Sāwā: "From Muḥammad the Prophet to Mundhir b. Sāwā. Peace be upon you. I praise to you God, besides whom there is no god. To proceed: your letter has come to me and I have heard what is in it; whoever prays our prayer, faces our qibla and eats our slaughtered meat, that is the Muslim; and whoever refuses that, upon him is the poll-tax."

249 – ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī related to me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to al-Mundhir b. Sāwā, who became Muslim and called the people of Hajar; they were divided between the willing and the unwilling. The Arabs became Muslim; as for the Magians and Jews, they accepted the poll-tax, and it was taken from them.

250 – Shaybān b. Farrūkh told us: Sulaymān b. al-Mughīra told us: Ḥumayd b. Hilāl told us, who said: al-ʿAlāʾ b. al-Ḥaḍramī sent to the Messenger of God ﷺ money from al-Baḥrayn amounting to eighty thousand; more than it never came to him before or after; and he gave from it to his uncle al-ʿAbbās.

Cairo page 99

251 – Hishām b. ʿAmmār related to me, from Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿUbayd Allāh, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ sent to Khosrow's waḍāʾiʿ (? estate-dependents/tenants) at Hajar, and they did not become Muslim, so he imposed on them the poll-tax of a dinar on each man.

252 – They said: The Messenger of God ﷺ dismissed al-ʿAlāʾ and then appointed Abān b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya over al-Baḥrayn. Some say al-ʿAlāʾ governed one region of al-Baḥrayn, including al-Qaṭīf, and Abān another region, including al-Khaṭṭ; but the first is better established.

253 – They said: When the Messenger of God ﷺ died, Abān left al-Baḥrayn and came to Medina. The people of al-Baḥrayn asked Abū Bakr ﵁ to return al-ʿAlāʾ to them, and he did. It is said that al-ʿAlāʾ remained governor until he died there in the year 20. ʿUmar then appointed Abū Hurayra al-Dawsī in his place. It is also said that ʿUmar ﵁ appointed Abū Hurayra before al-ʿAlāʾ's death, and al-ʿAlāʾ went to Tawwaj in the land of Persia and resolved to settle there. He said: Then he returned to al-Baḥrayn and died there. Abū Hurayra used to say: We buried al-ʿAlāʾ, then needed to lift a brick, and we lifted it and did not find him in the niche (laḥd).

254 – Abū Mikhnaf said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ wrote to al-ʿAlāʾ b. al-Ḥaḍramī, his governor over al-Baḥrayn, ordering him to come to him, and appointed ʿUthmān b. Abī l-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī over al-Baḥrayn and ʿUmān. When al-ʿAlāʾ came to Medina he appointed him over Basra in place of ʿUtba b. Ghazwān, but he did not reach it before he died, in the year

Cairo page 100

14, or at the beginning of the year 15.

Then ʿUmar appointed Qudāma b. Maẓʿūn al-Jumaḥī over the revenue of al-Baḥrayn and Abū Hurayra over the aḥdāth (police/security) and prayer; then dismissed Qudāma alone, on account of wine-drinking, and appointed Abū Hurayra over prayer and aḥdāth; then dismissed him and divided his property with him; then appointed ʿUthmān b. Abī l-ʿĀṣī over al-Baḥrayn and ʿUmān.

255 – al-ʿUmarī related to me, from al-Haytham, who said: Qudāma b. Maẓʿūn was over the revenue and aḥdāth, and Abū Hurayra over prayer and judgeship, and [Abū Hurayra] testified against Qudāma to what he testified. Then ʿUmar appointed [Abū Hurayra] over al-Baḥrayn after Qudāma, then dismissed him and divided his property, and ordered him to go back [to work], but he refused, so ʿUthmān b. Abī l-ʿĀṣī was appointed. ʿUmar died while he was his governor over it. His deputy over ʿUmān and al-Baḥrayn, while he was in Fārs, was his brother al-Mughīra b. Abī l-ʿĀṣī; it is also said Ḥafṣ b. Abī l-ʿĀṣī.

256 – Shaybān b. Farrūkh told us: Abū Hilāl al-Rāsibī told us: Muḥammad b. Sīrīn told us, from Abū Hurayra, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ appointed me over al-Baḥrayn, and twelve thousand accumulated with me. When I came to ʿUmar he said to me: O enemy of God and enemy of the Muslims! – or he said, enemy of His Book – have you stolen the property of God? I said: I am not an enemy of God nor of the Muslims – or he said of His Book – but an enemy of whoever is their enemy. Rather, horses bred and arrows accumulated. He said: So twelve thousand was taken from me. When I had prayed the dawn prayer I said: O God, forgive ʿUmar. He used to take from them and give them better than that; then after that he said: Will you not work, Abū Hurayra? I said: No. He said: Why? One better than you worked: Yūsuf — "Set me over the storehouses of the land" (1).

(1) Q 12:55

I said: "Joseph was a prophet, the son of a prophet, and I am Abu Hurayra, son of Umayma. And I fear three things from you, and two." He said: "Why not say five?" I said: "I fear that you will beat my back, insult my honor and take my wealth, and I dislike speaking without forbearance and judging without knowledge."

257Al-Qasim b. Sallam and Rawh b. Abd al-Mu'min told us, saying: Ya'qub b. Ishaq al-Hadrami told us, from Yazid b. Ibrahim al-Tustari, from Ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayra, that when he came back from Bahrain, Umar said to him: "Enemy of God and enemy of His Book! Did you steal God's money?" He said: "I am not the enemy of God or of His Book, but I am the enemy of whoever is their enemy, and I did not steal God's money." He said: "Then where did ten thousand dirhams come from?" He said: "Horses that bred, stipends that accumulated, and shares of spoils that added up." So Umar took it from him. The narrator then gave the rest of the report along the lines of what Abu Hilal related.

258They said: When al-Mundhir b. Sawa died, shortly after the death of the Prophet, those in Bahrain from the sons of Qays b. Tha'laba b. Ukaba apostatized, along with al-Hutam. His name was Shurayh b. Dubay'a b. Amr b. Marthad, of the Banu Qays b. Tha'laba. He was called al-Hutam ("the crusher") because of the verse: "Night has enfolded them, with a harsh driver, a crusher."

The rest of Rabi'a in Bahrain also apostatized, except al-Jarud, who is Bishr b. Amr al-Abdi, and those of his people who followed him. They set over themselves a son of al-Nu'man b. al-Mundhir, also named al-Mundhir. Al-Hutam went until he joined Rabi'a and merged with it along with his followers. When the news reached al-Ala' b. al-Hadrami, he marched with the Muslims until he camped at Juwatha, a fortress of Bahrain. Rabi'a advanced against him, and he went out against them with the Arabs and non-Arabs with him and fought them fiercely.

Then the Muslims took refuge in the fortress, and their enemy besieged them there. About this Abdallah b. Hadhaf al-Kilabi said:

"Take a message to Abu Bakr, and to the young men of Medina all together: / Do you care for the youths of yours who now are captives in Juwatha, besieged?"

Then al-Ala' led the Muslims out one night and fell on Rabi'a by surprise. They fought fiercely, and al-Hutam was killed.

259Someone other than Hisham b. al-Kalbi said: Al-Hutam came to Rabi'a while they were at Juwatha, whose people had all become unbelievers and set al-Mundhir b. al-Nu'man over them, so he stayed with them. Al-Ala' besieged them until he took Juwatha, broke up that gathering and killed al-Hutam. But the first account is better established.

On the killing of al-Hutam, Malik b. Tha'laba al-Abdi said:

"We left Shurayh covered in blood-red, like the edge of a variegated Yemeni cloth." (Basira is blood that falls on the ground.) "We bereaved Umm Ghadban of her son, and we broke the spear in the eye of Hubtar. We left Musma' sprawled on the ground, a prey for a hyena that comes at him, and vultures."

260They said: Al-Mundhir b. al-Nu'man used to be called "al-Ghurur" (the deceived/deceiver). When the Muslims prevailed, he said: "I am not al-Ghurur but al-Maghrur (the one deceived)." He and the remnant of Rabi'a fled to al-Khatt, and al-Ala' came to it and conquered it, killing al-Mundhir and those with him. It is also said that al-Mundhir escaped and entered al-Mushaqqar and released water around it so that no one could reach him, until al-Ghurur made peace on condition that he would evacuate the town, and he did. He joined Musaylima and was killed with him.

261Some said al-Mundhir was killed on the day of Juwatha. Others say he asked for safe-conduct, then fled, was caught and killed. Al-Ala' had written to Abu Bakr asking for reinforcements, and Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid b. al-Walid ordering him to leave al-Yamama and go to his aid. Khalid came to him after al-Hutam had been killed and besieged al-Khatt with him. Then Abu Bakr's letter reached him ordering him to proceed to Iraq, and he left Bahrain, in the year 12. Al-Waqidi said: "Our companions say that Khalid came to Medina and then went from there to Iraq."

Among those martyred at Juwatha was Abdallah b. Suhayl b. Amr of the Banu Amir b. Lu'ayy, whose kunya was Abu Suhayl, and whose mother was Fakhita bint Amir b. Nawfal b. Abd Manaf. Abdallah had come out with the polytheists at Badr, then deserted to the Muslims as a convert and fought at Badr with the Prophet. When the news of his death reached his father, Suhayl b. Amr, he said: "I leave it to God to reward him." Abu Bakr met him in Mecca, where he was on pilgrimage, and consoled him. Suhayl said: "I have heard that the Messenger of God said: 'The martyr will intercede for seventy of his family,' and I hope my son will not begin with anyone before me." He was thirty-eight years old when he was martyred.

Abdallah b. Abdallah b. Ubayy was also martyred at Juwatha. Someone other than al-Waqidi said he was martyred at al-Yamama.

262They said: Al-Muka'bir the Persian, Khosrow's agent whom he had sent to kill the Banu Tamim when they raided his caravan, and whose name was Firuz b. Jushaysh, fortified himself at al-Zara. Zoroastrians who had gathered at al-Qatif joined him and refused to pay the poll-tax. Al-Ala' stayed at al-Zara but did not take it in Abu Bakr's caliphate; he took it at the beginning of Umar's. Al-Ala' also took al-Sabun and Darin by force in Umar's caliphate, and there is a place there known as "al-Ala's trench."

263Ma'mar b. al-Muthanna said: Al-Ala' campaigned with the Abd al-Qays against villages of al-Sabun in Umar b. al-Khattab's caliphate and took them. Then he raided the city of al-Ghaba and killed the non-Arabs there, then came to al-Zara, where al-Muka'bir was, and besieged him. Then the marzban of al-Zara called for single combat and al-Bara' b. Malik fought him, killed him and took his spoils, which came to forty thousand. Then a man came out of al-Zara asking for safe-conduct in return for showing where the people got their water, and he showed them the spring flowing out of al-Zara. Al-Ala' blocked it, and when they saw this they made peace, giving him a third of the city and a third of the gold and silver in it, and half of what they owned outside it.

Then al-Akhnas al-Amiri came to al-Ala' and said: "They have not made peace on behalf of their families, who are at Darin." Kuraz al-Nukari showed him the ford to them, and al-Ala' plunged into the sea with a group of Muslims. The people of Darin knew nothing until they heard the takbir. They came out and fought the Muslims from three directions, but the Muslims killed their fighters and took the families and captives. When al-Muka'bir saw this, he became Muslim. Kuraz said:

"Al-Ala' feared the sea's pools, but I plunged ahead, going on to the unbelievers of Darin."

264Khalaf al-Bazzaz and Affan told us, saying: Hushaym told us: Ibn Awn and Yunus informed us, from Muhammad b. Sirin, who said: Al-Bara' b. Malik fought the marzban of al-Zara, speared him above the back and threw him down. Then he dismounted, cut off his hands, and took his bracelets, his robe, and a belt. Umar took a fifth of it because it was so great, and it was the first spoil on which a fifth was taken in Islam.

Chapter 18

Al-Yamāma

AL-YAMAMA

265They said: Al-Yamama was called Jaww. A woman of Jadis named al-Yamama bint Murr was crucified on its gate, and it was named after her, and God knows best.

266They said: When the Messenger of God wrote to the rulers of the lands in early year 7 (some say year 6), he wrote to Hawdha b. Ali al-Hanafi and the people of al-Yamama calling them to Islam, and sent his letter with Sulayt b. Qays b. Amr al-Ansari of the Khazraj. They sent a delegation to the Messenger of God. In the delegation was Mujja'a b. Murara, and the Messenger of God granted him a piece of uncultivated land that he asked for. Also among them was al-Rajjal b. Unfuwa, who became Muslim and learned Surat al-Baqara and other suras of the Qur'an, but later apostatized. Among them too was Musaylima the Liar, Thumama b. Kabir b. Habib. Musaylima said to the Messenger of God: "If you wish, we will leave the matter to you and pledge allegiance to you, on condition that it is ours after you." The Messenger of God said to him: "No, and no favor to you. But God will kill you."

Hawdha b. Ali al-Hanafi had also written to the Prophet asking him to make the rule his after him, on condition that he would convert, come to him and support him. The Messenger of God said: "No, and no honor. O God, spare me him." And he died shortly after.

When the delegation of the Banu Hanifa returned to al-Yamama, Musaylima the Liar claimed prophethood, and al-Rajjal b. Unfuwa testified for him that the Messenger of God had made him a partner in the matter. The Banu Hanifa and others in al-Yamama followed him. He wrote to the Messenger of God by the hand of Ubada b. al-Harith of the Banu Amir b. Hanifa, who is Ibn al-Nawwaha, whom Abdallah b. Mas'ud later killed in Kufa when he learned that he and a group with him believed in Musaylima's lie:

"From Musaylima, the messenger of God, to Muhammad, the messenger of God. To proceed: half the earth is ours and half belongs to Quraysh, but Quraysh are not fair. Peace upon you." (It was written by Amr b. al-Jarud al-Hanafi.)

The Messenger of God wrote back (and Ubayy b. Ka'b wrote it): "In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. From Muhammad the Prophet to Musaylima the Liar. To proceed: 'The earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the outcome is for the God-fearing' (1), 'and peace upon whoever follows guidance' (2)."

When the Messenger of God died and Abu Bakr became caliph, he dealt with the apostates of Najd and its surroundings within a few months, then sent Khalid b. al-Walid b. al-Mughira al-Makhzumi to al-Yamama and ordered him to fight Musaylima the Liar. As he approached, Khalid captured a group of the Banu Hanifa including Mujja'a b. Murara b. Salma. He killed them but spared Mujja'a and took him along in fetters. Khalid camped a mile from al-Yamama, and the Banu Hanifa came out against him, including al-Rajjal and Muhakkam b. al-Tufayl b. Subay', called Muhakkam al-Yamama. Khalid saw the gleam of weapons among them and said: "Muslims! God has spared you the burden of your enemy. Don't you see them drawing swords on one another? I think they have fallen out and turned their strength against each other." Mujja'a, in his chains, said: "Not so! Those are Indian blades. They feared they would shatter, so they brought them out in the sun to soften their steel."

Then the armies met. The first of them to be met was al-Rajjal b. Unfuwa, whom God killed, and the noblest men and Qur'an reciters among the Muslims were martyred. Then the Muslims rallied and regrouped, and God sent down His help upon them and the people of al-Yamama were routed. The Muslims pursued them, killing them in droves. Abd al-Rahman b. Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, A'isha's half-brother, shot Muhakkam with an arrow and killed him. They drove the unbelievers

(1) Qur'an 7:128. (2) Qur'an 20:47.

into the garden, which was named that day "the Garden of Death," and God killed Musaylima in the garden. The Banu Amir b. Lu'ayy b. Ghalib say that Khidash b. Bashir b. al-Asamm, of the Banu Mu'ays b. Amir b. Lu'ayy, killed him. Some of the Ansar say Abdallah b. Zayd b. Tha'laba of the Banu al-Harith b. al-Khazraj killed him, the man who was shown the call to prayer in a dream. Others say Abu Dujana Simak b. Kharasha killed him and was then martyred. Others say it was Abdallah b. Zayd b. Asim, the brother of Habib b. Zayd of the Banu Mabdhul of the Banu al-Najjar. (Musaylima had cut off Habib's hands and feet.) Wahshi b. Harb the Abyssinian, the killer of Hamza, also claimed to have killed him and used to say: "I killed the best of men and the worst of men." Some say that all of these took part in killing him. Mu'awiya b. Abi Sufyan also claimed to have killed him, and the Banu Umayya claim this for him.

267Abu Hafs al-Dimashqi told me: al-Walid b. Muslim told us, from Khalid b. Dihqan, from a man who was present, that Abd al-Malik b. Marwan asked a man of the Banu Hanifa who had witnessed the battle of al-Yamama about the killer of Musaylima. He said: "A man of such and such a description killed him." Abd al-Malik said: "By God, I have settled it in Mu'awiya's favor." He added: When the Liar was being strangled, he kept saying: "Banu Hanifa! Fight for your honor!" and kept repeating it until God killed him.

268Abd al-Wahid b. Ghiyath told me: Hammad b. Salama told us, from Hisham b. Urwa, from his father, who said: The Arabs apostatized, and Abu Bakr sent Khalid b. al-Walid, who met them. Then Khalid said: "By God, I will not stop until I butt heads with Musaylima." The Ansar said: "This is an opinion you have formed alone. Abu Bakr did not order you to do it. Return to Medina so we can rest our horses." He said: "By God, I will not stop until I butt heads with him." The Ansar turned back from him, then said: "What have we done? If our companions win, we will have lost out, and if they flee, we will have abandoned them." So they returned and went on with him. The Muslims and the polytheists met, and the Muslims turned and fled until they reached the baggage camps. Then al-Sa'ib b. al-Awwam stood up and said: "People! You have reached the baggage. No man has anywhere to flee beyond his own saddle." So God routed the polytheists and Musaylima was killed. Their battle cry that day was: "People of Surat al-Baqara!"

269Some of the people of al-Yamama told me that a man who lived under the protection of the Banu Hanifa recited, when Muhakkam was killed:

"If I escape from this, I have escaped a calamity; if not, I shall drink the cup of Muhakkam."

270They said: The war had worn down the Muslims and taken its toll. Mujja'a said to Khalid: "Most of the people of al-Yamama did not come out to fight you. You have killed only a few of them, and they have inflicted on you what you see. I will make peace with you on their behalf." Khalid agreed to terms of half the captives, half the gold and silver, the mail and the horses. Khalid took security from him and sent him back to them. When he entered al-Yamama, he ordered the boys, women and old men there to put on armor and stand on the fortresses, and they did. When Khalid and the Muslims saw them, they never doubted that they were fighters, and said: "Mujja'a told us the truth."

Then Mujja'a came out to the Muslim camp and said: "The people have not accepted what I made peace for on their behalf. They have prepared to fight you, and the fortresses of al-Arid are full of men. I kept working on them until they agreed to make peace for a quarter of the captives and half the gold and silver, the mail and the horses." The settlement was fixed on that basis and Khalid accepted and ratified it, and Mujja'a took Khalid into al-Yamama. When he saw who was left there, he said: "You tricked me, Mujja'a." The people of al-Yamama became Muslim and the alms-tax was collected from them. Then Abu Bakr's letter reached Khalid, telling him to reinforce al-Ala' b. al-Hadrami, and he went to Bahrain, leaving Samura b. Amr al-Anbari in charge of al-Yamama. The conquest of al-Yamama was in the year 12.

271Abu Rabah al-Yamami told me: elders of the people of al-Yamama told me that Musaylima the Liar was short, very yellow, flat-nosed with a snub nose, and his kunya was Abu Thumama.

272Another said his kunya was Abu Thumala. He had a muezzin called Hujayr, who used to say in the call to prayer: "I testify that Musaylima claims to be the messenger of God." Musaylima said: "Hujayr spoke plainly." And it became a proverb.

Among those martyred at al-Yamama were: Abu Hudhayfa b. Utba b. Rabi'a b. Abd Shams, whose name was Hushaym (or Muhashshim); Salim, freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, whose kunya was Abu Abdallah, a freedman of Thubayta bint Ya'ar the Ansari woman (some narrators say Nubayta); Khalid b. Usayd b. Abi al-Ays b. Umayya; Abdallah, who is al-Hakam b. Sa'id b. al-As b. Umayya (it is said he was killed at Mu'ta); Shuja' b. Wahb al-Asadi, ally of the Banu Umayya, kunya Abu Wahb; al-Tufayl b. Amr al-Dawsi of the Azd; Yazid b. Ruqaysh al-Asadi, ally of the Banu Umayya; Makhrama b. Shurayh al-Hadrami, ally of the Banu Umayya; al-Sa'ib b. al-Awwam, brother of al-Zubayr b. al-Awwam; al-Walid b. Abd Shams b. al-Mughira al-Makhzumi; al-Sa'ib b. Uthman b. Maz'un al-Jumahi; and Zayd b. al-Khattab b. Nufayl, brother of Umar b. al-Khattab. It is said that Abu Maryam al-Hanafi, whose name was Subayh b. Muharrish, killed him. Ibn al-Kalbi said that Labid b. Burghuth al-Ijli killed him, who later came to Umar, who said: "You are al-Jawaliq" (and Labid is al-Jawaliq). Zayd's kunya was Abu Abd al-Rahman, and he was older than Umar. Some say Abu Maryam's name was Iyas b. Subayh; he was the first to act as judge in Basra in Umar's time and died at Sunbul in al-Ahwaz.

Also martyred were Abu Qays b. al-Harith b. Adi b. Sahm; Abdallah b. al-Harith b. Qays; Sulayt b. Amr, brother of Suhayl b. Amr, of the Banu Amir b. Lu'ayy; and Iyas b. al-Bukayr al-Kinani.

From the Ansar: Abbad b. al-Harith b. Adi of the Banu Jahjaba of the Aws; Abbad b. Bishr b. Waqsh al-Ashhali of the Aws, kunya Abu al-Rabi' (some say Abu Bishr); Malik b. Aws b. Atik al-Ashhali; Abu Aqil b. Tha'laba Bayhan al-Balawi, ally of the Banu Jahjaba, whose name had been Abd al-Uzza and whom the Prophet renamed Abd al-Rahman, "enemy of idols"; Suraqa b. Ka'b b. Abd al-Uzza al-Najjari of the Khazraj; Umara b. Hazm b. Zayd b. Lawdhan al-Najjari (some say he died in Mu'awiya's time); Habib b. Amr b. Mihsan al-Najjari; Ma'n b. Adi b. al-Jadd b. al-Ajlan al-Balawi of Quda'a, ally of the Ansar; Thabit b. Qays b. Shammas b. Abi Zuhayr, the Prophet's orator, of the Banu al-Harith b. al-Khazraj, kunya Abu Muhammad, who commanded the Ansar that day; Abu Hanna b. Ghaziyya b. Amr of the Banu Mazin b. al-Najjar; al-As b. Tha'laba al-Dawsi of the Azd, ally of the Ansar; Abu Dujana Simak b. Aws b. Kharasha b. Lawdhan al-Sa'idi of the Khazraj; Abu Usayd Malik b. Rabi'a al-Sa'idi (some say he died in year 60 in Medina); Abdallah b. Abdallah b. Ubayy b. Malik, whose name had been al-Hubab and whom the Messenger of God renamed after his father, though his father was a hypocrite and is the one called Ibn Ubayy b. Salul (Salul was Ubayy's mother, a Khuza'i woman to whom he is attributed; his father was Malik b. al-Harith of the Banu al-Khazraj). It is said he was martyred at Juwatha in Bahrain. Also Uqba b. Amir b. Nabi of the Banu Salima of the Khazraj, and al-Harith b. Ka'b b. Amr of the Banu al-Najjar.

The Messenger of God had sent Habib b. Zayd b. Asim of the Banu Mabdhul b. Amr b. Ghanm b. Mazin b. al-Najjar, and Abdallah b. Wahb al-Aslami,

to Musaylima. He did not touch Abdallah, but cut off Habib's hands and feet. Habib's mother was Nusayba bint Ka'b.

273Al-Waqidi said: The two had come with Amr b. al-As from Oman, and Musaylima kept them back. Amr and those with him escaped except these two, who were seized. Nusayba fought at al-Yamama and came away with wounds. She is the mother of Habib and Abdallah, sons of Zayd, and had fought at Uhud too. She is one of the two women who gave their pledge at al-Aqaba.

Also martyred at al-Yamama were A'idh b. Ma'is al-Zuraqi of the Khazraj, and Yazid b. Thabit al-Khazraji, brother of Zayd b. Thabit, the expert in inheritance law. There is disagreement about the number of those martyred at al-Yamama: the lowest figure reported is seven hundred and the highest one thousand seven hundred. Some say they numbered twelve hundred.

274Al-Qasim b. Sallam told us: al-Harith b. Murra al-Hanafi told us, from Hisham b. Isma'il, that Mujja'a al-Yamami came to the Messenger of God, who granted him land and wrote him a document: "In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is a writing by Muhammad, the Messenger of God, for Mujja'a b. Murara b. Salma. I have granted you al-Ghawra, Ghurāba and al-Habl. Whoever disputes with you, let him come to me." (Al-Ghawra is a village of the Gharabat, adjoining Qarat.) He said: Mujja'a later came as a delegate to Abu Bakr after the Prophet's death, and Abu Bakr granted him al-Khadrama. Then he came to Umar, who granted him al-Riya. Then he came to Uthman, who granted him an estate. Al-Harith said: "I don't remember its name."

275Al-Qasim b. Sallam told us: Abu Ayyub al-Dimashqi told us, from Sa'dan b. Yahya, from Sadaqa b. Abi Imran, from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from Adi b. Hatim, that the Messenger of God granted Furat b. Hayyan al-Ijli land in al-Yamama.

276Muhammad b. Thumal al-Yamami told me, from their elders: The garden was called the Garden of Death because of the number killed in it. He said: Ishaq b. Abi Khumaysa, a freedman of Qays, built a congregational mosque in it in the days of al-Ma'mun, and the garden used to be called Abad. Muhammad b. Thumal said: Qasr al-Ward is named after al-Ward b. al-Samin b. Ubayd al-Hanafi. Another said the fortress was called Mu'taq ("freed") because of its strength, meaning that whoever took refuge in it was freed from his enemy. He said: al-Riya is a spring from which the Sa'fuqa irrigation drew water (an estate named for a manager called Sa'fuq), and the Khuyayba and al-Khadrama irrigation too.

Chapter 19

The apostasy of the Arabs in the caliphate of Abū Bakr

The Account of the Apostasy of the Arabs in the Caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq

277They said: When Abu Bakr became caliph, groups of Arabs apostatized and withheld the alms-tax. Some of them said: "We will keep up prayer but not pay zakat." Abu Bakr said: "If they withhold from me even a camel's hobble, I will fight them." Some narrators say "even a young kid." (The 'iqal is the year's alms.)

278Abdallah b. Salih al-Ijli told me, from Yahya b. Adam, from Awana b. al-Hakam, from Jarir b. Yazid, from al-Sha'bi, who said Abdallah b. Mas'ud said: "After the Messenger of God we stood in a position in which we nearly perished, had God not favored us with Abu Bakr. All of us had agreed that we would not fight over a bint makhad or an ibn labun (young camels due as alms), that we would eat the villages of Arabia and worship God until certainty came to us. But God made Abu Bakr resolve to fight them, and by God he accepted nothing from them but the shameful plan or the exiling war. The shameful plan was that they admit that those of them who were killed are in the Fire, and that what they had taken of our property be returned to us. The exiling war was that they be driven from their homes."

279Ibrahim b. Muhammad told us, from Ar'ara: Abd al-Rahman b. Mahdi told us: Sufyan al-Thawri informed us, from Qays b. Muslim, from Tariq b. Shihab, who said: The delegation of Buzakha came to Abu Bakr, and he gave them the choice between the exiling war and the shameful peace. They said: "We know the exiling war, but what is the shameful peace?" He said: "That we take from you the mail and the horses, and keep what we took from you; that you return what you took from us and pay blood-money for our dead, while your dead are in the Fire."

280Shuja' b. Makhlad al-Fallas told us: Bishr b. al-Mufaddal told us: Abd al-Aziz b. Abdallah b. Abi Salama al-Majishun told us, from Abd al-Wahid, from al-Qasim b. Muhammad b. Abi Bakr, from his aunt A'isha, Mother of the Believers, who said: "The Messenger of God died, and there fell upon my father what, had it fallen on the towering mountains, would have broken them. Hypocrisy raised its head in Medina and the Arabs apostatized. By God, they never disagreed over a single matter without his carrying off for Islam its share and its benefit."

281They said: Abu Bakr went out to al-Qassa in the land of Muharib to dispatch troops against the apostates, with the Muslims accompanying him. Kharija b. Hisn b. Hudhayfa b. Badr al-Fazari and Manzur b. Zabban b. Sayyar al-Fazari, of the Banu al-Ushara in Ghatafan, came against them, and they fought fiercely. The polytheists were routed, and Talha b. Ubaydallah al-Taymi pursued them and caught up with them below the passes of Awsaja. He killed one man, but the rest escaped him by flight. Kharija b. Hisn kept saying: "Woe to the Arabs from Ibn Abi Quhafa!"

Then, at al-Qassa, Abu Bakr gave the command of the people to Khalid b. al-Walid b. al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, and put Thabit b. Qays b. Shammas al-Ansari (one of those martyred at al-Yamama) over the Ansar, though under Khalid's authority. He ordered Khalid to head for Tulayha b. Khuwaylid al-Asadi, who had claimed prophethood and was then at Buzakha, a watering place of the Banu Asad b. Khuzayma. Khalid marched against him, sending ahead Ukasha b. Mihsan al-Asadi, an ally of the Banu Abd Shams, and Thabit b. Aqram al-Balawi, an ally of the Ansar. Hibal b. Khuwaylid met them and they killed him. Then Tulayha and his brother Salama came out, having heard the news, met Ukasha and Thabit and killed them. Tulayha said:

"I remembered my brother when I knew their faces, and was sure I was his avenger, Hibal's. The evening I left Ibn Aqram lying dead, and Ukasha al-Ghanami at the place of battle."

Then the Muslims and their enemy met and fought fiercely. Uyayna b. Hisn b. Hudhayfa b. Badr was with Tulayha with seven hundred of the Banu Fazara. When he saw the Muslims' swords cutting down the polytheists, he came to Tulayha and said: "Don't you see what Abu al-Fasil's army is doing? Has Gabriel brought you anything?" He said: "Yes. He came to me and said: 'You will have a mill like his mill, and a day you will not forget.'" Uyayna said: "I think you will indeed have a day you will not forget. Banu Fazara, this man is a liar!" And he turned away from his camp, and the people were routed, the Muslims prevailed, and Uyayna b. Hisn was captured. He was brought to Medina, and Abu Bakr spared his life and let him go.

Tulayha b. Khuwaylid fled, entered a tent of his, washed, came out, mounted his horse, declared the intention of the umra and went to Mecca, then came to Medina as a Muslim. Others say he went to Syria, where the Muslim raiders seized him and sent him to Abu Bakr in Medina, and he became Muslim and later distinguished himself in the conquest of Iraq and Nihawand. Umar said to him: "Did you kill the righteous servant Ukasha b. Mihsan?" He said: "Ukasha b. Mihsan was made happy by me and I was made wretched by him, and I ask God's forgiveness."

282Dawud b. Hibal al-Asadi told me, from elders of his people : Umar b. al-Khattab said to Tulayha: "You are the one who lied about God when you claimed He had revealed to you: 'God does nothing with the dusting of your faces and the ugliness of your backsides. So remember God, standing chaste, for the froth is on top of the pure milk.'" He said: "Commander of the Faithful, that was one of the trials of unbelief, all of which Islam has torn down, so do not rebuke me for part of it." Umar fell silent.

283They said: Khalid b. al-Walid came to Ruman and Abanan, where the remnant of Buzakha was. They did not fight him but gave him allegiance for Abu Bakr. Khalid sent Hisham b. al-As b. Wa'il al-Sahmi, brother of Amr b. al-As, an early convert and one of the emigrants to Abyssinia, to the Banu Amir b. Sa'sa'a. They did not fight him; they professed Islam and made the call to prayer, and he turned back from them. Qurra b. Hubayra al-Qushayri had refused to pay the alms-tax and had reinforced Tulayha. Hisham b. al-As seized him and brought him to Khalid, who sent him to Abu Bakr. Qurra said: "By God, I have not disbelieved since I believed. Amr b. al-As passed by me on his return from Oman and I honored and treated him well." Abu Bakr asked Amr about it, and he confirmed it, so Abu Bakr spared his life. It is also said that Khalid marched to the lands of the Banu Amir, seized Qurra and sent him to Abu Bakr.

284He said: Then Khalid b. al-Walid went to al-Ghamr, where there was a group of the Banu Asad, Ghatafan and others under Kharija b. Hisn b. Hudhayfa. It is said they were each led by a separate chief of their own. They fought Khalid and the Muslims, killed a number of them, and the rest were routed. About the day of al-Ghamr, al-Hutay'a al-Absi said:

"Alas, all short spears are humble things; a ransom for the spears of the horsemen at al-Ghamr."

Then Khalid came to Jaww Qaraqir (some say al-Naqira), where there was a force of the Banu Sulaym under Abu Shajara Amr b. Abd al-Uzza al-Sulami, whose mother was al-Khansa'. They fought him. One Muslim was martyred, and then God broke up the polytheists' gathering. That day Khalid began burning the apostates. Abu Bakr was told of it and said: "I will not sheathe a sword that God has drawn against the unbelievers."

Abu Shajara became Muslim and came to Umar as he was distributing to the poor, and asked for a share. Umar said to him: "Aren't you the one who said:

'I watered my spear from Khalid's squadron, and I hope after this to live long'?"

and struck him with his whip. He said: "Islam has wiped that out, Commander of the Faithful."

285They said: Al-Fuja'a, that is Bujayr b. Iyas b. Abdallah al-Sulami, came to Abu Bakr and said: "Mount me and equip me so I can fight the apostates." Abu Bakr mounted him and gave him weapons. He went out waylaying people, killing Muslims and apostates alike, and gathered a band. Abu Bakr wrote to Turayfa b. Hajiza, brother of Ma'n b. Hajiza, ordering him to fight him. He fought him and Ibn Hajiza captured him and sent him to Abu Bakr, who ordered him burned at the edge of the prayer ground. Some say Abu Bakr wrote to Ma'n about al-Fuja'a, and Ma'n sent his brother Turayfa, who captured him.

Then Khalid marched against those at al-Bita and al-Bu'uda of the Banu Tamim. They fought him, he broke up their gathering, and Malik b. Nuwayra, brother of Mutammim b. Nuwayra, was killed. Malik had been the Prophet's agent over the alms of the Banu Hanzala. When the Prophet died, he released what he held of the obligatory dues and said: "Take your property, Banu Hanzala." It is also said that Khalid did not meet anyone at al-Bita and al-Bu'uda but sent out detachments among the Banu Tamim, one of them under Dirar b. al-Azwar al-Asadi. Dirar met Malik and they fought, and he captured him and some men with him. They were brought and their necks struck, and Dirar himself struck Malik's neck. It is said Malik told Khalid: "By God, I did not apostatize." And Abu Qatada al-Ansari testified that the Banu Hanzala had laid down their arms and made the call to prayer.

Umar b. al-Khattab said to Abu Bakr: "You have sent a man who kills Muslims and tortures with fire."

It is reported that Mutammim b. Nuwayra came in to Umar b. al-Khattab, who said to him: "How far did your grief for your brother Malik go?" He said: "I wept for him a year, until my blind eye gave tears for my sound one. I never saw a fire without nearly breaking with sorrow for him, because he used to keep his fire burning until dawn for fear a guest might come and not find his place." Umar said: "Describe him to me." He said: "He would ride the slow horse and lead the heavy camel, between two dripping water-skins on the bitterly cold night, in a thin cloak, holding a long lance, traveling by night and arriving at morning, and his face was a slice of the moon." Umar said: "Recite me some of what you said of him." So he recited the elegy that includes:

"We were like Jadhima's two drinking companions for a stretch of time, so that it was said they would never part."

Umar said: "If I were good at composing verse, I would lament my brother Zayd." Mutammim said: "It is not the same, Commander of the Faithful. Had my brother fallen as yours fell, I would not have wept for him." Umar said: "No one has consoled me better than you have."

286 (the second numbered 286 in the printed text; properly 289). They said: Umm Sadir Sajah bint Aws b. Haqq b. Usama b. al-Ghunayz b. Yarbu' b. Hanzala b. Malik b. Zayd Manat b. Tamim claimed prophethood (some say she was Sajah bint al-Harith b. Uqfan b. Suwayd b. Khalid b. Usama) and practiced divination. A group of the Banu Tamim followed her, and some of her maternal kin from the Banu Taghlib. Then one day she spoke in rhymed prose: "The Lord of the clouds commands you to raid the Rabab." She raided them and they defeated her; no one but they fought her. Then she went to Musaylima the Liar, who was at Hajr, married him, and made her religion and his one. When he was killed, she went back to her brothers and died among them.

Ibn al-Kalbi said: Sajah became Muslim, emigrated to Basra and was a good Muslim. Abd al-A'la b. Hammad al-Narsi said: I heard elders of Basra say that Samura b. Jundub al-Fazari prayed over her while governing Basra for Mu'awiya, before Ubaydallah b. Ziyad came from Khurasan and became governor of Basra. Ibn al-Kalbi said Sajah's muezzin was al-Janba b. Tariq b. Amr b. Hawt al-Riyahi; some say Shabath b. Rib'i al-Riyahi used to call the prayer for her.

287They said: Khawlan in Yemen apostatized, and Abu Bakr sent Ya'la b. Munya against them (Munya was his mother, of the Banu Mazin b. Mansur b. Ikrima b. Khasafa b. Qays b. Aylan b. Mudar; his father was Umayya b. Abi Ubayda, of the descendants of Malik b. Hanzala, an ally of the Banu Nawfal b. Abd Manaf). He defeated them and took booty and captives. It is also said he met no fighting and the people returned to Islam.

Chapter 20

The apostasy of the Banū Walīʿa and al-Ashʿath b. Qays

The Apostasy of the Banu Wali'a and al-Ash'ath b. Qays b. Ma'dikarib b. Mu'awiya al-Kindi

288They said: The Messenger of God appointed Ziyad b. Labid al-Bayadi of the Ansar over Hadramawt, then added Kinda to his charge. (Some say it was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq who added Kinda.) Ziyad b. Labid was a firm and resolute man. He took a young she-camel as alms from one of the Kinda, and the Kindi asked him to return it and take another. But he had already branded it with the alms-brand and refused, and al-Ash'ath b. Qays spoke to him about it and got no answer. He said: "I will not return something the brand has fallen on." So all Kinda rose against him except the Sakun, who stayed with him, and their poet said:

"We aided the faith when our people strayed in wretchedness, and we followed the son of Ziyad's mother. We did not turn aside from the truth of the Bayadi by a span, and fear of the Merciful was the best provision."

The Banu Amr b. Mu'awiya b. al-Harith al-Kindi gathered against him, but he fell on them by night with the Muslims who were with him and killed a number of them, among them Mikhwas, Mishrah, Hamd and Abdi'a, sons of Ma'dikarib b. Wali'a b. Shurahbil b. Mu'awiya b. Hujr al-Qird (al-qird meaning "the generous" in their speech) b. al-Harith b. al-Walida b. Amr b. Mu'awiya b. al-Harith. These brothers held valleys they ruled, so they were called "the Four Kings." They had come to the Prophet as a delegation and then apostatized. A sister of theirs called al-Amrada was killed; her killer had taken her for a man.

Then Ziyad came back with the captives and the property and passed by al-Ash'ath b. Qays and his people. The women and children cried out and wept, and al-Ash'ath was filled with anger and came out with a group of his people and confronted Ziyad and those with him. Some Muslims were killed, but then they were beaten. The great men of Kinda gathered around al-Ash'ath b. Qays. When Ziyad saw this he wrote to Abu Bakr asking for help, and Abu Bakr wrote to al-Muhajir b. Abi Umayya ordering him to aid him. The two met al-Ash'ath b. Qays with the Muslims who were with them, broke up his force, fell on his companions and killed many of them. Then they took refuge in al-Nujayr, a fortress of theirs, and the Muslims besieged them until they were worn out. Al-Ash'ath asked for safe-conduct for a number of them and left himself out of the number, because al-Jafshish al-Kindi, whose name was Ma'dan b. al-Aswad b. Ma'dikarib, seized him by the waist and said: "Put me in the number." So he put him in and left himself out. He came down to Ziyad b. Labid and al-Muhajir, who sent him to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu Bakr pardoned him and married him to his sister Umm Farwa bint Abi Quhafa. She bore him Muhammad, Ishaq, Qurayba , Hubaba and Ja'da. Some say he married him to his sister Qurayba. When he married her he went to the market and, seeing no camel there, hamstrung every one of them, paid for them and fed the people. He lived in Medina, then went raiding in Syria and Iraq, and died in Kufa, where al-Hasan b. Ali b. Abi Talib prayed over him after his settlement with Mu'awiya. Al-Ash'ath's kunya was Abu Muhammad and his nickname was "Urf al-Nar" ("Cock's Comb of Fire").

289 (printed 286). Some narrators said: The Banu Wali'a apostatized before the death of the Prophet. When news of his death reached Ziyad b. Labid, he called the people to give allegiance to Abu Bakr, and they did, except the Banu Wali'a, whom he fell on by night and killed. Al-Ash'ath apostatized and fortified himself in al-Nujayr, and Ziyad b. Labid and al-Muhajir joined forces and besieged him. Abu Bakr reinforced them with Ikrima b. Abi Jahl after his return from Oman. He reached them when al-Nujayr had already been taken. Abu Bakr asked the Muslims to let him share in the booty and they did.

290They said: There were women in al-Nujayr who had rejoiced at the death of the Messenger of God, so Abu Bakr wrote ordering their hands and feet to be cut off. Among them were al-Thabja' al-Hadramiyya and Hind bint Yamin the Jewess.

291Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: Abd al-Razzaq b. Hammam al-Yamani told me, from elders of Yemen who told him, that the Messenger of God appointed Khalid b. Sa'id b. al-As over Sana'a, but al-Ansi the Liar drove him out of it, and that he appointed al-Muhajir b. Abi Umayya over Kinda and Ziyad b. Labid al-Ansari over Hadramawt and the Sadaf (the descendants of Malik b. Murta' b. Mu'awiya b. Kinda). He was called Sadaf because Murta' married a Hadrami woman and stipulated to her that she would stay with him, and that if she bore a child he would not remove her from her people's house. She bore him Malik. The judge ruled against him, that he must send her back to her family. When Malik left him with her, he said: "Malik has turned away (sadafa) from me." So he was called al-Sadaf.

Abd al-Razzaq said: Elders of Yemen told me: Abu Bakr wrote to Ziyad b. Labid and al-Muhajir b. Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi, who was then over Kinda, ordering them to unite, so that their hands were one hand and their command one, to take allegiance for him and fight those who refused to pay alms, and to seek help from the believers against the unbelievers and from the obedient against the disobedient and opposed.

They took from a man of Kinda a young camel as alms, and he asked them to take another. Al-Muhajir was lenient with him, but Ziyad refused to take anything else and said: "I will not return it after the alms-brand has fallen on it." The Banu Amr b. Mu'awiya gathered a force. Ziyad b. Labid said to al-Muhajir: "You see this gathering. It is not wise for both of us to leave our place, but I will detach myself from the army with a band, which will be more concealed and discreet, and then fall on these unbelievers by night." (Ziyad was firm and resolute.) He went to the Banu Amr and found them at night and fell on them, destroying most of them, and some began killing each other. Then he and al-Muhajir joined up with the booty and captives, and al-Ash'ath b. Qays and the leading men of Kinda confronted them and they fought them fiercely. Then the Kindites fortified themselves in al-Nujayr, and the two besieged them until the siege wore them out and exhausted them. Al-Ash'ath surrendered to judgment.

292They said: Hadramawt had come to help Kinda, and Ziyad and al-Muhajir met them and defeated them. Khawlan apostatized, and Abu Bakr sent Ya'la b. Munya against them, who fought them until they submitted and acknowledged the alms-tax. Then Abu Bakr's letter came to al-Muhajir appointing him over Sana'a and its districts, and combining the work of Ziyad with what he already held. So Yemen was divided among three: al-Muhajir, Ziyad and Ya'la. Abu Sufyan b. Harb was given what lay between the farthest border of the Hijaz and the farthest border of Najran.

293Abu al-Tammar told me: Sharik told me: Ibrahim b. Muhajir informed us, from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: Al-Ash'ath b. Qays al-Kindi apostatized with some of Kinda, and they were besieged. He got safe-conduct for seventy of them but did not take it for himself. He was brought to Abu Bakr, who said: "We will kill you, for you have no safe-conduct since you left yourself out of the number." He said: "No, grant me your favor, Caliph of the Messenger of God, and marry me to your sister." He did so and married him to his sister.

294Al-Qasim b. Sallam Abu Ubayd told me: Abdallah b. Salih, secretary of al-Layth b. Sa'd, told us, from Alwan b. Salih, from Salih b. Kaysan, from Humayd b. Abd al-Rahman, from Abd al-Rahman b. Awf, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who said: "There are three things I did that I wish I had not done. I wish that on the day al-Ash'ath b. Qays was brought to me I had struck off his head, for it seemed to me that he sees no evil without striving in it and helping it. I wish that on the day al-Fuja'a was brought to me I had killed him and not burned him. And I wish that when I sent Khalid to Syria I had sent Umar b. al-Khattab to Iraq, so that I would have stretched out both my right hand and my left in the cause of God."

295Abdallah b. Salih al-Ijli informed me, from Yahya b. Adam, from al-Hasan b. Salih, from Firas or Bunan, from al-Sha'bi, that Abu Bakr returned the captives of al-Nujayr for ransom, four hundred dirhams a head, and that al-Ash'ath b. Qays borrowed their ransom from the merchants of Medina, ransomed them, and then they repaid him. Al-Ash'ath b. Qays lamented Bishr b. al-Awdah (who had been among the delegation to the Messenger of God and then apostatized) and Yazid b. Amana and those killed at al-Nujayr:

"By my life, and my life is no small thing to me, I was the one most deserving to grieve over the slain. No wonder, on the day their captives are divided, that after them time is not to be trusted. I was like a mother camel who bellowed, driven to distraction by her stuffed calf-skin, and she turned to it, yearning in a moan: for the generous son of Amana, and after him Bashir of bounty. So let the tears of eyes flow."

Chapter 21

Al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī and the apostates of Yemen

The Affair of al-Aswad al-Ansi and Those Who Apostatized with Him in Yemen

296They said: Al-Aswad b. Ka'b b. Awf al-Ansi practiced divination and claimed prophethood, and the Ans followed him. (The name Ans was Zayd b. Malik b. Udad b. Yashjub b. Arib b. Zayd b. Kahlan b. Saba'; Ans was the brother of Murad b. Malik, Khalid b. Malik and Sa'd al-Ashira b. Malik.) People other than the Ans also followed him. He called himself "Rahman of Yemen," as Musaylima called himself "Rahman of al-Yamama." He had a trained donkey, to which he would say "Prostrate to your Lord," and it would prostrate, and "Kneel," and it would kneel. So he was called "Dhu al-Himar" ("he of the donkey"). Others said he was called Dhu al-Khimar ("he of the veil") because he was always veiled and turbaned.

297Some people of Yemen informed me that he was black-faced, and so was called al-Aswad ("the Black") for his color, and that his name was Ayhala.

298They said: The Messenger of God sent Jarir b. Abdallah al-Bajali, in the year in which the Messenger of God died (the year Jarir became Muslim), to al-Aswad to call him to Islam, but he did not respond. Some narrators deny that the Prophet sent Jarir to Yemen.

299They said: Al-Aswad came to Sana'a and took control of it and drove Khalid b. Sa'id b. al-As out of it. (It is also said that he drove out al-Muhajir b. Abi Umayya, who withdrew to the side of Ziyad b. Labid al-Bayadi and stayed with him until Abu Bakr's letter came ordering him to help Ziyad; when they finished with their affair, he appointed him over Sana'a and its districts.) Al-Aswad was tyrannical and humiliated the Abna', the descendants of the Persians whom Khosrow sent to Yemen with Ibn Dhi Yazan under Wahriz. He put them into service and harmed them, and married al-Marzubana, the wife of Badhan, their king and Abarwiz's governor over them.

The Messenger of God sent Qays b. Hubayra al-Makshuh al-Muradi to fight him. (He was called al-Makshuh because he had been cauterized on his flank for an ailment he had.) He ordered him to win over the Abna', and sent Farwa b. Musayk al-Muradi with him. When they reached Yemen, the news of the Messenger of God's death reached them. Qays pretended to al-Aswad that he shared his view, until al-Aswad allowed him into Sana'a, and he entered with a group of Madhhij, Hamdan and others. Then he won over Fayruz al-Daylami, one of the Abna', who had become Muslim. Then they went to Badhan, the head of the Abna' (some say Badhan had died and the head of the Abna' after him was his successor Dadhawayh, which is better established). Dadhawayh became Muslim. Qays met Bab b. Dhi al-Jurra al-Himyari and won him over, and Dadhawayh sent out his missionaries among the Abna', who became Muslim. All these agreed to kill al-Aswad and assassinate him, and they secretly informed his wife al-Marzubana of what they intended. She hated him. She showed them a channel by which they could enter his place. They entered before dawn (some say they bored through his house wall with vinegar), then entered on him at daybreak when he was drunk and asleep, and Qays slaughtered him. He bellowed like a bull, which alarmed his guards, who said: "What is wrong with the Rahman of Yemen?" His wife hurried to say: "Revelation is coming down on him." So they calmed down and held back.

Qays cut off his head, then in the morning climbed the city wall and said: "God is greatest! God is greatest! I testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and that al-Aswad, so-and-so, is the enemy of God." Al-Aswad's followers gathered, and he threw his head to them and they dispersed except for a few. Qays's companions went out, opened the gate and put the rest of al-Ansi's followers to the sword, and none escaped but those who became Muslim. Some narrators report that the one who killed al-Aswad al-Ansi was Fayruz al-Daylami, and that Qays finished him off and cut off his head.

Some scholars mention that al-Aswad was killed five days before the death of the Prophet, who said in his illness: "God has killed al-Aswad al-Ansi. The righteous man Fayruz al-Daylami killed him." The news of the victory reached Abu Bakr ten nights after he became caliph.

300Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: Ibn Anas al-Yamani told me, from someone who told him, from al-Nu'man b. Barzaj, one of the Abna': The Prophet's governor whom al-Aswad drove out of Sana'a was Aban b. Sa'id b. al-As, and the one who killed al-Aswad al-Ansi was Fayruz al-Daylami. Qays and Fayruz both claimed the killing while in Medina. Umar said: "This lion killed him," meaning Fayruz.

301They said: Later Qays was accused of killing Dadhawayh, and it reached Abu Bakr that he intended to expel the Abna' from Sana'a. This angered him, and he wrote to al-Muhajir b. Abi Umayya, his governor over Sana'a, when he entered it, ordering him to send Qays to him. When al-Muhajir brought him, Abu Bakr made him swear fifty oaths at the Prophet's pulpit that he had not killed Dadhawayh. He swore, and Abu Bakr released him and sent him to Syria with those Muslims who had volunteered to fight the Byzantines.

Part Two

Syria, al-Jazīra and Armenia

Chapter 22

The conquest of Syria

302They said: When Abu Bakr finished with the apostates, he decided to send armies to Syria. He wrote to the people of Mecca, Ta'if and Yemen, and to all the Arabs of Najd and the Hijaz, calling them to jihad and encouraging them with the spoils of the Byzantines. People hurried to him, some seeking reward and some seeking gain, and came to Medina from every direction. He tied three banners for three men: Khalid b. Sa'id b. al-As b. Umayya; Shurahbil b. Hasana, ally of the Banu Jumah (according to al-Waqidi, Shurahbil is the son of Abdallah b. al-Muta' al-Kindi, and Hasana was his mother, a freedwoman of Ma'mar b. Habib b. Wahb b. Hudhafa b. Jumah; al-Kalbi says he is Shurahbil b. Rabi'a b. al-Tat', of the descendants of Sufa, that is, al-Ghawth b. Murr b. Udd b. Tabikha); and Amr b. al-As b. Wa'il al-Sahmi .

He tied these banners on Thursday, the first of Safar in the year 13. This was after the armies had camped at al-Jurf throughout Muharram, with Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah leading them in prayer. Abu Bakr had wanted to tie a banner for Abu Ubayda, but he asked to be excused. Some report that he did tie one for him, but that is not established. Umar appointed him over all of Syria when he became caliph.

303Abu Mikhnaf mentioned that Abu Bakr said to the commanders: "If you unite for a fight, your commander is Abu Ubayda Amir b. Abdallah b. al-Jarrah al-Fihri; otherwise it is Yazid b. Abi Sufyan." He also mentioned that Amr b. al-As was only a reinforcement for the Muslims and a commander over those attached to him. He said: When Abu Bakr tied the banner for Khalid b. Sa'id, Umar disliked it and spoke to Abu Bakr about removing him, saying: "He is a boastful man who turns his command into rivalry and partisanship." So Abu Bakr removed him and sent Abu Arwa al-Dawsi to take his banner. He met him at Dhu al-Marwa and took the banner from him, and brought it to Abu Bakr, who gave it to Yazid b. Abi Sufyan. Yazid set out with it, his brother Mu'awiya carrying it before him. Others say the banner was handed to him at Dhu al-Marwa, and he went on at the head of Khalid's army, while Khalid b. Sa'id went along seeking reward from God in Shurahbil's army.

Abu Bakr ordered Amr b. al-As to take the road by Ayla, heading for Palestine, and ordered Yazid to take the road by Tabuk, and wrote to Shurahbil to take the Tabuk road as well. At the outset each commander's force was three thousand men, but Abu Bakr kept sending reinforcements until each commander had seven thousand five hundred, and their total finally reached twenty-four thousand.

304It is related from al-Waqidi that Abu Bakr appointed Amr over Palestine, Shurahbil over Jordan and Yazid over Damascus, and said: "If you have to fight, your commander is the one in whose province you are." It is also related that he told Amr orally to lead the people in prayer when they were together, and when they separated each commander would pray with his own men . He also ordered the commanders to tie a banner for each tribe, to be among them.

305They said: When Amr b. al-As reached the first district of Palestine, he wrote to Abu Bakr informing him of the great number of the enemy, their equipment, the breadth of their land and the courage of their fighters. So Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid b. al-Walid b. al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, who was in Iraq, ordering him to march to Syria. It is said he made him commander over the commanders in war. Some say Khalid was commander only over the companions who had gone with him, and that when the Muslims gathered for battle the commanders put him in charge of it because of his bravery, cunning and good fortune.

306They said: The first battle between the Muslims and their enemy was at a village of the villages of Gaza called Da'in, against the patrician of Gaza. They fought fiercely, and God made His friends victorious, routed His enemies and broke up their gathering. This was before Khalid b. al-Walid arrived in Syria. Yazid b. Abi Sufyan set out in pursuit of that patrician, and learned that at al-Araba in Palestine there was a force of Byzantines. He sent Abu Umama al-Suda b. Ajlan al-Bahili against them, who fell on them, killed their chief and returned.

307Abu Mikhnaf related of the day of al-Araba that six Byzantine commanders had camped at al-Araba with three thousand men. Abu Umama marched against them with a body of Muslims, defeated them and killed one of the commanders. Then he pursued them until they reached al-Dabiya, that is al-Dabiya, and defeated them again, and the Muslims took fine booty.

308Abu Hafs al-Shami told me, from elders of the people of Syria, who said: The first of the Muslims' battles was al-Araba; they had not fought before that since they left the Hijaz. Everywhere they passed between the Hijaz and the site of this battle they prevailed over it without fighting and it came into their hands .

Chapter 23

The march of Khālid b. al-Walīd to Syria

The March of Khalid b. al-Walid to Syria and What He Conquered on the Way

309They said: When Abu Bakr's letter reached Khalid b. al-Walid at al-Hira, he left al-Muthanna b. Haritha al-Shaybani in charge of the Kufa region and set out in Rabi' II of the year 13 with eight hundred men (some say six hundred, some say five hundred). He came to Ayn al-Tamr and took it by force. (Some say Abu Bakr's letter reached him at Ayn al-Tamr after he had taken it.) From Ayn al-Tamr Khalid came to Sandawda', where there were people of Kinda, Iyad and non-Arabs. Its people fought him and he prevailed, and he left Sa'd b. Hiram al-Ansari there, so his descendants are there today.

Khalid learned that a force of the Banu Taghlib b. Wa'il, apostates, was at al-Mudabbih and al-Husayd under Rabi'a b. Bujayr. He came to them, they fought him, and he defeated them, took captives and booty, and sent the captives to Abu Bakr. Among them was Umm Habib al-Sahba' bint Habib b. Bujayr, who became the mother of Umar b. Abi Talib.

Then Khalid raided Qaraqir, a watering place of Kalb, then crossed the desert from it to Suwa, also a watering place of Kalb, where there were some of Bahra' with them. He killed Harqus b. al-Nu'man al-Bahrani of Quda'a and swept off their property. When Khalid entered the waterless desert, he took the camels and gave them their fill of water, then cut their lips and bound them so they would not chew the cud and become thirsty, and took a great deal of water with him. It ran out on the way, so he began slaughtering those camels one after another, and he and his companions drank the water from their stomachs. He had a guide called Rafi' b. Umayr al-Ta'i, about whom the poet said :

"What a marvel is Nafi', how he found his way and crossed from Qaraqir to Suwa, a water that if the stingy man sought it, he would recoil, that no man had crossed before you."

When the Muslims reached Suwa, they found Harqus and a group with him drinking and singing, and Harqus was saying:

"Come, console me before Abu Bakr's army comes; perhaps our deaths are near and we do not know it."

When the Muslims killed him, his blood ran into the bowl in which his drink was. It is said that his head fell into it too. Some narrators said the one singing this verse was a man of the Banu Taghlib whom Khalid had raided with Rabi'a b. Bujayr.

310Al-Waqidi said: Khalid went out from Suwa to al-Kawathil, then came to Qarqisiya. Its master came out against him with a host, but Khalid left him, moved off into the open country and went on his way. He came to Arka (that is, Ark), raided its people, besieged them and took it by treaty, receiving something from them for the Muslims. He came to Dumat al-Jandal and took it. Then he came to Qasm, and the Banu Mashja'a b. al-Tayim b. al-Namir b. Wabara b. Taghlib b. Hulwan b. Imran b. al-Haf b. Quda'a made peace with him and he wrote them a guarantee of safety. Then he came to Tadmur, whose people refused and fortified themselves, then asked for safety, and he granted it on condition that they be dhimmis, that they host the Muslims and give them gifts . Then he came to al-Qaryatayn, whose people fought him, and he prevailed and took booty. Then he came to Huwwarin in Sanir and raided its people's livestock. They fought him, though reinforcements had come to them from the people of Baalbek and Busra (the city of Hawran), and he defeated them and took captives and killed.

Then he came to Marj Rahit and raided Ghassan on the day of their Easter, when they were Christians, taking captives and killing. Khalid sent Busr b. Abi Arta'a al-Amiri of Quraysh and Habib b. Maslama al-Fihri to the Ghuta of Damascus, and they raided some of its villages. Khalid went to the pass known as Thaniyyat al-Uqab at Damascus. He stood on it for a while with his banner unfurled, a black banner that had belonged to the Messenger of God, and so it was named Thaniyyat al-Uqab ("the Eagle's Pass") that day. (The Arabs call a banner an uqab. Some say it was named for an eagle that had settled on it. The first account is sounder. I have heard someone say there was a stone image of an eagle there, but that is nothing.)

311They said: Khalid camped at the East Gate of Damascus (some say he camped at the Gate of al-Jabiya), and the bishop of Damascus brought out lodging and service for him and said: "Keep this covenant for me." He promised him that. Then Khalid went on until he reached the Muslims, who were at Qanat Busra. Some say he came to al-Jabiya, where Abu Ubayda was with a group of Muslims; they met and went on together to Busra.

Chapter 24

The conquest of Buṣrā

The Conquest of Busra

312They said: When Khalid b. al-Walid reached the Muslims at Busra, they gathered against it and made Khalid commander for its siege. Then they pressed right up to it and fought its patrician until they drove him and the best of his companions into the city. Some say Yazid b. Abi Sufyan was in charge of the war, because its governorship and command belonged to him, since it belongs to Damascus. In the end its people made peace on condition that they would be safe in their lives, property and children and would pay the poll-tax.

313Some narrators mentioned that the people of Busra made peace on condition of paying a dinar and a jarib of wheat for every adult male. The Muslims conquered all the land of the district of Hawran and prevailed over it. He said: Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah went with a large body of Muslims from the commanders' men who were attached to him and came to Ma'ab in the land of al-Balqa', where a force of the enemy was. He took it by treaty on the same terms as Busra. Some say Ma'ab was taken before Busra. Some say Abu Ubayda took Ma'ab when he was commander over all Syria in Umar's days.

Chapter 25

The day of Ajnadayn

The Day of Ajnadayn (also called Ajnadin)

314Then came the battle of Ajnadayn. About a hundred thousand Byzantines took part, most of them Heraclius's own troops, with the rest gathered from the surrounding regions, while Heraclius was then staying at Homs. The Muslims fought them fiercely, and Khalid b. al-Walid distinguished himself that day. Then God routed His enemies and tore them to pieces, and many of them were killed.

Martyred that day were Abdallah b. al-Zubayr b. Abd al-Muttalib b. Hashim; Amr b. Sa'id b. al-As b. Umayya and his brother Aban b. Sa'id (this is the established view; others say Aban died in year 29); and Tulayb b. Umayr b. Wahb b. Abd b. Qusayy. A foreigner fought him and struck him a blow that cut off his right hand, so that his sword fell with his palm, and then the Byzantines overwhelmed him and killed him. His mother was Arwa bint Abd al-Muttalib, aunt of the Messenger of God, and his kunya was Abu Adi. Also Salama b. Hisham b. al-Mughira (some say he was killed at Marj al-Suffar); Ikrima b. Abi Jahl b. Hisham al-Makhzumi; Hubbar b. Sufyan b. Abd al-Asad al-Makhzumi (some say he was killed at Mu'ta); Nu'aym b. Abdallah al-Nahham al-Adawi (some say he was killed at the Yarmuk); Hisham b. al-As b. Wa'il al-Sahmi (some say at the Yarmuk); Umar b. al-Tufayl b. Amr al-Dawsi (some say at the Yarmuk); Jundub b. Amr al-Dawsi; Sa'id b. al-Harith; al-Harith b. al-Harith; and al-Hajjaj b. al-Harith b. Qays b. Adi al-Sahmi.

315Hisham b. Muhammad al-Kalbi said: Al-Nahham was killed at Mu'ta; Sa'id b. al-Harith b. Qays was killed at the Yarmuk; Tamim b. al-Harith was killed at Ajnadayn; and his brother Ubaydallah b. Abd al-Asad was killed at the Yarmuk. He said: al-Harith b. Hisham b. al-Mughira was killed at Ajnadayn.

316They said: When news of this battle reached Heraclius, his heart quaked, he was dismayed and filled with terror, and he fled from Homs to Antioch. Some mention that his flight from Homs to Antioch took place when the Muslims first came to Syria. The battle of Ajnadayn was on Monday, twelve nights before the end of Jumada I, in the year 13 (some say on the second night of Jumada II, some say two nights before its end).

317They said: Then the Byzantines gathered a force at al-Yaqusa (al-Yaqusa is a valley whose mouth is al-Fawwara). The Muslims met them there and drove them back and routed them, killing many of them, and their fugitives joined the cities of Syria. Abu Bakr died in Jumada II of the year 13, and news of his death reached the Muslims while they were at al-Yaqusa .

Chapter 26

The day of Fiḥl in Jordan

The Day of Fihl in Jordan

318They said: The battle of Fihl in Jordan was on the second-to-last night of Dhu al-Qa'da, five months after the caliphate of Umar b. al-Khattab began, with Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah as commander of the people. Umar had written to him appointing him over Syria and as commander of the commanders, sending the letter by Amir b. Abi Waqqas, brother of Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas.

319Some say that Abu Ubayda's appointment over Syria reached him while the people were besieging Damascus, and that he concealed it from Khalid for some days, because Khalid was the people's commander in war. Khalid said to him: "What made you do what you did, may God have mercy on you?" He said: "I disliked breaking you and weakening your position while you were facing an enemy."

The cause of this battle was that when Heraclius reached Antioch, he called out the Byzantines and the people of the Jazira, and sent a man from among his closest and most trusted. They met the Muslims at Fihl in Jordan, and fought them with the fiercest and most grievous fighting until God gave the Muslims the upper hand. Their patrician was killed with some ten thousand with him, and the rest scattered into the cities of Syria, some joining Heraclius. The people of Fihl fortified themselves and the Muslims besieged them until they asked for safety, on condition of paying the poll-tax per head and the land-tax on their land. The Muslims guaranteed their lives and property and that their walls would not be torn down. Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah concluded this agreement; some say Shurahbil b. Hasana did.

Chapter 27

Jordan

The Affair of Jordan

320Hafs b. Umar al-Umari told me, from al-Haytham b. Adi, who said: Shurahbil b. Hasana conquered Jordan by force, except Tiberias, whose people made peace with him for half of their houses and churches.

321Abu Hafs al-Dimashqi told me, from Sa'id b. Abd al-Aziz al-Tanukhi, from a number of people including Abu Bishr, muezzin of the mosque of Damascus: When the Muslims came to Syria, each commander would head for a region to raid and spread his raiding parties through it. Amr b. al-As headed for Palestine, Shurahbil for Jordan, and Yazid b. Abi Sufyan for the land of Damascus. When the enemy massed against them, they united against him, and if one of them needed the support and aid of his companion, he hastened to it. Their commander when they were together in war, in the first days of Abu Bakr, was Amr b. al-As, until Khalid b. al-Walid came to Syria and became commander of the Muslims in every battle. Then Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah was given the whole of Syria and the command of the commanders in war and peace by Umar b. al-Khattab, for when Umar became caliph he wrote to Khalid removing him and appointed Abu Ubayda.

Shurahbil b. Hasana took Tiberias by treaty after a siege of some days, on condition that its people be safe in their lives, property, children, churches and houses, except what they had evacuated and abandoned, and he set aside a place for the Muslims' mosque. Then they broke the agreement in Umar's caliphate, and a group of Byzantines and others gathered to them, and Abu Ubayda ordered Amr b. al-As to attack them. He went against them with four thousand and took it on the same terms as Shurahbil's treaty. Some say Shurahbil took it a second time.

Shurahbil conquered all the cities and fortresses of Jordan on these terms, easily and without fighting: he took Baysan, Susiya, Afiq, Jarash, Bayt Ra's, Qudus and the Golan, and prevailed over the farmland of Jordan and all its territory.

322Abu Hafs said: Abu Muhammad Sa'id b. Abd al-Aziz said: I have heard that al-Wadin b. Ata' said: Shurahbil took Acre, Tyre and Sepphoris. Abu Bishr the muezzin said: Abu Ubayda sent Amr b. al-As to the coasts of Jordan, and the Byzantines grew numerous against him, with reinforcements reaching them from Heraclius, who was in Constantinople. Amr wrote to Abu Ubayda asking for help, and Abu Ubayda sent Yazid b. Abi Sufyan. Yazid set out with his brother Mu'awiya at the head of his vanguard. Yazid and Amr conquered the coasts of Jordan, and Abu Ubayda wrote of their conquest in their names, and Mu'awiya had good achievement and a fine record in it.

323Abu al-Yasa' al-Antaki told me, from his father, from elders of the people of Antioch and Jordan, who said: Mu'awiya moved some Persians of Baalbek, Homs and Antioch to the coasts of Jordan, to Tyre, Acre and others, in the year 42. In that year, or a year before or after, he also moved a group from the Asawira of Basra and Kufa and the Persians of Baalbek and Homs to Antioch. Among the Persian commanders was Muslim b. Abdallah, grandfather of Abdallah b. Habib b. al-Nu'man b. Muslim al-Antaki.

324Muhammad b. Sa'd told me, from al-Waqidi, and Hisham b. al-Layth al-Suri informed me, from elders of the people of Syria, who said: Mu'awiya repaired Acre when he sailed from it to Cyprus, and he repaired Tyre. Then Abd al-Malik b. Marwan restored both, which had fallen into ruin.

325Hisham b. al-Layth told me: Our elders told us: We settled in Tyre and on the coasts, where there was a force of Arabs and many Byzantines. Then people from various towns were drawn to us and settled with us, and so it was throughout all the coasts of Syria.

326Muhammad b. Sahm al-Antaki told me, from elders he had known, who said: In the year 49 the Byzantines came out to the coasts, and the shipyard was in Egypt only. Mu'awiya b. Abi Sufyan ordered the carpenters and craftsmen to be gathered, and they were gathered and he stationed them on the coasts. The shipyard in Jordan was at Acre. He said: Abu al-Khattab al-Azdi mentioned that a man of the descendants of Abu Mu'ayt had mills and income-producing properties at Acre. Hisham b. Abd al-Malik wanted him to sell them to him, but the Mu'ayti refused. So Hisham moved the shipyard to Tyre and built an inn and an income property at Tyre . Al-Waqidi said: The ships remained at Acre until the Banu Marwan took power, and they moved them to Tyre, where they are to this day. The Commander of the Believers al-Mutawakkil ordered, in the year 247, that the ships be stationed at Acre and all the coasts and manned with fighters.

Chapter 28

The day of Marj al-Ṣuffar

The Day of Marj al-Suffar

327They said: Then the Byzantines gathered a great host and Heraclius reinforced them. The Muslims met them at Marj al-Suffar as they were heading for Damascus, on the new moon of Muharram in the year 14. They fought fiercely until blood ran into the water and turned the mill, and about four thousand of the Muslims were wounded. Then the unbelievers turned and fled, broken and defeated, heedless of anything, until they reached Damascus and Jerusalem. Khalid b. Sa'id b. al-As b. Umayya, kunya Abu Sa'id, was martyred that day. He had consummated his marriage on the night before the battle, with Umm Hakim bint al-Harith b. Hisham al-Makhzumi, wife of Ikrima b. Abi Jahl. When news of his death reached her, she pulled up a tent pole and fought with it. It is said she killed seven men that day, with the traces of perfume still on her.

328In Abu Mikhnaf's account the battle of the Marj was twenty nights after Ajnadayn, with the conquest of the city of Damascus after it, and then, after the conquest of the city of Damascus, the battle of Fihl. Al-Waqidi's account is better established. About the day of the Marj, Khalid b. Sa'id b. al-As said:

"Who is the horseman who dislikes the thrust and taunts me about a spear, when they alight at Marj al-Suffar?"

And Abdallah b. Kamil b. Habib b. Umayr b. Khufaf b. Imri' al-Qays b. Buhtha b. Sulaym said:

"The clans of Malik were present, but Umayra stayed away from me on the day of Marj al-Suffar."

He means Malik b. Khufaf .

329Hisham b. Muhammad al-Kalbi said: Khalid b. Sa'id was martyred on the day of the Marj with his sword al-Samsama around his neck. The Prophet had sent him to Yemen as governor. He passed by the clan of Amr b. Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi of Madhhij and raided them, taking Amr's wife and a number of his people. Amr offered that he would spare them and they would become Muslim; Khalid agreed and they did, and Amr gave him his sword al-Samsama and said:

"A friend, whom I did not give it out of hatred for him, but gifts belong to the noble. A friend I did not betray, nor did he betray me; so it is with my friends or my drinking companions. I gave it to a noble man of Quraysh. Go with it, and may it be kept from the base."

He said: Mu'awiya took the sword from Khalid's neck on the day of the Marj when he was martyred and kept it. Then Sa'id b. al-As b. Sa'id b. al-As b. Umayya disputed it with him and Uthman ruled in his favor, and it stayed with him. On the day of the House, when Marwan was struck on the back of his neck and Sa'id was struck and fell down, a man of Juhayna took al-Samsama from him and kept it. Later he gave it to a sword-polisher to burnish, and the polisher doubted that a man like the Juhani could own such a thing, so he brought it to Marwan b. al-Hakam, who was then governor of Medina. Marwan questioned the Juhani about it and he told his story. Marwan said: "By God, my sword was taken from me on the day of the House, and Sa'id b. al-As's sword was taken too." Sa'id came, recognized the sword, took it, sealed it, and sent it to Amr b. Sa'id al-Ashdaq, who was governor of Mecca. Sa'id died and the sword stayed with Amr b. Sa'id. Then Amr b. Sa'id was killed at Damascus and his belongings plundered, and Muhammad b. Sa'id, Amr's half-brother on his father's side, took the sword. Then it passed to Yahya b. Sa'id. Then he died and it went to Anbasa b. Sa'id b. al-As. Then to Sa'id b. Amr b. Sa'id. Then he died and it went to Muhammad b. Abdallah b. Sa'id, whose descendants live at Bariq. Then it went to Aban b. Yahya b. Sa'id, who adorned it with gold and kept it with a concubine of his. Then Ayyub b. Abi Ayyub b. Sa'id b. Amr b. Sa'id sold it to al-Mahdi, the Commander of the Believers, for a little over eighty thousand, and al-Mahdi returned the ornament to him.

When al-Samsama came to Musa al-Hadi, the Commander of the Believers, he admired it and ordered the poet Abu al-Hawl to describe it, and he said:

"Amr al-Zubaydi's Samsama has been taken by the best of the creatures, Musa the Trustworthy. Amr's sword, so far as we know, was the best thing the scabbards ever enclosed. Green in color, with between its edges a drop of deadly poison, in which death sways. When you draw it, it dazzles the sun with brightness, so that one can hardly be made out. It does not care, when the stroke comes, whether it is wielded by left hand or right. What a fine cudgel of the zealous in battle, to be wielded, and what a fine companion."

Then the Commander of the Believers al-Wathiq billah called for a sword-polisher and ordered him to sharpen it, and when he did so, it changed.

Chapter 29

The conquest of Damascus and its territory

The Conquest of the City of Damascus and Its Territory

330They said: When the Muslims finished fighting the force that had gathered against them at the Marj, they stayed fifteen nights, then returned to the city of Damascus fourteen nights before the end of Muharram in the year 14. They took the Ghuta and its churches by force. The people of the city fortified themselves and closed its gate. Khalid b. al-Walid camped at the East Gate with some five thousand whom Abu Ubayda had attached to him. Some say Khalid was commander and that his dismissal reached him only while they were besieging Damascus. The monastery where Khalid camped was called Dayr Khalid. Amr b. al-As camped at Bab Tuma. Shurahbil camped at Bab al-Faradis. Abu Ubayda camped at Bab al-Jabiya. Yazid b. Abi Sufyan camped at the Small Gate up to the gate known as Kaysan. Abu al-Darda' Uwaymir b. Amir al-Khazraji was set over an outpost at Barza.

The bishop who had prepared the lodging for Khalid at the outset would sometimes stand on the wall and Khalid would call out to him; when he came, he greeted him and talked with him. One day he said to him: "Abu Sulayman, your cause is advancing, and I have some claim on you. Make peace with me over this city." Khalid called for an inkwell and paper and wrote: "In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is what Khalid b. al-Walid gave to the people of Damascus, if he enters it: he gave them safety for their persons, property and churches, and the wall of their city will not be torn down, and none of their houses will be settled. They have for this the covenant of God and the protection of His Messenger and the caliphs and the believers; nothing but good will befall them so long as they pay the poll-tax."

Then one of the bishop's companions came to Khalid one night and informed him that it was a feast night for the people of the city, that they were occupied, and that the East Gate had been blocked with stones and left (unguarded), and advised him to look for a ladder. People from the monastery near his camp brought two ladders, and a group of Muslims climbed them to the top of the wall and descended to the gate, where there was only one man or two. They overpowered him and opened it, at sunrise.

Meanwhile Abu Ubayda b. al-Jarrah had struggled to open the Jabiya Gate and had sent a group of Muslims up on its wall, and the Byzantine fighters rushed to his side and fought the Muslims fiercely. Then they turned and fled, and Abu Ubayda and the Muslims with him opened the Jabiya Gate by force and entered by it. Abu Ubayda and Khalid b. al-Walid met at al-Maqsalat, the place of the coppersmiths in Damascus, which is al-Barith that Hassan b. Thabit mentioned in his verse:

"They are given to drink from the water of al-Barith, above them the Barada, which ripples with clear, sweet wine."

330 (second).
