It is also related that the Byzantines took one of their dead out of the Jabiya Gate by night, with a crowd of their brave men and champions surrounding his bier, while the rest of them rushed to the gate and stood at it to prevent the Muslims from opening it and entering until their companions returned from burying the dead; they hoped the Muslims would be heedless of them. But the Muslims noticed them first and fought them at the gate with the fiercest and most grievous fighting until they opened it at sunrise.

When the bishop saw that Abu Ubayda was about to enter the city, he hurried to Khalid and made peace with him and opened the East Gate for him. Khalid entered with the bishop beside him displaying the document he had written for him. Some of the Muslims said: "By God, Khalid is not the commander, so how can his peace be valid?" Abu Ubayda said: "The least of the Muslims may grant protection on behalf of them all." He approved his peace and carried it out, paying no heed to what had been taken by force, so Damascus became wholly a peace-treaty city. Abu Ubayda wrote this to Umar and dispatched it, the gates of the city were opened, and all the people met.

331In the account of Abu Mikhnaf and others, Khalid entered Damascus by fighting and Abu Ubayda entered it by treaty, and they met at al-Zayatin . But the first account is better established.

332Al-Haytham b. Adi claimed that the people of Damascus made peace for half of their houses and churches.

333Muhammad b. Sa'd said: Abu Abdallah al-Waqidi said: I read Khalid b. al-Walid's document for the people of Damascus and did not see half-houses and churches in it. That has been related, and I do not know where whoever related it got it. But when Damascus was conquered, many of its people joined Heraclius at Antioch, so there were many empty houses, and the Muslims settled in them.

334Some have related that Abu Ubayda was at the East Gate and Khalid at the Jabiya Gate. This is a mistake. (1)

335Al-Waqidi said: The conquest of the city of Damascus was in Rajab of the year 14, and the date of Khalid's document of peace is Rabi' II of the year 15. That is because

(1) In the margin of manuscript A there is the following: Muhammad b. Asakir says: The author relied on the account that Damascus was taken by force through the Jabiya Gate at Abu Ubayda's hand, and he confirmed it by saying here "the first account is better established," but it is in truth the weakest of the accounts of the conquest of Damascus. What is sound and established by the reports and the surviving evidence is that Khalid entered it by force from the East Gate, and Abu Ubayda entered it by treaty from the Jabiya Gate. That is from the standpoint of the soundness of the reports. As for the evidence of the monuments, the Mosque of Damascus [before its rebuilding had no part held by the Muslims except the eastern side, by the sword]. Our proof is that the maqsura attributed to the Companions and the seven reciters is also there, and the church remained on its western side until al-Walid b. Abd al-Malik demolished it when he resolved to build the mosque during his caliphate. And in the author's own first account, that Khalid came with Muslims from the monastery next to his camp and his companions climbed them to the wall of the East Gate, there is evidence that supports what we have said here. And God knows best what is right.

(The bracketed phrase in the note is partly illegible in the source text, marked "؟ ؟ ؟", so I have reconstructed its sense.)

Khalid wrote the document without a date. When the Muslims assembled to march against those who had gathered against them at the Yarmuk, the bishop came to Khalid and asked him to renew the document for him and to have Abu Ubayda and the Muslims witness it. He did so and entered in the document the testimony of Abu Ubayda, Yazid b. Abi Sufyan, Shurahbil b. Hasana and others, and dated it with the time when he renewed it.

336Al-Qasim b. Sallam told me: Abu Mushir told us, from Sa'id b. Abd al-Aziz al-Tanukhi, who said: Yazid entered Damascus from the East Gate under treaty, and the two met at al-Maqsalat, so all of it was carried out on the basis of the treaty.

337Al-Qasim told me: Abu Mushir told us, from Yahya b. Hamza, from Abu al-Muhallab al-San'ani, from Abu al-Ash'ath al-San'ani or Abu Uthman al-San'ani, that Abu Ubayda stayed at the Jabiya Gate besieging them for four months.

338Abu Ubayd told me: Nu'aym b. Hammad told us, from Damra b. Rabi'a (?), from Raja' b. Abi Salama, who said: Hassan b. Malik brought a suit before Umar b. Abd al-Aziz on behalf of the non-Arabs of Damascus over a church that one of the commanders had granted him as a fief. Umar said: "If it is one of the fifteen churches that are in their covenant, you have no claim on it." Damra said, from Ali b. Abi Hamala: We brought a suit before Umar b. Abd al-Aziz on behalf of the non-Arabs of Damascus over a church in Damascus that so-and-so had assigned to the Banu Nasr, and Umar removed us from it and returned it to the Christians. When Yazid b. Abd al-Malik took office, he returned it to the Banu Nasr.

339Abu Ubayd told me: Hisham b. Ammar told us, from al-Walid b. Muslim, from al-Awza'i, who said: The poll-tax in Syria at the beginning was a jarib and a dinar on every head. Then Umar b. al-Khattab set it at four dinars on the gold people and forty dirhams on the silver people, and divided them into classes according to the wealth of the wealthy, the poverty of the poor and the means of the middle. Hisham said: I heard our elders mention that the Jews had been like dhimmis to the Christians, paying them tribute, and they entered with them into the peace. Some narrators have also mentioned that Khalid b. al-Walid made peace with the people of Damascus on terms that included imposing on every man a dinar of poll-tax and a jarib of wheat, with vinegar and oil for the Muslims' provisions.

340Amr al-Naqid told us: Abdallah b. Wahb al-Misri told us, from Umar b. Muhammad, from Nafi' , from Aslam, freedman of Umar b. al-Khattab, that Umar wrote to the commanders of the garrisons ordering them to impose the poll-tax on everyone on whom the razor had passed, to set it at forty dirhams per man on the silver people and four dinars on the gold people, and, in addition, to supply the Muslims' rations of wheat and oil: two mudd of wheat and three qist of oil per month for each person in Syria and the Jazira. He also set fat and honey on them, I don't know how much, and for each person in Egypt each month an ardabb, clothing and three days' hospitality.

341Amr b. Hammad b. Abi Hanifa told us: Malik b. Anas told us, from Nafi', from Aslam, that Umar imposed the poll-tax of four dinars on the gold people and forty dirhams on the silver people, in addition to the Muslims' rations and three days' hospitality.

342Mus'ab told me, from his father, from Malik, from Nafi', from Aslam, with the same text.

343They said: When Mu'awiya b. Abi Sufyan became ruler, he wanted to add the Church of St. John to the mosque in Damascus. The Christians refused, so he desisted. Then Abd al-Malik b. Marwan sought it in his time to enlarge the mosque and offered them money, but they refused to hand it over. Then al-Walid b. Abd al-Malik gathered them in his time and offered them a great sum for it, but they refused. He said: "If you will not, I will tear it down." One of them said: "Commander of the Believers, whoever demolishes a church goes mad and is struck by an affliction." This angered him, and he called for a pickaxe and began to tear down some of its walls with his own hand, wearing a yellow silk tunic. Then he gathered workmen and wreckers who demolished it, and he incorporated it into the mosque.

When Umar b. Abd al-Aziz became caliph, the Christians complained to him of what al-Walid had done to them over their church. He wrote to his governor ordering him to return to them what had been added to the mosque. The people of Damascus disliked this and said: "Our mosque will be demolished after we have called the prayer in it and prayed in it, and a church restored?" Among them then were Sulayman b. Habib al-Muharibi and other jurists. They turned to the Christians and asked them to take all the churches of the Ghuta that had been taken by force and had come into Muslim hands, on condition that they would pardon the Church of St. John and refrain from claiming it. They agreed and were pleased with it. He wrote this to Umar, who was glad and approved it.

In the mosque of Damascus, in the southern portico next to the minaret, there is an inscription on a marble slab near the ceiling: "Among what the Commander of the Believers al-Walid ordered built, in the year 86."

344I heard Hisham b. Ammar say: The wall of the city of Damascus stood until Abdallah b. Ali b. Abdallah b. al-Abbas tore it down after the end of the rule of Marwan and the Umayyads.

345Abu Hafs al-Dimashqi told me, from Sa'id b. Abd al-Aziz, from the muezzin of the mosque of Damascus and others, who said: The Muslims gathered when Khalid arrived at Busra and took it by treaty, and spread through the whole land of Hawran and prevailed over it. The master of Adhri'at came to them and asked for peace on the same terms as the people of Busra, with all the land of al-Bathaniyya being land subject to the land-tax. They agreed. Yazid b. Abi Sufyan went on until he entered it and made an agreement for its people. The Muslims were then in control of the two districts of Hawran and al-Bathaniyya. Then they went on to Palestine and Jordan and raided what had not been conquered. Yazid went to Amman and took it easily, by treaty on the same terms as Busra, and prevailed over the land of al-Balqa'. Abu Ubayda took charge when all this had been conquered, and he was commander of the people when Damascus was taken, except that the treaty was Khalid's, and he approved his treaty.

Yazid b. Abi Sufyan went out in Abu Ubayda's governorship and took Arandal by treaty and prevailed over the land of al-Shara and its mountains. He said: Sa'id b. Abd al-Aziz said: al-Wadin informed me that after the conquest of the city of Damascus, Yazid came to Sidon, Arqa, Jubayl and Beirut, which are coastal towns, with his brother Mu'awiya at the head of his vanguard, and took them easily and drove many of their people into exile. Mu'awiya himself took charge of the conquest of Arqa during Yazid's governorship. Then the Byzantines regained some of these coasts at the end of Umar b. al-Khattab's caliphate or the beginning of Uthman b. Affan's, and Mu'awiya set out against them and conquered them, then repaired them, garrisoned them with fighters and gave them land grants.

346They said: When Uthman became caliph and Mu'awiya was governor of Syria, Mu'awiya sent Sufyan b. Mujib al-Azdi to Tripoli, which is three cities joined together. He built a fort at a meadow a few miles from it, called the Fort of Sufyan, cut off supplies to its people from the sea and elsewhere and besieged them. When the siege grew severe on them, they gathered in one of the three fortresses and they wrote to the king of the Byzantines asking him to reinforce them or to send ships in which they could flee to his territory. He sent many ships, and they boarded them by night and fled. When morning came, Sufyān found the fortress they had been in empty and entered it. Sufyān used to spend every night in his own fort, lodging the Muslims in it, and go out against the enemy in the morning. He wrote of the conquest to Muʿāwiya, who settled a large group of Jews in it. This is the place that has the port today. Later ʿAbd al-Malik rebuilt and fortified it.

347They said: Every year Muʿāwiya sent a large body of troops to Tripoli to garrison it and appointed a governor over it. When the sea closed [for winter] they went home, and the governor stayed with a small group. This continued until ʿAbd al-Malik's reign. In his days a Byzantine patrician came with many of his people and asked for safe-conduct on condition that he settle there and pay the land-tax. His request was granted. Only two years, or a few months more, passed before the time came for the troops to leave the city. Then he shut its gate, killed its governor, captured the soldiers with him and a number of Jews, and rejoined the Byzantine lands with his companions. Afterwards the Muslims caught him at sea, heading in many ships toward a Muslim coast, and killed him. It is also said they captured him and sent him to ʿAbd al-Malik, who killed and crucified him. I also heard someone say that ʿAbd al-Malik sent a force that besieged him at Tripoli, then took him by peaceful surrender and brought him to ʿAbd al-Malik, who killed and crucified him. Some of his companions escaped and joined the Byzantine lands.

ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī said, from ʿAttāb b. Ibrāhīm: Sufyān b. Mujīb conquered Tripoli; its people then broke the treaty in ʿAbd al-Malik's days, and al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik conquered it in his time.

348Abū Ḥafṣ al-Shāmī told me, from Saʿīd, from al-Wāḍīn: Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān sent Muʿāwiya to the coasts of Damascus, except Tripoli, which he had no hope of taking. He would stay at a fort for two days or a few days; sometimes there was light fighting, sometimes it was pelted [with siege fire] and he took it. He said: Whenever the Muslims conquered a visible city or one on the coast, they stationed in it the number of Muslims it needed, and if anything happened there from the enemy's side, they sent reinforcements. When ʿUthmān became caliph he wrote to Muʿāwiya ordering him to fortify the coasts, garrison them, and give land grants to those who settled there. He did so.

349Abū Ḥafṣ told me, from Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: I reached people who were saying that after the death of his brother Yazīd, Muʿāwiya wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb describing the state of the coasts. ʿUmar wrote back about repairing their fortresses, arranging the fighters in them, posting guards on their watchtowers, and setting beacons for them. He did not permit him to raid by sea. Muʿāwiya kept at ʿUthmān until he permitted sea raids, and ordered him, whenever he raided or sent armies to raid, to keep a reserve on the coasts beyond the existing garrisons, to grant the garrison troops land, to give them the houses their people had abandoned, to build mosques, and to enlarge those built before his caliphate. Al-Wāḍīn said: After that people moved to the coasts from every direction.

350al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from Jaʿfar b. Kilāb al-Kilābī: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed ʿAlqama b. ʿAwf b. al-Aḥwaṣ b. Jaʿfar b. Kilāb over Ḥawrān, and his governorship was thereafter under Muʿāwiya. He died there. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa al-ʿAbsī, who set out to him but whose death came before his arrival, composed about him. [ʿAlqama] had heard he was on the way, and had willed him a share equal to one of his sons' shares:

Nothing would have stood between me and riches, had I met you safe,but a few nights.

351A number of scholars told me, among them a neighbour of Hishām b. ʿAmmār: Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb, in his trading days to Syria in the Jāhiliyya, had an estate in al-Balqāʾ called Qubaysh [reading uncertain]. It passed to Muʿāwiya and his son, was confiscated at the start of the [ʿAbbāsid] dynasty and went to one of the sons of the Commander of the Faithful al-Mahdī, then to a group of oil-sellers known as the Banū Nuʿaym of Kufa.

352al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from his grandfather: Tamīm b. Aws of the Banū al-Dār b. Ḥabīb of Lakhm, whose kunya was Abū Ruqayya, came to the Prophet with his brother Nuʿaym b. Aws. The Messenger of God granted them Ḥabrā, Bayt ʿAynūn and the Mosque of Abraham ﵇, and wrote them a document to that effect. When Syria was conquered, it was handed over to them. Whenever Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik passed this estate he would not turn aside, saying: "I fear the Prophet's curse will strike me."

353Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me that he heard elders say that when ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb came to al-Jābiya in the region of Damascus, he passed a group of leprous Christians and ordered that they be given alms and a regular food allowance. Hishām said: I heard al-Walīd b. Muslim say that Khālid b. al-Walīd stipulated a reduction in land-tax for the people of the monastery known as Dayr Khālid, when they gave him the ladder he climbed. Abū ʿUbayda implemented it for them.

When Abū ʿUbayda finished with the city of Damascus, he went to Homs and passed Baalbek. Its people asked for safe-conduct and peace, and he made peace on terms securing their lives, property and churches, and wrote for them:

"In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is a document of safety for so-and-so son of so-and-so and the people of Baalbek, their Byzantines, Persians and Arabs, for their persons, property, churches and houses, inside the city and outside, and their mills. The Byzantines may pasture their herds within fifteen miles of them, but may not settle in an inhabited village. When the months of Rabīʿ and Jumādā I have passed, they may go wherever they like. Whoever of them converts has what we have and owes what we owe. Their merchants may travel to any of the lands with which we have made peace. Those who stay owe the poll-tax and the land-tax. God is witness, and God suffices as witness."

Chapter 30

Homs

The affair of Homs

354al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf: When Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ finished with Damascus, he sent ahead Khālid b. al-Walīd and Malḥān b. Ziyār al-Ṭāʾī, then followed. When they all reached Homs, its people fought them, then took refuge in the city and asked for safety and peace. They made peace for 170,000 dinars.

Al-Wāqidī and others said: While the Muslims were at the gates of Damascus, a large force of enemy cavalry appeared. A group of Muslims went out and met them between Bayt Lihyā and al-Thaniyya, and they fled toward Homs by the road of Qāra. The Muslims pursued them as far as Homs and found [the Byzantines] had turned away from it. The people of Homs saw them. They were terrified because Heraclius had fled from them and because of what reached them of the Muslims' cunning, strength and success, so they submitted and cried out for safety. The Muslims granted it and held their hands from them. The people brought out fodder and food, and [the Muslims] stayed on the Araniṭ — meaning the Orontes, the river that comes to Antioch and then runs into the sea at its coast. The Muslim commander was al-Simṭ b. al-Aswad al-Kindī. When Abū ʿUbayda finished with Damascus he left Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān in charge of it, then came to Homs by way of Baalbek and camped at Bāb al-Rastan. The people of Homs made peace with him: he secured their lives, property, city wall, churches and mills, excepted from them a quarter of the Church of John for the mosque, and stipulated the land-tax on those who stayed.

Some narrators mention that al-Simṭ b. al-Aswad al-Kindī had made peace with the people of Homs, and when Abū ʿUbayda came he ratified it; and that al-Simṭ divided Homs into plots among the Muslims until they settled it, lodging them in each abandoned house whose people had left, or empty lot.

355Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me, from Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: When Abū ʿUbayda conquered Damascus he appointed Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān over Damascus, ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ over Palestine and Shuraḥbīl over Jordan. He came to Homs and made peace with its people on terms like Baalbek's. He left ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit al-Anṣārī in Homs and went toward Ḥamāh. Its people met him in submission, and he made peace on the poll-tax on their heads and the land-tax on their land. He went on to Shayzar; they came out with their crosses and the welcoming performers (muqallisūn), and accepted what Ḥamāh had accepted. His cavalry reached al-Zarāʿa and al-Qasṭal. Abū ʿUbayda passed Maʿarrat Ḥimṣ, which is attributed to al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr; they came out performing before him. Then he came to Fāmiya and its people did likewise and submitted to the poll-tax and land-tax. The matter of Homs was completed, and Homs and Qinnasrīn were one unit.

They differed about the naming of the ajnād (military districts). Some said the Muslims called Palestine a jund because it combined several districts, and likewise Damascus, Jordan, and Homs with Qinnasrīn. Others said each region that had soldiers drawing their stipends from it was called a jund. They mention that the Jazīra used to belong to Qinnasrīn, and ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān made it a separate jund, so its soldiers drew their stipends from its revenues; Muḥammad b. Marwān had asked ʿAbd al-Malik to do so. Qinnasrīn and its districts stayed joined to Homs until Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya made Qinnasrīn, Antioch, Manbij and their dependencies a jund. When the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd Hārūn b. al-Mahdī took office, he separated Qinnasrīn with its districts as one jund, and separated Manbij, Dulūk, Raʿbān, Qūrus, Antioch and Tīzīn, and called them the ʿAwāṣim ("protectors"), because the Muslims take refuge in them when they return from their raids and leave the frontier. He made Manbij the capital of the ʿAwāṣim, and ʿAbd al-Malik b. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī settled it in the year 173 and built structures there.

356Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me, from Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Mūsā b. Ibrāhīm al-Tanūkhī told me, from his father, from elders of Homs: Abū ʿUbayda left ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit al-Anṣārī in charge of Homs. ʿUbāda came to Latakia, and its people fought him. It had a huge gate that only a crowd of men could open. When he saw how hard it was to take, he camped some distance from the city, then ordered pits dug like tunnels, each large enough to hide a man and his horse. The Muslims worked hard until they finished them. Then they pretended to return to Homs, but when night fell they went back to their camp and pits. The people of Latakia were off guard, thinking [the Muslims] had gone. In the morning they opened their gate and let out their herds, and were startled by the Muslims attacking them at dawn and entering by the city gate. It was taken by force. ʿUbāda entered the fort, climbed its wall and shouted Allāhu akbar from it. A group of Latakia's Christians fled to al-Yasīd [reading uncertain], then asked for safe-conduct on condition they return to their land. They were assessed a land-tax to pay in any amount, large or small; their church was left to them; and the Muslims built a congregational mosque in Latakia by ʿUbāda's order, later enlarged. The Byzantines raided the coast of Latakia by sea, destroyed its city and took its people captive, in the caliphate of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz in the year 100. ʿUmar ordered it rebuilt and fortified, and sent to the Byzantine emperor to ransom the Muslims captured, but that was not completed before ʿUmar died in the year 101; Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik completed the city and garrisoned it.

357A man of Latakia told me: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz did not die until he had fortified the city of Latakia and finished it. What Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik did there was repair work and an increase in the garrison.

358Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me: Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Saʿīd b. Sulaymān al-Ḥimṣī told me: ʿUbāda and the Muslims came to the coasts and took by force a city known as Balda, two leagues from Jabala. It later fell into ruin and its people left. Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān founded Jabala. It had been a Byzantine fortress which they abandoned when the Muslims conquered and garrisoned Homs.

359Sufyān b. Muḥammad al-Bahrānī told me, from his elders: Muʿāwiya built a fort for Jabala outside the old Byzantine fort. The inhabitants of the Byzantine fort were monks and people devoted to worship in their religion.

360Sufyān b. Muḥammad told me: My father and our elders told me: ʿUbāda and the Muslims with him conquered Anṭarṭūs, which was a fort whose people then left. Muʿāwiya built Anṭarṭūs, made it a city, and gave land grants there; he did likewise at Marqiya and Balanyās.

361Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me, from his elders: Abū ʿUbayda conquered Latakia, Jabala and Anṭarṭūs at the hands of ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit. He assigned guards there until the sea closed [for winter]. When Muʿāwiya garrisoned and fortified the coasts, he garrisoned and fortified these and carried their affairs out as he did for the coasts generally.

362An old man of Homs told me: Near Salamiyya there was a city called al-Muʾtafika ("the overturned") which was overturned with its people, and only a hundred persons survived. They built a hundred houses and settled there, and their enclosure was called Salm Miʾa ("safe hundred"); people then corrupted the name to Salamiyya. Later Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās took it, built there with his sons, and made it a city, and some of his descendants settled it. Ibn Sahm al-Anṭākī said: Salamiyya is an old Byzantine name.

363Muḥammad b. Muṣaffā al-Ḥimṣī told me: Marwān b. Muḥammad tore down the wall of Homs. This was because they had rebelled against him, and when he passed through them fleeing the people of Khurasan, they cut off part of his baggage, money and armouries. The city of Homs had been paved with stone. In the days of Aḥmad b. Muḥammad b. Abī Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim billāh, they rioted against their governor al-Faḍl b. Qārin al-Ṭabarī, brother of Māzyār b. Qārin, who ordered the paving torn up, and it was. Then they openly rebelled, restored the paving and fought al-Faḍl b. Qārin until they overpowered him, plundered his property and women, and seized, killed and crucified him. Aḥmad b. Muḥammad sent against them Mūsā b. Bughā the Elder, client of the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim billāh. They fought him, with many of the city's Christians and Jews among them. He killed many of them and routed the rest until he drove them into the city and entered it by force, in the year 250. Homs has a granary into which wheat and oil come from the coasts and elsewhere, from what its people were assessed for, and decrees were drawn up for them recording their settlements.

Chapter 31

The day of the Yarmūk

364They said: Heraclius gathered large forces of Byzantines, Syrians, people of the Jazīra and Armenia, about 200,000, appointed one of his intimates over them, and sent Jabala b. al-Ayham al-Ghassānī in the vanguard with the Arabized tribes of Syria, Lakhm, Judhām and others. He resolved to fight the Muslims; if they prevailed [well], and if not he would go into Byzantine lands and stay in Constantinople. The Muslims gathered and advanced on them, and they fought on the Yarmūk with the fiercest and most grievous fighting. The Yarmūk is a river. The Muslims numbered 24,000 that day. The Byzantines and their followers were chained together that day so they would not be tempted to flee. God killed about 70,000 of them, and their fugitives fled to Palestine, Antioch, Aleppo, the Jazīra and Armenia.

Some of the Muslim women fought fiercely on the day of the Yarmūk. Hind bint ʿUtba, mother of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, kept saying: "Cut down the uncircumcised with your swords!" Her husband Abū Sufyān had gone to Syria as a volunteer, and also wanted to see his son, and took her with him. He later came to Medina and died there in the year 31, aged eighty-eight; some say he died in Syria. When the news of his death reached his daughter Ḥabība [Umm Ḥabība], she called on the third day for yellow perfume, rubbed it on her forearms and cheeks, and said: "I had no need of this, had I not heard the Prophet say: 'A woman shall not mourn for a dead person other than her husband for more than three days.'" It is also said she did this when the news of her brother Yazīd's death reached her. God knows best. Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb was one of the one-eyed; he lost his eye on the day of al-Ṭāʾif.

365They said: On the day of the Yarmūk, al-Ashʿath b. Qays lost an eye, as did Hāshim b. ʿUtba b. Abī Waqqāṣ al-Zuhrī (al-Mirqāl) and Qays b. Makshūḥ. ʿĀmir b. Abī Waqqāṣ al-Zuhrī was martyred; he is the one who had come to Syria with ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb's letter to Abū ʿUbayda appointing him over Syria. Some say he died in the plague, and some narrators said he was martyred at Ajnādayn, which is not established.

He said: Abū ʿUbayda tied a banner for Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī over the pursuit cavalry, and he killed whomever he overtook. Jabala b. al-Ayham went over to the Anṣār and said: "You are our brothers and the sons of our father," and professed Islam. When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb came to Syria in the year 17, Jabala quarrelled with a man of Muzayna and struck his eye. ʿUmar ordered him to submit to retaliation. He said: "Is his eye like my eye? By God, I will not stay in a land where someone has authority over me." So he entered the Byzantine lands as an apostate. Jabala was king of Ghassān after al-Ḥārith b. Abī Shimr.

It is also related that Jabala came to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb still a Christian. ʿUmar offered him Islam and paying the alms-tax, and he refused, saying: "I will stay in my religion and pay the alms-tax." ʿUmar said: "If you stay in your religion, pay the poll-tax." He scorned it. ʿUmar said: "We have for you only one of three: Islam, or paying the poll-tax, or going wherever you like." He entered Byzantine lands with 30,000 men. When this reached ʿUmar he regretted it. ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit reproached him: "If you had accepted the alms-tax from him and then won him over, he would have converted." In the year 21, ʿUmar sent ʿUmayr b. Saʿd al-Anṣārī into Byzantine lands with a great army and put him in charge of the summer raid (ṣāʾifa), the first summer raid ever. He ordered him to be gentle with Jabala b. al-Ayham, to appeal to the kinship between them, and to invite him back to the lands of Islam, on condition that he pay the alms-tax he had offered and remain in his religion. ʿUmayr marched into Byzantine lands, offered Jabala what ʿUmar had ordered, and he refused anything but staying in Byzantine lands. ʿUmayr reached a place called al-Ḥimār, a valley, fell on its people and ruined it, whence the saying "emptier than the belly of a donkey."

366They said: When Heraclius heard of the people of the Yarmūk and the Muslims' blow to his troops, he fled from Antioch to Constantinople. When he crossed the pass, he said: "Farewell to you, O Syria! What a fine country this is for the enemy" — meaning the land of Syria, for its abundant pastures. The battle of the Yarmūk was in Rajab of the year 15.

Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: Ḥubāsh b. Qays al-Qushayrī fought at the Yarmūk and killed many non-Arabs, and his leg was cut off without his noticing. Then he began to recite verses about it. Sawwār b. Awfā said:

Among us is Ibn ʿAttāb, and the one who called out for his leg;among us is the one who brought Ḥājib to the tribe

meaning Dhū al-Raqība [text uncertain].

367Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me: Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz told us: It has reached me that when Heraclius gathered forces against the Muslims, and the Muslims learned they were advancing for the battle of the Yarmūk, they returned to the people of Homs the land-tax they had taken from them, saying: "We are too occupied to help and defend you, so you are on your own." The people of Homs said: "We prefer your rule and justice to the injustice and oppression we were in, and we will indeed repel Heraclius's soldiers from the city with your governor." The Jews rose and said: "By the Torah, Heraclius's governor will not enter the city of Homs unless we are overcome and exhausted." They shut the gates and guarded them. The people of the [other] cities that had made peace, Christians and Jews alike, did the same, saying: "If the Byzantines and their followers prevail over the Muslims we return to what we were; otherwise we hold to our agreement as long as any Muslims remain." When God routed the unbelievers and gave victory to the Muslims, [the people] opened their cities, brought out the welcoming performers, who played, and paid the land-tax. Abū ʿUbayda went to the jund of Qinnasrīn and Antioch and conquered it.

368al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from his grandfather: al-Simṭ b. al-Aswad al-Kindī distinguished himself in Syria, in Homs especially, and on the day of the Yarmūk. He is the one who divided the houses of Homs among its people. His son Shuraḥbīl b. al-Simṭ in Kufa was a rival of al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī for leadership. Al-Simṭ came to ʿUmar and said: "Commander of the Faithful, you do not separate captives from their families, yet you have separated me from my son. Move him to Syria or move me to Kufa." He said: "I will move him to Syria." So he settled in Homs with his father.

Chapter 32

Palestine

The affair of Palestine

369Abū Ḥafṣ al-Dimashqī told me, from Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from his elders, and from Baqiyya b. al-Walīd, from elders of the people of knowledge: The first battle the Muslims fought against the Byzantines in Abū Bakr's caliphate was in Palestine, with ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ in command. Later ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered Gaza in Abū Bakr's caliphate; then he conquered Sebaste and Nablus, granting them safety for their persons, property and houses, on condition that the poll-tax fall on their heads and the land-tax on their land; then he conquered the city of Lydda and its land; then Yubnā, ʿImwās and Bayt Jibrīn, where he made an estate called ʿAjlān, named after a client of his; and Jaffa, though it is said Muʿāwiya took it. ʿAmr conquered Rafaḥ on the same terms.

Abū ʿUbayda came to him after conquering Qinnasrīn and its districts, in the year 16, while he was besieging Īliyā, which is the city of Bayt al-Maqdis [Jerusalem]. It is said he sent [Abū ʿUbayda] from Īliyā to Antioch, whose people had betrayed [the treaty]; he conquered it and returned, and stayed two or three days. Then the people of Īliyā asked Abū ʿUbayda for safety and peace on the same terms as the cities of Syria, paying the poll-tax and land-tax and entering what their peers had entered, on condition that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb himself conclude the agreement for them. Abū ʿUbayda wrote to ʿUmar about it. ʿUmar came, camped at al-Jābiya in the region of Damascus, then went to Īliyā, carried out the peace with its people and wrote it for them. The conquest of Īliyā was in the year 17. Another account of the conquest of Īliyā has also been related.

370al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent Khālid b. Thābit al-Fahmī to Bayt al-Maqdis with an army, while he was at al-Jābiya. [Khālid] fought them, and they gave him something to pay, assessed on what their fort enclosed, with what lay outside going to the Muslims. ʿUmar came, approved this, and went back to Medina.

371Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me, from al-Walīd, from al-Awzāʿī: Abū ʿUbayda conquered Qinnasrīn and its districts in the year 16. Then he came to Palestine and camped at Īliyā; they asked him to make peace with them. He made peace with them in the year 17, on condition that ʿUmar ﵀ come, carry it out and write it for them.

372Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me: al-Walīd b. Muslim told me, from Tamīm b. ʿAṭiyya, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays: I was among those who met ʿUmar with Abū ʿUbayda on his arrival in Syria. As ʿUmar rode, the welcoming performers of Adhriʿāt met him with swords and basil. ʿUmar said: "Stop! Stop them!" Abū ʿUbayda said: "Commander of the Faithful, this is their custom (or words to that effect), and if you stop them they will think you intend to break their covenant." He said: "Leave them."

He said: The plague of ʿImwās was in the year 18, and many Muslims died in it, among them Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ, who died aged fifty-eight, while governor; and Muʿādh b. Jabal of the Banū Salima of the Khazraj, whose kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who died in the area of al-Uqḥuwāna in Jordan aged thirty-eight. When Abū ʿUbayda was dying he appointed [Muʿādh] as successor; it is also said he appointed ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm al-Fihrī, and also said he appointed ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, who appointed his son and went to Egypt. Also [died]: al-Faḍl b. al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, kunya Abū Muḥammad (some say he was martyred at Ajnādayn, but it is established that he died in the plague of ʿImwās); Shuraḥbīl b. Ḥasana, kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who died aged sixty-nine; Suhayl b. ʿAmr of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy, kunya Abū Yazīd; and al-Ḥārith b. Hishām b. al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī, though it is said he was martyred at Ajnādayn.

373They said: When news of Abū ʿUbayda's death reached ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, he wrote to Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān appointing him to the governorship of Syria in his place, and ordered him to raid Caesarea. Some say ʿUmar only appointed Yazīd over Jordan and Palestine, and appointed Abū al-Dardāʾ over Damascus and ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit over Homs.

374Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Wāqidī told me: There was disagreement among us about Caesarea. Some said Muʿāwiya conquered it; others said ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm conquered it after Abū ʿUbayda's death, as his successor; others said ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered it; others said ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ went to Egypt and left his son ʿAbd Allāh. The established account, on which scholars agreed, is that the first to besiege it was ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, who camped before it in Jumādā I of the year 13. He would stay as long as he could, and when the Muslims gathered against their enemy he would march to them. He was at Ajnādayn, Fiḥl, al-Marj, Damascus and the Yarmūk, then returned to Palestine and besieged it after Īliyā, then went from Caesarea to Egypt. Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān was appointed after Abū ʿUbayda and entrusted the siege to his brother Muʿāwiya, and went to Damascus, struck by plague, and died there.

Someone other than al-Wāqidī said: ʿUmar appointed Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān over Palestine along with what he governed of the Syrian ajnād, and wrote to him ordering him to raid Caesarea, which had been besieged before. He marched on it with 17,000 and its people fought him, then he besieged them. He fell ill at the end of the year 18, went to Damascus and left his brother Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān in charge at Caesarea. [Muʿāwiya] conquered it and wrote of the conquest, and Yazīd wrote it to ʿUmar. When Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān died, ʿUmar wrote to Muʿāwiya appointing him to what [Yazīd] had governed, and Abū Sufyān thanked him for it and said: "You have maintained kinship ties with me, Commander of the Faithful."

375Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me: al-Walīd b. Muslim told me, from Tamīm b. ʿAṭiyya: ʿUmar appointed Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān over Syria after Yazīd, and appointed with him two Companions of the Messenger of God over prayer and judgeship: Abū al-Dardāʾ over the judgeship and prayer of Damascus and Jordan, and ʿUbāda over the judgeship and prayer of Homs and Qinnasrīn.

376Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, with his isnād: When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed Muʿāwiya over Syria, he besieged Caesarea until he conquered it. It had been besieged for about seven years. Its conquest was in Shawwāl of the year 19.

377Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from Muḥammad b. ʿUmar, from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir, with his isnād: Muʿāwiya besieged Caesarea until he despaired of taking it; ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ and his son had besieged it. Muʿāwiya took it by force. He found in it 700,000 salaried soldiers, 30,000 Samaritans and 200,000 Jews, and found 300 markets all standing, and 100,000 men guarded its wall every night [figures as printed].

The cause of its conquest was that a Jew named Yūsuf came to the Muslims by night and showed them a path through a tunnel with water up to a man's waist, on condition they spare him and his family. Muʿāwiya agreed to it. The Muslims entered at night and shouted takbīr inside; the Byzantines tried to flee through the tunnel and found the Muslims at it. The Muslims opened the gate, and Muʿāwiya and those with him entered. There were many Arabs in it, among them Shaqrāʾ, about whom Ḥassān b. Thābit said:

Shaqrāʾ says: "If you were sober from wine, you would become rich in number."

It is said her name was Shaʿthāʾ.

378Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, with his isnād: The captives of Caesarea numbered four thousand heads. When Muʿāwiya sent them to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, he ordered them lodged at al-Jurf, then divided them among the orphans of the Anṣār and put some of them to work as scribes and labourers for the Muslims. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq had given the daughters of Abū Umāma Asʿad b. Zurāra two servants from the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr; they died, so ʿUmar gave them replacements from the captives of Caesarea.

379They said: Muʿāwiya sent the news of the conquest with two men of Judhām, then feared they would be too weak to make the journey, so he sent a man of Khathʿam, who pushed himself hard in travelling by day and night, saying:

The brother of Judhām kept my eye awake,brother of Jusham and brother of Ḥarām.How can I sleep while they two are ahead of me,when they set out and the noon heat is at its height?

He got ahead of them, went in to ʿUmar, and ʿUmar shouted takbīr.

380Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me, with an isnād I do not remember: Caesarea was conquered by force in the year 19. When the news reached ʿUmar, he announced that Caesarea had been taken by force, and shouted takbīr, and the Muslims did too. It had been besieged seven years and Muʿāwiya conquered it.

381They said: Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān died at the end of the year 18 in Damascus. Whoever says Muʿāwiya conquered Caesarea in his brother's lifetime says it was taken at the end of the year 18; whoever says he conquered it during his own governorship of Syria says it was taken in the year 19, which is the established view. Some narrators said it was taken at the beginning of the year 20.

382They said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to Muʿāwiya ordering him to follow up what remained of Palestine. He conquered Ascalon by treaty after some stratagem. It is said ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ had conquered it, then its people broke the treaty and the Byzantines reinforced them; Muʿāwiya conquered it, settled frontier-guards (rawābiṭ) in it and assigned guards.

383Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: I heard Muḥammad b. Yūsuf al-Fāryābī relate, from elders of Ascalon, that the Byzantines ruined Ascalon and drove its people out in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr. When ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān took power he rebuilt and fortified it, and also repaired Caesarea.

384Muḥammad b. Muṣaffā told me: Abū Sulaymān al-Ramlī told me, from his father: The Byzantines came out in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr to Caesarea, damaged it and demolished its mosque. When ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān's authority was secure, he repaired Caesarea, restored its mosque, garrisoned it with men, and built the outer Tyre of Acre; their case was like Caesarea's.

385A number of people of knowledge of Syrian affairs told me: al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik over the jund of Palestine. He settled at Lydda. Then he founded the city of Ramla and made it a city. The first thing he built there was his palace and the house known as the Dyers' House, in which he made a cistern at its middle. Then he laid out a plot for the mosque and built it, but became caliph before finishing it, and built more on it during his caliphate. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz completed it and reduced the plot, saying: "The people of Ramla will make do with the size to which I have limited it." When Sulaymān built for himself, he permitted people to build, and they did. He dug for the people of Ramla their canal called Burda, dug wells, and put in charge of the expenditure on building at Ramla and the congregational mosque a Christian secretary of his from Lydda called al-Biṭrīq b. al-Nakā. The city of Ramla did not exist before Sulaymān; its site was [just] sand (ramla).

386They said: The Dyers' House passed to the heirs of Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās, because it was confiscated with the Umayyads' property.

387They said: The Umayyads, after Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik, kept paying for the wells and canal of Ramla. When the ʿAbbāsids took power, they paid for them. The order for this expenditure used to be issued every year, from caliph to caliph; when the Commander of the Faithful Abū Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim billāh took office, he issued a standing decree for this expenditure, so that annual authorization ceased, and it became a standing charge that the officials account for and have credited to them.

388They said: In Palestine there are separate decrees from the caliphs, apart from the general land-tax, in which there are takhfīf (reductions) and rudūd (restorations). That was because estates were abandoned in al-Rashīd's caliphate and left by their people, and the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd sent Harthama b. Aʿyan to repopulate them. He called some of the farmers and cultivators to return on condition that their land-tax be reduced and their treatment eased, and they returned: those are the aṣḥāb al-takhāfīf ("people of reductions"). Others came later and their lands were restored to them on the same terms as before: they are the aṣḥāb al-rudūd ("people of restorations").

389Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: I met an Arab man at Ascalon who told me his grandfather was among those ʿAbd al-Malik settled there and granted a plot, together with others of the frontier-guards. He showed me some land and said: "This is among the grants of ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān." Bakr said: I heard Muḥammad b. Yūsuf al-Fāryābī say: "Here at Ascalon there are grants made by order of ʿUmar and ʿUthmān; if a man entered them I would see no harm in it."

Chapter 33

The jund of Qinnasrīn and the ʿAwāṣim

The affair of the jund of Qinnasrīn and the cities called the ʿAwāṣim

390They said: After finishing with the land of the Yarmūk, Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ went to Homs and settled in it. Then he came to Qinnasrīn, with Khālid b. al-Walīd in his vanguard. The people of the city of Qinnasrīn fought him, then took refuge in their fort and asked for peace, and Abū ʿUbayda made peace on terms like Homs's. The Muslims prevailed over its land and farmland. The ḥāḍir of Qinnasrīn belonged to Tanūkh, who had settled it from the time they first became Tanūkh in Syria, living in hair tents, then built houses there. Abū ʿUbayda invited them to Islam; some converted, and the Banū Salīḥ b. Ḥulwān b. ʿImrān b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa stayed Christian.

391Some descendants of Yazīd b. Ḥunayn al-Ṭāʾī al-Anṭākī told me, from their elders: A group of the people of that ḥāḍir converted in the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Mahdī, and [a record] was written at their hands [wording garbled in the source: "bi'l-khaḍra Qinnasrīn"].

Then Abū ʿUbayda set out for Aleppo, and heard that the people of Qinnasrīn had broken the treaty and betrayed. He sent al-Simṭ b. al-Aswad al-Kindī against them, who besieged them and then conquered it.

392Hishām b. ʿAmmār al-Dimashqī told me: Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza told us, from Abū ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from ʿUbāda b. Nusayy, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ghanm: We garrisoned the city of Qinnasrīn with al-Simṭ (or he said Shuraḥbīl b. al-Simṭ). When he conquered it he found cattle and sheep in it, divided a portion among us and put the rest in the spoils.

The ḥāḍir of Ṭayyiʾ was settled long ago by them after the Ḥarb al-Fasād that occurred among them, when those of them who went to the two mountains settled there and the rest scattered in the lands. When Abū ʿUbayda came to them, some converted and many made peace on the poll-tax; shortly afterwards they converted, except those who were apart from their group.

Near the city of Aleppo there was a ḥāḍir called Ḥāḍir Ḥalab, which gathered various kinds of Arabs, Tanūkh and others. Abū ʿUbayda made peace with them on the poll-tax; then they converted, and they and their descendants remained there until shortly after the death of the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd. Then the people of that ḥāḍir fought the people of the city of Aleppo and wanted to expel them from it, so the Hāshimites among them wrote to all the Arab tribes around asking for help. The first to come to their help and rescue was al-ʿAbbās b. Zufar b. ʿĀṣim al-Hilālī, through maternal kinship, because the mother of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās was Lubāba bint al-Ḥārith b. Ḥazn b. Bujayr b. al-Hazm al-Hilāliyya. The people of that ḥāḍir had no power against him and those with him, so they were driven from their ḥāḍir and it was ruined. This was in the days of the civil war of Muḥammad b. al-Rashīd. They moved to Qinnasrīn, whose people met them with food and clothing; when they entered it they tried to dominate it, so they were expelled and scattered in the lands: some at Tikrīt, whom I have seen, others in Armenia and in many different places.

393The Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ﵀ told me: I heard an old man of the elders of the Banū Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās tell the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim billāh ﵀ in the year he raided ʿAmmūriya: When al-ʿAbbās b. Zufar al-Hilālī came to Aleppo to rescue the Hāshimites, some of their women called out to him: "Uncle! We are in God's hands, then yours!" He said: "You have nothing to fear, God willing; may God forsake me if I forsake you."

He said: Ḥiyār Banī al-Qaʿqāʿ was a well-known town before Islam, where al-Mundhir b. Māʾ al-Samāʾ al-Lakhmī, king of al-Ḥīra, spent the midday heat. The Banū al-Qaʿqāʿ b. Khulayd b. Juzʾ b. Zuhayr b. Jadhīma b. Rawāḥa b. Rabīʿa b. al-Ḥārith b. Quṭayʿa b. ʿAbs b. Baghīḍ settled it and it was named after them. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān granted al-Qaʿqāʿ a plot there, and granted his uncle al-ʿAbbās b. Juzʾ b. al-Ḥārith plots which he made tax-exempt for him up to Yemen, and which after him became tax-exempt. They were mostly, or in part, waste land. Wallāda bint al-ʿAbbās b. Juzʾ was [a wife] of ʿAbd al-Malik, and bore him al-Walīd and Sulaymān.

394They said: Abū ʿUbayda marched to Aleppo with ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm al-Fihrī in his vanguard. [ʿIyāḍ's] father was called ʿAbd Ghanm; when ʿIyāḍ converted he disliked being called "Servant of Ghanm" and said: "I am ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm." He found its people fortified and camped before it. They soon asked for peace and safety for their persons, property, city wall, churches, houses and the fortress there. They were given it, with the site of the mosque excepted. ʿIyāḍ was the one who made the treaty with them, and Abū ʿUbayda carried it out. Some narrators claimed they made peace on sparing their lives and sharing half of their houses and churches. Others said Abū ʿUbayda found no one in Aleppo, because its people had moved to Antioch, and that they made peace over their city while at Antioch, negotiating with him; when their peace was complete, they returned to Aleppo.

395They said: Abū ʿUbayda marched from Aleppo to Antioch, where many people of the jund of Qinnasrīn had fortified themselves. When he reached Mahrūba, about two leagues from the city of Antioch, a force of the enemy met him. He routed them and drove them into the city, and besieged its people from all its gates. The bulk of the army was at the Gate of Fārs and the gate called the Sea Gate. They made peace with him on the poll-tax and evacuation: some left and some stayed. He secured them and imposed on every adult male a dinar and a jarīb. Then they broke the treaty, and Abū ʿUbayda sent ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm and Ḥabīb b. Maslama, who conquered it on the first terms. Some say they broke it after he returned to Palestine, and ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ sent [troops] from Īliyā who conquered it, then returned and stayed a short while until the people of Īliyā asked for safety and peace. God knows best.

396Muḥammad b. Sahm al-Anṭākī told me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Farrāʾ: Mukhallad b. al-Ḥusayn said: I heard the elders of the frontier say: Antioch was of great renown and importance to ʿUmar and ʿUthmān. When it was conquered, ʿUmar wrote to Abū ʿUbayda: "Station in Antioch a group of Muslims of good character and public-minded (ahl nabāt wa ḥisba), make them frontier-guards there, and do not withhold their stipends." When Muʿāwiya took office, [ʿUmar's successor] wrote to him likewise. Then ʿUthmān wrote to him ordering him to keep a group of people in it and to give land grants, and he did. Ibn Sahm said: I was standing on the bridge of Antioch over the Orontes and heard a very old man of Antioch, when I was a boy, say: "This land is a grant from ʿUthmān to people who were with Abū ʿUbayda, which he gave them in the days of ʿUthmān's governorship of Muʿāwiya over Syria."

397They said: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān moved to Antioch in the year 42 a group of Persians and people of Baalbek, Homs and the two garrison cities [Basra and Kufa]. Among them was Muslim b. ʿAbd Allāh, grandfather of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥabīb b. al-Nuʿmān b. Muslim al-Anṭākī. Muslim was killed at one of the gates of Antioch known today as Bāb Muslim. The Byzantines came out from the coast and besieged Antioch; Muslim was on the wall, and a foreigner threw a stone at him and killed him.

398A group of the elders of Antioch told me, among them Ibn Burd the jurist: al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik granted soldiers at Antioch the land of Salūqiya by the coast, and set the falthar (that is, the jarīb) at a dinar and two mudd of wheat. They developed it, this arrangement continued for them, and he built the fort of Salūqiya.

399They said: The land of Baghrās belonged to Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik, who endowed it for charitable purposes. ʿAyn al-Salūr and its lake were also his. Alexandretta also belonged to him; then it became a grant to Rajāʾ, client of al-Mahdī, and was inherited by Manṣūr and Ibrāhīm, sons of al-Mahdī. Then it passed to Ibrāhīm b. Saʿīd al-Jawharī, then was bought by Aḥmad b. Abī Duʾād al-Iyādī, and then ownership passed to the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ﵀.

400Ibn Burd al-Anṭākī and others told me: Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik granted plots to some people of Rabīʿa; these were confiscated and later went to al-Maʾmūn, and their administration passed to Ṣāliḥ the Treasurer, [keeper of] Ṣāliḥ's House in Antioch.

401They said: It reached Abū ʿUbayda that a Byzantine force was between Maʿarrat Maṣrīn and Aleppo. He met them, killed several patricians, broke up that army, took captives and booty. He conquered Maʿarrat Maṣrīn on terms like Aleppo's. His cavalry ranged as far as Būqā, and conquered the villages of al-Jūma, Sarmīn, Martaḥwān and Tīzīn. The people of Dayr Ṭayāyā [as printed] and Dayr al-Fasīla made peace on condition they host Muslims passing by, and the Christians of Khunāṣira came to him and he made peace with them. Abū ʿUbayda conquered all the land of Qinnasrīn and Antioch.

402al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father: Khunāṣira is named after Khunāṣir b. ʿAmr b. al-Ḥārith al-Kalbī then al-Kinānī, who was its lord. Biṭnān Ḥabīb is named after Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī: Abū ʿUbayda, or ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm, sent him from Aleppo and he conquered a fort there, so it was named after him.

403They said: Abū ʿUbayda set out for Qūrus, sending ʿIyāḍ ahead. A monk of its monks met him asking for peace for its people. [ʿIyāḍ] sent him to Abū ʿUbayda, who was between Jibrīn and Tall Aʿzāz, and he made peace with him, then came to Qūrus and concluded a covenant for its people giving them what he had given the people of Antioch, and wrote the monk a document concerning a village of his called Sharqīnā. He spread his cavalry and prevailed over all the land of Qūrus to the farthest boundary of Nuqābulus.

404They said: Qūrus was like an outpost for Antioch; each year a [rotating] contingent of Antioch's soldiers and fighters came to it, then a quarter of Antioch's quarters was moved to it and the rotations stopped. It is said Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī was in Abū ʿUbayda's army with Abū Umāma al-Ṣudayy b. ʿAjlān, Companion of the Messenger of God, and took up quarters in a fort at Qūrus, which was named after him; it is known as the Fort of Salmān. Then he went back from Syria among those sent as reinforcements to Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ in Iraq. It is also said that Salmān b. Rabīʿa raided the Byzantines after the conquest of Iraq and before going to Armenia, and camped at this fort, having come out from the direction of Marʿash, so it was named for him. Salmān and Ziyād were among the Slavs whom Marwān b. Muḥammad stationed on the frontiers. I also heard someone say that this Salmān was a Slav, to whom the fort was attributed. God knows best.

405They said: Abū ʿUbayda came to Ḥalab al-Sājūr and sent ʿIyāḍ ahead to Manbij, then joined him after [ʿIyāḍ] had made peace with its people on terms like Antioch's; Abū ʿUbayda carried that out. ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm was sent to the area of Dulūk and Raʿbān, and their people made peace with him on terms like Manbij's, stipulating that they investigate news of the Byzantines and write it to the Muslims. Abū ʿUbayda appointed a governor over each district he conquered, attached a group of Muslims to him, and garrisoned the dangerous areas.

406They said: Then Abū ʿUbayda went on and camped at ʿArājīn. He sent his vanguard to Bālis, and sent an army under Ḥabīb b. Maslama to Qāṣirīn. Bālis and Qāṣirīn belonged to two brothers of the Byzantine nobles who had been granted the villages near them, and made guardians of the Byzantine cities between them in Syria. When the Muslims camped there, he made peace with them on the poll-tax and evacuation; most of them left for Byzantine lands, the land of the Jazīra, and the village of Jisr Manbij, which did not then exist but was made in ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān's caliphate for the summer raids (some say it had an old foundation).

407They said: Abū ʿUbayda stationed at Bālis a group of fighters and settled in it some of the Arabs who had been in Syria and had converted after the Muslims came to Syria, and some who were not from the [regular] expeditions, drawn from the desert tribes of Qays; he settled some people at Qāṣirīn, whom they or their descendants later left. Abū ʿUbayda reached the Euphrates and then returned to Palestine. Bālis and the villages attributed to it, in its upper, middle and lower reaches, were [lands] watered by natural flow subject to the tithe. When Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān set out to raid the Byzantines from the Jazīran frontiers, he camped at Bālis. Its people, and the people of Buwaylis [as printed] and Qāṣirīn, ʿĀbidīn and Ṣiffīn, villages attributed to it, came to him. The people of the upper reach asked him to dig them a canal from the Euphrates to water their land, on condition they give him a third of their yields after the sultan's tithe he used to take; he did so. He dug the canal known as Nahr Maslama, they fulfilled the condition, and he repaired the city wall and strengthened it. It is also said the initiative came from Maslama, who invited them to this arrangement. When Maslama died, Bālis and its villages went to his heirs and stayed in their hands until the blessed dynasty came and ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAlī seized the Umayyads' property, which included them. The Commander of the Faithful Abū al-ʿAbbās granted them to Sulaymān b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās, and they passed to his son Muḥammad b. Sulaymān. His brother Jaʿfar b. Sulaymān used to inform on him to the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd ﵀, writing to him that [Muḥammad] had no money or estate except what had exceeded many times its value, and that he spent it on what he promoted for himself and on the servants he had acquired, and that his property was lawfully the Commander of the Faithful's. Al-Rashīd ordered his letters to be preserved. When Muḥammad b. Sulaymān died, his letters were brought out to Jaʿfar and used against him. Muḥammad had no full brother other than him, so he acknowledged them, and Muḥammad's property went to al-Rashīd. Al-Maʾmūn ﵀ then granted Bālis and its villages, and they passed to his descendants after him.

408Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me: Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza told us, from Tamīm b. ʿAṭiyya, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays al-Hamdānī: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb came to al-Jābiya. He wanted to divide the land among the Muslims because it had been taken by force. Muʿādh b. Jabal said to him: "By God, if you divide it, what we dislike will result: a great deal will come into the hands of a few, then they will die out and it will remain with one person, and then people will come after them who will fill the gap of Islam and find nothing. So consider something that will suffice both the first and the last of them." He came round to Muʿādh's view.

409al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī b. al-Aswad al-ʿIjlī told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from elders of the Jazīrans, from Sulaymān b. ʿAṭāʾ, from Salama al-Juhanī, from his uncle: The lord of Buṣrā mentioned that he had made peace with the Muslims on food, oil and vinegar. He asked ʿUmar to write that for him, and Abū ʿUbayda contradicted him, saying: "We only made peace with him on something the Muslims could benefit from for their winter." So [ʿUmar] imposed on them the poll-tax by classes and the land-tax on land.

410al-Ḥusayn told me: Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Aḥdab told us: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar told us, from Nāfiʿ, from Aslam, client of ʿUmar: ʿUmar wrote to the commanders over the poll-tax not to impose it except on those on whom the razor had passed. He set it at four dinars for the gold people, and for the Muslims' provisions imposed two mudd of wheat per man and three qist of oil in Syria and the Jazīra, together with three days' hospitality for those who stayed with them.

411Abū Ḥafṣ al-Shāmī told me, from Muḥammad b. Rāshid, from Makḥūl: Every tithe-land in Syria is land whose people left and which the Muslims were granted and revived; it was uncultivated land in which no one had any right, and they revived it with the governors' permission.

Chapter 34

Cyprus

The affair of Cyprus

412Al-Wāqidī and others said: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān made the first Cyprus expedition by sea; the Muslims had not sailed the Byzantine sea before. Muʿāwiya had asked ʿUmar's permission to raid by sea and he did not allow it. When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān took office, [Muʿāwiya] wrote asking permission for a Cyprus expedition, informing him of its nearness and the ease of the matter. [ʿUthmān] wrote back: "You witnessed what ʿUmar ﵀ replied when you consulted him about raiding by sea." When the year 27 began, [Muʿāwiya] wrote to him making light of sailing to Cyprus. ʿUthmān wrote: "If you sail with your wife, then sail, permitted; otherwise not." So he sailed from Acre with many ships, taking his wife Fākhita bint Qaraẓa b. ʿAbd ʿAmr b. Nawfal b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Quṣayy, and ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit took his wife Umm Ḥarām bint Milḥān al-Anṣāriyya. This was in the year 28 after winter receded, some say the year 29.

When the Muslims reached Cyprus and landed on its coast (it is an island in the sea said to be eighty leagues by as many), its archon sent to them asking for peace, its people having submitted to it. [Muʿāwiya] made peace with them for 7,200 dinars to be paid each year; the Byzantines made peace with them on the same, so they pay two tributes. They stipulated that the Muslims would not stop them paying the settlement to the Byzantines. The Muslims stipulated that they would not fight on behalf of anyone who attacked them from behind and would notify the Muslims of the movement of their Byzantine enemy. So when the Muslims sailed they did not molest them, and the people of Cyprus neither helped them nor were helped against them. In the year 32 they aided the Byzantines against the raiders at sea with ships they gave them, so Muʿāwiya raided them in the year 33 with 500 ships and conquered Cyprus by force, killed and took captives, then confirmed them in their peace. He sent to it 12,000 men, all on the registry, who built mosques there. He moved to it a group from Baalbek and built a city there. They kept receiving stipends until Muʿāwiya died and his son Yazīd succeeded, who recalled that force and ordered the city demolished. Some narrators claim that Muʿāwiya's second Cyprus raid was in the year 35.

413Muḥammad b. Muṣaffā al-Ḥimṣī told me, from al-Walīd: It has reached us that Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya bribed [the Byzantines] with a great sum so that the Cyprus garrison was recalled, and when they left, the people of Cyprus demolished their city and mosques.

414Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd al-Salām b. Mūsā, from his father: When Cyprus was raided the first time, Umm Ḥarām bint Milḥān sailed with her husband ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit. When they reached Cyprus she left the ship and a mount was brought for her to ride; it stumbled with her and killed her. Her grave is at Cyprus, called the Grave of the Righteous Woman.

415They said: With Muʿāwiya raided Abū Ayyūb Khālid b. Zayd b. Kulayb al-Anṣārī, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit, Faḍāla b. ʿUbayd al-Anṣārī, ʿUmayr b. Saʿd b. ʿUbayd al-Anṣārī, Wāthila b. al-Asqaʿ al-Kinānī, ʿAbd Allāh b. Busr al-Māzinī, Shaddād b. Aws b. Thābit (nephew of Ḥassān b. Thābit), al-Miqdād, Kaʿb al-Aḥbār b. Māniʿ, and Jubayr b. Nufayr al-Ḥaḍramī.

416Hishām b. ʿAmmār al-Dimashqī told me: al-Walīd b. Muslim told us, from Ṣafwān b. ʿAmr: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān raided Cyprus in person with his wife. God gave a great victory and the Muslims took fine booty. The Muslims kept raiding them until Muʿāwiya in his time made a lasting peace with them for 7,000 dinars, with loyalty to the Muslims and warning them of their Byzantine enemy. This, or something like it.

417They said: al-Walīd b. Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik exiled many of them to Syria over a matter of which he suspected them. People objected to this, and Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik [sic, probably Yazīd b. al-Walīd] returned them to their country. Ḥumayd b. Maʿyūf al-Hamdānī raided them in al-Rashīd's caliphate for an offence they committed and captured many of them; then they behaved properly toward the Muslims, and al-Rashīd ordered those captured returned, and they were.

418Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, with his isnād: The people of Cyprus remained under Muʿāwiya's peace until ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān took office and added a thousand dinars. That continued until the caliphate of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who removed it. Then when Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik took office he restored it. That continued until the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, who said: "We are the most entitled to deal fairly with them and not to multiply by wronging them." He returned them to Muʿāwiya's settlement.

419Some people of knowledge among the Syrians and Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: The people of Cyprus committed an offence during the governorship of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās over the frontiers, and he wanted to break their treaty, with the jurists in abundance. He wrote to al-Layth b. Saʿd, Mālik b. Anas, Sufyān b. ʿUyayna, Mūsā b. Aʿyun, Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh, Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza, Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī and Mukhallad b. al-Ḥusayn about them, and they answered him.

Among what al-Layth b. Saʿd wrote: "The people of Cyprus are a people we have always suspected of deceiving the people of Islam and counselling God's enemies the Byzantines. God Almighty has said: 'And if you fear treachery from a people, throw [the treaty] back to them on equal terms' (8:58) — and He did not say, 'do not throw it back until you are certain of their treachery.' I think you should throw it back to them and give them a year to consider. Whoever wishes to join the Muslim lands as a dhimmī paying the land-tax, accept it; whoever wishes to withdraw to Byzantine lands, let him; whoever wishes to remain in Cyprus at war, let him remain, and they will be an enemy who is fought and raided. For in granting a year there is a cutting-off of their argument and a fulfilment of the promise to them."

Among what Mālik b. Anas wrote: "The safety of the people of Cyprus has long been openly acknowledged by the governors. That is because they saw that confirming them in their condition was a humiliation and belittlement for them and a strength for the Muslims over them, through what they take of their poll-tax and the opportunity they gain against their enemy. I have not found any governor who broke their peace or expelled them from their land. I think you should not hasten to break their covenant and throw it back at them until the proof is established against them, for God says: 'So fulfil their covenant until their term' (9:4). If after that they do not behave properly and give up their deceit, and you see that treachery is established on their part, strike them; then it will be after warning, and you will be granted victory, and they will have humiliation and disgrace, God Almighty willing."

Sufyān b. ʿUyayna wrote: "We do not know of the Prophet making a covenant with a people who then broke it without his permitting their killing, except the people of Mecca, to whom he showed favour; their breach was that they helped their allies against the Messenger of God's allies of Khuzāʿa. And among the conditions imposed on the people of Najrān was that they not consume usury, and when they did, ʿUmar ﵀ ruled that they be expelled. So the agreement of the people is that whoever breaks a covenant has no protection."

Mūsā b. Aʿyun wrote: "Such a thing has happened before, and governors dealt with it by granting a respite. I have not seen anyone of the past break [the covenant with] the people of Cyprus or others, and perhaps their common people and community did not conspire in what their elite did. I think we should keep faith with them and complete their stipulation, even if they did what they did. I heard al-Awzāʿī say, of a people who made peace with the Muslims and then informed the polytheists of their weak points and guided them to them: if they were dhimmīs they have broken their covenant and left their protection, and if the governor wishes he may kill and crucify; if they were under a peace treaty and not in the Muslims' protection, the governor throws it back to them on equal terms, 'God does not guide the plot of the treacherous' (12:52, quoted)."

Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh wrote: "The people of Cyprus are humbled and subdued; the Byzantines overpower them over their persons and women, so it is right for us to protect and defend them. Ḥabīb b. Maslama wrote for the people of Tiflis in their covenant that if the Muslims were occupied from you and your enemy overpowered you, that would not void your covenant provided you keep faith with the Muslims. I think they should be confirmed in their covenant and protection. Al-Walīd b. Yazīd had exiled them to Syria; the Muslims found this monstrous and the jurists thought it grave, and when Yazīd b. al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik took office he returned them to Cyprus, and the Muslims approved his act and considered it just."

Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza wrote: "The case of Cyprus is like the case of ʿArabsūs; in it there is a fine example and a followed precedent. Its story is that ʿUmayr b. Saʿd said to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb when he came to him: 'Between us and the Byzantines is a city called ʿArabsūs. They tell our enemy about our weak points and do not show us our enemy's.' ʿUmar said: 'When you return, give them the choice: for every sheep we will give them two sheep, for every cow two cows, for everything two of it. If they accept, give them that, let them leave, and ruin the town. If they refuse, throw the treaty back to them and give them a year to leave, then ruin it.' ʿUmayr went and they refused, so he gave them a year and then ruined it. They had a covenant like that of the people of Cyprus. Leaving the people of Cyprus to their settlement and using what warns about the Muslims' affairs is better. Any covenanted people for whom the Muslims do not fight those behind them, and on whom their own laws run in their own land, are not dhimmīs but people of ransom: they are left alone as long as they leave [us] alone, their covenant is kept as long as they keep it and are content, and their pardon is accepted as long as they pay. It is related of Muʿādh b. Jabal that he disliked making peace with any enemy for a fixed amount unless the Muslims were compelled to make peace with them, since one does not know whether making peace might be of benefit and strength for the Muslims."

Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī and Mukhallad b. al-Ḥusayn wrote: "We have seen nothing more like the case of Cyprus than the case of ʿArabsūs and what ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ruled in it, for he offered them double their property if they would leave it, or a year's respite after throwing their covenant back at them; they refused the first, so they waited; then it was ruined. Al-Awzāʿī used to relate that Cyprus was conquered and its people left as they were and made peace for 14,000 dinars, 7,000 for the Muslims and 7,000 for the Byzantines, on condition that they not conceal the Muslims' affairs from the Byzantines. He used to say: 'The people of Cyprus never kept faith with us, but we regard them as covenant-people, whose peace was concluded on terms with a condition for them and a condition on them, and it cannot rightly be broken except for something in which their treachery and breach is known.'"

Chapter 35

The Samaritans

The affair of the Samaritans

420Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me, from al-Walīd b. Muslim, from Ṣafwān b. ʿAmr: Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ made peace with the Samaritans in Jordan and Palestine, who had been spies and guides for the Muslims, on the poll-tax on their heads and a food-share from their land. When Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya came, he imposed the land-tax on their land.

421A group of people versed in the affairs of the two junds of Jordan and Palestine told me: Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya imposed the land-tax on the lands of the Samaritans in Jordan and set two dinars on each person's head, and also imposed the land-tax on their lands in Palestine and set five dinars on each person's head. The Samaritans are Jews, in two kinds: one called the Dūsitān, the other the Kūshān.

422They said: In Palestine, at the start of the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd ﵀, there was a sweeping plague that sometimes struck whole households. Their lands became ruined and idle. The authority appointed someone to cultivate them and gathered farmers and cultivators to them, so they became caliphal estates, with Samaritans on them. In the year 246, the people of a village of those estates called Bayt Māmā, in the district of Nablus, Samaritans, petitioned complaining of their weakness and inability to pay the land-tax at five dinars. The Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ordered them reduced to three dinars each.

423Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me: al-Walīd b. Muslim told us, from Ṣafwān b. ʿAmr and Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: The Byzantines made peace with Muʿāwiya on condition that he pay them money, and Muʿāwiya took hostages from them and placed them at Baalbek. Then the Byzantines betrayed, but Muʿāwiya and the Muslims did not consider it lawful to kill the hostages in their hands, and released them, saying: "Faithfulness in the face of betrayal is better than betrayal for betrayal." Hishām said: That is the view of the scholars, al-Awzāʿī and others.

Chapter 36

The Jarājima

The affair of the Jarājima

424Elders of Antioch told me: The Jarājima come from a city on Mount al-Lukkām near the vitriol mine, between Bayyās and Būqā, called al-Jurjūma. Their affair, in the days of Byzantine domination over Syria and Antioch, depended on the patrician of Antioch and its governor. When Abū ʿUbayda came to Antioch and conquered it, they kept to their city and meant to join the Byzantines if they feared for themselves; the Muslims did not notice them and nobody alerted them. Then the people of Antioch broke the treaty and betrayed, and Abū ʿUbayda sent someone who conquered it a second time, and after the conquest appointed Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī over it. He raided al-Jurjūma; its people did not fight him but hurried to ask for safety and peace. They made peace with him on condition that they be helpers, spies and outpost-guards for the Muslims on Mount al-Lukkām, that the poll-tax not be taken from them, and that they receive as extra shares the spoils [stripped] from those they killed of the Muslims' enemy when they joined them in war on their campaigns. Those in their city, merchants, hired men and dependants, Nabateans and others, and the villagers entered this peace, and were called the Rawādīf because they came after them and were not of them; it is also said they brought them to the Muslim camp as riders behind them (ardāf), so they were called rawādīf.

The Jarājima were loyal to governors at times and crooked at others, writing to the Byzantines and siding with them. In the days of Ibn al-Zubayr, after the death of Marwān b. al-Ḥakam, when ʿAbd al-Malik sought the caliphate after him by virtue of [Marwān's] appointing him heir, and was preparing to set out to Iraq to fight Muṣʿab b. al-Zubayr, Byzantine cavalry came out to Mount al-Lukkām under one of their commanders, then went to Lebanon, with a large number of Jarājima, Nabateans and fugitive slaves of Muslims having joined them. ʿAbd al-Malik was compelled to make peace with them for a thousand dinars every Friday, and made peace with the Byzantine emperor for money he would pay him, being occupied from fighting him and fearing he might come out to Syria and overpower him. In his peace he followed Muʿāwiya, who when occupied with the Iraqis made peace with them on paying them money and took hostages whom he placed at Baalbek. This also coincided with ʿAmr b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ seeking the caliphate and shutting the gates of Damascus when ʿAbd al-Malik left it, which increased his burden; this was in the year 70.

Then ʿAbd al-Malik sent Suḥaym b. al-Muhājir to the Byzantine [commander], who cleverly entered his presence in disguise, feigned support for him, and drew close to them by disparaging, cursing and belittling ʿAbd al-Malik, until [the commander] trusted him and was taken in. Then he turned on him with some of ʿAbd al-Malik's clients and soldiers he had prepared for an attack and stationed at a place he knew, and killed him and those of the Byzantines with him, and proclaimed safety to all who had joined him. The Jarājima scattered among the villages of Homs and Damascus; most returned to their city on al-Lukkām, the Nabateans went to their villages, and the slaves returned to their masters.

Maymūn al-Jurjumānī was a Byzantine slave of the sons of Umm al-Ḥakam, sister of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, who were Thaqafīs; he was attributed to the Jarājima because he mixed with them and went out with them on Mount Lebanon. ʿAbd al-Malik heard of his courage and bravery and asked his masters to free him, and they did. He put him in command of a group of soldiers and stationed him at Antioch, and he raided with Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik at Ṭuwāna, commanding a thousand men of Antioch. He was martyred after good service and a famous stand. ʿAbd al-Malik was grieved by his death and sent a great army against the Byzantines to avenge him.

425They said: In the year 89 the Jarājima gathered in their city and some Byzantines came to them from the side of Alexandretta and Rūsus. Al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik sent Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik against them; he camped against them with a great force and took the city on condition that they settle wherever they liked in Syria, that each of them receive eight dinars and their families rations of wheat and oil (two mudd of wheat and two qisṭ of oil), that neither they nor their children and women be compelled to abandon Christianity, that they wear Muslim dress, that no poll-tax be taken from them or their children and women, that they raid with the Muslims and receive as extra the spoils of those they kill in single combat, and that from their trade and the property of their wealthy be taken what is taken from Muslims' property.
