He ruined their city and settled them in Jabal al-Ḥawār, Sanḥ al-Lūlūn [as printed] and the ʿUmq of Tīzīn. Some went to Homs, and the patrician of al-Jurjūma with a group went to Antioch, then fled to Byzantine lands. Some officials later imposed the poll-tax on the Jarājima at Antioch; they petitioned al-Wāthiq billāh ﵀ while he was caliph, and he ordered it removed from them.

426One of the secretaries I trust told me: al-Mutawakkil ﵀ ordered the poll-tax taken from these Jarājima and rations paid to them, since they were among those used for outposts and other duties. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb al-Azdī claimed that the people of al-Jurjūma used to raid in ʿAbd al-Malik's days the villages of Antioch and al-ʿUmq, and when the summer expeditions went out they cut off stragglers, latecomers and whoever they could reach at the rear of the army, and did excessive harm to the Muslims. So ʿAbd al-Malik ordered stipends assigned to people of Antioch and its Nabateans, who were made outposts and placed behind the summer armies' rear to deter the Jarājima, and were called the Rawādīf. Each of them was paid eight dinars. The first account is better established.

427Abū Ḥafṣ al-Shāmī told me, from Muḥammad b. Rāshid, from Makḥūl: In the year 49 or 50, Muʿāwiya moved to the coasts some of the Zuṭṭ of Basra and the Sayābija, and settled some in Antioch. Abū Ḥafṣ said: In Antioch there is a quarter called al-Zuṭṭ, and at Būqā in the Antioch district there are some of their descendants called the Zuṭṭ. Al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik also moved to Antioch some Sindī Zuṭṭ whom Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim had sent to al-Ḥajjāj, and al-Ḥajjāj sent them to Syria.

428Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī: Some people on Mount Lebanon rebelled complaining of the land-tax official of Baalbek. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās sent forces who killed their fighters, left the rest in their religion and returned them to their villages, and expelled some people of Lebanon.

429al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me that Muḥammad b. Kathīr told him that al-Awzāʿī wrote Ṣāliḥ a long letter, of which he memorized: "Concerning the expulsion of the dhimmīs from Mount Lebanon, those who had not conspired with the rebels in their rebellion, some of whom you killed and the rest of whom you returned to their villages, you know what happened: how can the many be taken for the sins of the few, until they are driven from their homes and property, when God Almighty's ruling is that 'no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another'? That is the most worthy thing to stand by and follow, and the most deserving of all instructions to be kept and heeded is the Messenger of God's instruction, for he said: 'Whoever wrongs a covenant-protected person and burdens him beyond his capacity, I am his adversary.'" Then he mentioned further words.

430Muḥammad b. Sahm al-Anṭākī told me: Muʿāwiya b. ʿAmr told me, from Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī: The Umayyads used to raid the Byzantines with the people of Syria and the Jazīra, summer and winter, from the Syrian and Jazīran frontiers, maintaining ships for raiding and posting guards on the coasts, with neglect and negligence mixed with prudence and vigilance. When Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr took office he inspected the fortresses and cities of the coasts, repaired and fortified them, and built what needed building, and did the same for the frontier cities. When al-Mahdī took office he completed what remained of the cities and fortresses and increased their garrisons. Muʿāwiya b. ʿAmr said: We have seen from the Commander of the Faithful Hārūn's effort in raiding and his penetrating insight into jihad something great. He set up shipyard facilities no one had before, distributed funds on the frontiers and coasts, and distressed and subdued the Byzantines. Al-Mutawakkil ordered the ships stationed on all the coasts and manned with fighters, in the year 247.

Chapter 37

The Syrian frontiers

431Elders of Antioch and others told me: The Muslims' Syrian frontiers in the days of ʿUmar and ʿUthmān ﵃ and after were Antioch and the other cities Hārūn al-Rashīd called the ʿAwāṣim. The Muslims raided beyond them, as they raid today beyond Tarsus. Between Alexandretta and Tarsus were Byzantine forts and outposts like the forts and outposts the Muslims pass today. Sometimes their people left them and fled to Byzantine lands in fear, and sometimes fighters were moved to them to garrison them. It is also said Heraclius took the people of these cities with him when he moved from Antioch, so the Muslims would not be able to settle the area between Antioch and Byzantine lands. God knows best.

432Ibn Ṭasūn (?) al-Baghrāsī told me, from their elders, that they said: What is commonly known among us is that Heraclius took the people of these forts with him and damaged them, so when the Muslims raided they found no one in them, and sometimes Byzantines hid by them and attacked stragglers from the army and those cut off from it; so the governors of the winter and summer expeditions, when entering Byzantine lands, left a large force there until they came out. They differed over who first crossed the pass, the Darb Baghrās. Some said Maysara b. Masrūq al-ʿAbsī crossed it, sent by Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ, and met a Byzantine force with some Arabized Ghassān, Tanūkh and Iyād wanting to join Heraclius, and fell on them and killed many. Then Mālik al-Ashtar al-Nakhaʿī joined him as reinforcement from Abū ʿUbayda, who was at Antioch. Others said the first to cross the pass was ʿUmayr b. Saʿd al-Anṣārī when he went about the matter of Jabala b. al-Ayham.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb al-Azdī said: It has reached me that Abū ʿUbayda himself raided in a summer expedition, passed al-Maṣṣīṣa and Tarsus, whose people and the people of the forts adjoining them had left, entered the pass, and reached Zandaʾ [as printed] on his raid. Others said only Maysara b. Masrūq was sent, and he reached Zandaʾ.

433Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Farrāʾ told me, from a man of Damascus called ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Walīd, from Hishām b. al-Ghāzī, from ʿUbāda b. Nusayy, as Abū Ṣāliḥ thinks: When Muʿāwiya made the ʿAmmūriya expedition in the year 25, he found the forts between Antioch and Tarsus empty, and a group from Syria, the Jazīra and Qinnasrīn stood guard at them until he returned from his raid. A year or two later he sent Yazīd b. al-Ḥurr al-ʿAbsī on the summer raid and ordered him to do likewise, and governors continued to do it. This man said: I found in the book of Muʿāwiya's expeditions that he raided in the year 31 from the direction of al-Maṣṣīṣa and reached Darūliya; when he came back, he did not pass any fort between there and Antioch without demolishing it.

434Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī and others: In the year 84, ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān led the summer raid; he entered by the Antioch pass and came to al-Maṣṣīṣa. He rebuilt its fort on its old foundation and placed soldiers in it, including 300 men he had selected from the known brave and doughty; the Muslims had not lived there before. He built a mosque on the hill of the fort. Then he marched in his army and raided and conquered the Fort of Sinān, and sent Yazīd b. Ḥunayn al-Ṭāʾī al-Anṭākī, who raided and returned to him.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb al-Azdī said: The first to build the fort of al-Maṣṣīṣa in Islam was ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān, through his son ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Malik, in the year 84, on its old foundation. Its construction and garrisoning was completed in the year 85. In the fort there was a church that was made a granary. Each year the [rotating] contingents from Antioch went up to it, wintered there and then left; the number who went up was 1,500 to 2,000. He said: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz went until he camped at the granary of al-Maṣṣīṣa and wanted to demolish it and the forts between it and Antioch, saying: "I dislike that the Byzantines besiege its people." People informed him that it was built only to repel the Byzantines in it from Antioch, and that if he ruined it there would be nothing to stop the enemy short of Antioch. He desisted and built for its people a congregational mosque on the side of Kafarbayyā, with a cistern in it and his name written on it. The mosque later fell into ruin in al-Muʿtaṣim billāh's caliphate and is called the Fort Mosque.

He said: Then Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik built the suburb (rabaḍ), then Marwān b. Muḥammad built al-Khuṣūṣ east of the Jayḥān, built a wall around it, set a wooden gate in it and dug a moat. When Abū al-ʿAbbās took office he assigned stipends in al-Maṣṣīṣa for 400 men as an addition to its garrison and gave them grants. Then when al-Manṣūr took office he assigned stipends in al-Maṣṣīṣa for 400 men. Then when the year 139 began, he ordered the city of al-Maṣṣīṣa built up; its wall was damaged by earthquakes and its people few inside the city. He built the city wall and settled its people in the year 140, calling it al-Maʿmūra ("the Populated"), and built in it a congregational mosque on the site of a temple there, making it like the Mosque of ʿUmar [in size] several times. Al-Maʾmūn added to it in the days of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṭāhir b. al-Ḥusayn's governorship of the West. Al-Manṣūr assigned stipends there for a thousand men, then moved the people of al-Khuṣūṣ, who are Persians, Slavs and Christian Nabateans. Marwān had settled them there and given them plots in the city in exchange for their houses, by measure, demolished their houses and helped them build, and gave the stipend-holders grants and dwellings. When al-Mahdī took office he assigned stipends in al-Maṣṣīṣa for two thousand men and did not give them grants because it had already been garrisoned with soldiers and volunteers; the rotating contingents kept coming from Antioch each year until Sālim al-Burullusī took charge, and in his place 500 fighters were assigned stipends, ten dinars each. Those there increased and grew strong. This was in al-Mahdī's caliphate.

435Muḥammad b. Sahm told me, from elders of the frontier: The Byzantines pressed on the people of al-Maṣṣīṣa at the start of the blessed dynasty until they left. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī sent Jibrīl b. Yaḥyā al-Bajalī to it, who repaired it and settled people in it in the year 140. Al-Rashīd built Kafarbayyā, though some say it was begun in al-Mahdī's caliphate and then al-Rashīd changed its construction and fortified it with a moat. Then a petition was submitted to al-Maʾmūn about a charge on its houses and he cancelled it. Its houses were like caravanserais. He ordered a wall made for it and it was raised, but it was not completed before he died, so al-Muʿtaṣim billāh ordered it completed and crowned with battlements.

436They said: The one who fortified al-Muthaqqab was Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik, through Ḥassān b. Māhawayh al-Anṭākī. When its moat was dug, a leg-bone of excessive length was found, and he sent it to Hishām. Hishām built the fort of Qaṭarghāṣ through ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ḥayyān al-Anṭākī, and built the fort of Mūra through a man of Antioch. The reason for building it was that the Byzantines had intercepted a messenger of his in the Darb al-Lukkām at al-ʿAqaba al-Bayḍāʾ; he stationed forty men in it and a group of Jarājima, and placed at Baghrās an outpost of fifty men and built a fort for it. Hishām built the fort of Būqā in the Antioch district, later renewed and repaired recently. Muḥammad b. Yūsuf al-Marwazī, known as Abū Saʿīd, built a fort on the coast of Antioch after the Byzantine raid on its coast in al-Muʿtaṣim billāh's caliphate ﵀.

437Dāwūd b. ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, judge of al-Raqqa, told me, from his father, from his grandfather: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁ wanted to demolish al-Maṣṣīṣa and move its people away because of what they suffered from the Byzantines, but he died before that.

438Some people of Antioch and Baghrās told me: When Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik raided ʿAmmūriya he took his women with him, and some of those with him took theirs. The Umayyads did that to ensure earnestness in fighting, out of protective jealousy for the women's honour. When he reached the Baghrās ascent, at the narrow road overlooking the valley, a litter with a woman in it fell to the bottom. Maslama ordered the rest of the women to walk, and they walked, so that ascent was named ʿAqabat al-Nisāʾ ("the Women's Ascent"). Al-Muʿtaṣim billāh ﵀ built a low stone wall along the edge of that road.

Abū al-Nuʿmān al-Anṭākī said: The road between Antioch and al-Maṣṣīṣa was infested with lions that would attack people on it. When al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik reigned, this was reported to him, and he sent 4,000 water buffalo, male and female, and God benefited by them. Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim al-Thaqafī, al-Ḥajjāj's governor over Sind, had sent thousands of buffalo, and al-Ḥajjāj sent al-Walīd the 4,000 and released the rest into the marshes of Kaskar. When Yazīd b. al-Muhallab rebelled and was killed, and Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik seized the property of the Banū al-Muhallab, he got from them 4,000 buffalo in the districts of the Tigris and Kaskar, which Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik also sent to al-Maṣṣīṣa with their Zuṭṭ [keepers], so the original buffalo at al-Maṣṣīṣa numbered 8,000. The people of Antioch and Qinnasrīn had taken many of them and chosen them for themselves in the days of the civil war of Marwān b. Muḥammad b. Marwān; when al-Manṣūr took office he ordered them returned to al-Maṣṣīṣa. As for the buffalo of Antioch, their origin was what the Zuṭṭ brought with them, and likewise the buffalo of Būqā.

Abū al-Khaṭṭāb said: The bridge on the Adhana road from al-Maṣṣīṣa, nine miles from al-Maṣṣīṣa, was built in the year 125. It is called Jisr al-Walīd, after al-Walīd b. Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik, the one who was killed. Abū al-Nuʿmān al-Anṭākī and others said: Adhana was built in the year 141 or 142, with soldiers from the people of Khurasan camped over it with Maslama b. Yaḥyā al-Bajalī, and from the people of Syria with Mālik b. Adham al-Bāhilī, both sent by Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī.

439They said: In the year 165, al-Mahdī sent his son Hārūn al-Rashīd to raid the Byzantine lands. He camped at the Gulf, then went out and repaired al-Maṣṣīṣa and its mosque, increased its garrison, strengthened its people, and built the palace at the bridge of Adhana on the Sayḥān. Al-Manṣūr had sent Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī to raid Byzantine lands, and he sent Hilāl b. Ḍayghum with a group of people of Damascus, Jordan and elsewhere, who built that palace; its construction was not solid, so al-Rashīd tore it down and rebuilt it. Then in the year 194, Abū Salīm Faraj the eunuch built Adhana, made its construction solid and fortified it, and called to it men from Khurasan and others with an increase in pay, by order of Muḥammad b. al-Rashīd. He repaired the palace of the Sayḥān. Al-Rashīd had died in the year 193 while Abū Salīm was his official over the frontier tithes, and Muḥammad kept him on. This Abū Salīm is the owner of the house in Antioch.

440Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī: al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba al-Ṭāʾī raided Byzantine lands in the year 162 with the people of Khurasan, Mosul and Syria, reinforcements from Yemen, and volunteers from Iraq and the Hijaz. He went out from the direction of Tarsus and informed al-Mahdī of the great benefit to Islam, the subjugation of the enemy and the thwarting of what he tried and plotted, that lay in building, fortifying and garrisoning it with fighters. Al-Ḥasan had performed well on that raid and overran the Byzantine land until they called him al-Shaytan. With him on his raid were Mindal al-ʿAnazī, the Kufan ḥadīth scholar, and Muʿtamir b. Sulaymān of Basra.

441Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Ḥasan's son told me: When al-Ḥasan left the Byzantine lands, he camped at Marj Ṭarsūs, rode to its city, which was in ruins, looked at it and went around all its sides, and estimated the number who could live there and found them to be 100,000. When he came to al-Mahdī he described its situation to him, and what its building and garrisoning would mean in terms of rage and subjugation of the enemy and the might of Islam and its people, and also told him a report about al-Ḥadath that made him want to build its city. [Al-Mahdī] ordered him to build Tarsus, beginning with the city of al-Ḥadath, and it was built. Al-Mahdī left instructions to build Tarsus. When the year 171 came, it reached al-Rashīd that the Byzantines had conspired among themselves to go out to Tarsus to fortify it and station fighters in it. So in the year 171 he sent Harthama b. Aʿyan on the summer raid and ordered him to repair, build and settle Tarsus, and he did. Its affair was managed by Faraj b. Salīm the eunuch by al-Rashīd's order; Faraj was put in charge of building it, and Abū Salīm went to Madīnat al-Salām [Baghdad] and sent out the first contingent from the people of Khurasan, 3,000 men, who arrived at Tarsus. Then he sent out the second contingent. They were two thousand men: one thousand from the people of al-Maṣṣīṣa and one thousand from the people of Antioch, with an increase of ten dinars for each man in his original stipend .

They encamped with the first levy (nadba) at al-Madāʾin, at the Gate of Jihad, at the beginning of Muḥarram in the year 172, until the building of Tarsus, its fortification, and the building of its mosque were completed.

Faraj surveyed the area from river to river, and it came to four thousand plots, each plot twenty cubits by twenty. The plots were assigned to the people of Tarsus, and the two levies settled them in the month of Rabīʿ II of 172.

442They said: ʿAbd al-Malik b. Ṣāliḥ had appointed Yazīd b. Mukhallad al-Fazārī over Tarsus, and he expelled the Khurasanis there, who had come to dislike him on account of the Hubayriyya. So he [ʿAbd al-Malik] appointed Abū l-Fawāris as deputy, and ʿAbd al-Malik b. Ṣāliḥ confirmed him. That was in 173.

443Muḥammad b. Saʿd said: al-Wāqidī told me: The people of Sīsiya evacuated and joined the upper Byzantine lands in 194 or 193. Sīsiya is the city of Tall ʿAyn Zarba. It was rebuilt in the caliphate of al-Mutawakkil at the hands of ʿAlī b. Yaḥyā the Armenian, then the Byzantines ruined it.

444They said: The one who burned "Burnt Antioch" in the land of the Byzantines was al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

445They said: Tall Jubayr is named after a man of the Persians of Antioch who had an engagement there. It is less than ten miles from Tarsus.

446They said: The fortress known as Dhū l-Kalāʿ is really al-Ḥiṣn Dhū l-Qilāʿ ("the Fortress of the Citadels"), because it stands on three citadels, and its name was corrupted. The meaning of its name in Greek is "the fortress that is with the stars."

447They also said: The Church of the Truce (Kanīsat al-Ṣulḥ) was so named because when the Byzantines carried their peace [offer] to al-Rashīd, they stayed there. Marj Ḥusayn is attributed to Ḥusayn b. Muslim al-Anṭākī, because he fought an engagement there and inflicted losses on the enemy.

448They said: In 163 al-Mahdī sent his son Hārūn al-Rashīd on a campaign. He besieged the people of Ṣamālū, which the common people call Samālū. They asked him for safe-conduct for ten households, including the qūmus [count/komes], and he granted it. Their condition was that they not be separated. They were settled in Baghdad at the Shammāsiyya Gate, and they called their place Samālū, as it is still known. It is also said that they surrendered to al-Mahdī's judgment and he spared them and gathered them in that place, and ordered that it be named Samālū. Al-Rashīd ordered a proclamation made over those who remained in the fortress, and they were sold. An Ethiopian who used to curse al-Rashīd and the Muslims was seized and crucified on one of its towers.

449Aḥmad b. al-Ḥārith al-Wāsiṭī told me, from Muḥammad b. Saʿd, from al-Wāqidī, who said: In the year 180 al-Rashīd ordered the building and fortification of the city of ʿAyn Zarba, and levied a contingent to it from the people of Khurasan and others, and assigned them dwellings there. Then in 183 he ordered the building of al-Hārūniyya. It was built and likewise garrisoned with fighters and with volunteers who migrated to it, and it was named after him. It is also said that he built it [began it] in the caliphate of al-Mahdī, and it was completed in his own.

450They said: The Black Church was of black stones, built by the Byzantines in ancient times, and it had an old fortress, which was ruined. Al-Rashīd ordered the city of the Black Church built and fortified, and levied fighters to it with increased stipend.

451Someone from the people of the frontier, ʿAzūn b. Saʿd, informed me that the Byzantines raided it while al-Qāsim b. al-Rashīd was staying at Dābiq. They drove off its people's livestock and captured a number of them. The people of al-Maṣṣīṣa and its volunteers rushed out against them and rescued everything that had fallen into their hands, and killed some of them, and the rest returned afflicted and broken. Al-Qāsim then fortified the city's fortress, repaired it, and increased its garrison. Al-Muʿtaṣim billāh had also transferred to ʿAyn Zarba and its environs a number of the Zuṭṭ who had gained control of the marshes between Wāsiṭ and Basra, and its people benefited from them.

452Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Anṭākī told me: Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī disliked

(p. 203 → 204) buying land on the frontier, and used to say: "A people overcame it at the start of the affair and were driven out of it; it was not divided, and it passed to others. A doubt has entered into this matter which a sensible person ought to avoid." There were also īghārāt [fiscal exemptions/fixed-sum assessments] on the frontier that had eaten into what came in from its tithes until they fell short of its expenses. So in 243 al-Mutawakkil ordered those īghārāt abolished, and they were abolished .

Chapter 38

The conquest of al-Jazīra

453Dāwūd b. ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, judge of al-Raqqa, told me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Maymūn b. Mihrān, who said: All of al-Jazīra was conquered by ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm after the death of Abū ʿUbayda. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed him over it. Abū ʿUbayda had made him his deputy over Syria; then ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān, then Muʿāwiya after him, over Syria, and ordered ʿIyāḍ to raid al-Jazīra.

454al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from a number of Jazīrans, from Sulaymān b. ʿAṭāʾ al-Qurashī, who said: Abū ʿUbayda sent ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm to al-Jazīra, and Abū ʿUbayda died while he was there. ʿUmar then appointed him over it afterward.

455Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: al-Nufaylī ʿAbdallāh b. Muḥammad told us: Sulaymān b. ʿAṭāʾ told us: When ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm conquered al-Ruhā [Edessa], Abū ʿUbayda having sent him, he stood at its gate on a bay horse of his. They made peace with him on the terms that they keep their temple (haykal) and what surrounds it, that they not build any new church except what they already had, and that they help the Muslims against their enemy; and that if they neglected any of what was stipulated, they would have no protection (dhimma). The people of al-Jazīra entered into what the people of al-Ruhā entered into.

456Muḥammad b. Saʿd said: al-Wāqidī said: The best-established account we have heard about ʿIyāḍ is that Abū ʿUbayda died in the plague of ʿAmwās in 18 and appointed ʿIyāḍ as his successor. Then ʿUmar's letter reached him appointing him over Ḥimṣ, Qinnasrīn and al-Jazīra. He set out for al-Jazīra on Thursday, mid-Shaʿbān of 18, with five thousand men, with Maysara b. Masrūq al-ʿAbsī commanding his vanguard, Saʿīd b. ʿĀmir b. Ḥidhyam al-Jumaḥī his right wing, and Ṣafwān b. al-Muʿaṭṭal al-Sulamī his left wing. [Another statement:] Khālid b. al-Walīd had been on his left wing. It is said that Khālid never marched under anyone's banner after Abū ʿUbayda, but stayed at Ḥimṣ until he died there in 21, bequeathing [his affairs] to ʿUmar. Some claim he died in Medina, but his death at Ḥimṣ is better established.

457They said: ʿIyāḍ's scouts reached al-Raqqa and raided an encampment of Arabs around it and some peasants, and took booty; those who escaped fled and entered the city of al-Raqqa. ʿIyāḍ advanced with his army until he halted at the Gate of al-Ruhā, one of its gates, in battle formation. The Muslims shot for a while until some of them were wounded. Then he drew back from them so that their stones and arrows would not reach him, rode around the city, placed pickets at its gates, returned to his camp and sent out raiding parties. They kept bringing captives from the villages and abundant provisions, the crops being ripe for harvest. After five or six days of this, the patriarch of the city sent to ʿIyāḍ asking for safe-conduct. ʿIyāḍ made peace with him, granting security to all its people for their lives, children, property and city. ʿIyāḍ said: "The land is ours; we have trodden it and secured it." So he left it in their hands subject to kharāj, and he assigned to the Muslims, at the tithe, such of it as the dhimmīs did not want and abandoned. He laid the jizya on their necks, imposing on each man of them one dinar a year; he exempted women and boys; and he imposed on them, along with the dinar, qafīz-measures of wheat and some oil, vinegar and honey. When Muʿāwiya took charge, he made that a jizya upon it [the city]. Then they opened the gates of the city and set up a market for the Muslims at the Gate of al-Ruhā. ʿIyāḍ wrote for them:

"In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is what ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm granted to the people of al-Raqqa on the day he entered it. He granted them security for their persons, their property and their churches, which are not to be destroyed or inhabited, provided they pay the jizya due from them and do not introduce a mughayyila [meaning uncertain], and provided that they not build a church or synagogue, nor display a clapper (nāqūs), nor a bāʿūth [litany procession], nor a cross. God is witness, and God suffices as witness." And ʿIyāḍ sealed it with his seal.

It is said that ʿIyāḍ imposed four dinars on every adult male of the people of al-Raqqa. The established account is that ʿUmar afterward wrote to ʿUmayr b. Saʿd, who was his governor: "Impose on every man of them four dinars, as he imposed on the people of gold."

458They said: Then ʿIyāḍ marched to Ḥarrān and encamped at Bājaddā, and sent out his vanguard. The people of Ḥarrān shut their gates against them; then he followed them. When he encamped before it, the Ḥarrānians among its people sent to him, informing him that they held a section of the city and asking him to go on to al-Ruhā: whatever terms the people of al-Ruhā made with him, they would be content with, and they would clear the way between him and the Christians until they came to him. The Christians learned of this and sent to him their acceptance of what the Ḥarrānians had proposed, and they offered [terms]. He came to al-Ruhā, whose people had mustered against him; they shot at the Muslims for a while, then their fighters came out and the Muslims routed them and forced them back into the city. It was not long before they asked for peace and safe-conduct, and ʿIyāḍ agreed and wrote them a document, a copy of which is:

"In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is a letter from ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm to the bishop of al-Ruhā. If you open the gate of the city to me, on the condition that you pay me, for every man, a dinar and two mudds of wheat, then you are secure in your persons, your property, and those who follow you. And it is incumbent on you to guide the lost, repair bridges and roads, and give sincere counsel to the Muslims. God is witness, and God suffices as witness."

459Dāwūd b. ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd told me, from his father, from his grandfather, that ʿIyāḍ's letter to the people of al-Ruhā was: "In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful. This is a letter from ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm and those Muslims with him to the people of al-Ruhā. I have granted them security for their blood, their property, their offspring, their women, their city and their mills, provided they render the obligation that is due from them; and we have it upon them that they repair our bridges and guide our lost. God and His angels and the Muslims are witnesses." He said: Then ʿIyāḍ came to Ḥarrān and sent Ṣafwān b. al-Muʿaṭṭal and Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī to Samīsāṭ. ʿIyāḍ made peace with the people of Ḥarrān on the like of the peace of al-Ruhā, and they opened its gates to him, and he appointed a man over it. Then he went to Samīsāṭ and found Ṣafwān b. al-Muʿaṭṭal and Ḥabīb b. Maslama encamped before it , having overcome villages and fortresses in its district. Its people made peace with him on the like of the peace of the people of al-Ruhā. ʿIyāḍ used to raid from al-Ruhā and then return to it.

460Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, who said: Not a foot's place remained in al-Jazīra that was not conquered in the time of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ at the hands of ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm: he conquered Ḥarrān, al-Ruhā, al-Raqqa, Qarqīsiyā, Nuṣaybīn and Sinjār.

461Muḥammad told me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Maslama, from Furāt b. Salmān, from Thābit b. al-Ḥajjāj, who said: ʿIyāḍ conquered al-Raqqa, Ḥarrān, al-Ruhā, Nuṣaybīn, Mayyāfāriqīn, Qarqīsiyā, and the villages and towns of the Euphrates, by treaty as to the towns and by force as to the land.

462Muḥammad told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Thawr b. Yazīd, from Rāshid b. Saʿd, that ʿIyāḍ conquered al-Jazīra and its towns by treaty and its land by force. It is also reported that when ʿIyāḍ came to Ḥarrān from al-Raqqa he found it empty, its people having moved to al-Ruhā. When al-Ruhā was conquered they made peace for their city while remaining in it, and their peace was like the peace of al-Ruhā.

463Abū Ayyūb al-Raqqī the tutor told me: al-Ḥajjāj b. Abī Manīʿ al-Ruṣāfī told me, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: ʿIyāḍ conquered al-Raqqa, then al-Ruhā, then Ḥarrān, then Samīsāṭ, on a single treaty. Then he came to Sarūj, Rāsakīfā and al-Arḍ al-Bayḍāʾ, and gained control of their land, and made peace with the people of their fortresses on the like of al-Ruhā. Then the people of Samīsāṭ renounced [their faith/treaty]; when that reached him he went back to it and besieged it until he conquered it. Then it reached him that the people of al-Ruhā had broken [the treaty]; when he encamped against them they opened the gates of their city to him, and he entered it and left his governor there with a force. Then he came to the Euphrates villages, which are the bridge of Manbij and its dependencies, and conquered them on that basis. He came to ʿAyn al-Warda, which is Raʾs al-ʿAyn, but it held out against him and he left it. He came to Tall Mawzan and conquered it on the like of the peace of al-Ruhā, and that was in the year 19. ʿIyāḍ sent Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī to Qarqīsiyā, and he conquered it by treaty like al-Raqqa. ʿIyāḍ conquered Āmid without fighting, on the like of the peace of al-Ruhā. He conquered Mayyāfāriqīn on the like of that. He conquered the fortress of Kafar Tūthā. He conquered Nuṣaybīn after fighting, on the like of the peace of al-Ruhā. He conquered Ṭūr ʿAbdīn, the fortress of Mārdīn, and Dārā on the like of that. He conquered Qardā and Bāzabdā on the like of the peace of Nuṣaybīn. The patriarch of al-Zawzān came to him and made peace on his land for a tribute, all of that in the year 19 and days of Muḥarram of the year 20. Then he marched to Arzan and conquered it on the like of the peace of Nuṣaybīn. He entered the Pass (al-darb) and reached Bidlīs, passed it to Khilāṭ, and made peace with its patriarch, and reached al-ʿAyn al-Ḥāmiḍa of Armenia and did not go beyond it. Then he returned, and the lord of Bidlīs guaranteed the kharāj of Khilāṭ and its poll-taxes (lit. "skulls"), and what was due from its patriarch. Then he withdrew to al-Raqqa and went on to Ḥimṣ, ʿUmar having appointed him over it, and he died in 20. ʿUmar appointed Saʿīd b. ʿĀmir b. Ḥidhyam, who did not last long before he died. Then ʿUmar appointed ʿUmayr b. Saʿd al-Anṣārī, who conquered ʿAyn al-Warda after fierce fighting.

464al-Wāqidī said: One who heard Isḥāq b. Abī Farwa narrate from Abū Wahb al-Jayshānī Daylam b. al-Mūsiʿ told me that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ wrote to ʿIyāḍ ordering him to send ʿUmayr b. Saʿd to ʿAyn al-Warda, and he sent him to it. He sent scouts ahead of him, who seized some peasants and took livestock from the enemy's herds. Then the people of the city shut its gates and set up ʿarrādāt [light catapults] on it, and a number of Muslims were killed by stones and arrows. One of its patriarchs looked out at them, cursed them and said: "We are not like those you have met." Then it was conquered afterward by treaty.

465ʿAmr b. Muḥammad told me, from al-Ḥajjāj b. Abī Manīʿ, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: Raʾs al-ʿAyn held out against ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm, and ʿUmayr b. Saʿd, ʿUmar's governor over al-Jazīra, conquered it after its people had fought the Muslims fiercely. The Muslims entered it by force, and afterward made peace with them on the terms that the land be handed over to them and the jizya be laid on their heads, four dinars a head; their women and children were not taken captive.

al-Ḥajjāj said: I heard elders of the people of Raʾs al-ʿAyn mention that when ʿUmayr entered it he said to them, "No harm, no harm; come to me, come to me," and that was security for them. Al-Haytham b. ʿAdī claimed that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ sent Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī to ʿAyn al-Warda and that he raided it with the troops of al-Jazīra after ʿIyāḍ's death. The established view is that ʿUmayr conquered it by force, that its people were not enslaved, and that he imposed kharāj and jizya on them; no one besides al-Haytham said this. al-Ḥajjāj b. Abī Manīʿ said: A multitude of the people of Raʾs al-ʿAyn evacuated, and the Muslims worked their lands and cultivated them by grants (iqṭāʿ).

466Muḥammad b. al-Mufaḍḍal al-Mawṣilī told me, from elders of the people of Sinjār, who said: Sinjār was in the hands of the Byzantines. Then Chosroes, known as Abarwīz, wished to kill a hundred Persian men who had been brought to him because of a dispute and disobedience. He was spoken to on their behalf and ordered that they be sent to Sinjār, which he was then trying to conquer. Two of them died, and ninety-eight reached it and joined the fighters who were facing it; they conquered it [without the others / ahead of them; the Arabic dūnahum is ambiguous], and settled there and multiplied. When ʿIyāḍ returned from Khilāṭ and came to al-Jazīra, he sent to Sinjār and conquered it by treaty and settled Arabs in it. Some transmitters have said that ʿIyāḍ conquered a fortress of al-Mawṣil, but that is not established.

467Ibn al-Kalbī said: ʿUmayr b. Saʿd, ʿUmar's governor, is ʿUmayr b. Saʿd b. Shuhayd b. ʿAmr, of the Aws. Al-Wāqidī said: He is ʿUmayr b. Saʿd b. ʿUbayd. His father Saʿd was killed at al-Qādisiyya. This Saʿd is the one whom the Kufans report to have been among those who collected the Qurʾān in the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

468al-Wāqidī said: Some have reported that Khālid b. al-Walīd was made governor by ʿUmar over part of al-Jazīra, and that he was anointed/smeared in a bathhouse at Āmid or elsewhere with something containing wine, so ʿUmar dismissed him. That is not established.

469ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: al-Ḥajjāj b. Abī Manīʿ told me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Maymūn b. Mihrān, who said: Oil, vinegar and food were taken for the support of the Muslims in al-Jazīra for a period; then it was lightened for them and limited to forty-eight dirhams, twenty-four, and twelve, out of ʿUmar's consideration for the people. Upon each person, together with his jizya, were two mudds of wheat, two qisṭs of oil and two qisṭs of vinegar.

470A number of the people of al-Raqqa told me: When ʿIyāḍ died and Saʿīd b. ʿĀmir b. Ḥidhyam took over al-Jazīra, he built the mosque of al-Raqqa and the mosque of al-Ruhā. Then he died, and ʿUmayr b. Saʿd built the mosques in Diyār Muḍar and Diyār Rabīʿa. Later, when Muʿāwiya governed Syria and al-Jazīra for ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵁ [ʿUthmān] ordered him to settle the Arabs in places remote from the cities and villages and to permit them to cultivate the lands in which no one had any right. So he settled Banū Tamīm at al-Rābiya, and settled al-Māziḥīn and al-Mudaybir, mixed groups of Qays, Asad and others; and he did likewise in all districts of Diyār Muḍar, and arranged Rabīʿa in its territories on the same basis. He assigned to the cities, villages and frontier posts those from among the stipend-holders who would guard and defend them, and then placed them with his governors.

471Abū Ḥafṣ al-Shāmī told me, from Ḥammād b. ʿAmr al-Naṣībī, who said: The governor of Nuṣaybīn wrote to Muʿāwiya, who was ʿUthmān's governor over Syria and al-Jazīra, complaining that a number of the Muslims with him had been stung by scorpions. He wrote back ordering him to impose on the people of each quarter of the city a stated number of scorpions every night. He did so, and they would bring them to him and he would order them killed.

472Abū Ayyūb al-Muʾaddib al-Raqqī told me, from Abū ʿAbdallāh al-Qarqasānī, from his elders, that when ʿUmayr b. Saʿd conquered Raʾs al-ʿAyn he went along the Khābūr and its vicinity until he reached Qarqīsiyā, whose people had broken [the treaty], and made peace with them on the like of their first peace. Then he came to the fortresses of the Euphrates, fortress by fortress, and conquered them on the terms on which Qarqīsiyā had been conquered, and met with much fighting at none of them. Some of their people at times threw stones. When he had finished with Talbus [sic] and ʿĀnāt, he came to al-Nāʾūsa, Ālūsa and Hīt, and found ʿAmmār b. Yāsir, who was then ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb's governor over Kufa, and who had sent an army to raid what lies above al-Anbār, commanded by Saʿd b. ʿAmr b. Ḥarām al-Anṣārī; the people of these fortresses had come to him asking for safe-conduct. He granted them security, excepting from the people of Hīt half of their church. ʿUmayr then returned to al-Raqqa.

473Some men of learning told me: The one who went to Hīt and the fortresses beyond it from Kufa was Mudlāj b. ʿAmr al-Sulamī, an ally of Banū ʿAbd Shams, who had companionship [with the Prophet]; he took charge of their conquest. He built al-Ḥadītha on the Euphrates. His descendants are at Hīt, and among them was a man with the kunya Abū Hārūn, [described as] "bālqy al-dhikr" there [the phrase is unintelligible as printed; perhaps "of established renown"]. It is said that Mudlāj acted on behalf of Saʿd b. ʿAmr b. Ḥarām. And God knows best.

474They said: The site of the canal of Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān, the one called Saʿīd al-Khayr, who made a show of asceticism, was a thicket (ghayḍa) full of wild beasts. Al-Walīd granted it to him as a fief (iqṭāʿ). He dug the canal and developed everything there. Some say that it was ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz who granted him that.

475They said: Al-Rāfiqa had no ancient remains. It was built by the Commander of the Faithful al-Manṣūr ﵀ in 155, on the plan of his city at Baghdad, and he stationed in it troops from Khurasan. Its building went forward at the hands of al-Mahdī, while he was crown prince. Then al-Rashīd built its palaces, and between al-Raqqa and al-Rāfiqa there was open ground of fields. When ʿAlī b. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī came as governor of al-Jazīra, he moved the markets of al-Raqqa to that land. The great market of al-Raqqa in earlier times was known as the Old Market of Hishām. Then, when al-Rashīd came to al-Raqqa, he enlarged those markets, and they continued to be collected [for revenue] together with the crown estates (ṣawāfī). As for Ruṣāfat Hishām, Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik founded it; before that he used to stay at al-Zaytūna. He dug al-Hanīʾ and al-Marīʾ, brought into production the estate known as al-Hanīʾ wa-l-Marīʾ, and founded in it the Wāsiṭ of al-Raqqa. That estate was later confiscated at the beginning of the dynasty. Then it passed to Umm Jaʿfar Zubayda bt. Jaʿfar b. al-Manṣūr, who built in it the allotment (qaṭīʿa) attributed to her and increased its development.

The Raḥba below Qarqīsiyā had no ancient remains. It was built and founded by Mālik b. Ṭawq b. ʿAttāb al-Taghlibī in the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn. Adhrama, in Diyār Rabīʿa, was an ancient village. Al-Ḥasan b. ʿAmr b. al-Khaṭṭāb al-Taghlibī took it from its owner, built a palace there, and fortified it. Kafar Tūthā was an old fortress; the sons of Abū Rimtha took it as a residence, made it a town, and fortified it.

476Muʿāfā b. Ṭāwūs told me, from his father, who said: I asked the elders about the tithes of the land and of the territories of Rabīʿa and the desert (al-bādiya). He said: They are the tithes of what the Arabs accepted Islam on, or developed from waste land held by no one, or what the Christians abandoned, so that it went to ruin and became overgrown with scrub, and it was assigned as a fief to the Arabs.

477Abū ʿAffān al-Raqqī told me, from elders among the scribes of al-Raqqa and others, who said: ʿAyn al-Rūmiyya and its water belonged to al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, who gave it to Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī. Then it passed to Abū l-ʿAbbās, the Commander of the Faithful, who granted it as a fief to Maymūn b. Ḥamza, a client of ʿAlī b. ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAbbās. Then al-Rashīd bought it from his heirs. It belongs to the land of al-Raqqa.

478They said: Ibn Hubayra granted the Ibn Hubayra woodland (ghāba); it was confiscated, and was granted to Bishr b. Maymūn, the owner of the arcades (ṭāqāt) in Baghdad in the Bāb al-Shām district. Then al-Rashīd bought it. It belongs to the land of Sarūj. Hishām granted his daughter ʿĀʾisha an allotment at Raʾs Kayfā, known by her name; it was confiscated. ʿAbd al-Malik and Hishām owned a village called Salʿūs and half of a village called Kafar Jadā, near al-Ruhā. At Ḥarrān, al-Ghamr b. Yazīd owned Tall ʿAfrāʾ, the land of Tall Mudhābā [sic], the land of al-Muṣallā, and crown estates in the suburb of Ḥarrān and its income-producing properties.

Marj ʿAbd al-Wāḥid was a preserve (ḥimā) of the Muslims before al-Ḥadath and Zibaṭra were built. When those two were built, it was no longer needed, so it was developed, and al-Ḥusayn the eunuch annexed it to the estates (aḥwāz) in the caliphate of al-Rashīd. Then people rose up [the text here is garbled] and seized its farmland, until ʿAbdallāh b. Ṭāhir came to Syria and returned it to the estates. Abū Ayyūb al-Raqqī said: I heard that the ʿAbd al-Wāḥid after whom the meadow is named was ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. al-Ḥārith b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī l-ʿĀṣ, a cousin of ʿAbd al-Malik. The meadow was his, and he made it a preserve for the Muslims. He is the one whom al-Quṭāmī praised, saying: "Let not the affair of the people of the city grieve you, once ʿAbd al-Wāḥid, the most exalted, has passed them over." [The second hemistich is uncertain.]

Chapter 39

The Christians of Banū Taghlib b. Wāʾil

The Affair of the Christians of Banū Taghlib b. Wāʾil

479Shaybān b. Farrūkh told us: Abū ʿAwāna told us, from al-Mughīra, from al-Saffāḥ al-Shaybānī [as printed; the name is probably corrupt], that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ wished to take the jizya from the Christians of Banū Taghlib. They set off in flight, and a group of them reached a distant land. Al-Nuʿmān b. Zurʿa, or Zurʿa b. al-Nuʿmān, said: "I adjure you by God, concerning Banū Taghlib! They are a people of the Arabs who disdain the jizya, and they are a people whose harm to the enemy is severe, so do not help your enemy against you through them." So ʿUmar sent after them and brought them back, and doubled the ṣadaqa upon them.

480Shaybān told us: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Muslim told us: Layth told us, from a man, from Saʿīd b. Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The slaughtered animals of the Christians of Banū Taghlib are not to be eaten, and their women are not to be married. They are neither of us nor of the People of the Book.

481ʿAbbās b. Hishām told us, from his father, from ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam and Abū Mikhnaf, who both said: ʿUmayr b. Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ informing him that he had come to the Syrian bank of the Euphrates and conquered ʿĀnāt and the rest of the Euphrates fortresses. He had wanted those of Banū Taghlib who were there to accept Islam; they refused and intended to join the Byzantine land. Before that he had wanted the same of those on the eastern bank, and they refused and asked his permission to evacuate, and he sought ʿUmar's opinion about them. ʿUmar ﵁ wrote to him ordering him to double on them the ṣadaqa taken from the Muslims on every grazing animal and every piece of land, and, if they refused, to fight them until he destroyed them or they became Muslim. They accepted that double the ṣadaqa be taken from them and said: "Since it is not a jizya like the jizya of the non-Arab infidels (aʿlāj), we are content, and we keep our religion."

482ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Abū Muʿāwiya told me, from al-Shaybānī, from al-Saffāḥ, from Dāwūd b. Kurdūs, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb made peace with Banū Taghlib, after they had crossed the Euphrates and intended to join the Byzantine land, on the terms that they would not "dip" (yaṣbughū) any child [in baptism] and would not force him into their religion, and that they would owe doubled ṣadaqa. He said: Dāwūd b. Kurdūs used to say: They have no protection (dhimma), because they have dipped [children] in their religion, meaning baptism.

483al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from Ibn al-Mubārak, from Yūnus b. Yazīd al-Aylī, from al-Zuhrī, who said: There is no ṣadaqa on the livestock of the People of the Book, except for the Christians of Banū Taghlib, or he said the Christians of the Arabs, most of whose wealth is livestock; upon them is double what is on the Muslims.

484Saʿīd b. Sulaymān Saʿdawayh told us: Hushaym told us, from Mughīra, from al-Saffāḥ b. al-Muthannā, from Zurʿa b. al-Nuʿmān, that he spoke to ʿUmar about the Christians of Banū Taghlib and said: "They are an Arab people who disdain the jizya; they are only owners of crops and livestock." ʿUmar had been intending to take the jizya from them, and they scattered through the lands. So he made peace with them on the basis that he doubled what is taken from the Muslims in ṣadaqa on land and livestock, and stipulated that they not make their children Christians.

Mughīra said: ʿAlī ﵇ used to say: "If I ever have leisure for Banū Taghlib, I shall have a decision about them. I shall kill their fighters and enslave their offspring, for they have broken the covenant and protection is withdrawn from them, since they have made their children Christians."

485Abū Naṣr al-Tammār told me: Sharīk b. ʿAbdallāh told us, from Ibrāhīm b. Muhājir, from Ziyād b. Ḥudayr al-Asadī, who said: ʿUmar sent me to the Christians of Banū Taghlib to take from them a half-tithe of their property, and forbade me to levy the tithe on a Muslim or on a dhimmī who pays kharāj.

486Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from ʿAbd al-Malik b. Nawfal, from Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm b. al-Ḥārith, that ʿUthmān ordered that nothing be accepted from Banū Taghlib in jizya except dahīk gold and silver [dahīk is unclear to me]. Then the established report reached him that ʿUmar had taken double the ṣadaqa from them, and he withdrew from that.

al-Wāqidī said: Sufyān al-Thawrī, al-Awzāʿī, Mālik b. Anas, Ibn Abī Laylā, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf said: From the Taghlibī is taken double what is taken from the Muslim on his land, livestock and wealth. As for the boy and the mentally impaired among them, the Iraqis hold that double ṣadaqa is taken from his land but nothing from his livestock, while the Hijazis say it is taken from his livestock and his land. They all said: What is taken from the property of Banū Taghlib has the status of kharāj property, because it is a substitute for the jizya.

Chapter 40

The frontiers of al-Jazīra

487They said: When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵁ became caliph, he wrote to Muʿāwiya confirming him in the governorship of Syria. He appointed ʿUmayr b. Saʿd al-Anṣārī over al-Jazīra, then dismissed him, and he combined for Muʿāwiya Syria and al-Jazīra and their frontiers. He ordered him to raid Shimshāṭ, which is Fourth Armenia, or to have it raided. Muʿāwiya sent against it Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī and Ṣafwān b. Muʿaṭṭal al-Sulamī, who conquered it after some days of encamping before it, on the like of the peace of al-Ruhā. Ṣafwān stayed there, and died there at the end of Muʿāwiya's caliphate. It is also said that Muʿāwiya himself raided it, with these two accompanying him, and appointed Ṣafwān over it, who made it his home and died there.

488They said: Constantine the tyrant [Constantine V] besieged it after encamping at Malaṭya in 133 but could accomplish nothing against it, so he raided the surrounding area and withdrew. Shimshāṭ remained kharāj-land until al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh ﵀ made it tithe-land (ʿushriyya) like the other frontier towns.

489They said: Ḥabīb b. Maslama raided the fortress of Kamkh after the conquest of Shimshāṭ but could not take it. Ṣafwān raided it and could not conquer it. Then he raided it in 59, the year in which he died, with ʿUmayr b. al-Ḥubāb al-Sulamī. ʿUmayr climbed its wall and kept fighting on it alone until he drove back the Byzantines and the Muslims climbed up. It was conquered through ʿUmayr b. al-Ḥubāb, and he used to boast of that, and was boasted of for it. Then the Byzantines overcame it, and Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik conquered it. It went on being conquered and the Byzantines retaking it.

In the year 149, al-Manṣūr set out from Baghdad and halted at Ḥadīthat al-Mawṣil. From there he sent on campaign al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba, and after him Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath, placing al-ʿAbbās b. Muḥammad over them and ordering him to raid Kamkh with them. Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath died at Āmid, and al-ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan went on until they reached Malaṭya. They took provisions from there, then encamped against Kamkh. Al-ʿAbbās ordered a mangonel set up against it. The defenders put juniper timber on their fortress so that the mangonel stones would not damage it, and they shot at the Muslims and killed two hundred of them with stones. The Muslims made siege-sheds (dabbābāt) and fought hard until they conquered it. With al-ʿAbbās b. Muḥammad b. ʿAlī on this campaign was Maṭar al-Warrāq. Then the Byzantines shut Kamkh again.

In 177, Muḥammad b. ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī ʿAmra al-Anṣārī, the governor of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Ṣāliḥ over Shimshāṭ, raided it, conquered it, and entered it on the fourteenth night of Rabīʿ II of that year. It stayed in Muslim hands until the upheaval of Muḥammad b. al-Rashīd, when its people fled and the Byzantines overcame it. It is said that ʿUbaydallāh b. al-Aqṭaʿ handed it over to them and thereby freed his son, who was their prisoner. Then ʿAbdallāh b. Ṭāhir conquered it in the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn, and it remained in Muslim hands, until some Christians of Shimshāṭ, together with Qālīqalā and Baqrāṭ b. Ashūṭ, patriarch of Khilāṭ, schemed to hand it over to the Byzantines and win their favor, because of estates they held in the district of Shimshāṭ.

Malatya (Malaṭya)

490They said: ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm sent Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī from Shimshāṭ against Malaṭya. He conquered it, but it was subsequently closed against the Muslims. When Muʿāwiya was appointed over Syria and al-Jazīra, he sent Ḥabīb b. Maslama against it again. He conquered it by force and stationed a Muslim garrison there alongside its governor. Muʿāwiya came to Malaṭya when he intended to enter Byzantine territory and filled it with men from Syria, al-Jazīra, and elsewhere. It became a route for the summer campaigns (ṣawāʾif).

Then its inhabitants left it during the days of ʿAbdallāh b. al-Zubayr. The Byzantines came out and damaged it, then abandoned it; afterward, some Christian Armenians and Nabataeans settled there.

491Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to me, from al-Wāqidī, through his chain: The Muslims had settled in Ṭaranda after ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAbd al-Malik attacked it in the year 83 and had built dwellings there. It lay three stages from Malaṭya, deep within Byzantine territory. Malaṭya was then in ruins, with no one in it except some protected subjects (ahl al-dhimma), Armenians and others. A mounted detachment from the troops of al-Jazīra would come to them in summer and remain until winter arrived and snow fell, at which point they would return home.

When ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁ became caliph, he had the inhabitants of Ṭaranda leave it, though they were unwilling, out of concern for their safety from the enemy. They carried off everything and left nothing for the enemy, even breaking the jars of vinegar and oil. He then settled them at Malaṭya, demolished Ṭaranda, and appointed Jaʿwana b. al-Ḥārith, one of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa, over Malaṭya.

492They said: In the year 123, twenty thousand Byzantines came out and encamped against Malaṭya. Its inhabitants shut its gates, and the women appeared on the walls wearing turbans and fought. An envoy went out from the inhabitants to seek help. He rode the postal relay until he caught up with Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik at al-Ruṣāfa. Hishām called upon the people to march to Malaṭya, but news then reached him that the Byzantines had withdrawn. He summoned the envoy, told him the news, and sent horsemen back with him to serve as a garrison there.

Hishām himself then went on campaign, encamped at Malaṭya, and remained while it was rebuilt. His route passed through al-Raqqa, which he entered wearing a sword at his side, something he had not done previously during his reign.

493Al-Wāqidī said: In the year 133, Constantine the tyrant advanced toward Malaṭya. Kamkh was then in Muslim hands, under a man of the Banū Sulaym. The people of Kamkh sent an urgent appeal to the inhabitants of Malaṭya, who dispatched eight hundred horsemen against the Byzantines. Byzantine cavalry engaged and routed them. Constantine then turned toward Malaṭya, encamped before it, and besieged its inhabitants. Al-Jazīra was at that time troubled by civil strife, and its governor, Mūsā b. Kaʿb, was at Ḥarrān. The inhabitants sent an envoy to him, but he was unable to relieve them.

When Constantine learned this he told them: “People of Malaṭya! I came against you only because I know your condition and how occupied your ruler is. Come out under a guarantee of safety and evacuate the city. I will demolish it and go away, leaving you alone.” They refused, so he set up mangonels against it. When hardship overcame them and the siege grew severe, they asked him to give them a binding guarantee, and he did so. They prepared to depart, carrying what light possessions they could, and throwing much of what was too heavy into the wells and hiding places. Then they came out.

The Byzantines formed two ranks, with drawn swords, from the gate of the city to the end of their formation, the point of each man's sword touching the point of the sword held by the man opposite him, so that the blades resembled the arch of a bridge. They escorted the inhabitants until they reached safety; the inhabitants then headed toward al-Jazīra and dispersed throughout it. The Byzantines demolished Malaṭya, leaving only a granary (hary), which they damaged slightly. They also demolished the fortress of Qalawdhiyya.

In the year 139, al-Manṣūr wrote to Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī ordering him to rebuild and fortify Malaṭya. He then decided instead to send ʿAbd al-Wahhāb b. Ibrāhīm al-Imām as governor of al-Jazīra and its frontier districts. ʿAbd al-Wahhāb set out in the year 140, accompanied by al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba with troops from Khurāsān. He assigned troop levies to the people of Syria and al-Jazīra, until seventy thousand men had assembled with him. He encamped at Malaṭya, brought laborers together from every district, and began rebuilding it.

Al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba would sometimes carry a stone himself and hand it to a mason. He also provided breakfast and supper to the men out of his own wealth, establishing his kitchens openly. This irritated ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, who wrote to Abū Jaʿfar [al-Manṣūr] saying that he himself fed the men, but that al-Ḥasan fed many times as many, seeking to outdo him and to spoil and discredit his own efforts by extravagance and ostentation, and that al-Ḥasan had criers calling the people to his meals.

Abū Jaʿfar wrote back: “Boy! Al-Ḥasan feeds them out of his own wealth, while you feed them out of mine. This comes only from your low standing, your lack of ambition, and the foolishness of your judgment.” He wrote to al-Ḥasan: “Feed them, but do not employ a crier.” Al-Ḥasan would then say, “Whoever is first to reach a battlement shall receive such-and-such.” The men worked energetically until they had completed Malaṭya and its mosque in six months.

For each ʿirāfa of soldiers settled there, they built two ground-floor rooms, two upper rooms above them, and a stable. An ʿirāfa comprised ten to fifteen men. They established a military outpost thirty miles from the city, and another by a river called Qubāqib, which flows into the Euphrates. Al-Manṣūr settled four thousand fighting men from al-Jazīra in Malaṭya, as it belonged to their frontier districts, giving each man an extra ten dinars in his stipend and an allowance of one hundred dinars, apart from payments agreed between the tribes themselves. He stocked the city with weapons, assigned farms as grants to the soldiers, and rebuilt the fortress of Qalawdhiyya. Constantine the tyrant advanced with more than a hundred thousand men and halted at the Jayḥān River, but when he learned how numerous the Arabs were, he held back from attacking.

494I heard someone mention that Naṣr b. Mālik al-Khuzāʿī and Naṣr b. Saʿd, the secretary and freedman of the Anṣār, accompanied ʿAbd al-Wahhāb on this campaign. A poet said:

The two Naṣrs encompassed you—Naṣr b. Mālikand Naṣr b. Saʿd: how mighty your naṣr [victory] with such Naṣrs!

In the year 141, Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm sent an expedition to Malaṭya with troops from Khurāsān, with al-Musayyab b. Zuhayr commanding his police. He remained on frontier duty there so that the enemy would not be tempted to attack it, and those of its former inhabitants who survived returned to it. The Byzantines attacked Malaṭya during the caliphate of al-Rashīd but could not take it; al-Rashīd ﵀ campaigned against them, inflicted hardship upon them, and subdued them.

Marʿash and al-Ḥadath

495They said: While Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ was at Manbij, he sent Khālid b. al-Walīd toward Marʿash. Khālid took its fortress on condition that its inhabitants depart, then demolished it. When Sufyān b. ʿAwf al-Ghāmidī campaigned against the Byzantines in the year 30, he traveled by way of Marʿash and ranged through Byzantine territory.

Muʿāwiya built the city of Marʿash and settled troops there, but when Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya died, Byzantine raids against them increased and they abandoned it. After the death of his father Marwān b. al-Ḥakam, when ʿAbd al-Malik was seeking the caliphate, he made peace with the Byzantines in exchange for a payment he undertook to make them. In the year 74, Muḥammad b. Marwān campaigned against the Byzantines and the agreement was broken. He again led the summer expedition in the year 75.

In Jumādā I, Byzantine forces came from the direction of Marʿash toward the valleys (al-Aʿmāq). The Muslims advanced against them under Abān b. al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, together with Dīnār b. Dīnār, freedman of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān and governor of Qinnasrīn and its districts. They met in the valley of Marʿash and fought fiercely. The Byzantines were routed, and the Muslims pursued them, killing and taking captives. In that same year Dīnār had encountered a group of Byzantines at Ḥasr Yaghrā, about ten miles from Shimshāṭ, and defeated them.

Later, al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik went to Marʿash, restored and fortified it, brought settlers there, and built a congregational mosque. Every year he required Qinnasrīn to provide a contingent for it. In the days of Marwān b. Muḥammad, while he was occupied fighting the people of Ḥimṣ, the Byzantines came out and besieged Marʿash. Its people agreed to evacuate it and departed with their families toward al-Jazīra and the military district of Qinnasrīn; the Byzantines then destroyed it. Marwān's governor there was al-Kawthar b. Zufar b. al-Ḥārith al-Kilābī, and the Byzantine ruler at the time was Constantine b. Leo.

When Marwān had finished with Ḥimṣ and demolished its walls, he sent an army to rebuild Marʿash, and it was rebuilt and restored as a town. During the civil strife against him the Byzantines again came out and destroyed it. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī rebuilt and fortified it during the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr and summoned settlers by offering an increase in their stipends. When al-Mahdī became caliph, he increased its military stores and strengthened its inhabitants.

496Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to me, from al-Wāqidī: Michael came out through the pass of al-Ḥadath with eighty thousand men and advanced to the valley of Marʿash, killing, burning, and taking many Muslims captive. He reached the gate of Marʿash, where ʿĪsā b. ʿAlī was stationed, having gone on campaign that year. ʿĪsā's freedmen and the inhabitants and fighting men of the city went out and shot arrows at Michael's forces. He feigned retreat and drew them away from the city, then wheeled around and killed eight of ʿĪsā's freedmen. The survivors took refuge in the city, closed its gates, and were besieged there. Michael then withdrew and encamped at the Jayḥān.

News reached Thumāma b. al-Walīd al-ʿAbsī at Dābiq, who had been appointed commander of the summer campaign in the year 161. He sent a large cavalry force against Michael; the men were struck down, except those who escaped. This deeply angered al-Mahdī, who made thorough preparations to send al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba on campaign the following year, 162.

497They said: The fortress of al-Ḥadath was among the places conquered in the days of ʿUmar. Ḥabīb b. Maslama took it on behalf of ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm, and Muʿāwiya attended to it afterward.

The Umayyads called the pass of al-Ḥadath “al-Salāma” [Safety] to avoid an ill omen, because Muslims had suffered losses there, and some said that this was the ḥadath [incident] from which the place was named. Others said a young boy (ghulām ḥadath) met the Muslims in the pass and fought them with his companions, so it was called the Pass of al-Ḥadath.

During the turmoil of Marwān b. Muḥammad, the Byzantines came out, demolished the city of al-Ḥadath, and expelled its inhabitants, as they had done at Malaṭya. Then, in the year 161, Michael came out toward the valley of Marʿash, and al-Mahdī dispatched al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba to range through Byzantine territory. His attacks weighed so heavily upon its inhabitants that they depicted him in their churches. He entered through the pass of al-Ḥadath, saw the site of the city, and was told that Michael had marched out from there. Al-Ḥasan selected a site for its reconstruction. On his return he spoke to al-Mahdī about building it and Ṭarsūs, and al-Mahdī ordered that the building of al-Ḥadath take precedence.

Mandal al-ʿAnazī, the Kufan traditionist, and Muʿtamir b. Sulaymān, the Basran, accompanied al-Ḥasan on this expedition. ʿAlī b. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī, then governor of al-Jazīra and Qinnasrīn, founded the city, which was called al-Muḥammadiyya. Al-Mahdī died just as its construction was completed, so it was also known as al-Mahdiyya. It was built of mudbrick, and his death occurred in the year 169.

His son Mūsā al-Hādī succeeded him, dismissed ʿAlī b. Sulaymān, and appointed Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad b. ʿAlī governor of al-Jazīra and Qinnasrīn. ʿAlī b. Sulaymān had completed al-Ḥadath, while Muḥammad assigned troops from Syria, al-Jazīra, and Khurāsān to it, with stipends of forty dinars. He allotted them homes and gave every man three hundred dirhams. Construction was completed in the year 169. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb said: ʿAlī b. Sulaymān enrolled four thousand men for al-Ḥadath and settled them there, and transferred another two thousand from Malaṭya, Shimshāṭ, Kaysūm, Dulūk, and Raʿbān.

498Al-Wāqidī said: After al-Ḥadath was built, winter set in with snow and heavy rain. Its construction had not been made secure or undertaken with sufficient precautions, so the city's walls crumbled and it was damaged. The Byzantines came against it, and its garrison and other inhabitants dispersed. When the news reached Mūsā [al-Hādī], he assigned one contingent under al-Musayyab b. Zuhayr, another under Rawḥ b. Ḥātim, and another under Ḥamza b. Mālik, but he died before they could set out. Al-Rashīd then became caliph and ordered the city rebuilt, fortified, and stocked with troops and supplies, with homes and land grants allotted to its fighting men.

499Someone other than al-Wāqidī said: A leading Byzantine commander encamped with a large force against the newly built city of al-Ḥadath. It had been constructed of mudbricks piled upon one another, and the snow had damaged it. Its governor and inhabitants fled. The enemy entered, burned its mosque, devastated it, and carried away the inhabitants' possessions. Al-Rashīd rebuilt it when he became caliph.

500A man from Manbij related to me: Al-Rashīd wrote to Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm confirming him in his office. Accordingly, the affairs and rebuilding of al-Ḥadath proceeded under his supervision on al-Rashīd's behalf. Al-Rashīd subsequently dismissed him.

501They said: Mālik b. ʿAbd al-Khathʿamī, known as “Mālik of the summer campaigns,” a man of Palestine, raided Byzantine territory in the year 46 and acquired abundant booty. On his return, he stopped at a place called al-Rahwa, fifteen miles from the pass of al-Ḥadath, and remained there for three days. He sold the booty and apportioned its shares, and that place came to be called Rahwat Mālik.

Zibaṭra and Ḥiṣn Manṣūr

502They said: Marj ʿAbd al-Wāḥid had been a protected pasture for Muslim horses. When al-Ḥadath and Zibaṭra were built, it was no longer needed for that purpose and was put under cultivation.

They said: Zibaṭra was an old Byzantine fortress, conquered along with the original fortress of al-Ḥadath by Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī. It remained standing until the Byzantines devastated it in the days of al-Walīd b. Yazīd. It was rebuilt, but without strong construction. During the turmoil of Marwān b. Muḥammad, the Byzantines encamped against it and demolished it. Al-Manṣūr rebuilt it. They came out again and damaged it; al-Rashīd rebuilt it through Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm and supplied it with a garrison.

During the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn, the Byzantines made a surprise attack upon it, damaged it, and raided the livestock pastures of its inhabitants, driving off their animals. Al-Maʾmūn ordered it repaired and fortified. In the year 210, envoys from the Byzantine ruler came asking for peace, but he refused them. He wrote to the commanders of the frontier districts, who ranged through Byzantine territory, killing many, overrunning its lands, and gaining a notable victory, though Yaqẓān b. ʿAbd al-Aʿlā b. Aḥmad b. Yazīd b. Usayd al-Sulamī was killed.

Later, during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim billāh, Abū Isḥāq b. al-Rashīd, the Byzantines attacked Zibaṭra, killed its men, took its women captive, and destroyed it. This enraged and angered al-Muʿtaṣim. He campaigned against them as far as ʿAmmūriyya [Amorium], destroying fortresses on the way. He laid siege to ʿAmmūriyya until he captured it, killed its fighting men, took the women and children captive, and destroyed it. He ordered Zibaṭra rebuilt, fortified, and stocked with a garrison. The Byzantines attempted to take it afterward, but were unable to do so.

503Abū ʿAmr al-Bāhilī and others related to me: Ḥiṣn Manṣūr [the Fortress of Manṣūr] took its name from Manṣūr b. Jaʿwana b. al-Ḥārith al-ʿĀmirī of Qays, because he had overseen its construction and repair. He was stationed there in the days of Marwān to repel the enemy, with a large garrison from Syria and al-Jazīra.

This Manṣūr had been in command of the people of al-Ruhā when they rebelled at the beginning of the [Abbasid] dynasty. Al-Manṣūr, while governor of al-Jazīra and Armenia for Abū al-ʿAbbās, besieged them. When he captured al-Ruhā, Manṣūr fled; he was later given a guarantee of safety and reappeared. When ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAlī renounced allegiance to Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, he appointed Manṣūr chief of his police. When ʿAbdallāh fled to Basra, Manṣūr went into hiding. He was betrayed in the year 141 and brought before al-Manṣūr, who had him killed at al-Raqqa on his return from Jerusalem.

Others say that after Ibn ʿAlī fled, Manṣūr received a guarantee of safety and reappeared, but letters he had sent to the Byzantines were then discovered, showing treachery against Islam. When al-Manṣūr arrived at al-Raqqa from Jerusalem in the year 141, he sent for Manṣūr and had him beheaded there, then departed for al-Hāshimiyya near Kūfa. Al-Rashīd rebuilt Ḥiṣn Manṣūr and provided it with a garrison during al-Mahdī's caliphate.

Chapter 41

The transfer of the registers from Greek

504They said: The fiscal registers (dīwān) of Syria continued to be kept in Greek until ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān came to power. In the year 81 he ordered their transfer [into Arabic]. This came about because one of the Greek-speaking secretaries needed to write something and, finding no water, urinated in the inkwell. When ʿAbd al-Malik learned of it, he punished him and ordered Sulaymān b. Saʿd to transfer the registers. Sulaymān asked to be supported with a year's land-tax revenue from al-Urdunn [the Jordan district]. ʿAbd al-Malik agreed and appointed him governor of al-Urdunn. Before the year was over, Sulaymān had finished the transfer and brought the registers to ʿAbd al-Malik.

The caliph summoned Sarjūn, his secretary, and showed him the work. Sarjūn was distressed and left downcast. A group of Greek-speaking secretaries met him, and he said: “Seek a livelihood other than this profession, for God has cut it off from you.”

He said: The assigned revenue (waẓīfa) of al-Urdunn, which had been granted as assistance, was 180,000 dinars; that of Palestine was 350,000 dinars; that of Damascus was 400,000 dinars; and that of Ḥimṣ, together with Qinnasrīn and the districts now called the ʿAwāṣim, was 800,000 dinars, though it is also said to have been 700,000 dinars.

Chapter 42

The conquest of Armenia

505Muḥammad b. Ismāʿīl, one of the inhabitants of Bardhaʿa, and others related to me from Abū Barāʾ ʿAnbasa b. Baḥr al-Armanī. Muḥammad b. Bishr al-Qālī also related to me from his teachers, as did Barmak b. ʿAbdallāh al-Dabīlī, Muḥammad b. al-Mukhayyis al-Khilāṭī, and others, from people knowledgeable about the affairs of Armenia. I have set out their reports, combining portions of one with another. They said:

Shimshāṭ, Qālīqalā, Khilāṭ, Arjīsh, and Bājnays were called Fourth Armenia; the district of al-Busfurrajān, Dabīl, Sirāj Ṭayr, and Baghravand was called Third Armenia; Jurzān was called Second Armenia; and al-Sīsajān and Arrān were called First Armenia.

It is also said that Shimshāṭ alone was Fourth Armenia; that Qālīqalā, Khilāṭ, Arjīsh, and Bājnays were Third Armenia; Sirāj Ṭayr, Baghravand, Dabīl, and al-Busfurrajān were Second Armenia; and al-Sīsajān, Arrān, and Tiflīs were First Armenia.

Jurzān and Arrān were in the hands of the Khazars; the rest of Armenia was in the hands of the Byzantines and governed by the ruler of Armeniakōn. The Khazars would go out on raids, sometimes reaching al-Dīnawar. King Qubādh b. Fīrūz therefore sent one of his great commanders with twelve thousand men. He overran Arrān and conquered the land from the river known as al-Rass to Shirwān. Qubādh then followed him, building the city of al-Baylaqān in Arrān, Bardhaʿa, the chief city of the entire frontier, and the city of Qibala, which is Khazar [territory]. He then built the mudbrick barrier between Shirwān and the Gate of the Alans (Bāb al-Lān), and along this barrier established 360 cities, which fell into ruin after the building of al-Bāb wa'l-Abwāb.

Qubādh was succeeded by his son Anūshirwān, Kisrā b. Qubādh. He built the cities of al-Shābarān and Masqaṭ, and afterward the city of al-Bāb wa'l-Abwāb [the Gate and the Gates]. They were called “gates” because they had been built across a mountain passage. He populated these places with people he called the Siyāsījīn.

In Arrān he built the Gates of Shakkan, al-Qamībarān, and the Gates of the Dūdāniyya, a people who claim descent from Dūdān b. Asad b. Khuzayma. He built al-Dardhaqiyya, comprising twelve gates, each a stone fortress. In Jurzān he built a city called Sughdabīl, settled Sogdians and descendants of Persians there, and made it a military outpost. On the Byzantine side of Jurzān he built fortresses called Bāb Fīrūzqubādh, Bāb Lādhiqa, and Bāb Bāriqa, the latter by the Sea of Ṭarābazunda. He built Bāb al-Lān and Bāb Samsakhī, and the fortresses of al-Jardamān and Shamshaldī.

Anūshirwān conquered all the parts of Armenia that had been in Byzantine hands. He restored and fortified Dabīl, built the city of al-Nashawā, the chief city of al-Busfurrajān, and built the fortress of Wayṣ and other fortresses in al-Sīsajān, including Qalʿat al-Kilāb and Sāhyūnus. He settled the forts with strong and courageous men of the Siyāsījīn.

Anūshirwān then wrote to the king of the Turks proposing a truce and peace, so that the two rulers might act together. To reassure him, he sought the hand of the Turk's daughter in marriage and professed a desire for kinship through marriage. He sent the Turk a slave girl whom one of his wives had adopted, pretending she was his daughter. The Turk sent Anūshirwān his own daughter.

The Turk then came to meet him. They met at al-Barshaliyya, spent several days drinking together, became familiar with one another, and each showed the other goodwill. Anūshirwān secretly instructed a group of his trusted intimates to attack and burn a section of the Turk's camp by night. They did so. In the morning the Turk complained, but Anūshirwān denied ordering it or knowing that any of his men had done it. Several nights later he ordered the same men to repeat the attack. When they did so, the Turk protested bitterly, until Anūshirwān treated him kindly and offered apologies, and he calmed down.

Anūshirwān next ordered a fire to be started in a part of his own camp containing only huts made of grass and twigs. In the morning he complained to the Turk: “Your men nearly destroyed my camp, and there was reason to suspect them.” The Turk swore that he had been responsible for none of it. Anūshirwān replied: “My brother, our soldiers and yours have come to dislike our peace because it deprives them of the spoils they used to obtain in the raids and wars between us. I cannot be sure that they will not create incidents which poison our hearts, after we have become reconciled and sincere with one another, so that we return to hostility after marriage ties and affection. The wisest course is for you to permit me to build a wall between us with a gate, so that none may pass from our side to yours, or yours to ours, except those whom you and we approve.” The Turk agreed.

The Turk returned to his country, and Anūshirwān remained to construct the wall. On the seaward side he made it of rock and lead, three hundred cubits wide, and joined it to the mountain peaks. He ordered stones brought out in boats and sunk into the sea; when they rose above the water's surface, he built on them, extending the wall three miles into the sea. When the construction was complete, he hung iron gates across its entrance and assigned one hundred horsemen to guard it, where formerly the place had needed fifty thousand soldiers. He also placed a protective siege structure (dabbāba) upon it [the precise object intended is uncertain]. Later someone told the Khāqān: “He deceived you, gave you someone other than his daughter in marriage, and fortified himself against you.” The Khāqān could devise no remedy.

Anūshirwān installed subordinate kings and assigned each a region to rule under a royal title. Among them were the Khāqān of the Mountain, ruler of al-Sarīr, called Waharārzānshāh; the ruler of Fīlān, called Fīlānshāh; Ṭabarsarānshāh; the ruler of al-Lakz, called Jarshānshāh; the ruler of Masqaṭ, whose kingship later ceased; the ruler of Līrān, called Līrānshāh; the ruler of Shirwān, called Shirwānshāh; the ruler of Bakh, who ruled Bakh; and the ruler of Zarīkarān. He left the kings of the Caucasus Mountains in possession of their kingdoms and concluded agreements with them for tribute. [The Arabic page reference printed in the supplied digital text here reads “p. 166,” apparently an error for p. 196.]

Armenia remained in Persian hands until the advent of Islam. Many of the Siyāsījīn then abandoned their fortresses and towns, which fell into ruin, while the Khazars and Byzantines took control of what had formerly been in their hands.

506They said: At one time the Byzantine dominions became divided, with their rulers resembling independent petty kings. One of these men ruled Armeniakōn. When he died, his wife, named Qālī, succeeded him. She founded Qālīqalā and named it Qālīqāla, meaning “Qālī's beneficence.” He said that her likeness was carved on one of its gates. The Arabs Arabized Qālīqāla as Qālīqalā.

507They said: When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān became caliph, he wrote to Muʿāwiya, his governor over Syria, al-Jazīra, and their frontiers, ordering him to send Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī to Armenia. Ḥabīb had distinguished himself in the conquests of Syria and the campaigns against the Byzantines, as ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān ﵃—and those who came afterward knew. It is also said, more reliably, that ʿUthmān wrote directly to Ḥabīb ordering him to attack Armenia.

Ḥabīb marched against it with six thousand troops, or according to another account eight thousand, from Syria and al-Jazīra. He came to Qālīqalā and encamped against it. The inhabitants came out and fought him, but he drove them back into the city. They requested safe-conduct to leave and an agreement for payment of the jizya. Many departed for Byzantine territory. Ḥabīb remained there with his men for several months.

Then he learned that the Byzantine governor of Armeniakōn had mustered a great force against the Muslims, reinforced by men from the Alans, the Abkhaz, and Samandar among the Khazars. He wrote to ʿUthmān requesting reinforcements. ʿUthmān wrote to Muʿāwiya asking him to send men from Syria and al-Jazīra eager for campaigning and booty. Muʿāwiya sent two thousand men, whom he settled at Qālīqalā, granting them allotments of land and making them a frontier garrison.

When Ḥabīb's letter reached ʿUthmān, he also wrote to Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya, his governor of Kūfa, ordering him to send an army under Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī, known as Salmān al-Khayl [Salmān of the Horses], a virtuous and accomplished campaigner. Salmān set out toward Ḥabīb with six thousand Kufans. The Byzantines and their allies had meanwhile advanced and encamped on the Euphrates, and the reinforcements were slow to reach Ḥabīb. The Muslims therefore attacked the enemy by night, annihilated them, and killed their commander.

That night, Ḥabīb's wife, Umm ʿAbdallāh bt. Yazīd al-Kalbiyya, asked him: “Where shall I meet you?” He replied, “At the tyrant's pavilion—or in Paradise.” When he reached the pavilion, he found her there.
