508They said: Salmān arrived after the Muslims had finished with their enemy. The Kufans asked to share in the booty, but the others refused. Ḥabīb and Salmān exchanged harsh words, and some of the Muslims threatened to kill Salmān. A poet said:

If you kill Salmān, we shall kill your Ḥabīb;if you set out toward Ibn ʿAffān, we shall set out too.

The matter was reported in writing to ʿUthmān, who replied: “The booty belongs to the Syrians, ready for the taking [bārida, literally ‘cold’].” He wrote to Salmān ordering him to attack Arrān.

Some, however, have related that Salmān b. Rabīʿa marched to Armenia during ʿUthmān's caliphate, took captives and booty, and returned to al-Walīd b. ʿUqba at Ḥadīthat al-Mawṣil in the year 25. There a letter from ʿUthmān reached al-Walīd, reporting that Muʿāwiya had written of great Byzantine forces assembled against the Muslims and had requested reinforcements, and ordering al-Walīd to send eight thousand men. He sent them under Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī, while Muʿāwiya sent Ḥabīb b. Maslama al-Fihrī with an equal number. They captured fortresses and took prisoners but disputed over command. The Syrians plotted to kill Salmān, whereupon the poet said, “If you kill [Salmān]”—the verse cited above.

The first account is more firmly established. Several elders of Qālīqalā related it to me, and al-ʿAṭṭāf b. Sufyān Abū al-Aṣbagh, its judge, wrote it to me.

509Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Jaʿfar, from his father: Ḥabīb b. Maslama besieged the people of Dabīl and remained before it. Al-Mūriyān the Byzantine met him; Ḥabīb surprised him in a night attack, killed him, and seized the goods in his camp. Salmān then arrived to join him. Yet the established account among the people there is that Ḥabīb met him at Qālīqalā.

510Muḥammad b. Bishr and Ibn Warz al-Qāliyyān related to me from elders of Qālīqalā: From the time Qālīqalā was conquered, the city and its inhabitants continued to hold out securely, until the tyrant came out in the year 133, besieged Malaṭya, demolished its walls, and expelled its Muslim inhabitants toward al-Jazīra. He then encamped at Marj al-Ḥaṣā and sent Kūsān the Armenian against Qālīqalā. Kūsān encamped there and besieged it. Its inhabitants were few in number and its governor was Abū Karīma.

Two Armenian brothers from among the inhabitants of Qālīqalā dug through a blocked passage in its wall and went out to Kūsān. They brought him into the city, and he gained control of it. He killed and took captives, demolished the city, and carried its contents to the tyrant, who distributed the captives among his men.

511Al-Wāqidī said: In the year 139, al-Manṣūr ransomed those captives from Qālīqalā who were still alive. He rebuilt and restored the city, sent those whom he had ransomed back to it, and called upon troops from al-Jazīra and elsewhere to settle there. The Byzantine ruler later attacked Qālīqalā during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim billāh and battered its wall until it nearly collapsed. Al-Muʿtaṣim spent five hundred thousand dirhams on it until it was securely fortified.

512They said: After taking Qālīqalā, Ḥabīb went on to Marbālā. The governor (baṭrīq) of Khilāṭ came to him bearing a letter from ʿIyāḍ b. Ghanm. ʿIyāḍ had guaranteed his person, wealth, and territory and had agreed with him on a fixed tribute. Ḥabīb ratified that agreement. Then Ḥabīb halted between al-Harak and Dasht al-Wark, where the governor of Khilāṭ brought him the money he owed and offered him a gift, which Ḥabīb refused. He entered Khilāṭ and proceeded to a place whose name is corrupted in the source as “al-Ṣaṣā(?)h.” There the ruler of Maks, a district of al-Busfurrajān, met him. Ḥabīb settled the tribute due from his lands, assigned a man to accompany him, and wrote a document of peace and safe-conduct.

He sent forces into the villages of Arjīsh and Bājnays, took control of them, and collected poll-tax from their inhabitants. Their leading men came to him, and he agreed upon the land-tax due from their districts. He did not interfere with Lake al-Ṭarīkh, whose fishing remained unrestricted until Muḥammad b. Marwān b. al-Ḥakam was appointed over al-Jazīra and Armenia. Muḥammad appropriated its fishery and sold its catch, deriving revenue from it. It later passed to Marwān b. Muḥammad, from whom it was confiscated.

Ḥabīb then went to Azdasāṭ, the village of the crimson dye (qirmiz), crossed the River of the Kurds, and encamped on the plain of Dabīl. He sent cavalry parties ahead, then advanced and encamped before its gate. Its inhabitants fortified themselves and shot at him, so he set up a mangonel and bombarded them. They eventually asked for safe-conduct and peace, which he granted. His cavalry ranged through Jarnā and reached Ashūsh, Dhāt al-Lujum, al-Jabal [a corrupted place-name follows], and Wādī al-Aḥrār, and took control of all the villages of Dabīl. He sent to Sirāj Ṭayr and Baghravand, whose governor came to him and concluded peace for a tribute to be paid, pledging sincere dealings with the Muslims, hospitality toward them, and help against their enemies.

The text of the treaty with Dabīl was:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This is a document from Ḥabīb b. Maslama to the Christians, Magians, and Jews of Dabīl, those present and those absent. I grant you safety for your persons, your property, your churches, your places of worship, and the wall of your city. You are secure, and we are bound to keep our covenant with you so long as you keep it and pay the jizya and kharāj. God is witness, and God suffices as witness.

Sealed by Ḥabīb b. Maslama.

Ḥabīb next came to al-Nashawā and took it on the same terms as Dabīl. The governor of al-Busfurrajān came before him, and he concluded peace for all his lands, on terms including a tax to be paid annually. [The supplied Arabic has two corrupted words in this clause, “هصايلته” and “افارستة,” which cannot safely be interpreted.] Then he came to al-Sīsajān. Its inhabitants fought him, but he routed them and took Wayṣ. He made peace with the inhabitants of its fortresses on condition that they pay a fixed tax, then marched toward Jurzān.

513Elders of Dabīl, among them Barmak b. ʿAbdallāh, related to me: Ḥabīb b. Maslama set out with his men toward Jurzān. When they reached Dhāt al-Lujum [the Place of Bridles], they let some of their animals graze and gathered up their bridles. A group of non-Arabs came out against them and forced them away before they could collect the bridles. The Muslims fought them, but the attackers drove them back and took the bridles and whatever animals they could capture. The Muslims then attacked them again, killed them, and recovered what had been taken. The place was therefore called Dhāt al-Lujum.

They said: An envoy from the governor and people of Jurzān came to Ḥabīb as he was heading toward them. He delivered their message and requested a document of peace and safety. Ḥabīb wrote to them:

To proceed: Your envoy came before me and the believers accompanying me and conveyed your message. We are a community whom God has honored and favored; such has God done, and abundant praise belongs to Him. May God bless Muḥammad, His prophet and His chosen one among His creatures, and grant him peace.

You have stated that you have accepted our peace. I have assessed your gift and credited it against your jizya. I have written you a guarantee of safety and stipulated a condition in it. If you accept and fulfill it, [the guarantee stands]; otherwise, know that you face war from God and His Messenger. Peace be upon those who follow guidance.

He then arrived at Tiflīs and wrote its inhabitants the following treaty:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This is a document from Ḥabīb b. Maslama to the people of Ṭiflīs, in Manjlīs of Jurzān al-Qirmiz, granting them safety for their persons, churches, monasteries, prayers, and religion, on condition that they acknowledge submission and pay the jizya: one dinar for every household. You are not to combine separate households to reduce the jizya, nor are we to divide households to increase it.

It is incumbent upon us to give you sincere counsel and support you against the enemies of God and His Messenger ﷺ as far as we are able. You must provide a needy Muslim with one night's customary hospitality, from such lawful food as the People of the Book have and as we may eat. If a Muslim is stranded among you, you must convey him to the nearest body of believers unless you are prevented from doing so. If you turn [to God] and establish the prayer, you are our brothers in religion; otherwise the jizya remains due from you.

Should the Muslims become occupied elsewhere and an enemy subdue you, you will not be held responsible for that, nor will it invalidate your covenant.

These are your rights and your obligations. God and His angels bear witness, and God suffices as witness.

Al-Jarrāḥ b. ʿAbdallāh al-Ḥakamī wrote the people of Tiflīs another document. Its text was:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

This is a document from al-Jarrāḥ b. ʿAbdallāh to the inhabitants of Tiflīs in the district of Manjlīs, of the province of Jurzān. They brought me a guarantee of safety from Ḥabīb b. Maslama, on condition that they acknowledge the obligations of the jizya. [The document also shows] that he had made an agreement with them concerning their lands, vineyards, and mills called Awārī and Sābīnā in the district of Manjlīs, and concerning Ṭaʿām and Dīdūnā in the district of Qaḥwīṭ of Jurzān, that they should pay one hundred dirhams each year for these mills and vineyards, without a second payment.

I have confirmed their guarantee of safety and their treaty and have ordered that nothing be added to their dues. Whoever has this letter read to him must not exceed these terms in his dealings with them, God willing. Written [accordingly].

514They said: Ḥabīb took Ḥawāriḥ, Kasfaras [uncertain reading], Kasāl, Khanān, Samsakhī, al-Jardamān, Kastasjī, Shūsht, and Bāzalīt by treaty, on condition that their inhabitants' blood be spared, their places of worship and walls be left intact, and tribute be paid on their lands and persons. He also concluded agreements with the people of Qalarjīt, Tharyālīt, Khākhīṭ, Khūkhīṭ, Arṭahāl, and Bāb al-Lāl, and made terms with the Ṣanāriyya and Dūdāniyya for tribute.

515They said: When ʿUthmān ordered Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī to march to Arrān, he conquered al-Baylaqān by treaty, granting its inhabitants safety for their lives, property, and city walls, while stipulating payment of the jizya and kharāj. Salmān then advanced to Bardhaʿa and encamped beside al-Tharthūr, a river less than a farsakh from it. Its inhabitants shut their gates against him. He pressed them for several days and raided their villages, whose crops were ready for harvesting. They agreed to peace on the same terms as al-Baylaqān, opened their gates, and he entered and remained there.

He dispatched cavalry who conquered Shafshīn, al-Masfuwān, Awdh, al-Miṣriyān [reading marked uncertain in the source], al-Harḥaliyān, and Tabār, all of them rural districts, together with other parts of Arrān. He called the Kurds of al-Balāsajān to Islam, but they fought him. He overcame them; some agreed to pay jizya, while others, few in number, paid ṣadaqa [the Muslim alms-tax].

516A group of inhabitants of Bardhaʿa related to me: Shamkūr was an ancient city, and Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī sent a force which conquered it. It remained settled and prosperous until it was destroyed by the Sāwardiyya, a people who gathered together in the days following the departure of Yazīd b. Usayd from Armenia. They became powerful and their depredations increased. Later, in the year 240, Bughā, freedman of al-Muʿtaṣim billāh ﵀—restored Shamkūr while governor of Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Shimshāṭ. He settled there Khazars who had come to him seeking protection because they wished to embrace Islam, transferred merchants from Bardhaʿa to it, and renamed it al-Mutawakkiliyya.

517They said: Salmān traveled to the confluence of the al-Rass and al-Kurr beyond Bardīj, crossed the al-Kurr, and conquered Qibala. The ruler of Shakkan and al-Qamībarān concluded peace with him for a tribute. He likewise made agreements with the people of Khīzān, the king of Shirwān, the other mountain kings, and the people of Masqaṭ, al-Shābarān, and the city of al-Bāb. But al-Bāb subsequently closed against the Muslims. The Khāqān met him with his cavalry beyond the River al-Balanjar. Salmān, may God have mercy upon him, was killed along with four thousand Muslims, and the cry of Allāhu akbar was heard at the place where they were hemmed in.

Salmān b. Rabīʿa had been the first appointed to the judgeship in Kūfa. He remained forty days without a litigant coming before him, and he transmitted reports from ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb. Concerning Salmān and Qutayba b. Muslim, Ibn Jumāna al-Bāhilī said:

We have two graves: a grave at Balanjar,and a grave in China—what graves they are!

The one in China spread his conquests far and wide;at the other rain is sought to water the paths.

Qaraẓa b. Kaʿb al-Anṣārī was with Salmān at Balanjar and brought news of his death to ʿUthmān.

518They said: After Ḥabīb had conquered the portions of Armenia mentioned above, he wrote to ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān reporting the matter. His letter reached ʿUthmān when the news of Salmān's death had also arrived. ʿUthmān considered appointing Ḥabīb over all Armenia, but then decided to keep him campaigning on the frontiers of Syria and al-Jazīra, because he had proved so useful in such operations. He appointed Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān al-ʿAbsī over the Armenian frontier instead.

Ḥudhayfa traveled to Bardhaʿa and dispatched his officials to the places between it and Qālīqalā, and toward Jīzān. Then ʿUthmān's letter reached him ordering him to return and to leave in charge Ṣila b. Zufar al-ʿAbsī, who was with him. He did so and departed. Ḥabīb returned to Syria, where he continued to campaign against the Byzantines. He settled at Ḥimṣ, but Muʿāwiya transferred him to Damascus, where he died in the year 42, aged thirty-five. Muʿāwiya had sent Ḥabīb with an army to help ʿUthmān when he was besieged. When Ḥabīb reached Wādī al-Qurā, he learned of ʿUthmān's death and turned back.

519They said: ʿUthmān appointed al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba over Azerbaijan and Armenia, then dismissed him and appointed al-Qāsim b. Rabīʿa b. Umayya b. Abī al-Ṣalt al-Thaqafī over Armenia. It is also said that he appointed ʿAmr b. Muʿāwiya b. al-Muntafiq al-ʿUqaylī. Some say a man of the Banū Kilāb governed Armenia for fifteen years after al-Mughīra, before al-ʿUqaylī was appointed.

Al-Ashʿath b. Qays governed Armenia and Azerbaijan for ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵁. Thereafter ʿAbdallāh b. Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān b. ʿAmr al-Bāhilī was appointed by Muʿāwiya. He died in Armenia and was succeeded by his brother ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān, who built and fortified Dabīl, enlarged its mosque, built al-Nashawā, repaired Bardhaʿa—or, according to some, rebuilt it—and thoroughly dug the trenches surrounding it. He also rebuilt al-Baylaqān. These towns had previously been damaged and partly ruined.

Others say that Muḥammad b. Marwān rebuilt Bardhaʿa in the days of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān. Al-Wāqidī said that ʿAbd al-Malik built Bardhaʿa under the supervision of Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān al-Bāhilī or his son. ʿAbd al-Malik had also appointed ʿUthmān b. al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ over Armenia.

520They said: During the civil war of Ibn al-Zubayr, Armenia rebelled, and its nobles and their followers withdrew their allegiance. When Muḥammad b. Marwān was appointed over Armenia by his brother ʿAbd al-Malik, he fought and defeated them, killing and taking captives, and gained control of the territory. He then promised the survivors that he would review their standing among the nobles. They assembled for this purpose in churches in the district of Khilāṭ. He locked the doors, posted guards at them, and burned the people inside. On that campaign the mother of Yazīd b. Usayd, a daughter of the governor of al-Sīsajān, was taken captive.

521They said: Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed ʿAdī b. ʿUmayra al-Kindī governor of Armenia. ʿAdī had been one of those who settled in al-Raqqa after separating from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz later also appointed him there. The Nahr ʿAdī at al-Baylaqān bears his name. Some relate that ʿUmar's governor was Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān, but this is not firmly established.

Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik then appointed Muʿallaq b. Ṣaffār al-Bahrānī, whom he dismissed in favor of al-Ḥārith b. ʿAmr al-Ṭāʾī. Al-Ḥārith attacked the people of al-Lakz, conquering the districts of Rastāq and Ḥasmadān. Al-Jarrāḥ b. ʿAbdallāh al-Ḥakamī of Madhḥij was then appointed governor of Armenia. He settled at Bardhaʿa. Complaints about differences in its measures and weights were brought before him, so he standardized them fairly and accurately. He instituted a measure called the Jarrāḥī, by which the people still transact business today.

Al-Jarrāḥ crossed the al-Kurr, continued over the river known as al-Samūr, and advanced against the Khazars, killing a great number of them. He fought the people of Ḥamzīn, then concluded a treaty with them whereby he moved them into the district of Jīzān and gave them two villages there. He attacked the people of Ghūmīk and took captives, then returned to Shakkī, while his troops wintered at Bardhaʿa and al-Baylaqān.

The Khazars rose up and crossed the al-Rass. He fought them on the plain of Warthān. They then withdrew toward Ardabīl; he engaged them four farsakhs from it, on the Armenian side. They fought for three days, and al-Jarrāḥ and his men were killed. That river therefore came to be called Nahr al-Jarrāḥ, and a bridge over it also bore his name.

Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik then appointed Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik over Armenia. Maslama sent ahead Saʿīd b. ʿAmr b. Aswad al-Jurashī, accompanied by Isḥāq b. Muslim al-ʿUqaylī and his brothers, Jaʿwana b. al-Ḥārith b. Khālid of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Rabīʿa b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa, Dhufāfa and Khālid the sons of ʿUmayr b. al-Ḥubāb al-Sulamī, al-Furāt b. Salmān al-Bāhilī, and al-Walīd b. al-Qaʿqāʿ al-ʿAbsī. They engaged the Khazars, who were besieging Warthān, raised the siege, and routed them.

The Khazars went to Maymadh in Azerbaijan. As Saʿīd prepared to fight them, a letter arrived from Maslama reproaching him for having attacked them before his arrival and informing him that command of the army had been assigned to ʿAbd al-Malik b. Muslim al-ʿUqaylī. Once Saʿīd had handed over the army, Maslama's envoy arrested him, bound him, and took him to Bardhaʿa, where he was imprisoned.

The Khazars withdrew, and Maslama pursued them and wrote to Hishām about it. Hishām replied in verse:

You leave them at Maymadh, although you can see them,and seek them out at the farthest end of the earth!

He also ordered al-Jurashī released from prison.

522They said: Maslama concluded peace with the people of Jīzān and ordered its fortress demolished. He took estates for himself there, now known as Ḥawz Jīzān. The mountain kings sought peace with him: Shirwānshāh, Līrānshāh, Ṭabarsarānshāh, Fīlānshāh, and Jarshānshāh came to him, as did the ruler of Masqaṭ.

Maslama then made for al-Bāb and captured it. A thousand Khazar households were in its citadel. He besieged them and bombarded them with stones, then with pieces of iron made in the shape of stones, but to no effect. He then went to the spring from which Anūshirwān had channeled water into their reservoir. He slaughtered cattle and sheep and threw their dung and asafoetida (ḥiltīt) into it. Within a night their water became worm-infested, foul, and spoiled. Under cover of darkness they fled and evacuated the citadel.

Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik settled twenty-four thousand Syrians in al-Bāb wa'l-Abwāb on military stipends. The inhabitants of al-Bāb therefore do not permit a governor to enter their city today unless he brings money to distribute among them. Maslama built a granary for food, another for barley, and a storehouse for weapons. He ordered the reservoir filled in and the city and its battlements repaired.

Marwān b. Muḥammad accompanied Maslama and fought fiercely alongside him against the Khazars. After Maslama, Hishām appointed Saʿīd al-Jurashī, who remained on the frontier two years. Then Marwān b. Muḥammad was appointed. He settled at Kasāl and built its town, forty farsakhs from Bardhaʿa and twenty from Tiflīs.

He entered Khazar territory by the direction of Bāb al-Lān, guided there by Usayd b. Ẓāfir al-Sulamī, Abū Yazīd, along with the mountain kings from the district of al-Bāb wa'l-Abwāb. Marwān raided the Slavs (Ṣaqāliba) living in Khazar territory, captured twenty thousand households of them, and settled them at Khākhīṭ. Later they killed their commander and fled. He pursued and killed them.

523They said: When the Khazar ruler learned how many men Marwān had brought to overrun his country, and how well armed and powerful they were, his heart quailed and he was filled with fear. As Marwān approached, he sent an envoy calling upon him to accept Islam or face war. The ruler replied, “I have accepted Islam. Send someone to explain it to me.” Marwān did so. The ruler outwardly professed Islam, and Marwān made peace with him on condition that he remain in possession of his kingdom. Marwān departed with a large number of Khazars and settled them between al-Samūr and al-Shābarān on the plain of al-Lakz.

Marwān then entered the land of al-Sarīr, attacked its inhabitants, and conquered fortresses there. The king of al-Sarīr submitted and obeyed him, agreeing to deliver one thousand persons every year—five hundred boys and five hundred girls with black hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes—and one hundred thousand mudd of grain to be deposited in the granaries of al-Bāb. Marwān took hostages from him.

He made peace with the people of Tūmān for one hundred persons annually—fifty girls and fifty boys, five years old, with black hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes—and twenty thousand mudd for the granaries every year. He then entered Zarīkarān and agreed with its king on fifty persons and ten thousand mudd for the granaries each year.

He next came to Ḥamzīn, whose ruler refused to make peace. Marwān besieged their fortress for a month, captured it, burned it, and devastated it. The agreement imposed on the ruler was to deliver five hundred persons as a single payment, after which there would be no further claim against him on that account, together with thirty thousand mudd carried to the granaries of al-Bāb annually. He then came to Sandān, which he took by treaty: its ruler was to pay him one hundred persons once, with no further liability in future, and to deliver five thousand mudd to the granaries of al-Bāb every year. He assessed the people of Ṭabarsarānshāh at ten thousand mudd annually for the granaries of al-Bāb.

He imposed nothing on Fīlānshāh because of his effective service, distinguished fighting, and commendable conduct. Marwān then encamped before the fortress of the ruler of al-Lakz, who had refused to pay any of his assessed dues. The ruler went out intending to reach the Khazar ruler, but a shepherd, not recognizing him, shot and killed him with an arrow. The people of al-Lakz made peace on condition that twenty thousand mudd be conveyed to the granaries, and Marwān placed Khashrama al-Sulamī in charge of them.

Marwān marched to the fortress of the ruler of Shirwān, called Kharsh, situated on the sea. Its ruler submitted to obedience and agreed to come down to the plain, and Marwān imposed an annual payment of ten thousand mudd. He further stipulated that the ruler of Shirwān was to serve in the vanguard whenever the Muslims began a campaign against the Khazars and in the rearguard when they returned; Fīlānshāh was simply to campaign with them; and Ṭabarsarānshāh was to serve in the rearguard on the outward march and the vanguard on the return. Marwān then marched against the Dūdāniyya and attacked them.

News then reached him of the killing of al-Walīd b. Yazīd, and Thābit b. Nuʿaym al-Judhāmī rose against him. Musāfir al-Qaṣṣāb, one of those who had helped al-Ḍaḥḥāk the Khārijite gain a foothold at al-Bāb, went to al-Ḍaḥḥāk, embraced his position, and was appointed by him over Armenia and Azerbaijan. Musāfir entered Ardabīl secretly, where some of the Shurāt [Khārijites] joined him. They went to Bājrawān, where others holding their views joined them; then to Warthān, where many residents of like mind accompanied them. They crossed to al-Baylaqān, where another large group joined, and then encamped at a place whose name is corrupted in the source as “?wanān.”

Marwān b. Muḥammad appointed Isḥāq b. Muslim over Armenia, and Isḥāq continued to fight Musāfir, who was at Qalʿat al-Kilāb in al-Sīsajān. When the blessed [Abbasid] dynasty came to power and Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr became governor of al-Jazīra and Armenia during the caliphate of al-Saffāḥ Abū al-ʿAbbās ﵀—he dispatched a Khurāsānī commander against Musāfir and his companions. The commander fought them, defeated them, and killed Musāfir. The people of al-Baylaqān had fortified themselves at Qalʿat al-Kilāb under their leader Qudad b. Aṣfar al-Baylaqānī. They were induced to descend from the fortress under a guarantee of safety.

When al-Manṣūr became caliph ﵀ he appointed Yazīd b. Usayd al-Sulamī over Armenia. Yazīd conquered Bāb al-Lān and stationed a registered frontier garrison there. He subdued the Ṣanāriyya until they paid kharāj. Al-Manṣūr then wrote ordering him to establish a marriage alliance with the Khazar ruler; Yazīd did so. His wife, the ruler's daughter, bore him a son, but the son died and she died in childbirth.

Yazīd took charge of the naphtha deposits and saltworks of Shirwān, collecting their revenues and assigning officials over them. He built Lesser Arjīl and the city of Greater Arjīl, settling people from Palestine in both.

524Muḥammad b. Ismāʿīl related to me from a group of elders of Bardhaʿa: Al-Shammākhiyya in the district of Shirwān was named after al-Shammākh b. Shujāʿ, who was ruler of Shirwān during Saʿīd b. Sālim al-Bāhilī's governorship of Armenia.

525Muḥammad b. Ismāʿīl related to me from the elders: The inhabitants of Armenia rebelled during the governorship of al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba al-Ṭāʾī, after the removal of Ibn Usayd and Bakkār b. Muslim al-ʿUqaylī. Their leader was Mūshāʾīl the Armenian. Al-Manṣūr ﵀ sent reinforcements to al-Ḥasan under ʿĀmir b. Ismāʿīl. Al-Ḥasan fought Mūshāʾīl, killed him, dispersed his forces, and restored order. The Nahr al-Ḥasan at al-Baylaqān, the garden known as Bāgh al-Ḥasan at Bardhaʿa, and the estates called al-Ḥasaniyya all bear his name.

After al-Ḥasan b. Qaḥṭaba, Armenia was governed in succession by ʿUthmān b. ʿUmāra b. Khuraym, Rawḥ b. Ḥātim al-Muhallabī, Khuzayma b. Khāzim, Yazīd b. Mazyad al-Shaybānī, ʿUbaydallāh b. al-Mahdī, al-Faḍl b. Yaḥyā, Saʿīd b. Sālim, and Muḥammad b. Yazīd b. Mazyad. Khuzayma governed with the greatest severity of them all. He introduced land surveying in Dabīl and al-Nashawā, where it had not previously been practiced.

The Armenian governors (baṭāriqa) continued to reside in their own territories, each defending his district. When a frontier governor arrived, they dealt cautiously with him: if they found him upright, firm, well supplied with men and equipment, they paid him the kharāj and submitted; otherwise they perceived his weakness and treated his authority lightly. During al-Maʾmūn's caliphate, Khālid b. Yazīd b. Mazyad was appointed over them. He accepted their gifts and became familiar with them. His conduct corrupted their attitude and emboldened them against later governors of al-Maʾmūn.

Al-Muʿtaṣim billāh then appointed al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī al-Bādhighīsī, known as al-Maʾmūnī, over the frontier. He neglected its governors and nobles and treated them indulgently, so that they grew more rebellious against the government and more oppressive toward their subjects. Isḥāq b. Ismāʿīl b. Shuʿayb, a freedman of the Banū Umayya, seized control of Jurzān. Sahl b. Sunbāṭ, a local governor, attacked an official whom Ḥaydar b. Kāwūs al-Afshīn had appointed over Armenia, killed his secretary, and the official barely escaped with his life.

Further governors of Armenia accepted whatever contributions its inhabitants volunteered and were content with whatever kharāj they could obtain. Then the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh appointed Yūsuf b. Muḥammad b. Yūsuf al-Marwazī governor of Armenia in the second year of his caliphate. When Yūsuf came to Khilāṭ he seized its governor, Baqrāṭ b. Ashūṭ, and sent him to Sāmarrāʾ. This alienated the local governors, nobles, and dominant chiefs.

One of Yūsuf's officials, called al-ʿAlāʾ b. Aḥmad, then went to a monastery in al-Sīsajān known as Dayr al-Aqdāḥ [Monastery of the Cups], long revered and endowed with gifts by the Christians of Armenia. He seized everything in it and mistreated its people. The governors were deeply angered and regarded this as a grave offense. They corresponded among themselves, urging one another to rebellion. They secretly encouraged the Khuwāythiyya, non-Arabs known as the Arṭān, to attack Yūsuf, stirring them up against him because of his arrest of their governor Baqrāṭ. Each of the governors and dominant chiefs supplied cavalry and infantry to support them. They attacked Yūsuf at a place whose reading is uncertain in the supplied Arabic (“?ṭrūn”), while he had scattered his men among the villages. They killed him and seized the possessions in his camp.

Al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh then appointed Bughā al-Kabīr over Armenia. When Bughā reached Bidlīs, he seized Mūsā b. Zurāra, who had approved and assisted in the killing of Yūsuf out of anger over Baqrāṭ's arrest. He fought the Khuwāythiyya, killed many, and took numerous captives. He then besieged Ashūṭ b. Ḥamza [reading uncertain] b. Jājiq, the governor of al-Busfurrajān, at al-Bāq. He induced him to come down from his fortress and sent him to Sāmarrāʾ.

Bughā proceeded to Jurzān, captured Isḥāq b. Ismāʿīl, and executed him after taking him prisoner. He conquered Jurzān and carried away people from Arrān and the outer districts of Armenia, including al-Sīsajān, who had rebelled or disobeyed, Christians and others, until that frontier was restored to a condition of order it had not known before. He returned to Sāmarrāʾ in the year 241.

Part Three

Egypt and the West

Chapter 43

The conquests of Egypt and the Maghrib

526They said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ had besieged Caesarea after the people returned from the Battle of al-Yarmūk. When Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān became governor, ʿAmr left his son in charge of the siege and proceeded to Egypt on his own initiative with 3,500 men. ʿUmar was angered by this and wrote rebuking and sharply censuring him for acting on his own judgment without authorization. He ordered him to return to his post if the letter reached him before he entered Egypt. The letter arrived while he was at al-ʿArīsh.

It is also said that ʿUmar wrote ordering ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ to set out for Egypt, and that the letter reached him while he was besieging Caesarea. The messenger who brought it was Sharīk b. ʿAbda. ʿAmr offered him one thousand dinars, but Sharīk refused them. He then asked Sharīk to conceal the matter and not tell ʿUmar about it.

527They said: ʿAmr marched to Egypt in the year 19. He stopped at al-ʿArīsh and then came to al-Faramā, whose inhabitants had prepared themselves for battle. He fought and defeated them, seized their camp, and advanced toward al-Fusṭāṭ , encamping at the Gardens of al-Rayḥān. The people of al-Fusṭāṭ had dug a defensive trench. The city's name was al-Yūna, but the Muslims called it al-Fusṭāṭ because they said, “This is the fusṭāṭ [encampment or gathering place] of the people.” Others say that ʿAmr pitched a tent (fusṭāṭ) there, and that it was named for that reason.

528They said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ had not been besieging the people of al-Fusṭāṭ for long when al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām b. Khuwaylid arrived with ten thousand men—or, according to another account, twelve thousand—including Khārija b. Ḥudhāfa al-ʿAdawī and ʿUmayr b. Wahb al-Jumaḥī.

Al-Zubayr had intended to go on campaign and wished to travel to Antioch. ʿUmar said to him: “Abū ʿAbdallāh, would you accept the governorship of Egypt?” He replied: “I have no need of it, but I will go out as a fighter and a helper to the Muslims. If I find that ʿAmr has already conquered it, I will not interfere with his administration, but will go to one of the coastal regions and station myself there as a frontier guard. If I find him still engaged in battle, I will join him.” And he set out on this understanding.

529They said: Al-Zubayr fought from one direction and ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ from another. Then al-Zubayr brought a ladder, climbed it until he reached the top of the fortress, and, with his sword drawn, proclaimed Allāhu akbar. The Muslims likewise proclaimed Allāhu akbar and followed him. The fortress was taken by force, and the Muslims seized what was inside it. ʿAmr allowed its inhabitants to remain as protected subjects (ahl al-dhimma), imposing poll tax (jizya) upon their persons and land-tax (kharāj) upon their lands.

He wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb about this, and ʿUmar approved it. Al-Zubayr marked out an allotment in Egypt and built a well-known house. ʿAbdallāh b. al-Zubayr stayed there when he campaigned in Ifrīqiya with Ibn Abī Sarḥ. Al-Zubayr's ladder remains in Egypt.

530ʿAffān b. Muslim related to us: Ḥammād b. Salama related to us, from Hishām b. ʿUrwa, that al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām was sent to Egypt. Someone said to him: “There is stabbing and plague there.” He replied: “It is precisely for stabbing and plague that we have come.” He said: They placed ladders against the walls and climbed them.

531ʿAmr al-Nāqid related to me: ʿAbdallāh b. Wahb al-Miṣrī related to me, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ entered Egypt with 3,500 men. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb was apprehensive when he was informed about the situation there. He therefore sent al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām with twelve thousand men . Al-Zubayr took part in the conquest of Egypt and marked out a property allotment there.

532ʿAmr al-Nāqid related to me, from ʿAbdallāh b. Wahb al-Miṣrī, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from ʿAbdallāh b. al-Mughīra b. Abī Burda, from Sufyān b. Wahb al-Khawlānī, who said: “When we conquered Egypt without a treaty, al-Zubayr stood up and said: ‘Divide it, ʿAmr!’ But he refused. Al-Zubayr said: ‘By God, we shall certainly divide it as the Messenger of God divided Khaybar.’” ʿAmr wrote to ʿUmar about this. ʿUmar wrote back: “Leave it in its present condition, so that the descendants of descendants may campaign from it.” [The expression ḥabl al-ḥabala requires checking against the printed text and its usage.]

ʿAbdallāh b. Wahb also said: Ibn Lahīʿa related to me, from Khālid b. Maymūn, from ʿAbdallāh b. al-Mughīra, from Sufyān b. Wahb, something similar.

533Al-Qāsim b. Sallām related to me: Abū al-Aswad related to us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ entered Egypt with 3,500 men. ʿUmar was alarmed by this and sent al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām with twelve thousand men, and he witnessed the conquest of Egypt alongside ʿAmr. He said: Al-Zubayr marked out two property allotments, one in Egypt and another in Alexandria.

534Ibrāhīm b. Muslim al-Khwārizmī related to me, from ʿAbdallāh b. al-Mubārak, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from Abū Firās, from ʿAbdallāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, who said:

“People disagreed about Egypt. Some said it was conquered by force, while others said it was conquered by treaty. The reliable account of its affair is that my father came there and the people of al-Yūna fought him. He took the city by force and admitted the Muslims into it; al-Zubayr was the first to climb its fortress.

“Then its ruler said to my father: ‘We have heard what you did in Syria: your imposition of the poll tax on Christians and Jews, and your leaving the land in the hands of its inhabitants to cultivate it and pay the land-tax. If you deal with us in the same way, that would be preferable to us than killing us, taking us captive, or expelling us.’

“My father consulted the Muslims, who advised him to do so, except for a few who asked that the land be divided among them. He therefore imposed a poll tax of two dinars upon every adult, except someone who was poor. He also obligated every landholder, in addition to the two dinars, to provide three ardabbs of wheat, two qisṭs of oil, two qisṭs of honey, and two qisṭs of vinegar , as provisions for the Muslims, to be collected in the House of Provisions and distributed among them.

“The Muslims were counted, and all the people of Egypt were obligated to provide each Muslim every year with a woolen cloak, a hooded cloak (burnus) or turban, trousers, and two leather socks, or a Coptic garment in place of the woolen cloak. A written agreement was drawn up recording these obligations. He stipulated that, provided they fulfilled them, their women and children would not be sold or taken captive, and their property and treasures would remain in their hands.

“He wrote about this to the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar, who approved it, and the land thereby became land subject to kharāj. But because this condition and written agreement had been made, some people supposed that it had been conquered by treaty.

“When the ruler of al-Yūna had settled the affair of himself and those with him in his city, he made a settlement on behalf of all the people of Egypt on the same terms as the settlement of al-Yūna. They agreed to it, saying: ‘These people who could resist have accepted and been satisfied with this; we are all the more content with it, for we are defenseless people without the power to resist.’

“The land-tax was imposed on the lands of Egypt at one dinar and three ardabbs of food for every jarīb, and the poll tax at two dinars for every adult. He wrote about this to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb.”

535ʿAmr al-Nāqid related to me, from ʿAbdallāh b. Wahb al-Miṣrī, from al-Layth, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that al-Muqawqis concluded a settlement with ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ whereby any of the Byzantines who wished to depart might do so, while those who wished to remain would stay on specified terms, and a tax of two dinars would be imposed on the Copts. When the Byzantine emperor learned of this, he was displeased and sent armies. They closed the gates of Alexandria and announced war against ʿAmr.

Al-Muqawqis went out to him and said: “I ask three things of you: Do not grant the Byzantines the same terms you granted me, for they have treated me as a traitor; do not break the agreement with the Copts, for the breach did not come from their side; and, if I die, order me to be buried in a certain church in Alexandria.” ʿAmr replied: “These are among the easiest requests for me to grant.”

Certain Egyptian villages had fought, and captives were taken from them. The villages were Balhīt, al-Khays, and Sulṭays. Their captives reached Medina, but ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb returned them and made them, together with the other Copts, protected subjects. They had an agreement that they had not violated .

ʿAmr wrote to ʿUmar announcing the conquest of Alexandria: “To proceed: God has granted us the conquest of Alexandria by force and compulsion, without treaty or covenant.” Yet, according to Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, all of Egypt was conquered by treaty.

Translation note: This continuation follows the Cairo Arabic OCR transcription, printed pages 211–215. The reading of the fiscal quantities and the idiom ḥabl al-ḥabala in report 532 should be verified in the printed edition prior to publication. Distinct reports about conquest by force versus treaty have deliberately not been reconciled.

Codex continuation; original translation above preserved byte for byte.

536Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb told me, from Abū Ayyūb al-Raqqī, from ʿAbd al-Naffār, from Ibn Lahīʿa, who said: ʿAmr collected Egypt’s land tax and poll tax, amounting to two million; ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ collected four million. ʿUthmān said to ʿAmr, “The milch camels in Egypt have let down their milk after you.”

He said, “That is because you have made their young lean.”

He said: In the year 21, ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ informing him of the hardship endured by the people of Medina and ordering him to send to Medina by sea whatever surplus food there was in the land tax.

That food was sent, together with oil.

When it arrived at al-Jār, Saʿd al-Jār took charge of receiving it.

It was then placed in a house in Medina and distributed among the people by measure.

This ceased during the First Civil War; then it was sent during the days of Muʿāwiya and Yazīd, and ceased again until the time of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān. It continued to be sent until the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar, or shortly before it.

537Bakr b. al-Haytham told me; he said: Abū Ṣāliḥ ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told me, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that, during ʿUmar’s caliphate, after the first agreement, in place of the wheat, oil, honey, and vinegar, they were assessed two dinars each. Each man was thus required to pay four dinars. They accepted this and welcomed it.

538Abū Ayyūb al-Raqqī told me; he said: ʿAbd al-Ghaffār al-Ḥarrānī told me, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from al-Jayshānī, who said: I heard a group of those who participated in the conquest of Egypt relate that, when ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered al-Fusṭāṭ, he dispatched ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī to ʿAyn Shams. He gained control of its territory and concluded agreements with the inhabitants of its villages on terms like those governing al-Fusṭāṭ.

He dispatched Ḥārija b. Ḥudhāfa al-ʿAdawī to al-Fayyūm, al-Ashmūnayn, Ikhmīm, al-Bashrūdāt, and the villages of Upper Egypt, and he did likewise.

He dispatched ʿUmayr b. Wahb al-Jumaḥī to Tinnīs, Dimyāṭ, Tūna, Damīra, Shaṭā, Daqahla, Banā, and Būṣīr, and he did likewise.

He dispatched ʿUqba b. ʿĀmir al-Juhanī—or, it is said, his client Wardān, associated with the market of Wardān in Egypt—to the remaining villages of the lower country, and he did likewise.

ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ thus completed the conquest of Egypt, and its land became kharāj land.

539Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us; he said: ʿAbd al-Ghaffār al-Ḥarrānī told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad, from Ayyūb b. Abī al-ʿĀliya, from his father, who said: I heard ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ say from the pulpit: “I have taken this seat of mine with no Copt of Egypt having any covenant or compact binding upon me.

“If I wish, I kill; if I wish, I take a fifth; and if I wish, I sell—except for the inhabitants of Anṭābulus, for they have a covenant which will be fulfilled for them.”

540Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me; he said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told me this, from Mūsā b. ʿAlī b. Rabāḥ al-Lakhmī, from his father, who said: The whole Maghrib was conquered by force.

541Abū ʿUbayd told us, from Saʿīd b. Abī Maryam, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from al-Ṣalt b. Abī ʿĀṣim, the secretary of Ḥayyān b. Shurayḥ, that he read ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s letter to Ḥayyān, who was his governor over Egypt, stating that Egypt had been conquered by force, without covenant or compact.

542Abū ʿUbayd told me; he said: Saʿīd b. Abī Maryam told us, from Yaḥyā b. Ayyūb, from ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Jaʿfar, who said: Muʿāwiya wrote to Wardān, ʿAmr’s client: “Increase the levy on every Copt by one qīrāṭ.”

He wrote back to him: “How can I increase the levy on them when their covenant stipulates that it shall not be increased?”

543Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Jaʿfar, from his father, who said: I heard ʿUrwa b. al-Zubayr say: “I stayed in Egypt for seven years and married there. I found its inhabitants sorely afflicted, burdened beyond their capacity. ʿAmr conquered it only by an agreement and a covenant , with a specified levy imposed upon them.”

544Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Yazīd b. Abī ʿAlāqa, from ʿUqba b. ʿĀmir al-Juhanī, who said: The inhabitants of Egypt had a covenant and a compact.

ʿAmr wrote for them that their property, lives, women, and children were secure, that none of them would be sold,

and imposed upon them a kharāj which would not be increased, and that the threat of their enemy would be warded off from them.

ʿUqba said: I was a witness to that.

545Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me; he said: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Mubārak, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from someone who heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Mughīra b. Abī Burda say: I heard Sufyān b. Wahb al-Khawlānī say: When we conquered Egypt without a covenant, al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām stood up and said: “ʿAmr! Divide it among us.”

ʿAmr replied: “No, by God! I shall not divide it until I write to ʿUmar.”

He wrote to ʿUmar, who wrote in reply to his letter: “Leave it as it is, so that the offspring of the offspring may campaign from it”—or he said, “may go forth in the morning.”

546Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, Muḥammad b. ʿUmar, from Usāma b. Zayd b. Aslam, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered Egypt in the year twenty, with al-Zubayr accompanying him.

When he had conquered it, the inhabitants of the country concluded an agreement with him for a fixed levy which he imposed upon them, namely two dinars on every man. He excluded women and children from this.

Egypt’s kharāj during his governorship reached two million dinars.

After that it used to reach four million dinars.

547Abū ʿUbayd told me; he said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Layth, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt, concluded an agreement with ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ under which he imposed two dinars on each of the Copts.

News of this reached Heraclius, the ruler of the Byzantines. He became exceedingly angry, dispatched armies to Alexandria, and blockaded it.

ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered it by force.

548Ibn al-Qattāt, who is Abū Masʿūd, told me, from al-Haytham, from al-Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, that ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn, or al-Ḥusayn himself, spoke to Muʿāwiya concerning the jizya of the inhabitants of the village of the mother of Ibrāhīm, the son of the Messenger of God ﷺ in Egypt; he remitted it for them.

The Prophet ﷺ used to enjoin kind treatment of the Copts.

549ʿAmr told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Wahb, from Mālik and al-Layth, from al-Zuhrī, from a son of Kaʿb b. Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When you conquer Egypt, treat the Copts kindly, for they have a covenant of protection and ties of kinship.”

Al-Layth said: “The mother of Ismāʿīl was one of them.”

550Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Mubārak, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb used to record the property of his officials when he appointed them, then divide with them whatever exceeded that amount; sometimes he took it from them.

He wrote to ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ: “You have acquired a proliferation of goods, slaves, vessels, and livestock that you did not possess when you were appointed over Egypt.”

ʿAmr wrote to him: “Our land is a land of cultivation and commerce, and we obtain a surplus beyond what we need for our expenses.”

He wrote to him: “I have had sufficient experience of bad officials, and your letter to me is the letter of someone distressed at being held to what is right. I have come to think ill of you, and I have sent Muḥammad b. Maslama to you to divide your property with you. Acquaint him fully with it, produce for him what he demands of you, and spare him the need to deal harshly with you, for concealment has ceased.”

He then divided his property with him.

551Al-Madāʾinī, from ʿĪsā b. Yazīd, who said: When Muḥammad b. Maslama divided ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ’s property with him, ʿAmr said: “An age in which the son of Ḥantama treats us in this manner is indeed an evil age. Al-ʿĀṣ used to wear khazz with brocade edging.”

Muḥammad said: “Enough! Were it not for this age of the son of Ḥantama that you dislike, you would be found holding a she-goat between your legs in the courtyard of your house, pleased at her abundant milk and distressed at her scant yield.”

He said: “I adjure you by God not to tell ʿUmar what I said, for gatherings are held in confidence.”

He said: “I shall mention nothing of what passed between us while ʿUmar is alive.”

552ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Wahb, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Hubayra, that Egypt was conquered by force.

553ʿAmr told me, from Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Ibn Anʿum, from his father, from his grandfather, who was among those who witnessed the conquest of Egypt, who said: “Egypt was conquered by force, without a covenant or an agreement.”

Chapter 44

The conquest of Alexandria

554They said: When ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered Egypt, he remained there. Then he wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb seeking his instructions about advancing against Alexandria. He wrote back ordering him to do so. He marched against it in the year twenty-one, leaving Khārija b. Ḥudhāfa b. Ghānim b. ʿĀmir b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUbayd b. ʿUwayj b. ʿAdī b. Kaʿb b. Luʾayy b. Ghālib in charge of Egypt.

The Byzantines and Copts on the nearer side of Alexandria had gathered against him and said: “We shall attack him at al-Fusṭāṭ before he reaches us and attempts Alexandria.” He met them at al-Karyūn, defeated them, and killed a great many of them. Among them were people from Sakhā, Yalhīt, al-Khays, Salṭīs, and elsewhere who had reinforced and assisted them.

Then ʿAmr marched until he reached Alexandria and found its inhabitants prepared to fight him, although the Copts, in these circumstances, preferred a peaceful settlement. Al-Muqawqis sent to him requesting a peace settlement and a truce for a specified period, but ʿAmr refused.

Al-Muqawqis ordered the women to stand on the city wall with their faces turned inward, and stationed the men under arms with their faces turned toward the Muslims, to frighten them by this means. ʿAmr sent to him: “We have seen what you have done. It was not through superior numbers that we overcame those whom we overcame. We met Heraclius, your king, and what happened to him happened.”

Al-Muqawqis said to his companions: “These people have spoken the truth. They drove our king from the seat of his kingdom until they forced him into Constantinople, so we have greater reason to submit.” They spoke harshly to him and insisted on fighting.

The Muslims fought them fiercely and besieged them for three months. Then ʿAmr took it by the sword and took as booty what was in it. He spared its inhabitants and took no captives, making them protected subjects like the inhabitants of al-Yūna. He wrote to ʿUmar announcing the conquest, sending the letter with Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj al-Kindī, then al-Sakūnī, and sent the fifth to him with him.

It is said that al-Muqawqis made peace with ʿAmr for thirteen thousand dinars, on condition that whoever wished to leave Alexandria could leave, whoever wished to remain there could remain, and two dinars would be assessed on every adult male Copt. He wrote them a document to that effect.

Then ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ left ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥudhāfa b. Qays b. ʿAdī b. Saʿd b. Sahm b. ʿAmr b. Huṣayṣ b. Kaʿb b. Luʾayy in charge of Alexandria with a garrison of Muslims, and departed for al-Fusṭāṭ.

The Byzantines wrote to Constantine b. Heraclius, who was king at that time, informing him of the small number of Muslims among them, and of their own humiliation and payment of the jizya. He sent a man from among his companions called Manuwīl in three hundred vessels filled with fighting men. He entered Alexandria and killed the Muslim garrison troops there, except those who contrived to flee and escaped. This was in the year twenty-five.

The news reached ʿAmr, and he marched against them with fifteen thousand. He found that their fighting men had gone out to ravage the Egyptian villages near Alexandria. The Muslims met them, and they showered them with arrows for a while, as the Muslims sheltered behind their shields. Then they charged them in earnest, battle was joined between them, and they fought fiercely.

Then those unbelievers turned in flight, neither stopping nor turning aside before Alexandria. They fortified themselves within it and set up ʿarrādas. ʿAmr fought them there with the utmost intensity and set up mangonels, with which he demolished its walls. He pressed the fighting until he entered it by the sword, taking it by force; he killed the fighting men and took the children captive. Some of its Byzantines fled to Byzantine territory, and Manuwīl, the enemy of God, was killed.

ʿAmr and the Muslims demolished the wall of Alexandria. ʿAmr had vowed that, if he conquered it, he would do so.

Some transmitters said: “This expedition was in the year twenty-three.” Some of them transmitted that they broke their agreement in the year twenty-three and the year twenty-five. God knows best.

555They said: ʿAmr imposed the kharāj on the land of Alexandria and the jizya on its inhabitants.

It is transmitted that al-Muqawqis dissociated himself from the inhabitants of Alexandria when they broke their agreement, so ʿAmr confirmed him and those with him in their former terms. It is also transmitted that he had died before this expedition.

556Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Isḥāq b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Farwa, from Ḥibbān b. Shurayḥ, from ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁ that he said: “We conquered no town in the Maghrib by a peace agreement except three: Alexandria, Kafarṭīs, and Salṭīs.”

ʿUmar used to say: “Whoever among the inhabitants of these places embraces Islam shall be left free, together with his property.”

557ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Ibn Wahb al-Miṣrī told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that he said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered Alexandria, and the Muslims lived there during their garrison service. Then they returned home; then they went on campaign and raced to the lodgings. A man would come to the lodging where he had stayed and find that his companion had already occupied it, having reached it first.

ʿAmr said: “I fear that the lodgings will fall into ruin if you keep occupying them in turn.” When he went on campaign and they reached al-Karyūn, he said to them: “Proceed with God’s blessing. Whoever among you plants a spear in a house, it belongs to him and to the sons of his father.”

A man would enter a house and plant his spear in one of its rooms, and another would come and likewise plant his spear. A house would thus be shared between two or three persons. They would live in it, and when they returned home, the Byzantines would live in it.

Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb used to say: “None of its rent is lawful for anyone, and it may neither be sold nor inherited. They had only the right to reside there during their garrison service.”

When the later fighting over it occurred, and Manuwīl the Byzantine eunuch came to it, its inhabitants closed its gates. ʿAmr conquered it and demolished its wall.

558They said: When ʿAmr appointed his client Wardān over Alexandria and returned to al-Fusṭāṭ, only a short time passed before his dismissal reached him. After him, ʿUthmān appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ b. al-Ḥārith, one of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy. He was ʿUthmān’s foster brother. His appointment was in the year twenty-five.

It is said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd had been in charge of Egypt’s kharāj on ʿUthmān’s behalf. Words passed between him and ʿAmr. ʿAbd Allāh wrote complaining of ʿAmr, so ʿUthmān dismissed him and combined the two offices for ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd. He wrote to him informing him that Alexandria had been conquered once by force and had broken its agreement twice, and ordering him to station there a garrison that would not leave it, to provide its members with regular allowances, and to rotate them every six months.

559Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, that Ibn Hurmuz al-Aʿraj, the Qurʾān reciter, used to say: “The best of your coastal towns for garrison service is Alexandria.” He went out to it from Medina to serve in its garrison and died there in the year one hundred and seventeen.

560Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ, from Mūsā b. ʿAlī, from his father, who said: “The jizya of Alexandria was eighteen thousand dinars. During the rule of Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik, it reached thirty-six thousand dinars.”

561ʿAmr told me, from Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, who said: ʿUthmān had dismissed ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ from Egypt and appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd over it. When the Byzantines landed at Alexandria, the people of Egypt asked ʿUthmān to retain ʿAmr until he had finished fighting the Byzantines, because he had knowledge of warfare and inspired awe

in the hearts of the enemy.

He did so, until he defeated them. ʿUthmān then wished to put ʿAmr in charge of warfare and ʿAbd Allāh in charge of the kharāj. ʿAmr refused this and said: “I am like someone holding the cow’s two horns while the commander milks her.” So ʿUthmān appointed Ibn Saʿd over Egypt.

Then the Abyssinians of al-Bīmā continued fighting for seven years after the conquest of Egypt. They could not be overcome because they caused waters to gush forth in the thickets.

ʿAbd Allāh b. Wahb said: Al-Layth b. Saʿd informed me, from Mūsā b. ʿAlī, from his father, that ʿAmr conquered Alexandria by force in the later conquest, during the caliphate of ʿUthmān, after the death of ʿUmar ﵀ .

Chapter 45

The conquest of Barqa and Zawīla

562Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Shuraḥbīl b. Abī ʿAwn, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Hubayra, who said: When ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ conquered Alexandria, he marched with his army toward the Maghrib until he reached Barqa, which is the city of Anṭābulus. He made peace with its inhabitants for the jizya, which was thirteen thousand dinars, toward which they could sell whichever of their children they wished to sell.

563Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Suhayl b. ʿAqīl, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Hubayra, who said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ made peace with the inhabitants of Anṭābulus, whose city is Barqa, which lies between Egypt and Ifrīqiya, after besieging and fighting them, for the jizya, on condition that they could sell whichever of their children they wished toward their jizya. He wrote them a document to that effect.

564Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Maslama b. Saʿīd, from Isḥāq b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Farwa, who said: The inhabitants of Barqa used to send their kharāj to the governor of Egypt without anyone coming to urge or press them. They were the most prosperous people in the Maghrib, and no civil strife entered it.

Al-Wāqidī said: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ used to say: “Were it not for my property in the Ḥijāz, I would settle in Barqa, for I know no dwelling place safer or more secluded than it.”

565Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Muʿāwiya b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb informing him that he had appointed ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ al-Fihrī over the Maghrib and that he had reached Zawīla, and that those between Zawīla

and Barqa were all at peace and obedient, their Muslims having paid the alms-tax and their treaty-protected inhabitants having acknowledged the jizya; and that he had imposed on the people of Zawīla and those between him and it what he considered them able to bear.

He ordered all his officials to collect the alms-tax from the wealthy and return it to the poor, to collect the jizya from the protected communities so that it could be brought to him in Egypt, and to collect the tenth and the half-tenth from Muslim lands, and from the people under treaty what their treaty stipulated.

566Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, who said: I asked ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ about the Berbers, and he said: They claim that they are descendants of Barr b. Qays, but God gave Qays no son called Barr. Rather, they are descended from the mighty men whom David ﵇ fought.

Their dwellings in ages past were in Palestine. They were tent-dwellers, and they came to the Maghrib and multiplied there.

567Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us, who said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ wrote among the conditions he imposed on the Lawāta Berbers of Barqa: “You must sell your sons and your women to meet the jizya you owe.”

Al-Layth said: Had they been slaves, that would not have been lawful in their case.

568Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, who said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote concerning Lawāta women that anyone who had a Lawāta woman with him should ask her father for her hand or return her to her people.

He said: Lawāta was a Berber village whose inhabitants had a treaty.

Chapter 46

The conquest of Tripoli

569Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ, from Muʿāwiya b. Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥa, who said: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ marched until he encamped at Tripoli in the year twenty-two.

He encountered resistance, then conquered it by force. There he obtained many loads of zayūn in the possession of some of its merchants; he sold them and divided their price among the Muslims.

He wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb: “We have reached Tripoli, and between it and Ifrīqiya are nine days’ journey.

“If the Commander of the Faithful sees fit to permit us to invade it, let him do so.”

He wrote back forbidding him to do so, saying: “It is not Ifrīqiya, but a divider, treacherous and betrayed.”

That was because its inhabitants used to pay something to the king of the Byzantines, but frequently betrayed him; the king of al-Andalus had made a treaty with them and then betrayed them.

News of them had reached ʿUmar.

570ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me, who said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Wahb told us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, who said: Our elders told me that Tripoli was conquered under a treaty granted by ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ.

Chapter 47

The conquest of Ifrīqiya

571They said: When ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ became governor of Egypt and the Maghrib, he dispatched the Muslims in cavalry detachments. They struck the borderlands of Ifrīqiya and took booty.

ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵁ had hesitated to invade it, but then resolved to do so after taking counsel on the matter.

He wrote to ʿAbd Allāh in the year twenty-seven—it is also said in the year twenty-eight, and it is also said in the year twenty-nine—ordering him to invade it. He reinforced him with a great army that included Maʿbad b. al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; Marwān b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya; his brother al-Ḥārith b. al-Ḥakam; ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām; al-Miswar b. Makhrama b. Nawfal b. Uhayb b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Zuhra b. Kilāb; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Zayd b. al-Khaṭṭāb; ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb; ʿĀṣim b. ʿUmar; ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakr; ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ; Busr b. Arṭāt b. ʿUwaymir al-ʿĀmirī; and the poet Abū Dhuʾayb Khuwaylid b. Khālid al-Hudhalī. He died there, and Ibn al-Zubayr attended to his affairs until he laid him in his grave’s niche.

A great multitude of Arabs from around Medina went out on this expedition.

572Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Usāma b. Zayd b. Aslam, from Nāfiʿ, the client of the family of al-Zubayr, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, who said: ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān sent us to invade Ifrīqiya.

There was a patrician there whose authority extended from Tripoli to Tangier.

ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ marched until he encamped at ʿAqūba. He fought him for several days, and God killed him; I was the one who killed him.

His army fled and scattered.

Ibn Abī Sarḥ sent out raiding parties, dispersing them throughout the country. They took much booty and drove away as many livestock as they could.

When the magnates of Ifrīqiya saw this,

they assembled and asked ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd to accept three hundred qinṭārs of gold from them, on condition that he desist from attacking them and leave their country.

He accepted this.

573Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Usāma b. Zayd al-Laythī, from Ibn Kaʿb, that ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ made a treaty with the patrician of Ifrīqiya for two million dinars and five hundred thousand dinars.

574Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Mūsā b. Ḍamra al-Māzinī, from his father, who said: When ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd made a treaty with the patrician of Ifrīqiya, he returned to Egypt without appointing anyone over Ifrīqiya.

At that time it had neither a military settlement nor a central garrison town.

He said: When ʿUthmān was killed and Muḥammad b. Ḥudhayfa b. ʿUtba b. Rabīʿa assumed authority over Egypt, he sent no one there.

When Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān assumed power, he appointed Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj al-Sakūnī governor of Egypt.

In the year fifty, he dispatched ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ b. ʿAbd Qays b. Laqīṭ al-Fihrī, who invaded it and laid out its settlement.

575They said: ʿUqba sent Busr b. Arṭāt to a fortress in the region of al-Qayrawān. He conquered it, killed people, and took captives. Today it is known as the Fortress of Busr. It is near a town called Majjāna, by the silver mine.

576I have heard someone mention that Mūsā b. Nuṣayr sent Busr, when Busr was eighty-two years old, to this fortress, and he conquered it.

Busr’s birth was before

the death of the Prophet ﷺ by two years.

Someone other than al-Wāqidī claims that he transmitted reports from the Prophet ﷺ.

God knows best.

577Al-Wāqidī said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd remained governor until Muḥammad b. Abī Ḥudhayfa gained control of Egypt; it was he who had stirred it up against ʿUthmān.

Then ʿAlī ﵁ appointed Qays b. Saʿd b. ʿUbāda al-Anṣārī governor of Egypt. He then dismissed him and appointed Muḥammad b. Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq over it. He then dismissed him and appointed Mālik al-Ashtar, who fell ill at al-Qulzum.

Then he appointed Muḥammad b. Abī Bakr a second time and sent him back to it.

Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj killed him and burned him inside a donkey.

The governor was ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, on behalf of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān.

ʿAmr died in Egypt on the day of the Feast of Breaking the Fast in the year forty-two—it is also said in the year forty-three—and his son ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr assumed the governorship after him.

Then Muʿāwiya dismissed him and appointed Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj, who remained there for four years, then went on an expedition and took booty.

Then he came to Egypt and dispatched ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ b. ʿAbd Qays al-Fihrī. It is also said that Muʿāwiya instead appointed him over the Maghrib. He invaded Ifrīqiya with ten thousand Muslims.

He conquered Ifrīqiya and laid out its settlement of al-Qayrawān.

The site of al-Qayrawān was a thicket of tamarisks and trees, unapproachable because of the wild beasts, snakes, and deadly scorpions.

Ibn Nāfiʿ was a righteous man whose prayers were answered.

He prayed to his Lord, who removed all of that, so that even the wild beasts carried away their young as they fled with them.

578Al-Wāqidī said: I said to Mūsā b. ʿAlī: “Tell me, the continuous, compact buildings of Ifrīqiya that we see today—who built them?” He replied: “The first to build it was ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ al-Fihrī. He laid it out, then built, and the people built houses and dwellings along with him. He built the congregational mosque there.”

He said: In Ifrīqiya, Maʿbad b. al-ʿAbbās ﵀ was martyred during Ibn Abī Sarḥ’s expedition in the caliphate of ʿUthmān. It is also said that he instead died during the days of fighting.

His martyrdom is more firmly established.

579Al-Wāqidī and others said: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān dismissed Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj.

He appointed Maslama b. Mukhallad al-Anṣārī over Egypt and the Maghrib.

He appointed his client Abū al-Muhājir over the Maghrib.

When Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya assumed power, he restored ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ to his post.

He invaded al-Sūs al-Adnā, which lies beyond Tangier, and ranged through that region without anyone opposing or fighting him; then he returned.

Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya died, and allegiance was pledged to his son Muʿāwiya b. Yazīd, who was Abū Laylā.

He proclaimed: “Assemble for prayer!”

Then he renounced the caliphate and remained in his house. He died after two months.

Then came the rule of Marwān b. al-Ḥakam and the dissension of Ibn al-Zubayr.

Then ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān assumed power, and the people submitted to him.

He appointed his brother ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz over Egypt, and he appointed Zuhayr b. Qays al-Balawī over Ifrīqiya.

He conquered Tunis, then returned to Barqa.

News reached him that a group of Byzantines had disembarked from their ships and wrought havoc. He set out against them with a cavalry detachment and encountered them. He and those with him were martyred, and his grave is there.

Their graves are called the Graves of the Martyrs.

Then he appointed Ḥassān b. al-Nuʿmān al-Ghassānī, who attacked the Berber queen al-Kāhina, but she defeated him.

He came to some fortified buildings in the territory of Barqa and settled in them.

These were buildings enclosed by a fortified building whose roofs were vaults, and they were named the Fortified Buildings of Ḥassān.

Then Ḥassān attacked her a second time, killed her, and took Berber captives, whom he sent to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

The poet Abū Miḥjan Naṣb used to say: “I was present when Berber captives were with ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz; I have never seen faces more beautiful than theirs.”

580Ibn al-Kalbī said: Hishām appointed Kulthūm b. ʿIyāḍ b. Waḥwaḥ al-Qushayrī over Ifrīqiya. Its inhabitants rebelled against him, and he was killed there.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: Ifrīqīs b. Qays b. Ṣayfī al-Ḥimyarī had gained control of Ifrīqiya in the pre-Islamic period, and it was named after him.

He killed Jirjīr, its king.

He said of the Berbers: “How much babbling these people do!” Thus they were called the babblers.

581A group of people from Ifrīqiya told me, from their elders, that when ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ al-Fihrī wished to establish al-Qayrawān as a garrison town, he considered where within it the mosque should stand.

He was shown in his sleep what seemed to be a man giving the call to prayer at the spot where he placed his minaret.

When morning came, he built the minarets where the man had stood, then built the mosque.

582Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, who said: Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath al-Khawāʿī governed Ifrīqiya on behalf of Abū al-ʿAbbās, Commander of the Faithful.

He repaired the city of al-Qayrawān and its mosque.

Then al-Manṣūr dismissed him and appointed ʿUmar b. Ḥafṣ Hazār Mard in his place.

Chapter 48

The conquest of Tangier

583Al-Wāqidī said: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Marwān dispatched Mūzsā b. Nuṣayr, a client of the Banū Umayya—originally from ʿAyn al-Tamr; it is also said that he was instead from Arāsha of Balī, and it is also said that he was from Lakhm—as governor of Ifrīqiya.

It is also said that he instead became its governor in the time of al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik, in the year eighty-nine.

He conquered Tangier and settled there. He was the first to settle there and lay out plots for the Muslims within it.

His cavalry reached al-Sūs al-Adnā, between which and al-Sūs al-Aqṣā are twenty-odd days’ journey. He overran them and took captives from among them. They submitted to him, and his official collected the alms-tax from them.

Then he appointed his client Ṭāriq b. Ziyād over it and returned to al-Qayrawān in Ifrīqiya.

Chapter 49

The conquest of al-Andalus

584Al-Wāqidī said: Ṭāriq b. Ziyād, the governor appointed by Mūsā b. Nuṣayr, campaigned against al-Andalus. He was the first to campaign against it, in the year 92.

Alyān, who governed the crossing to al-Andalus, met him. Ṭāriq granted him security on condition that he transport him and his companions to al-Andalus in ships.

When he reached it, its inhabitants fought him, and he conquered it. That was in the year 92.

Its king, according to what they claim, belonged to the Ashbān, whose origin was from Iṣbahān.

Then Mūsā b. Nuṣayr wrote Ṭāriq a stern letter for exposing the Muslims to danger and undertaking his campaign on his own judgment without consulting him. He ordered him not to go beyond Córdoba.

Mūsā proceeded to Córdoba in al-Andalus, and Ṭāriq sought to appease him, so he became reconciled to him.

Ṭāriq conquered the city of Toledo, the royal capital of al-Andalus, situated on the side toward the Franks. There he acquired a great table, which Mūsā b. Nuṣayr presented to al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik in Damascus when he returned in the year 96, while al-Walīd was ill.

When Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik assumed power, he exacted one hundred thousand dinars from Mūsā b. Nuṣayr.

Yazīd b. al-Muhallab spoke to him on his behalf, and he desisted from pursuing him.

Then, during the caliphate of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁ he appointed Ismāʿīl b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī al-Muhājir, a client of Banū Makhzūm, to govern the Maghrib.

He conducted himself most excellently and called the Berbers to Islam.

ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz subsequently wrote letters to them calling them to it.

Ismāʿīl read these to them throughout the districts, and Islam became predominant in the Maghrib.

585They said: When Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik assumed power, he appointed Yazīd b. Abī Muslim, the client of al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf, to govern Ifrīqiya and the Maghrib.

He arrived in Ifrīqiya in the year 102.

His guards were Berbers, and he branded each man's hand with the mark “guardsman.”

They objected to this and grew weary of

his conduct. They approached one another secretly and joined together to kill him. One evening he went out for the sunset prayer, and they killed him in his place of prayer.

Yazīd appointed Bishr b. Ṣafwān al-Kalbī, and he had ʿAbd Allāh b. Mūsā b. Nuṣayr beheaded in retaliation for Yazīd.

That was because he was accused of killing him and inciting the people against him.

Then Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik also appointed Bishr b. Ṣafwān. He died in al-Qayrawān in the year 109.

He appointed ʿUbayda b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qaysī in his place.

Then, after him, he appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥabḥāb, a client of Banū Salūl.

He sent ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Ibman Ḥabīb b. Abī ʿUbayda b. ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ al-Fihrī to campaign in al-Sūs and the land of the Sūdān.

He achieved a victory the like of which no one had ever seen, and captured two slave girls from the women there. Each of their women has only one breast, and they are called Tarājān.

Then, after Ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, Kulthūm b. ʿIyāḍ al-Qushayrī was appointed. He arrived in Ifrīqiya in the year 23 and was killed.

Then, after him, Ḥanẓala b. Ṣafwān al-Kalbī, the brother of Bishr b. Ṣafwān, was appointed. He fought the Khārijites and died there while serving as governor.

Al-Walīd b. Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik assumed power, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥabīb al-Fihrī rebelled against him. He was much loved in that frontier district because of the deeds of his grandfather ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ there. He gained control of it, and Ḥanẓala withdrew from it.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān remained in control of it.

Yazīd b. al-Walīd assumed the caliphate but sent no governor to the Maghrib.

Marwān b. Muḥammad assumed power, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥabīb wrote to him, professed obedience to him, and sent him gifts.

His secretary was Khālid b. Rabīʿa al-Ifrīqī, between whom and ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Yaḥyā there was friendship and correspondence. Marwān confirmed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān in charge of the frontier district.

Then, after him, Ilyās b. Ḥabīb was appointed, then Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Then the Berbers and the Ibāḍīs among the Khārijites gained the upper hand.

Then Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath al-Khuzāʿī entered Ifrīqiya as its governor toward the end of Abū al-ʿAbbās's caliphate, with seventy thousand men—or, it is said, forty thousand. He governed it for four years and repaired the city of al-Qayrawān.

Then the troops of the country and others rose against him.

He heard someone relate that the inhabitants of the country and the troops stationed there rose against him. He remained in his palace fighting them for forty days, until those loyal to the government among the people of Khurāsān and others who had set out with him rallied to him. He prevailed over those who had fought him and reviewed them by name: anyone whose name was Muʿāwiya, Sufyān, Marwān, or a name corresponding to the names of Banū Umayya, he killed; anyone whose name was otherwise, he spared.

Al-Manṣūr dismissed him and appointed ʿUmar b. Ḥafṣ b. ʿUthmān b. Qabīṣa b. Abī Ṣufra al-ʿAtakī, who was called Hazārmard. Al-Manṣūr admired him.

He entered Ifrīqiya and campaigned from it until he reached the furthest reaches of the Berbers' country, where he built a city that he named al-ʿAbbāsiyya.

Then Abū Ḥātim al-Sadrātī, the Ibāḍī, a man of Sadrāta and a client of Kinda, fought him.

He was martyred, together with a group of his household. The frontier district revolted, and that city which he had built was demolished.

After Hazārmard, Yazīd b. Ḥātim b. Qabīṣa b. al-Muhallab was appointed.

He set out with fifty thousand men. Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr accompanied him as far as Jerusalem to see him off and spent a great sum of money on him. Yazīd proceeded until he met Abū Ḥātim at Tripoli, killed him, and entered Ifrīqiya.

It became obedient to him.

Then, after Yazīd b. Ḥātim, Rawḥ b. Ḥātim was appointed, then al-Faḍl b. Rawḥ. The troops rose against him and cut his throat.

586Aḥmad b. Naqd, a client of Banū al-Aghlab, told me, who said: Al-Aghlab b. Sālim al-Tamīmī was a man of Marw al-Rūdh, among those who came from Khurāsān with the wearers of black, and he was appointed by

Mūsā al-Hādī to govern the Maghrib.

Ḥarīsh, a man who had belonged to the frontier troops from Tunis, gathered a force against him and marched against him while he was at al-Qayrawān in Ifrīqiya, and besieged him.

Then al-Aghlab went out against him and fought him. An arrow struck him in the battle, and he fell dead, while his companions were unaware of what had befallen him.

Ḥarīsh's companions did not know of it either.

Then Ḥarīsh and his army were routed. Al-Aghlab's companions pursued them for three days, killing them, and killed Ḥarīsh at a place known as Sūʿ al-Aḥad.

Al-Aghlab was therefore called “the Martyr.”

He said: Ibrāhīm b. al-Aghlab was one of the leading men among the troops of Egypt.

He rose up, together with twelve men, and they took from the treasury the amount of their stipends, taking nothing beyond that, and fled. They reached a place called al-Zāb, more than ten days' journey from al-Qayrawān. The governor of the frontier district at that time, appointed by al-Rashīd Hārūn, was Harthama b. Aʿyan.

Ibrāhīm b. al-Aghlab assumed leadership over the troops and others in that region. He began sending gifts to Harthama, courting his favor, and writing to inform him that he had not withdrawn his hand from obedience or embraced disobedience, and that only want and necessity had driven him to what he had done.

Harthama appointed him over his region and entrusted him with its affairs.

When Harthama was removed from the frontier district, Ibn al-ʿAkkī governed it after him.

His conduct there was bad, until it revolted against him.

Al-Rashīd consulted Harthama about a man whom he could appoint over it and entrust with its affairs.

He advised him to win over Ibrāhīm, take him into his service, and appoint him over the frontier district.

Al-Rashīd wrote to him, informing him that he had pardoned his offense, excused his lapse, and decided to appoint him over the lands of the Maghrib as a mark of favor toward him, so that he might henceforth treat him with kindness and receive loyal service from him.
