Ibrāhīm took charge of that frontier district, administered it, and brought it under control.

Then a man of the country's troops called ʿImrān b. Mujālid rebelled and broke his allegiance.

The frontier troops joined him, demanded their stipends, and besieged Ibrāhīm in al-Qayrawān.

Before long, the muster officers and paymasters came to them with money from the land tax of Egypt.

When they were paid, they dispersed.

Ibrāhīm built the White Palace, which lies on the qibla side of al-Qayrawān, two miles from it.

He laid out plots for the people around it

and they built, and made what was there into a city and built a congregational mosque with plaster, baked brick, and marble columns, roofed it with cedar, and made it two hundred cubits by approximately two hundred cubits.

He purchased slaves whom he freed, their number reaching five thousand, and settled them around him.

He named that city al-ʿAbbāsiyya, and today it is populated and flourishing.

Muḥammad b. al-Aghlab b. Ibrāhīm b. al-Aghlab had founded a city near Tāhart in the year 239, which he likewise named al-ʿAbbāsiyya. Aflaḥ b. ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, the Ibāḍī, destroyed it and wrote to the Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus informing him of this, seeking thereby to gain his favor.

The Umayyad sent him one hundred thousand dirhams.

587In the Maghrib there is a land known as the Great Land. Between it and Barqa is a journey of fifteen days, or a little less or a little more.

There is a city there on the seacoast called Bāra. Its inhabitants were Christians, but were not Romans.

Ḥabla, the client of al-Aghlab, campaigned against it but was unable to take it.

Then Khalfūn the Berber campaigned against it—it is said that he was a client of Rabīʿa— and conquered it at the beginning of the caliphate of al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh.

After him, a man called al-Mufarrij b. Sallām assumed power. He conquered twenty-four fortresses and took possession of them. He wrote to the director of the post in Egypt, informing him of his circumstances and that he considered prayer invalid for himself and the Muslims with him unless the imam formally appointed him over his district and entrusted it to him, so that he might cease to belong to the category of those who seized power by force.

He built a congregational mosque.

Then his companions mutinied against him and killed him.

After him, Sūrān assumed power and sent his envoy to the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, asking him for a formal appointment and a document of investiture.

He died before his envoy returned to him.

Al-Muntaṣir bi-llāh died, his caliphate having lasted six months.

Al-Mustaʿīn bi-llāh Aḥmad b. Muḥammad b. al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh assumed power and ordered his governor over the Maghrib, Ūtāmish, the client of the Commander of the Faithful, to appoint him over his district.

His envoy had not yet departed from Surr Man Raʾā when Ūtāmish was killed and Waṣīf, the client of the Commander of the Faithful, was appointed over the region. He issued the appointment for him and dispatched it.

Chapter 50

The islands in the sea

The Conquest of Islands in the Sea

588They said: Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj al-Kindī campaigned against Sicily in the days of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān. He was the first to campaign against it.

Campaigns against it continued thereafter.

The family of al-Aghlab b. Sālim al-Ifrīqī has conquered more than twenty cities there, and they are in Muslim hands.

During the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, Aḥmad b. Muḥammad b. al-Aghlab conquered Qaṣriyāna and the fortress of Ghaliyāna there.

589Al-Wāqidī said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays b. Makhlad al-Duzaqī took captives in Sicily and acquired idols of gold and silver encrusted with jewels.

He sent them to Muʿāwiya, who forwarded them to Baṣra to be carried to India and sold there, so that their value might be realized.

590They said: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān used to send expeditions by land and sea. He sent Junāda b. Abī Umayya al-Azdī to Rhodes—Junāda was one of those from whom hadith was transmitted; he met Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and Muʿādh b. Jabal, and died in the year 80—and he conquered it by force.

It was a wooded thicket in the sea.

Muʿāwiya ordered him to settle a body of Muslims there, and he did so.

That was in the year 52.

591They said: Rhodes is among the most fertile islands. It measures approximately sixty miles and has olive trees, vineyards, fruits, and fresh water.

592Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī and others, who said: The Muslims remained on Rhodes for seven years in a fortress established for them.

When Muʿāwiya died, Yazīd wrote to Junāda ordering him to demolish the fortress and return.

Muʿāwiya used to rotate the men stationed there.

Mujāhid b. Jabr resided there, teaching the people to recite the Qurʾān.

In the year 54, Junāda b. Abī Umayya conquered Arwād, and Muʿāwiya settled Muslims there.

Among those who conquered it were Mujāhid and Tubayʿ, the son of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār's wife. There Mujāhid taught Tubayʿ to recite the Qurʾān.

It is said that he taught him to recite the Qurʾān on Rhodes.

Arwād is an island near Constantinople.

Junāda campaigned against Iqrīṭish.

In al-Walīd's time, part of it was conquered.

Then it was closed off.

Ḥumayd b. Maʿyūf al-Hamdānī campaigned against it during al-Rashīd's caliphate and conquered part of it.

Then, during al-Maʾmūn's caliphate, Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar b. ʿĪsā al-Andalusī, known as al-Iqrīṭish, campaigned against it.

He conquered a single fortress there and settled in it.

He then continued conquering one part after another until not a single Roman remained there, and he destroyed their fortresses.

Chapter 51

The peace agreement with Nubia

593Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, who said: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Wāqidī told me, from al-Walīd b. Kathīr, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, from Abū al-Khayr, who said: When the Muslims conquered Egypt, ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ sent cavalry to the villages around it to overrun them.

He sent ʿUqba b. Nāfiʿ al-Fihrī; Nāfiʿ was the maternal brother of al-ʿĀṣ.

Their cavalry entered the land of Nubia as the summer expeditions enter the Romans' country.

The Muslims encountered fierce fighting in Nubia.

They met them, and they showered them with arrows until most of them were wounded.

They withdrew with many wounds and gouged-out eyes, and they were called “the marksmen of the eyes.”

They continued in this situation until ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ became governor of Egypt.

They asked him for peace and a cessation of hostilities, and he agreed to this without imposing jizya, but on the basis of a truce providing for three hundred slaves each year, and on condition that the Muslims present them with a corresponding quantity of food.

594Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, who said: Al-Wāqidī told me, who said: Ibrāhīm b. Jaʿfar told us, from ʿUmar b. al-Ḥārith, from Abū Qabīl Ḥuyayy b. Hāniʾ al-Maʿāfirī, from an elder of Ḥimyar, who said: I took part in two expeditions to Nubia during the rule of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, and I have never seen a people fiercer in warfare than they.

I saw one of them say to a Muslim, “Where would you like me to place my arrow in you?” Sometimes a young man of ours would answer playfully, “In such-and-such a place.”

He would not miss it.

They shot arrows in great numbers, yet scarcely any of their arrows could be seen on the ground.

One day they came out against us and drew up in battle formation opposite us. We intended to make it a single charge with swords, but we were unable to engage them.

They shot at us until eyes were lost: one hundred and fifty gouged-out eyes were counted.

We said, “There is nothing better for dealing with these people than peace. The spoils to be taken from them are meager, and the harm they inflict is severe.”

But ʿAmr did not make peace with them. He continued to fight them fiercely until he was removed and ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ was appointed; he then made peace with them.

Al-Wāqidī said: It was in Nubia that Muʿāwiya b. Ḥudayj al-Kindī lost his eye; he was one-eyed.

595Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, who said: There is neither a treaty nor a covenant between us and the Blacks. It is only a truce between us and them, on condition that we give them some wheat and lentils and they give us slaves. There is therefore no harm in buying their slaves from them or from others.

596Abū ʿUbayd told us, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, who said: The peace between us and the Nubians stipulates only that we shall not fight them and they shall not fight us, and that they shall give us slaves and we shall give them a corresponding quantity of food. If they sell their women, I see no harm in their being purchased.. According to the transmission of Abū al-Bakhtarī and others, ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ made peace with the people of Nubia on condition that they present four hundred persons annually, delivering them and receiving food in exchange.

597Al-Mahdī, Commander of the Faithful, had ordered that the Nubians be required to deliver three hundred and sixty persons and a giraffe each year, on condition that they be given wheat, wine vinegar, clothing, and bedding, or its value.

They have recently claimed that the baqṭ is not due from them every year, and that, when it was demanded of them during the caliphate of al-Mahdī, they submitted to him that this baqṭ consisted of slaves whom they took from their enemies; when they could find none of these, they turned to their own children and supplied this number from among them. He therefore ordered that they be treated in this matter on the basis that one year's baqṭ should be taken from them every three years.

No record of this claim was found in the registers of the capital, but one was found in the register in Egypt.

Al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh had ordered that a man called Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh, known as al-Qummī, be sent to the mine in Egypt as its governor. He also placed him in charge of al-Qulzum, the road to the Ḥijāz, and the escort of the Egyptian pilgrims.

When he reached the mine, he sent provisions aboard ships from al-Qulzum to the land of the Beja and reached a stretch of coast known as ʿAydhāb.

The ships met him there.

He made use of those provisions, and he and his companions subsisted on them until he reached the fortress of the king of the Beja.

He advanced against him.

He had only a small force, and the Beja ruler came out against him with a multitude mounted on girt camels.

Al-Qummī thereupon took bells and hung them around the horses' necks.

When the camels heard their sounds, they scattered with the Beja riders through the valleys and mountains.

The ruler of the Beja was killed.

His sister's son then succeeded him; his father was one of the kings of the Beja.

He requested a truce.

Al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh refused this unless he set foot upon his carpet.

He came to Surra Man Raʾā, and peace was made with him in the year two hundred and forty-one on condition that he pay the tribute and the baqṭ, and he returned with al-Qummī.

The people of the Beja remain under the truce, making payments and not preventing the Muslims from working in the gold mine.

This was among the conditions imposed upon their ruler.

Chapter 52

Papyrus

Concerning Papyrus

598They said: Papyrus used to enter the land of the Romans from Egypt, while dinars came to the Arabs from the Romans.

ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān was the first to introduce the inscription written at the heads of the papyrus rolls, consisting of “Say: He is God, One,” and other words mentioning God.

The king of the Romans wrote to him: “You have introduced into your papyrus an inscription that we dislike. If you abandon it, well and good; otherwise, there will come to you on the dinars a mention of your prophet that you will dislike.”

He said: This weighed heavily upon ʿAbd al-Malik.

He was reluctant to abandon a good practice that he had instituted.

He sent for Khālid b. Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya and said to him: “Abū Hāshim! Here is a calamity!”

He told him what had happened.

He said: “Let your fear subside, Commander of the Faithful.

Prohibit their dinars so that they are not used in transactions, mint coinage for the people, and do not spare these unbelievers what they dislike in the papyrus rolls.”

ʿAbd al-Malik said: “You have relieved me of it; may God relieve you.”

He minted the dinars.

599ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam said: The Copts used to mention the Messiah at the heads of the papyrus rolls and ascribe lordship to him—exalted is God, far above that—and place the cross in the position of “In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful.”

That was why the king of the Romans disliked what he disliked, and why ʿAbd al-Malik's alteration of what he altered weighed heavily upon him.

Concerning Papyrus

598. They said: Papyrus used to enter the land of the Romans from Egypt, while dinars came to the Arabs from the Romans.

ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān was the first to introduce the inscription written at the heads of the papyrus rolls, consisting of “Say: He is God, One,” and other words mentioning God.

The king of the Romans wrote to him: “You have introduced into your papyrus an inscription that we dislike. If you abandon it, well and good; otherwise, there will come to you on the dinars a mention of your prophet that you will dislike.”

He said: This weighed heavily upon ʿAbd al-Malik.

He was reluctant to abandon a good practice that he had instituted.

He sent for Khālid b. Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya and said to him: “Abū Hāshim! Here is a calamity!”

He told him what had happened.

He said: “Let your fear subside, Commander of the Faithful.

Prohibit their dinars so that they are not used in transactions, mint coinage for the people, and do not spare these unbelievers what they dislike in the papyrus rolls.”

ʿAbd al-Malik said: “You have relieved me of it; may God relieve you.”

He minted the dinars.

599. ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam said: The Copts used to mention the Messiah at the heads of the papyrus rolls and ascribe lordship to him—exalted is God, far above that—and place the cross in the position of “In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful.”

That was why the king of the Romans disliked what he disliked, and why ʿAbd al-Malik's alteration of what he altered weighed heavily upon him.

600Al-Madāʾinī said: Maslama b. Muḥārib said: Khālid b. Yazīd advised ʿAbd al-Malik to prohibit their dinars and prevent their use in transactions, and to allow no papyrus to enter the land of the Romans.

For a time, none was sent to them.

Title page of volume 2 of the Cairo edition

Part Four

Central Iraq and the armies of Kūfa

Chapter 53

The Sawād in the caliphate of Abū Bakr

The Conquests of the Sawād during the Caliphate of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁

601They said: Al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha b. Salama b. Ḍamḍam al-Shaybānī used to raid the Sawād with men of his people.

News of him reached Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﵁ who asked about him. Qays b. ʿĀṣim b. Sinān al-Minqārī said to him: “This is a man whose reputation is not obscure, whose lineage is not unknown, and whose standing is not lowly. This is al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha al-Shaybānī.”

Then al-Muthannā came to Abū Bakr and said to him: “O successor of the Messenger of God! Appoint me over those of my people who have embraced Islam, so that I may fight these non-Arabs of Persia.”

Abū Bakr wrote him a letter of appointment to that effect. He set out until he encamped at Khuffān, and called his people to Islam, whereupon they embraced it.

Then Abū Bakr ﵁ wrote to Khālid b. al-Walīd al-Makhzūmī, ordering him to proceed to Iraq. It is also said that he dispatched him from Medina. Abū Bakr wrote to al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha, ordering him to hear and obey him and to meet him.

Madhʿūr b. ʿAdī al-ʿIjlī had written to Abū Bakr, informing him of his circumstances and those of his people, and asking him to place him in charge of fighting the Persians.

He wrote to him, ordering him to join Khālid, to remain with him when he remained, and to depart when he departed.

When Khālid encamped at al-Nibāj, al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha met him there. Khālid advanced until he reached Baṣra, where Suwayd b. Quṭba al-Dhuhlī was.

602Someone other than Abū Mikhnaf said: Quṭba b. Qatāda al-Dhuhlī, of Bakr b. Wāʾil, was there with a group of his people, intending to do at Baṣra what al-Muthannā had done at Kūfa.

Kūfa did not exist at that time; it was only al-Ḥīra.

Suwayd said to Khālid:

“The people of al-Ubulla have mustered against me, and I think they have held back from me only because of your presence.”

Khālid said to him: “The course to take is for me to leave Baṣra by day, then return by night and enter your camp with my companions. If they attack you in the morning, we shall fight them” .

— Khālid did so and headed toward al-Ḥīra.

When night enveloped him, he turned back until he reached Suwayd’s camp and entered it with his companions.

In the morning, the people of al-Ubulla, having heard that Khālid had departed from Baṣra, advanced toward Suwayd.

When they saw how many men were in his camp, they were dismayed and lost heart.

Khālid said: “Charge them, for I see the appearance of a people into whose hearts God has cast terror.”

They charged them and routed them. God killed many of them, and a group drowned in the Tigris of Baṣra.

Then Khālid passed through al-Khurayba, conquered it, and took its inhabitants captive. According to what al-Kalbī related, he left Shurayḥ b. ʿĀmir b. Qayn, of Banū Saʿd b. Bakr b. Hawāzin, in charge there.

It had been a garrison post of the non-Arabs.

It is also said that he came to the river known as Nahr al-Marʾa and made terms with its people, and that he fought a force at al-Madhār. Then he set out for al-Ḥīra, leaving Suwayd b. Quṭba in charge of his district, and said to him: “We have given these non-Arabs in your district a pounding that has humbled them before you.”

It has been reported that, when Khālid was in the region of al-Yamāma, he wrote to Abū Bakr requesting reinforcements. He reinforced him with Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh. Jarīr met him as he was returning from al-Yamāma and accompanied him.

He engaged the commander of al-Madhār on his orders. God knows best.

Al-Wāqidī said: The account accepted by our associates among the people of the Ḥijāz is that Khālid came to Medina from al-Yamāma, then departed from it for Iraq by way of Fayd and al-Thaʿlabiyya, and then came to al-Ḥīra.

603They said: Khālid b. al-Walīd passed through Zandaward, in Kaskar, and conquered it. He conquered Darnā and its dependencies under a guarantee of safety, after the people of Zandaward had exchanged missile fire with the Muslims for a time.

He came to Hurmuzjird, granted its inhabitants safety as well, and conquered it.

He came to Ullays, and Jābān, the chief of the non-Arabs, came out against him. He sent al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha al-Shaybānī ahead against him, and he met him at the River of Blood.

Khālid made terms with the people of Ullays on condition that they serve the Muslims as informants against the Persians, and as guides and helpers.

Khālid advanced to the confluence of the rivers. There Azādhbih, the commander of Kisrā’s garrison posts in the territory between him and the Arabs, met him. The Muslims fought him and routed him.

Then Khālid encamped at Khuffān. It is also said that he proceeded directly toward al-Ḥīra. ʿAbd al-Masīḥ b. ʿUmar b. Qays b. Ḥayyān b. Buqayla—Buqayla’s name was al-Ḥārith, and he was of al-Azd—came out to him, together with Hāniʾ b. Qabīṣa b. Masʿūd al-Shaybānī and Iyās b. Qabīṣa al-Ṭāʾī; it is also said, Farwa b. Iyās. Iyās had been the governor of al-Ḥīra for Kisrā Abarwīz after al-Nuʿmān b. al-Mundhir. They made terms with him for one hundred thousand dirhams.

It is also said: for eighty thousand dirhams each year, on condition that they serve the Muslims as informants against the people of Persia, and that no church or palace of theirs be demolished.

604Abū Mikhnaf reported, from Abū al-Muthannā al-Walīd b. al-Qaṭāmī, who is al-Sharqī b. al-Qasṭāmī al-Kalbī, that ʿAbd al-Masīḥ went out to meet Khālid. He was advanced in age. Khālid said to him: “From where does your earliest trace come, old man?” He said: “From my father’s back.”

He said: “Then where did you come out from?” He said: “From my mother’s belly.”

He said: “Woe to you! What are you in?” He said: “In my clothes.”

He said: “Woe to you! What are you on?” He said: “On the earth.”

He said: “Do you understand?” He said: “Yes, and I fetter as well.”

He said: “Woe to you! I am only speaking to you in the language of people.”

He said: “And I am only answering you with the answers of people.”

He said: “Are you at peace or at war?”

He said: “At peace.”

He said: “Then what are these fortresses?” He said: “We built them for the fool, until the forbearing man comes.”

Then they discussed peace and agreed upon one hundred thousand

to be paid every year. What was taken from them was the first money carried to Medina from Iraq. He stipulated that they should plot no harm against the Muslims and should serve as informants against the people of Persia. This was in the year 12.

605Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, who said: I heard that the people of al-Ḥīra numbered six thousand men. Each man was required to pay fourteen dirhams at a weight of five. That amounted to eighty-four thousand at a weight of five, making sixty at a weight of seven.

He wrote them a document to that effect, which I have read.

It was reported from Yazīd b. Nubaysha al-ʿĀmirī that he said: We came to Iraq with Khālid b. al-Walīd and reached the garrison post of al-ʿUdhayb. Then we came to al-Ḥīra, whose people had fortified themselves in the White Palace, the palace of Ibn Buqayla, and the palace of the ʿAdasiyyūn. We sent the cavalry ranging through their open grounds, and then they made terms with us.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: The ʿAdasiyyūn are of Kall. They were named after their mother, who was also a woman of Kalb.

606Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from Ibn Mujālid, from his father, from al-Shaʿbī, that Khuraym b. Aws b. Ḥāritha b. Lām al-Ṭāʾī said to the Prophet ﷺ: “If God grants you the conquest of al-Ḥīra, give me the daughter of Buqayla.”

When Khālid intended to make peace with the people of al-Ḥīra, Khuraym said to him: “The Prophet ﷺ assigned the daughter of Buqayla to me, so do not include her in your peace agreement.”

Bashīr b. Saʿd and Muḥammad b. Maslama, the two Anṣārīs, testified on his behalf.

He excluded her from the peace agreement and handed her over to Khuraym. She was bought from him for one thousand dirhams.

She was an old woman, changed from when he had known her.

He was told: “Woe to you! You sold her cheaply. Her family would have paid you

many times what you asked for her.”

He said: “I did not think any number could be greater than ten hundred.”

It has been related in the tradition that the man who asked the Prophet ﷺ for the daughter of Buqayla was a man of Rabīʿa. The first account is more firmly established.

607They said: Khālid b. al-Walīd sent Bashīr b. Saʿd, the father of al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr al-Anṣārī, to Bānqiyā. The cavalry of the non-Arabs met him, commanded by Farrukhbundādh, and shot arrows at those accompanying him. He charged them, routed them, and killed Farrukhbundādh.

Then he returned with a wound that reopened while he was at ʿAyn al-Tamr, and he died of it.

It is also said that Khālid himself met Farrukhbundādh, with Bashīr accompanying him.

Then Khālid sent Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī to the people of Bānqiyā. Baṣbuhrī b. Ṣalūbā came out to him, apologized to him for the fighting, and offered peace.

Jarīr made terms with him for one thousand dirhams and a ṭaylasān.

It is also said that Ibn Ṣalūbā came to Khālid, apologized to him, and concluded with him this peace agreement.

When Mihrān had been killed and the day of al-Nukhayla had passed, Jarīr came to them and collected from them and from the people of al-Ḥīra the payments stipulated in their peace agreements. He wrote them a document acknowledging receipt of that.

Some people deny that Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh came to Iraq before the caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb. Abū Mikhnaf and al-Wāqidī used to say: “He came there twice.”

608They said: Khālid wrote a document for Baṣbuhrī b. Ṣalūbā and sent the ṭaylasān to Abū Bakr, together with the money from al-Ḥīra and the one thousand dirhams.

He gave the ṭaylasān to al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī ﵄.

609Abū Naṣr al-Tammār told me: Sharīk b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Nakhaʿī told us, from al-Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāh, from al-Ḥakam, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Mughaffal al-Muzanī, who said: The people of the Sawād have no covenant except al-Ḥīra, Ullays, and Bānqiyā.

610Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from al-Mufaḍḍal b. al-Muhalhal, from Manṣūr, from ʿUbayd b. al-Ḥasan or Abū al-Ḥasan,

from Ibn Mughaffal, who said: It is not permissible to sell land on this side of al-Jabal, except the land of Banū Ṣalūbā and the land of al-Ḥīra.

611Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, from al-Aswad b. Qays, from his father, who said: We reached al-Ḥīra and made terms with them for such-and-such an amount and a saddle.

He said: I asked, “What did you do with the saddle?” He said: “One of our companions had no saddle, so we gave it to him.”

612Abū ʿUbayd told us: Ibn Abī Maryam told us, from al-Samarī b. Yaḥyā, from Ḥumayd b. Hilāl, that when Khālid encamped at al-Ḥīra, he made terms with its people, and they did not fight.

Ḍirār b. al-Azwar al-Asadī said:

I lay sleepless at Bānqiyā; whoever encounters the like of what I encountered at Bānqiyā in wounds will lie sleepless.

Al-Wāqidī said: The account agreed upon among our associates is that Ḍirār was killed at al-Yamāma.

613They said: Khālid came to al-Falālīj on his return from Bānqiyā. A force of the non-Arabs was there, but they dispersed, and he encountered no hostile action.

He turned back to al-Ḥīra, where news reached him that Jābān was with a force

of great size at Tustar.

He sent against him al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha al-Shaybānī and Ḥanẓala b. al-Rabīʿ b. Ribāḥ al-Usayyidī, of Banū Tamīm, who is called Ḥanẓala the Scribe.

When the two reached him, he fled.

Khālid proceeded to al-Anbār, and its people fortified themselves.

Then someone came to him who directed him to the market of Baghdad, the old market that was at Qarn al-Ṣarāt.

Khālid sent al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha, who raided it. The Muslims filled their hands with gold and silver and goods that were light to carry.

Then they spent the night at al-Saylaḥīn and came to al-Anbār, where Khālid was. They besieged its people and set fires in its environs.

Al-Anbār was so named because the granaries of the non-Arabs were there.

Al-Nuʿmān’s companions and protégés used to receive their provisions from them.

When the people of al-Anbār saw what had befallen them, they made terms with Khālid

for something with which he was satisfied, and he left them in place.

It is also said that Khālid sent al-Muthannā ahead to Baghdad, then proceeded after him and himself conducted the raid upon it, before returning to al-Anbār.

That is not firmly established.

614Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me: Al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Jābir, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: The people of al-Anbār have a covenant and an agreement.

615Elders from the people of al-Anbār told me that terms were made with them during the caliphate of ʿUmar, may God have mercy upon him, for their ṭassūj, at four hundred thousand dirhams and one thousand Qaṭawānī cloaks every year. Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī conducted the peace negotiations.

It is also said that he made terms with them for eighty thousand. God knows best.

616They said: Jarīr conquered Bawāzīj al-Anbār, where there were some of his clients.

617They said: A man came to Khālid b. al-Walīd and directed him to a market above al-Anbār where Kalb, Bakr b. Wāʾil, and groups of Quḍāʿa gathered.

He sent al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha there. He raided it, seized what was in it, killed, and took captives.

Then Khālid came to ʿAyn al-Tamr and drew close to its fortress.

There was a large garrison of non-Arabs in it.

The people of the fortress came out and fought.

Then they kept to their fortress. Khālid and the Muslims besieged them until they asked for safe-conduct, but he refused to grant it to them. He took the fortress by force, killed, and took captives. In a church there he found a group whom he took captive. Among those captives was Ḥumrān b. Abān b. Khālid al-Tamrī.

Some people say: His father's name was Abā.

Ḥumrān was the client of ʿUthmān. He had belonged to al-Musayyab b. Najaba al-Fazārī, and he bought him from him and freed him.

Then he sent him to Kūfa to inquire about his governor, but he judged him to have lied and expelled him from his neighborhood, so he settled in Baṣra.

Also Sīrīn, the father of Muḥammad b. Sīrīn and his brothers, namely Yaḥyā b. Sīrīn, Anas b. Sīrīn, and Maʿbad b. Sīrīn, who was the eldest of his brothers. They were the clients of Anas b. Mālik al-Anṣārī.

Among those captives was also Abū ʿAmra, the grandfather of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Aʿlā the poet.

Also Yasār, the grandfather of Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, the author of the biography, who was the client of Qays b. Makhrama b. al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf.

Among them was Murra, the father of ʿUbayd, the grandfather of Muḥammad b. Zayd b. ʿUbayd b. Murra and Nafīs b. Muḥammad b. Zayd b. ʿUbayd b. Murra, the owner of the palace by al-Ḥarra.

The son of this Muḥammad and his sons say: ʿUbayd b. Murra b. al-Muʿallā al-Anṣārī, then al-Zuraqī.

Also Nuṣayr, the father of Mūsā b. Nuṣayr, the commander in the Maghrib. He was a client of the Banū Umayya, and he has clients in the frontier districts, descendants of those whom he freed, who say this.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: Abū Farwa ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Aswad and Nuṣayr, the father of Mūsā b. Nuṣayr, were two Arabs from Arāsha of Balī. They were taken captive in the days of Abū Bakr ﵀ from Mount al-Jalīl in Syria.

Nuṣayr's name had been Naṣr, and it was put into the diminutive. One of the Banū Umayya freed him, and he returned to Syria. Mūsā was born to him in a village called Kafr Marā, and he was lame.

Al-Kalbī said: It has also been said that they were two brothers from among the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr and that their clientage belonged to the Banū Ḍabba.

ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī said: It is said that Abū Farwa and Nuṣayr were among the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr.

Nāʿim al-Asadī bought Abū Farwa, and then ʿUthmān bought him from him and set him to digging graves.

When the people rose against him, he joined them against him and said to him: “Restore what was wrongfully taken.”

He said to him: “You are the first of those things. I bought you with the alms funds to dig graves, but you abandoned that.”

His son ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Farwa was one of the leading clients.

Al-Rabīʿ, the associate of al-Manṣūr, was al-Rabīʿ b. Yūnus b. Muḥammad b. Abī Farwa.

He was only nicknamed Abū Farwa; it was upon him when he was taken captive. It has also been said that Khālid made a settlement with the people of the fortress of ʿAyn al-Tamr, and that these captives were found in a church in one of the districts.

It was said that Sīrīn was from Jarjarāyā, and that he was visiting relatives of his and was seized with them in the church.

618Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me, who said: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, from Ashʿath, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: Khālid b. al-Walīd made a settlement with the people of al-Ḥīra and the people of ʿAyn al-Tamr. He wrote to Abū Bakr about it, and he approved it.

Yaḥyā said: I said to al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ: “Then are the people of ʿAyn al-Tamr like the people of al-Ḥīra, with merely something imposed upon them and nothing imposed upon their lands?”

He said: “Yes.”

619They said: Hilāl b. ʿAqqa b. Qays b. al-Bishr al-Namarī was in command of al-Namir b. Qāsiṭ at ʿAyn al-Tamr. He gathered forces against Khālid and fought him, but he defeated him, killed him, and crucified him.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: In command of al-Namir that day was ʿAqqa b. Qays b. al-Bishr himself.

620They said: Bashīr b. Saʿd al-Anṣārī's wound reopened, and he died and was buried at ʿAyn al-Tamr.

Buried beside him was ʿUmayr b. Riʾāb b. Muhashshim b. Saʿīd b. Sahm b. ʿAmr. An arrow had struck him at ʿAyn al-Tamr, and he was martyred.

While at ʿAyn al-Tamr, Khālid b. al-Walīd sent al-Nusayr b. Daysam b. Thawr to a watering place belonging to the Banū Taghlib. He came upon them by night, killed, and took prisoners. A man among the prisoners asked him to release him in return for directing him to a clan of Rabīʿa.

He did so, and al-Nusayr came to that clan.

He attacked them by night, took booty, and took captives.

He proceeded toward Tikrīt through the open country , and the Muslims took booty.

621Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from Muḥammad b. Marwān, that al-Nusayr came to ʿUkbarā and granted its people safe-conduct. They brought out food and fodder for those with him.

Then he passed through al-Bardān. Its people began running away before the Muslims, and he said to them: “There is no harm.”

That constituted safe-conduct.

He said: Then he came to al-Mukharrim—Abū Masʿūd said: It was not called Mukharrim at that time. Some of the descendants of Mukharrim b. Ḥazn b. Ziyād b. Anas b. al-Dayyān al-Ḥārithī settled there, and it was named after him, according to what Hishām b. Muḥammad al-Kalbī related—then the Muslims crossed a bridge that had been laid at

the palace of Sābūr, known today as the palace of ʿĪsā b. ʿAlī. Khurzād b. Māhbandādh, who was entrusted with it, came out against him, and they fought him and defeated him.

Then they pressed on and came to ʿAyn al-Tamr.

Al-Wāqidī said: Al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha sent al-Nusayr and Ḥudhayfa b. Miḥṣan with cavalry to Khuffān after the Day of the Bridge and after his withdrawal with the Muslims. This was during the caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb.

They attacked a group of the Banū Taghlib and crossed over to Tikrīt, taking livestock and sheep.

ʿAttāb b. Ibrāhīm said, according to what Abū Masʿūd related to me from him, that al-Nusayr and Ḥudhayfa granted the people of Tikrīt safe-conduct and wrote them a document that ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī ratified for him when he conquered al-Ṭayrahān and al-Mawṣil.

He also related that al-Nusayr went out on behalf of Khālid b. al-Walīd and raided villages in Maskin and Quṭrabbul, taking substantial booty from them.

They said: Then Khālid marched from ʿAyn al-Tamr to Syria. He said to al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha: “Return, may God have mercy on you, to your jurisdiction, neither remiss nor slack.”

The poet said: “We came at dawn with battalions upon a clan of Bakr, / and a clan of Quḍāʿa, no fainthearts. We laid their abode open to plunder, while the horses galloped / bearing every lordly warrior, high of neck.” He means those who were in the market above al-Anbār.

“Al-Muthannā has a battle at al-ʿĀl, / witnessed by men of his tribe.” By al-ʿĀl he means al-Anbār, Quṭrabbul, Maskin, and Bādūrayā; thus he meant the market of Baghdad. “A battalion whose onslaught terrified / Kisrā, and the Īwān nearly split apart.”

“He emboldened the Muslims when they were afraid; / in the vicissitudes of experience are lessons. He made the course of the road easy, and they followed / his tracks; affairs are followed in their tracks.”

622One of them said when they encountered Khurzād: “The wary Persian sought escape from us / when we met him just short of the lookout, With every lean-bellied, swift, slender mare; / with such mounts the host of the unbelievers is defeated.” By the lookout he means the mound of ʿAqarqūf.

Khālid's departure for Syria was in the month of Rabīʿ al-Ākhir; it is also said to have been in the month of Rabīʿ al-Awwal, in the year thirteen.

623Some people said that Khālid came to Dūma from ʿAyn al-Tamr and conquered it, then proceeded toward Syria. The sounder account of this is his departure from ʿAyn al-Tamr.

Chapter 54

The caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb

The Caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁

624They said: When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ became caliph, he sent Abū ʿUbayd b. ʿAmr ʿUmayr b. ʿAwf b. ʿUqda b. Ghiyara b. ʿAwf b. Thaqīf—he was the father of al-Mukhtār b. Abī ʿUbayd—to Iraq with one thousand men. He wrote to al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha, ordering him to receive him and to hear and obey him. He sent Salīṭ b. Qays b. ʿAmr al-Anṣārī with Abū ʿUbayd, saying to him: “Were it not for your impetuosity, I would have appointed you commander. But war is fierce, and only a deliberate man is suited to it.”

Abū ʿUbayd advanced, passing no group of Arabs without encouraging them to undertake jihad and acquire booty.

A multitude accompanied him.

When he reached al-ʿUdhayb, news reached him that Jābān , the non-Arab, was at Tustar with a large force.

He met him, defeated his force, and took some of them prisoner.

Then he came to Durnā, where there was a force of non-Arabs, and routed them toward Kaskar.

He marched against al-Jālīnūs, who was at Bārūsmā. Ibn al-Andarzaʿz (sic) made a settlement with him for four dirhams per head, on condition that he withdraw.

Abū ʿUbayd sent al-Muthannā to Zandaward. He found that they had broken their agreement, so he fought them, prevailed, and took captives.

He sent ʿUrwa b. Zayd al-Khayl al-Ṭāʾī to al-Zawābī, and he made a settlement with its dihqān on the same terms as the settlement of Bārūsmā.

Chapter 55

The day of Quss al-Nāṭif, the day of the Bridge

The Day of Quss al-Nāṭif, Which Is the Day of the Bridge

625They said: When the Persians learned that the Arabs had assembled, they sent against them Dhū al-Ḥājib Mardānshāh. Anūshirwān had given him the name Bahman because he sought blessing through him. He was called Dhū al-Ḥājib because he used to trim his eyebrows to raise them above his eyes, out of arrogance.

It is also said that his name was Rustam.

Abū ʿUbayd ordered the bridge to be repaired and secured. The people of Bāniqyā helped him lay it.

It is also said that this bridge was an old one belonging to the people of al-Ḥīra, over which they crossed to their estates. Abū ʿUbayd repaired it, for it had been damaged and broken.

Then Abū ʿUbayd and the Muslims crossed from al-Marwaḥa over the bridge. They met Dhū al-Ḥājib, who had four thousand armored men and an elephant with him; it is also said that there were several elephants. They fought fiercely, and wounds became numerous and widespread among the Muslims.

Salīṭ b. Qays said: “Abū ʿUbayd! I had forbidden you to cross this bridge to them and advised you to withdraw to one of the surrounding areas and write to the Commander of the Faithful requesting reinforcements, but you refused.”

Salīṭ fought until he was killed.

Abū ʿUbayd asked: “Where is this beast's vulnerable spot?” He was told: “Its trunk.”

He charged and struck the elephant's trunk. Abū Miḥjan b. Ḥabīb al-Thaqafī charged it and struck its leg, leaving it hanging. The polytheists charged, and Abū ʿUbayd was killed ﵀.

It is also said that the elephant knelt upon him and he died beneath it.

His brother took the standard and was killed.

His son Jabr took it and was killed.

Then al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha took it for a time and withdrew with the men, some protecting the others. ʿUrwa b. Zayd al-Khayl fought fiercely that day, his fighting equaling that of a whole group. Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī the poet fought out of zeal for the Muslims at al-Gharbiyya. He had come to al-Ḥīra on some business of his, and he was a Christian.

Al-Muthannā came to Ullays and encamped there. He wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb with the news, sending it with ʿUrwa b. Zayd.

Among those killed on the Day of the Bridge, according to what Abū Mikhnaf related, was Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī, one of

those who collected the Qurʾān in the time of the Prophet ﷺ.

626They said: The Battle of the Bridge took place on Saturday at the end of the month of Ramaḍān in the year thirteen.

Abū Miḥjan b. Ḥabīb said: “How did Umm Yūsuf travel by night? Ḥawnā— / with unknown wastelands lying short of her night's destination, To young men at al-Ṭaff whose leading men were struck down, / and horses and riding camels of theirs were left behind. I passed the Anṣār amid their baggage / and said to them: ‘Is any of you returning home today?’”

627Abū ʿUbayd b. Sallām told me, who said: Muḥammad b. Kathīr told us, from Zāʾida, from Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid, from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, who said: Abū ʿUbayd crossed Bāniqyā with some of his companions. The polytheists cut the bridge, and some of his companions were struck down.

Ismāʿīl said: Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: The Day of Mihrān was at the beginning of the year, and al-Qādisiyya at its end.

Chapter 56

The battle of Mihrān, the battle of al-Nukhayla

The Battle of Mihrān, Which Is the Battle of al-Nukhayla

628Abū Mikhnaf and others said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ spent a year without mentioning Iraq because of the calamity that had befallen Abū ʿUbayd and Sulayṭ.

Al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha remained in the vicinity of Ullays, calling the Arabs to jihad.

Then ʿUmar ﵁ summoned the people to Iraq, but they began avoiding it and showing reluctance, until he considered campaigning in person.

A large body of men from al-Azd came to him, intending to campaign in Syria. He called them to Iraq and encouraged them with the riches of the house of Kisrā. They left the choice to him, and he ordered them to depart.

Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh arrived from al-Sarāt with Bajīla and asked to go to Iraq on condition that he and his people receive a quarter of whatever they conquered.

ʿUmar agreed to this, and he set out toward Iraq.

Some people claim that he passed along the Baṣra road and engaged the marzbān of al-Madhār, defeating him.

Others claim that he engaged the marzbān while he was with Khālid b. al-Walīd.

Some people say that he took the road through Fayd and al-Thaʿlabiyya to al-ʿUdhayb.

629ʿAffān b. Muslim told me: Ḥammād b. Salama told us: Dāwūd b. Abī Hind told us: Al-Shaʿbī informed me that ʿUmar dispatched Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh to Kūfa after the killing of Abū ʿUbayd, the first man he dispatched. He said, “Would you go to Iraq if I grant you a third as an additional share after the fifth?” He said, “Yes.”

630They said: The Muslims assembled at Dayr Hind in the year fourteen. Shīrūya had died, and Būrān daughter of Kisrā had assumed the kingship until Yazdajird b. Shahriyār should come of age.

He sent against them Mihrān b. Mihr Bundādh al-Hamadhānī with twelve thousand men. The Muslims gave him time until he had crossed the bridge and reached the side adjoining Dayr al-Aʿwar.

Sayf related that, on crossing the bridge, Mihrān reached a place called al-Buwayb, and this is the place where he was killed. It is said that the two sides of al-Buwayb were filled with bones until it became level, and that dust covered them during the time of the civil strife. Nothing is stirred up there [without their coming upon some of them]. This is between al-Sakūn and Banū Sulaym.

It was a drainage channel for the Euphrates in the days of the Kisrās, discharging into al-Jawf.

The Muslims’ camp was at al-Nukhayla. According to what Bajīla claim, Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh commanded the people; according to what Rabīʿa say, it was al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha.

It has also been said that they shared authority, each people having its own chief.

The Muslims and their enemy met. Shuraḥbīl b. al-Simṭ al-Kindī acquitted himself well that day, and Masʿūd b. Ḥāritha, the brother of al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha, was killed.

Al-Muthannā said, “O Muslims! Do not be alarmed by my brother’s fall, for thus do the best of you fall.”

They charged as one man, steadfast in their resolve and endurance, until God killed Mihrān and routed the unbelievers.

The Muslims pursued them, killing them, and few of them escaped.

Qurṭ b. Jimāḥ al-ʿAbdī fought that day until his sword bent. Night came, and they gathered back at their camp. This was in the year fourteen.

Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh and al-Mundhir b. Ḥassān b. Ḍirār al-Ḍabbī undertook the killing of Mihrān. This one said, “I killed him,” and that one said, “I killed him,” and they disputed fiercely.

Al-Mundhir took his belt, and Jarīr took the rest of his spoils.

It is said that al-Ḥiṣn b. Maʿbad b. Zurāra b. ʿUdas al-Tamīmī was among those who killed him.

631Then the Muslims continued launching raids in succession between al-Ḥīra and Kaskar, between Kaskar and Sūrā, Barbīsmā, and Ṣarāt Jāmāsb, and between the two Fallūjas

and al-Nahrayn and ʿAyn al-Tamr.

They came to the fortress of Malīqyā, which was a lookout post, and conquered it.

They drove the non-Arabs from lookout posts in al-Ṭaff.

They were demoralized; their authority had become feeble and their position weak.

Some of the Muslims crossed the Sūrā canal and came to Kūthā, Nahr al-Malik, and Bādūrayā.

Some of them reached Kalwādhā.

They lived on what they obtained from the raids.

It is said that eighteen months elapsed between Mihrān and al-Qādisiyya.

Chapter 57

The battle of al-Qādisiyya

632They said: The Muslims wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ informing him of the great number of Persians who had assembled against them and asking him for reinforcements.

He intended to campaign in person and encamped for that purpose.

Al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and a group of the senior Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ advised him to remain and dispatch armies and detachments.

He did so.

ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib advised him to set out.

He said to him, “I have resolved to remain.”

He offered ʿAlī ﵁ the opportunity to depart, but he declined it.

ʿUmar intended to dispatch Saʿīd b. Zayd b. ʿAmr b. Nufayl al-ʿAdawī, but then changed his mind and dispatched Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ—the name of Abū Waqqāṣ was Mālik b. Uhayb b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Zuhra b. Kilāb—and said, “He is a brave man and an archer.”

It is said that Saʿīd b. Zayd b. ʿAmr was campaigning in Syria at that time.

633They said: He set out for Iraq and stayed at al-Thaʿlabiyya for three months until the people had joined him.

Then he arrived at al-ʿUdhayb in the year fifteen.

Al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha was ill. He advised him to fight the enemy between al-Qādisiyya and al-ʿUdhayb. Then his illness became severe, and he was carried to his people and died among them.

Saʿd married his wife.

Al-Wāqidī said: Al-Muthannā died before Rustam encamped at al-Qādisiyya.

634They said: Rustam advanced—he was from al-Rayy, though it is said that he was instead from Hamadhān—and encamped at Burs.

Then he marched and remained between al-Ḥīra and al-Saylaḥīn for four months, without advancing

against the Muslims or fighting them, while the Muslims were encamped between al-ʿUdhayb and al-Qādisiyya.

Rustam sent Dhū al-Ḥājib ahead, and he was encamped at Ṭīzanābādh.

The polytheists numbered approximately one hundred thousand and twenty thousand. They had thirty elephants and their great banner, called Dirafshkābiyān.

The Muslims altogether numbered between nine thousand and ten thousand. When they needed fodder and food, they sent cavalry out into the open country, and it raided the lower Euphrates.

ʿUmar used to send them sheep and carrots from Medina.

635They said: Baṣra had been established as a garrison town between the battle of al-Nukhayla and the battle of al-Qādisiyya. ʿUtba b. Ghazwān established it.

Then he requested permission to perform the pilgrimage and left al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba in charge.

ʿUmar wrote to him with his commission. Before long he was charged with what he was charged with, so he appointed Abū Mūsā over Baṣra and summoned al-Mughīra to Medina.

Then ʿUmar sent him and those who had testified against him back to Baṣra.

When the battle of al-Qādisiyya was at hand, ʿUmar wrote to Abū Mūsā, ordering him to reinforce Saʿd. He reinforced him with al-Mughīra at the head of eight hundred men, or, it is said, four hundred. He took part in it and then departed for Medina.

ʿUmar wrote to Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ, who reinforced Saʿd with Qays b. Hubayra b. al-Makshūḥ al-Murādī.

It is said that he took part in al-Qādisiyya, and it is said instead that he reached the Muslims after its fighting had ended. Qays had seven hundred men with him.

The battle of al-Qādisiyya was at the end of the year sixteen.

It has also been said that the man who reinforced Saʿd with al-Mughīra was ʿUtba b. Ghazwān; that al-Mughīra assumed the governorship of Baṣra only after his return from al-Qādisiyya; and that, when ʿUmar had summoned him to Medina because of what he had been charged with, he sent him out from Medina only as governor of Kūfa.

636Al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd al-Narsī told me: ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. Ziyād told us, from Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: ʿUmar wrote to Abū ʿUbayda, “Send Qays b. Makshūḥ to al-Qādisiyya with those who volunteer to accompany him.”

A large number volunteered to accompany him.

He hurried forward with seven hundred men, and Saʿd had already been granted victory.

They asked him for booty.

He wrote to ʿUmar about this, and ʿUmar wrote back to him, “If Qays arrived before the dead were buried, allot him his share.”

637They said: Rustam sent to Saʿd, asking him to send some of his companions to him.

He sent al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba.

He made for Rustam’s throne to sit upon it with him, but the asāwira prevented him from doing so. Rustam spoke to him at length.

Then he said to him, “I know that nothing has driven you to your present undertaking except straitened means and severe hardship.

“We will give you enough to fill your bellies and send you away with some of what you desire.”

Al-Mughīra said, “God sent His Prophet to us ﷺ and we attained felicity by answering and following him. He commanded us to wage jihad against those who oppose our religion, ‘until they pay the jizya out of hand, being humbled.’ (1) We call you to worship God alone and to believe in His Prophet ﷺ. If you do so, well; otherwise, the sword stands between us and you.”

Rustam snorted in anger.

Then he said, “By the sun and the moon, tomorrow’s forenoon will not be far advanced before we kill you all.”

Al-Mughīra said, “There is no power and no strength except through God.”

He left him.

He was riding a lean horse of his, and wore a notched sword with rags wrapped around it.

638ʿUmar wrote to Saʿd, ordering him to send men to the ruler of the Persians to call him to Islam.

He sent ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Kab al-Zubaydī and al-Ashʿath b. Qays

[Source note 1: Sūra 9, verse 29.]

(*)

al-Kindī with a group. They passed by Rustam and were brought before him. He said, “Where are you headed?” They said, “To your master.”

Much conversation passed between them, until they said, “Our Prophet has promised us that we shall conquer your land.”

He called for a basket of earth and said, “This is yours from our land.”

ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib rose quickly, spread out his cloak, took some of that earth in it, and departed.

He was asked, “What prompted you to do what you did?” He said, “I took it as a favorable omen that their land would become ours and that we would conquer it.”

Then they came to the king and called him to Islam. He became angry, ordered them to leave, and said, “Were you not messengers, I would kill you.”

He wrote to Rustam, rebuking him for sending them to him.

639Then the Muslims’ foraging party, commanded by Zuhra b. Ḥawiyya b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Qatāda al-Taymī, then al-Saʿdī—it is also said that Qatāda b. Ḥawiyya commanded it—encountered cavalry of the non-Arabs. That was the cause of the battle.

The non-Arabs reinforced their cavalry, and the Muslims reinforced their foraging party. Battle was joined between them, after noon. ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib al-Zubaydī charged, grappled with a Persian noble, placed him before him on his saddle, and said, “I am Abū Thawr. Do likewise.”

Then he struck down one of the elephants and said, “Keep your swords upon their trunks, for the elephant’s vulnerable point is its trunk.”

640Saʿd had placed Khālid b. ʿUrfuṭa al-ʿUdhrī, an ally of Banū Zuhra, in charge of the camp and the people because of an ailment that afflicted him.

He was staying in the fortress of al-ʿUdhayb. His wife—she was Salmā daughter of Ḥafṣa, of Banū Taym Allāh b. Thaʿlaba, the wife of al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha—began saying, “Alas for al-Muthannā! There is no Muthannā for the cavalry!” He slapped her.

She said, “O Saʿd! Jealousy and cowardice?”

641Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī was at Bāḍiʿ, to which ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ had banished him for drinking wine. He escaped and joined Saʿd.

He was not among those who had departed with him, according to what al-Wāqidī mentioned. He drank wine in Saʿd’s camp, so Saʿd flogged him and imprisoned him in the fortress of

al-ʿUdhayb.

He asked Zabrāʾ, Saʿd’s slave woman who had borne him a child, to release him so that he could fight and then return to his irons.

She made him swear by God that he would do so if she released him.

He mounted Saʿd’s horse, charged the non-Arabs, broke through their ranks, and struck down the white elephant with his sword while Saʿd watched him.

He said, “As for the horse, it is my horse; as for the charge, it is Abū Miḥjan’s charge.”

Then he returned to his irons.

It is said that Salmā daughter of Ḥafṣa gave him the horse, but the first account is more correct and better established.

When the affair of Rustam was over, Saʿd said to him, “By God, after what I have seen of you, I shall never flog you for wine again.”

He said, “And I, by God, shall never drink it again.”

642Ṭulayḥa b. Khuwaylid al-Asadī acquitted himself well that day and struck al-Jālīnūs a blow that split his mail head covering but had no effect on his head.

Qays b. Makshūḥ said, “My people! The death of noble men is to be killed. Do not let these uncircumcised men have a greater claim to endurance or be more willing to meet death than you.”

Then he fought fiercely. God killed Rustam, and his body was found covered with sword blows and spear wounds, so it was not known who had killed him.

ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib, Ṭulayḥa b. Khuwaylid al-Asadī, Qurṭ b. Jimāḥ al-ʿAbdī, and Ḍirār b. al-Azwar al-Asadī had advanced against him.

Al-Wāqidī used to say: Ḍirār was killed at the battle of al-Yamāma.

It has also been said that Zuhayr b. ʿAbd Shams al-Bajalī killed him.

It has also been said that his killer was ʿAwwām b. ʿAbd Shams.

It has been said that his killer was Hilāl b. ʿUllafa al-Taymī.

The fighting at al-Qādisiyya took place on Thursday, Friday, and the night of Saturday, which was the Night of Clamor.

The night at Ṣiffīn was named after it.

It is said that Qays b. Makshūḥ did not take part in the fighting at al-Qādisiyya, but arrived there after the Muslims had finished fighting.

643Aḥmad b. Salmān al-Bāhilī told me, from al-Sahmī, from his elders, that Salmān b. Rabīʿa campaigned in Syria with Abū Umāma al-Ṣudayy b. ʿAjlān al-Bāhilī and took part in the Muslims’ engagements there. He then went out to Iraq among those who hastened out as reinforcements to al-Qādisiyya. He witnessed the battle, settled in Kūfa, and was killed at Balanjar.

644Al-Wāqidī said in his chain of transmission: A group of non-Arabs dug a trench for their banner and said, “We shall not leave our position until we die.” Salmān b. Rabīʿa al-Bāhilī charged them, killed them, and took the banner.

645They said: Saʿd sent Khālid b. ʿUrfuṭa in command of the pursuing cavalry. They killed those whom they overtook until they reached Burs. Khālid lodged with a man called Bisṭām, who honored him and treated him generously. A river there was named the River of Bisṭām.

Khālid passed through al-Ṣarāḥ and caught up with Jālīnūs. Kathīr b. Shihāb al-Ḥārithī charged him and stabbed him; it is said that he killed him. Ibn al-Kalbī said: Zuhra b. Ḥawiyya al-Saʿdī killed him. This is the more firmly established account.

The Persians fled to al-Madāʾin and joined Yazdajird. Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar reporting the victory and the losses of those who had fallen.

646Abū Rajāʾ al-Fārisī told me, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: I was present at the battle of al-Qādisiyya while I was a Magian. When the Arabs shot arrows at us , we began saying, “Dūk, dūk,” meaning spindles. Those spindles kept at us until they brought down our rule.

A man among us would shoot from a nāwak bow, and its arrow would do no more than catch in one of their garments. Yet an arrow from their arrows would pierce the stout coat of mail and the doubled jawshan armor that we wore.

Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: The first person to kill a non-Arab on the day of al-Qādisiyya was Rabīʿa b. ʿUthmān b. Rabīʿa, one of the Banū Naṣr b. Muʿāwiya b. Bakr b. Hawāzin b. Manṣūr.

647Ṭulayḥa said concerning the day of al-Qādisiyya: “I struck al-Jālīnūs a blow, when the noble horses were amid the press.”

Abū Miḥjan al-Thaqafī said when he saw the fighting: “It is grief enough that horses are thrust at with spears, while I am left, my bonds drawn tight around me. When I rise, the iron restrains me, and doors are shut before me, deafening anyone who calls.”

Zuhayr b. ʿAbd Shams b. ʿAwf al-Bajalī said: “I am Zuhayr and the son of ʿAbd Shams; with the sword I brought down the great man of the Persians, Rustam, possessed of pride and figured silk. I obeyed my Lord and satisfied my soul.”

Al-Ashʿath b. ʿAbd al-Ḥajar b. Surāqa al-Kilābī, who witnessed al-Ḥīra and al-Qādisiyya, said: “I hamstrung my mount at al-Saylaḥīn and at the palace only for fear of being reproached. Wretched is the man who boasts over me of his kinsmen, when my elders have held sway over Maʿadd and Ḥimyar.”

One of the Muslims said that day: “I fought until God sent down His victory, while Saʿd held himself secure at the gate of al-Qādisiyya. We returned with many women widowed, while among Saʿd’s women there was no widow.”

Qays b. al-Makshūḥ said—and it is said that these verses are by someone else: “I brought the horses from Ṣanʿāʾ, running, bearing every armored warrior, lofty as a lion, to Wādī al-Qurā, then the abodes of Kalb, to al-Yarmūk, then the Syrian land. We came to al-Qādisiyya after a month, the horses marked, their heels bleeding. There we rose against the host of Kisrā and the sons of the noble marzbāns. When I saw the cavalry wheel about, I made for the station of the king al-Mām. I struck his head, and he fell slain, with a sword neither notched nor blunt. God bestowed good there, and good deeds grow with God.”

ʿIṣām b. al-Muqshaʿirr said: “Had you witnessed me at al-Qawādis, you would have seen the swordplay of a resolute man when the people held back. I strike with the roughly forged sword until I notch it, and thrust with the casting spear and advance.”

Ṭulayḥa b. Khuwaylid said: “You came by night, Sulaymā, to the riders’ saddles; how did you find your way across a broad, empty plain? Since you departed, Salām, I have been enamored of sweeping raids and war. Had you been there on the day of al-Qādisiyya, when I engaged them with a keen Indian sword, you would have seen my charges and my withdrawals, and my standing firm to thrust and strike.”

Bishr b. Rabīʿa b. ʿAmr al-Khathʿamī said: “A phantom of Umayma visited deep in the night, when the earliest stars had begun to set, while we were in the desert of al-ʿUdhayb and her abode was in the Ḥijāz: the dwelling place was far away. The only wonder is her crossing the deserts in the darkness, with a lofty, immovable mountain spur between us.”

“My she-camel yearns at the gate of al-Qādisiyya, while Saʿd b. Waqqāṣ is commander over me. Saʿd is a commander whose harm is nearer than his good, far-reaching in injury, his fire steel yielding no spark, short. Remember—may God guide you—the blows of our swords at the gate of Qudays, when renewed attack was difficult, on the evening when the people wished that one of them might be lent a bird’s two wings and fly away.”

He said: Saʿd b. ʿUbayd al-Anṣārī was martyred that day. ʿUmar grieved at his loss and said, “His killing almost spoiled this victory for me.”

Chapter 58

The conquest of al-Madāʾin

648They said: The Muslims proceeded after al-Qādisiyya. When they passed Dayr Kaʿb, al-Nakhīrkhān Ilayhā wa-Badā met them with a great host from the people of al-Madāʾin, and they fought. Zuhayr b. Sulaym al-Azdī grappled with al-Nakhīrkhān, and he fell to the ground. Zuhayr took a dagger that was at al-Nakhīrkhān’s waist, slit open his belly, and killed him.

Saʿd and the Muslims marched on and encamped at Sābāṭ. They assembled at the city of Bahurasīr, which is the city on the Kūfa side. They remained for nine months; it is said eighteen months, until they had eaten fresh dates twice. The inhabitants of that city fought them, and when the two sides disengaged, they went back inside it.

When the Muslims conquered it, Yazdajird b. Shahriyār, king of Persia, resolved to flee. He was lowered from the White Palace of al-Madāʾin in a basket, so the Nabataeans called him Bar Zabīlā. He proceeded to Ḥulwān with the leading men of his asāwira, taking with him his treasury, his light belongings and his stores, and the women and children. The year in which he fled was a year of famine and plague that spread throughout the people of Persia.

Then the Muslims crossed by wading and conquered the eastern city.

649ʿAffān b. Muslim told me. He said: Hushaym informed us. He said: Ḥuṣayn informed us. He said: Abū Wāʾil informed us. He said: When the non-Arabs were defeated at al-Qādisiyya, we pursued them. They assembled at Kūthā, and we pursued them. Then we reached the Tigris, and the Muslims said, “What are you waiting for before wading through this stream?” So we waded through it and defeated them.

650Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from Ibn ʿAjlān, from Abān b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: When the Persians were defeated at al-Qādisiyya, their routed remnants arrived at al-Madāʾin,

and the Muslims reached the Tigris, which was overflowing with water the like of which had never been seen. The Persians had moved the boats and ferries to the eastern bank and burned the bridge. Saʿd and the Muslims were distressed because they could find no way to cross. A man among the Muslims volunteered, made his horse swim, and crossed. The Muslims then swam across. They afterward ordered the boatmen to take the baggage across. The Persians said, “By God, you are fighting none but jinn!” Then they fled in defeat.

651ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam; and Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ told me. They both said: Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ sent Khālid b. ʿUrfuṭa in command of his vanguard. Before Saʿd arrived, Khālid had conquered Sābāṭ.

Then he came and remained before al-Rūmiyya until he made a settlement with its inhabitants: those among them who wished could depart, and those who remained would do so on condition of obedience, sincere counsel, payment of the kharāj, and guiding the Muslims, harboring no deceit toward them.

He found no ferries, but was directed to a ford near the village of the fishermen. They made the horses wade through it, while the Persians shot at them. They came through unharmed , except for a man of Ṭayyiʾ called Sulayl b. Yazīd b. Mālik al-Sinbisī; no one else was struck that day.

652ʿAbdallāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us. He said: Someone whom I trust told me, from al-Mujālid b. Saʿīd, from al-Shaʿbī, that he said: On the day of al-Madāʾin, the Muslims took slave girls from among Kisrā’s slave girls who had been brought from distant regions and used to do work for him. My mother was one of them.

He said: The Muslims began taking camphor that day and throwing it into their pots, thinking it was salt.

Al-Wāqidī said: Saʿd finished with al-Madāʾin and Jalūlāʾ in the year sixteen.

Chapter 59

The day of Jalūlāʾ

The Day of Jalūlāʾ, the Battle

653They said: The Muslims remained at al-Madāʾin for some days. Then word reached them that Yazdajird had assembled a great host and sent it against them, and that the host was at Jalūlāʾ. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ dispatched Hāshim b. ʿUtba b. Abī Waqqāṣ against them with twelve thousand men. They found that the non-Arabs had fortified themselves, dug trenches, placed their families and baggage at Khāniqīn, and pledged to one another not to flee. Reinforcements kept coming to them from Ḥulwān and al-Jibāl.

The Muslims said, “We ought to engage them promptly before their reinforcements grow numerous.”

They met them with Ḥujr b. ʿAdī al-Kindī commanding the right wing, ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib commanding the cavalry, and Ṭulayḥa b. Khuwaylid commanding the infantry. Khurrazād, Rustam’s brother, commanded the non-Arabs that day.

They fought a fierce battle, the like of which they had never fought, shooting arrows and thrusting with spears until the spears shattered. They struck one another with swords until the swords bent.

Then the Muslims made a single charge, dislodging the non-Arabs from their position and defeating them. They turned and fled, and the Muslims pressed hard upon them, killing them in great numbers until darkness intervened between them.

Then they returned to their camp. Hāshim b. ʿUtba stationed Jarīr b. ʿAbdallāh at Jalūlāʾ with a large body of cavalry, to stand between the Muslims and their enemy.

Yazdajird departed from Ḥulwān, and the Muslims began raiding the districts of the Sawād on the eastern side of the Tigris. They came to Mahrūdh, and its dihqān made a settlement with Hāshim for a jarīb of dirhams, on condition that he kill none of them.

He killed the dihqān of al-Daskara because he suspected him of deceit toward the Muslims. He came to al-Bandanījayn, whose inhabitants sought safe conduct on condition of paying the jizya and kharāj, and he granted them safe conduct. Jarīr b. ʿAbdallāh came to Khāniqīn, where there were remnants of the non-Arabs, and killed them.

No district of the Sawād of the Tigris remained without the Muslims gaining mastery over it and its passing into their hands.

Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: The commander over the people on the day of Jalūlāʾ, appointed by Saʿd, was ʿAmr b. ʿUtba b. Nawfal b. Uhayb b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Zuhra. His mother was ʿĀtika bt. Abī Waqqāṣ.

654They said: Saʿd returned after Jalūlāʾ to al-Madāʾin. He stationed a force there, then proceeded toward al-Ḥīra. The battle of Jalūlāʾ took place at the end of the year sixteen.

655They said: Jamīl b. Baṣbahrī, the dihqān of al-Falālīj and al-Nahrayn; Bisṭām b. Narsī, the dihqān of Bābil and Khaṭarniyya; al-Rufayl, the dihqān of al-ʿĀl; Fīrūz, the dihqān of Nahr al-Malik and Kūthā; and other dihqāns embraced Islam. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb did not interfere with them or remove the land from their possession, and he lifted the jizya from their persons.

656Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from ʿAwāna, from his father, who said: Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ dispatched Hāshim b. ʿUtba b. Abī Waqqāṣ, accompanied by al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī. He passed through al-Rādhānāt and came to Daqūqā and Khānījār, gaining mastery over what was there. He conquered the whole district of Bājarmā and proceeded toward Sinn Bārmā and Bawāzīj al-Malik as far as the boundary of Shahrazūr.

657Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me. He said: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me. He said: Ibn al-Mubārak informed us, from Abū Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ when he conquered the Sawād: “To proceed: Your letter has reached me, in which you mention that the people have asked you to divide among them what God has bestowed upon them as fayʾ.

“When my letter reaches you, consider whatever the men of the army have attacked

with their horses and riding animals, whether property or mounts, divide it among them after taking the fifth, and leave the land and rivers to those who work them, so that this may provide for the Muslims’ stipends. For if you divide it among those present, those who remain after them will have nothing.

658Al-Ḥusayn told me: Wakīʿ told us, from Fuḍayl b. Ghazwān, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥāzim, who said: I asked Mujāhid about the land of al-Sawād, and he said: “It is neither to be bought nor sold.”

He said: We say this because it was conquered by force and was not divided, so it belongs to all the Muslims.

659Al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from Ṣāliḥ b. Kaysān, from Sulaymān b. Yasār, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb preserved al-Sawād for those in men’s loins and women’s wombs. He made its inhabitants protected subjects, from whom the jizya was collected and from whose land the kharāj was collected. They were protected subjects, under no bondage.

Sulaymān said: Al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik intended to make the inhabitants of al-Sawād fayʾ, but I informed him of what ʿUmar had done concerning this, and God restrained him from doing so to them.

660Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from Isrāʾīl, from Abū Isḥāq, from Ḥāritha b. Muḍarrib, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wished to divide al-Sawād among the Muslims. He ordered that they be counted, and each man’s share was found to be three cultivators.

He consulted the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ about this. ʿAlī said: “Leave them to be a source of support for the Muslims.”

He therefore sent ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf al-Anṣārī, who imposed upon it forty-eight, twenty-four, and twelve.

661Abū Naṣr al-Tammār told us: Sharīk told us, from al-Ajlaḥ, from Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit, from Thaʿlaba b. Yazīd, from ʿAlī, who said: “Were it not that some of you would strike others in the face, I would divide al-Sawād among you.”

662Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us: Isrāʾīl told us, from Jābir, from ʿĀmir, who said: “The inhabitants of al-Sawād have no covenant; they merely submitted to judgment.”

663Al-Ḥusayn told us: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us: Al-Ṣalt al-Zubaydī told me, from Muḥammad b. Qays al-Asadī, from al-Shaʿbī, that he was asked whether the inhabitants of al-Sawād had a covenant. He said: “They had no covenant, but when kharāj was accepted from them, they came to have a covenant.”

664Al-Ḥusayn told us, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from Sharīk, from Jābir, from ʿĀmir, that he said: “The inhabitants of al-Sawād have no covenant.”

665ʿAmr al-Nāqid told us: Ibn Wahb al-Miṣrī told us: Mālik told us, from Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad, from his father, who said: The Emigrants had a gathering place in the mosque.

ʿUmar would sit there with them and tell them what reached him concerning affairs in the regions.

One day he said: “I do not know how to deal with the Magians.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf sprang up and said: “I bear witness that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘Apply to them the practice applied to the People of the Book.’”

666Muḥammad b. al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Bazzāz told us: Hushaym told us: Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid told us,

from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, who said: Bajīla constituted a quarter of the men on the day of al-Qādisiyya.

ʿUmar had assigned them a quarter of al-Sawād.

When Jarīr came to him in a delegation, he said: “Were I not an accountable distributor, I would abide by what I assigned you.

But I see that the people have grown numerous, so return that to them.”

He did so, and they did so.

ʿUmar rewarded him with eighty dinars.

He said: A woman of Bajīla called Umm Kurz said: “My father died while his share in al-Sawād remained established.

I will not surrender it.”

He said to her: “Umm Kurz! Your people have agreed.”

She said to him: “I will not surrender it unless you mount me on a docile she-camel bearing a red velvet cloth and fill my hands with gold.”

ʿUmar did that.

667Al-Ḥusayn told me: Abū Usāma told us, from Ismāʿīl, from Qays, from Jarīr, who said: ʿUmar had given Bajīla a quarter of al-Sawād, and they received it for three years.

Qays said: Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh came to ʿUmar in a delegation with ʿAmmār b. Yāsir. ʿUmar said: “Were I not an accountable distributor, I would leave you as you were, but I think you should return it.” They did so.

He rewarded him with eighty dinars.

668Al-Ḥasan b. ʿUthmān al-Ziyādī said: ʿĪsā b. Yūnus told us, from Ismāʿīl, from Qays, who said: ʿUmar gave Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh four hundred dinars.

669Ḥumayd b. al-Rabīʿ told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: ʿUmar reached a settlement with Bajīla concerning their quarter of al-Sawād, on the condition that he assign them stipends of two thousand.

670Al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Jaʿfar, from Jarīr b. Yazīd b. Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh, from his father, from his grandfather, that ʿUmar assigned him and his people a quarter of what they conquered of al-Sawād.

When the spoils of Jalūlāʾ were gathered, he asked for his quarter.

Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar informing him of this.

ʿUmar wrote: “If Jarīr wishes that he and his people should have fought only for a payment like that of those whose hearts are reconciled, give them their payment. But if they fought only for God, seeking the reward that is with Him, they are among the Muslims, with the same rights and obligations as they have.”

Jarīr said: “The Commander of the Faithful has spoken truly and acted rightly. We have no need of the quarter.”

671Al-Ḥusayn told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me, from ʿAbd al-Salām b. Ḥarb, from Maʿmar, from ʿAlī b. al-Ḥakam, from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, who said: A man came to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb and said: “I have embraced Islam, so remove the kharāj from my land.”

He said: “Your land was taken by force.”

672Khalaf b. Hishām al-Bazzār told us: Hushaym told us, from al-ʿAwwām b. Ḥawshab, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, who said: When ʿUmar conquered al-Sawād, they said to him: “Divide it among us, for we conquered it by force with our swords.”

He refused and said: “Then what will there be for the Muslims who come after you? I fear that if I divide it, you will fall into disputes among yourselves over the waters.”

He said: He therefore left the inhabitants of al-Sawād on their land, imposed jizya on their persons and ṭasq on their land, and it was not divided among them.

673Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: Ismāʿīl b. Mujālid told us, from his father, from al-Shaʿbī, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf al-Anṣārī to survey al-Sawād.

He found it to comprise thirty-six million jarībs.

He imposed one dirham and one qafīz on every jarīb.

Al-Qāsim said: I have learned that this qafīz was a makkūk of theirs called al-shābarqān.

Yaḥyā b. Ādam said: It is the sealed measure of al-Ḥajjāj.

674ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Abū Muʿāwiya told us, from al-Shaybānī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī, who said: ʿUmar imposed on al-Sawād one dirham and one qafīz for every jarīb, cultivated or uncultivated, reached by water; five dirhams and five qafīzes for a jarīb of fresh fodder; and ten dirhams and ten qafīzes for a jarīb of trees. He did not mention date palms. On the persons of the men he imposed forty-eight, twenty-four, and twelve.

675Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us: Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī told us, from Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba, from Qatāda, from Abū Mijlaz Lāḥiq b. Ḥumayd, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent ʿAmmār b. Yāsir to oversee the prayers and armies of the people of Kūfa, ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd to oversee their adjudication and treasury, and ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf to oversee the surveying of the land.

He allotted them one sheep each day to share: half of it and its offal for ʿAmmār, and the other half between these two.

ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf surveyed the land and imposed ten dirhams on a jarīb of date palms, ten dirhams on a jarīb of vines, six dirhams on a jarīb of reeds, four dirhams on a jarīb of wheat, and two dirhams on a jarīb of barley.

He wrote about this to ʿUmar ﵀ and he approved it.

676Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from Mandal al-ʿAnazī, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm, from ʿAmr b. Maymūn, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān to oversee

what lay beyond the Tigris, and sent ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf to oversee what lay on this side of the Tigris.

They imposed one qafīz and one dirham on every jarīb.

677Al-Ḥusayn told us: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, from Mandal, from Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī, who said: Al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba wrote, while he was in charge of al-Sawād: “Among us are kinds of produce that yield more than wheat and barley.”

He mentioned mung beans, vines, fresh fodder, and sesame.

He said: He imposed eight apiece on them and exempted date palms.

678Khalaf al-Bazzār told us: Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh told us; and al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from Abū Bakr, who said: Abū Saʿīd al-Baqqāl informed me, from al-ʿAyzār b. Ḥurayth, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb imposed two dirhams and two jarībs on a jarīb of wheat, one dirham and one jarīb on a jarīb of barley, and one dirham for every two jarībs on all uncultivated land capable of being sown.

679Khalaf al-Bazzār told us, from Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh, from Abū Saʿīd, from al-ʿAyzār b. Ḥurayth, who said: ʿUmar imposed ten dirhams on a jarīb of vines, ten dirhams on a jarīb of fresh fodder, five dirhams on a jarīb of cotton, one dirham on a Persian date palm, and one dirham on two daqal date palms.

680ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Ḥafṣ b. Ghiyāth told us, from Ibn Abī ʿArūba, from Qatāda, from Abū Mijlaz, that ʿUmar imposed eight dirhams on a jarīb of date palms.

681Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Sulaymān told us, from al-Sarī b. Ismāʿīl, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf, who imposed on the inhabitants of al-Sawād five dirhams for a jarīb of fresh fodder and ten dirhams for a jarīb of vines, and imposed nothing on what was cultivated beneath it.

682Al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Wāqidī, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from al-Miswar b. Rifāʿa, who said: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “The kharāj of al-Sawād in the time of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb was one hundred million dirhams.

When al-Ḥajjāj came, it fell to forty million dirhams.”

683Al-Walīd told us, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Ayyūb b. Abī Umāma b. Sahl b. Ḥunayf, from his father, who said: ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf placed seals on the necks of five hundred and fifty thousand ʿiljs, and the kharāj during his administration reached one hundred million dirhams.

684Al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me: Yūnus b. Arqam al-Mālikī told us: Yaḥyā b. Abī al-Ashʿath al-Kindī told me, from Muṣʿab b. Yazīd Abī Zayd al-Anṣārī, from his father, who said: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib sent me to oversee what the Euphrates irrigated.

He mentioned rural districts and villages.

He named Nahr al-Malik, Kūthā, Bahurasīr, al-Rūmaqān, Nahr Jawbar, Nahr Darqīṭ, and al-Bahqubādhāt, and ordered me to impose on every jarīb densely sown with wheat one and a half dirhams and one ṣāʿ of food grain, and on every jarīb of middling density one dirham,

and on every jarīb sparsely sown with wheat two-thirds of a dirham, and on barley half of that.

He ordered me to impose ten dirhams on every jarīb of orchards combining date palms and other trees, and ten dirhams on a jarīb of vines once three years had passed over it, it had entered its fourth year, and it had borne fruit; to exempt every date palm standing apart from the villages whose fruit was eaten by passersby; and to impose nothing on vegetables: cucumber plots, grains, sesame, and cotton.

He ordered me to impose forty-eight dirhams per man on the dihqāns who rode bardhawn horses and wore gold rings; on those of middling means among them, the merchants, twenty-four dirhams per man annually; and on the tillers and all the rest of them, twelve dirhams per man.
