685Ḥumayd b. al-Rabīʿ told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: I said to al-Ḥasan: “What are these differing ṭasq assessments?” He said: “Each was imposed at one time after another according to the proximity of the lands and river landings to the markets

and what lies beyond them .”

He said: Yaḥyā b. Ādam said: As for the crop-sharing assessment of al-Sawād, the people requested it from the ruler at the end of al-Manṣūr’s caliphate. He died before they entered into crop sharing. Then al-Mahdī ordered it, and they were assessed by crop sharing in the territory on this side of the pass of Ḥulwān.

686ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-ʿIjlī told me, from ʿAbthar Abū Zubayd, from trustworthy authorities, who said: Ḥudhayfa surveyed the lands irrigated by the Tigris and died at al-Madāʾin.

The Bridges of Ḥudhayfa were named after him because he encamped by them.

It is also said that he rebuilt them.

His cubit and the cubit of Ibn Ḥunayf were the cubit of the arm, a fist, and an outstretched thumb.

Using these two, the inhabitants of al-Sawād were assessed by crop sharing at half, after the survey by which their land used to be measured.

687Some of the secretaries said: The tithe taken from land grants is a tenth of what is measured out, one-fifth of the half taken from the istān.

Accordingly, each jarīb of land in grants subject to measurement should likewise be assessed at one-fifth of what is taken from a jarīb of the istān. Practice proceeded on that basis.

688Abū ʿUbayd told me: Kathīr b. Hishām told us, from Jaʿfar b. Burqān, from Maymūn b. Mihrān, that ʿUmar ﵀ sent Ḥudhayfa and Ibn Ḥunayf to Khāniqīn, which was among the first places they conquered.

They placed seals on the necks of the protected non-Muslims and then collected the land tax.

689Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Wakīʿ told us: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Walīd told us: A man whose father was the most knowledgeable of people about this Sawād, named ʿAbd al-Malik b. Abī Ḥurra, told us, from his father, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb reserved ten categories of land from the Sawād. I remembered seven, and three escaped me: he reserved the reedbeds, the places where water collects, the land of Kisrā, and every monastery of Yazīd, the land of those killed in battle, and the land of those who fled.

He said: This remained established until the register was burned in the days of al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf, whereupon each group took what adjoined them.

390. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Juʿfī also told me: Ibn al-Mubārak told us, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Walīd, from ʿAbd al-Malik b. Abī Ḥurra, from his father, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb reserved from the Sawād the land of those killed in war, the land of those who fled, all the land of Kisrā, all the land belonging to his household, every place where water collects, every monastery of Yazīd, and every reserved estate that Kisrā had selected for himself.

His reserved estates thus amounted to seven thousand

thousand dirhams.

When the battle of al-Jamājim took place, the people burned the register, and each group took what adjoined them.

691Al-Ḥusayn and ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Muḥammad b. Fuḍayl told us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrāhīm b. Muhājir, from Mūsā b. Ṭalḥa, who said: ʿUthmān granted ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd land at al-Nahrayn, granted ʿAmmār b. Yāsir Istīniyā, granted Khabbāb b. al-Arath Ṣaʿnabā, and granted Saʿd the village of Hurmuz.

692ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-ʿIjlī also told us, from Ismāʿīl b. Mujālid, from his father, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān granted Ṭalḥa b. ʿUbayd Allāh al-Nashāstaj, and granted Usāma b. Zayd land that he sold.

693Shaybān b. Farrūkh told us: Abū ʿAwāna told us, from Ibrāhīm b. al-Muhājir, from Mūsā b. Ṭalḥa, that ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān made grants to five of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ among them ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd, Saʿd b. Mālik al-Zuhrī, al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām, Khabbāb b. al-Aratt, and Usāma b. Zayd.

He said: I saw Ibn Masʿūd and Saʿd, who were my neighbors, letting their land for a third and a quarter.

694Al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ also told me, from Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Aslamī, from Isḥāq b. Yaḥyā, from Mūsā b. Ṭalḥa, who said: The first to make land grants in Iraq was ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān.

He made grants from the reserved estates of Kisrā and from the land of those who had departed.

He granted Ṭalḥa al-Nashāstaj , granted Wāʾil b. Ḥujr al-Ḥaḍramī what adjoined Zurāra, and granted Khabbāb

b. al-Aratt Istīniyā, granted ʿAdī b. Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī al-Rawḥāʾ, granted Khālid b. ʿUrfuṭa land beside Ḥammām Aʿyan, granted al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī Ṭayzanābādh, and granted Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī his land on the bank of the Euphrates.

695Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ādam, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: It reached me that ʿAlī ﵀ imposed four thousand dirhams upon the people of Ajamat Burs and wrote them a document to that effect on a piece of leather.

696Aḥmad b. Ḥammād al-Kūfī also told me: Ajamat Burs is beside the tower of Nimrod at Babylon.

In the reedbed is a very deep pit, said to be a well. The last part of the tower was made from its clay. It is also said to be a place where the ground collapsed.

697Abū Masʿūd and others also told me that the dihqāns of al-Anbār asked Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ to dig them a canal that they had asked the ruler of the Persians to dig for them. He wrote to Saʿd b. ʿAmr b. Ḥarām, ordering him to dig it for them.

He assembled men for this, and they dug it until they reached a mountain that he could not cut through, so they abandoned it. When al-Ḥajjāj became governor of Iraq, he assembled laborers from every quarter and said to his overseers: “Look at the value of what one of the diggers eats in a day. If its weight is equal to the weight of what he removes, do not hold back from digging.”

They spent money on it until they completed it. That mountain was therefore named after al-Ḥajjāj, and the canal was named after Saʿd b. ʿAmr b. Ḥarām.

He said: Al-Khayzurān, the mother of the caliphs, ordered the digging of the canal known as Maḥdūd and named it al-Rayyān.

Her agent had divided it into sections, marked the limits of each section, and assigned a group to dig it; it was therefore called Maḥdūd.

As for the canal known as Shīlā, the descendants of Shīlā b. Farrukhzādān al-Marwazī claim

that Sābūr dug it for their ancestor when he stationed him at Naghiyā in the ṭassūj of al-Anbār.

Others say that it was named after a man called Shīlā who had contracted to dig it.

He had a vegetable plot beside it in the days of al-Manṣūr, Commander of the Faithful. This canal had long been silted up, and al-Manṣūr ordered it to be dug out. He did not complete it before he died; it was completed during the caliphate of al-Mahdī.

It is said that al-Manṣūr had ordered a new inlet to be made for it above its old inlet, but this was not finished until al-Mahdī ﵀ completed it.

Chapter 60

The founding of Kūfa

Account of the Founding of Kūfa

698Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Wāqidī told us, from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Jaʿfar and others, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ, ordering him to establish a place of migration for the Muslims and not to put a sea between himself and them.

He came to al-Anbār and intended to make it a place of settlement.

But flies became numerous around the people, so he moved to another place, which proved unsuitable. He then moved to Kūfa, laid it out, allotted dwelling sites to the people, settled the tribes in their quarters, and built its mosque. That was in the year seventeen.

699ʿAlī b. al-Mughīra al-Athram also told me: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā told me, from his elders. He said: Hishām b. al-Kalbī also informed me, from his father and the elders of the Kūfans:

They said: When Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ had finished the battle of al-Qādisiyya, he proceeded toward al-Madāʾin.

He made a settlement with the people of al-Rūmiyya and Bahurasīr.

Then he conquered al-Madāʾin and took Asbānbar and Kurdabandādh by force. He quartered his troops there, and they took possession of them.

Saʿd was then written to, being told to move them, so he moved them to Sūq Ḥakama.

Some say he moved them to Kuwayfa, short of Kūfa.

Al-Athram said: It has been said that takawwuf means assembling.

It has also been said that rounded areas of sand are called kūfānī.

Some call land containing pebbles together with clay and sand kūfa.

They said: Mosquitoes afflicted them, and Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar, informing him that the people had been bitten by mosquitoes and were suffering from this .

ʿUmar wrote to him: “The Arabs are like camels;

only what suits camels suits them. Seek out a place for them to settle, and do not put a sea between me and them.”

He appointed Abū al-Hayyāj al-Asadī, ʿAmr b. Mālik b. Junāda, to oversee the laying out of plots for the people.

Then ʿAbd al-Masīḥ b. Buqayla came to Saʿd and said to him: “I shall direct you to land that slopes down from the open desert and rises above the pestilential lowlands.”

He directed him to the site of present-day Kūfa.

It used to be called Sūristān.

When he reached the site of its mosque, he ordered a man to shoot an arrow as far as he could toward the direction of the qibla, and he marked where it fell. Then he shot another arrow toward the north wind and marked where it fell. Then he shot an arrow toward the south wind and marked where it fell. Then he shot an arrow toward the east wind and marked where it fell.

He then placed its mosque and governor’s residence at the archer’s station and around it. He drew two lots for Nizār and the people of Yemen, on the condition that whichever had its lot drawn first would have the left side, which was the better of the two.

The lot of the people of Yemen came out, so their plots were on the eastern side, while the plots of Nizār were on the western side, beyond those markers.

He left what lay within them as an open space for the mosque and the governor’s residence.

Then al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba enlarged it. Ziyād built it solidly and built the governor’s residence.

Ziyād used to say: “I spent eighteen hundred on each column of the mosque of Kūfa.”

ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth al-Makhzūmī erected a building in it.

Ziyād used to leave him in charge of Kūfa when he departed for Baṣra.

Then the governors built in it, narrowing its open spaces and courtyards.

He said: The owners of ʿAmr’s Lane in Kūfa are the descendants of ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth b. ʿAmr b. ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. Makhzūm b. Yaqaẓa.

700Wahb b. Baqiyya al-Wāsiṭī also told me: Yazīd b. Hārūn told us, from Dāwūd b. Abī Hind, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: We—meaning the people of Yemen—were twelve thousand.

Nizār were

eight thousand.

Do you not see that we are the majority of the people of Kūfa? Our lot fell on the eastern side, and that is why our plots are where they are.

701ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī also told me, from Maslama b. Muḥārib and others, who said: Al-Mughīra enlarged the mosque of Kūfa and built it; then Ziyād added to it.

The reason pebbles were spread in it and in the mosque of Baṣra was that people would pray and, when they raised their hands, which had become dusty, they would shake them off.

Ziyād said: “How greatly I fear that, in days to come, people will think that shaking the hands is an established practice in prayer.”

He therefore added to the mosque and enlarged it, and ordered pebbles to be collected and spread in the mosque’s courtyard.

Those appointed to collect them made unreasonable demands upon the people, saying to those whom they required to supply them: “Bring us pebbles like those we show you.” They selected particular kinds of them.

They would search for ones resembling them, and they acquired money.

Thus it was said: “How fine is authority, even over stones!”

Al-Athram said: Abū ʿUbayda said: This was said only because al-Ḥajjāj b. ʿAtīk al-Thaqafī, or his son, oversaw the quarrying of the stones for the columns of the mosque of Baṣra from the mountain of al-Ahwāz. Wealth became apparent in his possession, and the people said: “How fine is authority, even over stones!”

Abū ʿUbayda said: Kūfa was laid out as a settlement in the year eighteen.

He said: Ziyād had made a maqṣūra in the mosque of Kūfa, and Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī later renewed it.

702Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī also told me: Al-Haytham b. ʿAdī al-Ṭāʾī told me: The Muslims settled at al-Madāʾin, laid it out, and built mosques there.

Then the Muslims found it unhealthy and pestilential, and Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ wrote to ʿUmar about this.

ʿUmar wrote to him to settle them in a place to the west.

He sought out Kuwayfat Ibn ʿUmar.

They looked and found that water surrounded it.

They set out until they came to the site of present-day Kūfa and reached the elevated ground. It was called Khadd al-ʿAdhrāʾ and grew lavender, oxeye daisies, wormwood, southernwood, and anemones. They laid out the settlement there.

703An elder from among the Kūfans also told me that the area between Kūfa and al-Ḥīra was called al-Malṭāṭ.

He said: The house of ʿAbd al-Malik b. ʿUmayr was for guests.

ʿUmar ordered a house to be established for those arriving from the outlying regions, and they used to lodge there.

704Al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī also told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf, from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, who said: Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ installed a wooden gateway fitted with a door and erected a reed shelter over his palace.

ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent Muḥammad b. Maslama al-Anṣārī, who burned the door and the shelter.

He had Saʿd stand in the mosques of Kūfa, and nothing but good was said about him.

705Al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd al-Narsī and Ibrāhīm al-ʿAllāf al-Baṣrī also told me: Abū ʿAwāna told us, from ʿAbd al-Malik b. ʿUmayr, from Jābir b. Samura, that the people of Kūfa denounced Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ to ʿUmar, saying: “He does not know how to perform the prayer properly.”

Saʿd said: “As for me, I used to lead them in the prayer of God’s Messenger ﷺ departing from it in no respect. I prolong the first two units and shorten the last two.”

ʿUmar said: “That is what we expect of you, Abū Isḥāq.”

ʿUmar sent men to ask about him in Kūfa. They visited no mosque there without people speaking well of him and praising his good conduct, until they came to one of the mosques of the Banū ʿAbs. A man among them called Abū Saʿda said: “Now that

“You have asked us about him: he did not distribute equally or judge justly in cases.”

He said: Saʿd said: “O God, if he is lying, prolong his life, perpetuate his poverty, blind him, and expose him to temptations.”

ʿAbd al-Malik said: I myself saw him afterward accosting slave women in the streets. When he was asked, “How are you, Abū Saʿda?” he would say: “An old man afflicted by temptation, whom Saʿd’s supplication has struck.”

Al-ʿAbbās al-Narsī said, in a report other than this one: Saʿd said concerning the people of Kūfa: “O God, let no commander be pleased with them, and let them be pleased with no commander.”

706Al-ʿAbbās al-Narsī told me: It has reached me that al-Mukhtār b. Abī ʿUbayd, or someone else, said: “Love for the people of Kūfa is honor, and hatred of them is ruin.”

707Al-Ḥasan b. ʿUthmān al-Ziyādī told me: Ismāʿīl b. Mujālid told us, from his father, from al-Shaʿbī, that ʿAmr b. Maʿdīkarib al-Zubaydī came as a delegate to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb after the conquest of al-Qādisiyya. He asked him about Saʿd and whether the people were pleased with him. He replied: “I left him gathering for them as an ant gathers, and caring for them as a devoted mother cares. A Bedouin in his cloak, a Nabataean in his tax collection. He distributes equally, judges justly in cases, and dispatches the raiding party.”

ʿUmar said: “It seems that you two have exchanged praise”—Saʿd had written praising ʿAmr. He replied: “Certainly not, Commander of the Faithful! I have merely reported what I know.”

He said: “ʿAmr! Tell me about war.”

He replied: “Bitter to taste when it rises in full force. Whoever perseveres in it becomes known; whoever is unequal to it perishes.”

He said: “Then tell me about weapons.” He replied: “Ask, Commander of the Faithful, about whichever of them you wish.”

He said: “The spear.”

He replied: “Your brother, though it may betray you.”

He said: “And arrows?”

He replied: “Messengers of death: they miss and they hit.”

He said: “And the shield?”

He replied: “That is the buckler upon which the turns of fortune revolve.”

He said: “And the coat of mail?”

He replied: “An encumbrance to the horseman, exhausting to the foot soldier; yet it is indeed a strong fortress.”

He said: “And the sword?” He replied: “There is the thing! May your mother be bereaved of you!”

ʿUmar said: “Rather, may your mother be bereaved of you!”

ʿAmr replied: “Fever has humbled me before you.”

He said: ʿUmar dismissed Saʿd and appointed ʿAmmār b. Yāsir. They complained about him, saying: “He is weak and has no knowledge of governance.” So he dismissed him. His governorship of Kūfa lasted a year and nine months.

ʿUmar said: “Who will vindicate me against the people of Kūfa! If I appoint a strong man over them, they accuse him of wickedness; if I appoint a weak man over them, they despise him.”

Then he summoned al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba and said: “If I appoint you over Kūfa, will you return to any of the things of which you were accused?” He replied: “No.”

When al-Qādisiyya was conquered, al-Mughīra had gone to Medina. ʿUmar appointed him over Kūfa, and he remained over it until ʿUmar died. Then ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān appointed Saʿd over it, then dismissed him and appointed al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ b. Abī ʿAmr b. Umayya. When he arrived to take over from him, Saʿd said to him: “Either you have become clever since I last knew you, or I have become foolish since you last knew me.”

Then he dismissed al-Walīd and appointed Saʿd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Umayya.

708Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from one of the people of Kūfa, who said: I heard Misʿar b. Kidām relate: With Rustam on the day of al-Qādisiyya were four thousand men called the troops of the Shāhānshāh. They sought safe-conduct on condition that they settle wherever they wished, enter into alliance with whomever they wished, and be assigned stipends. They were granted what they requested. They entered into alliance with Zuhra b. Ḥawiyya al-Saʿdī, of Banū Tamīm. Saʿd settled them where they chose and assigned them stipends of a thousand thousand. They had a chief from among themselves called Daylam, so they were called Ḥamrāʾ Daylam.

Then Ziyād sent some of them to the lands of Syria at Muʿāwiya’s command; there they call themselves Persians. And he sent a group of them to Baṣra, where they joined the Asāwira who were there.

Abū Masʿūd said: The Arabs call non-Arabs al-Ḥamrāʾ, and they say, “I have come from Ḥamrāʾ Daylam,” just as they say, “I have come from Juhayna,” and similar expressions.

Abū Masʿūd said: I also heard someone mention that these Asāwira had been stationed opposite the Daylam. When the Muslims came upon them at Qazwīn, they embraced Islam on the same terms as the Asāwira of Baṣra had embraced it, and came to Kūfa and settled there.

709Al-Madāʾinī told me: Abarwīz had sent to the Daylam, and four thousand men were brought to him. They were his servants and intimates, and afterward retained that standing. They were present at al-Qādisiyya with Rustam. When he was killed and the Magians were routed, they withdrew and said: “We are not like these men, nor have we any refuge, and our record with them is unfavorable. The course for us is to join them in their religion, so that we may gain strength through them.” So they withdrew.

Saʿd said: “What is the matter with these men?” Al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba went to them and asked them about their situation. They told him their story and said: “We will enter your religion.” He returned to Saʿd and informed him. He granted them safe-conduct, and they embraced Islam. They took part in the conquest of al-Madāʾin with Saʿd and in the conquest of Jalūlāʾ. Then they moved and settled in Kūfa with the Muslims.

710Hishām b. Muḥammad b. al-Sāʾib al-Saklabī said: The cemetery of al-Sabīʿ was named after the descendants of al-Sabīʿ b. Sabʿ b. Ṣaʿb al-Hamdānī.

The open ground of Athīr was named after a man of Banū Asad called Athīr.

Dukkān ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd was named after ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Zayd b. al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s governor of Kūfa.

The open ground of Banū Qarār was named after Banū Qarār b. Thaʿlaba b. Mālik b. Ḥarb b. Ṭarīf b. al-Namir b. Yaqdum b. ʿAnaza b. Asad b. Rabīʿa b. Nizār.

He said: The House of the Byzantines was a rubbish dump for the people of Kūfa, where refuse and sweepings were thrown, until ʿAnbasa b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī requested it as a grant from Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik. He granted it to him, and he had its earth removed at a cost of one hundred thousand and fifty thousand dirhams.

710. Abū Masʿūd said: Yūsuf’s market in al-Ḥīra was named after Yūsuf b. ʿUmar b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī ʿAqīl al-Thaqafī, the paternal cousin of al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī ʿAqīl. He was Hishām’s governor of Iraq.

711Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī b. Muḥammad and Abū Masʿūd informed me, saying: The bathhouse of Aʿyan was attributed to Aʿyan, the client of Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ. This Aʿyan was the man whom al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf sent from Rustaqābādh to ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Jārūd al-ʿAbdī when the latter rebelled and the people followed him in seeking to expel al-Ḥajjāj from Iraq and asking ʿAbd al-Malik to appoint someone else. When he delivered the message, he said to him: “Were you not a messenger, I would kill you.”

712Abū Masʿūd said: I heard that before him the bathhouse belonged to a man of the ʿIbād called Jābir, the brother of Ḥayyān whom al-Aʿshā mentioned. He was the owner of Jābir’s embankment in al-Ḥīra. He purchased it from his heirs.

713Ibn al-Kalbī said: The church of Banū Māzin in al-Ḥīra belongs to a group of the Azd, of Banū ʿAmr b. Māzin of the Azd; they are of Ghassān.

He said: The bathhouse of ʿUmar was named after ʿUmar b. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ.

714They said: The Shahārsūj of Bajīla in Kūfa was actually named after Banū Bajla, the descendants of Mālik b. Thaʿlaba b. Buhtha b. Sulaym b. Manṣūr. Bajla was their mother, and her name predominates in their lineage. People made a mistake and said Bajīla.

The cemetery of ʿArzam was named after a man called ʿArzam who used to make mud bricks there. Its bricks are poor, containing reeds and potsherds; sometimes a fire would break out there and the walls would burn.

715Ibn ʿArafa told me: Ismāʿīl b. ʿUlayya told me, from Ibn ʿAwn, that Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī directed in his will that no ʿArzamī mud bricks be placed in his grave.

Some of the people of Kūfa have said that this ʿArzam was a man of Banū Nahd.

The cemetery of Bishr was named after Bishr b. Rabīʿa b. ʿAmr b. Manāra b. Qumayr al-Khathʿamī, who says: “My she-camel yearns at the gate of al-Qādisiyya, While Saʿd b. Waqqāṣ is commander over me.”

716Abū Masʿūd said: There was a place in Kūfa known as ʿAntara the Barber. He was black. When the people of Khurāsān entered Kūfa, they used to say “Barber ʿAntara,” and people continued to use that expression. Likewise, “Barber Faraj,” “Ḍaḥḥāk the head seller,” and “Farrier Ḥayyān.” It is also said: Rustam; and it is said: Ṣalīb. It is in al-Ḥīra.

717Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: Zurāra was named after Zurāra b. Yazīd b. ʿAmr b. ʿUdas, of Banū al-Bakkāʾ b. ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. It was his dwelling, and Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān took it from him. Later it was made crown property, until it was granted as an estate to Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath b. ʿUqba al-Khuzāʿī.

He said: The house of Ḥakīm in Kūfa, among the dealers in patterned coverings, was named after Ḥakīm b. Saʿd b. Thawr al-Bakkāʾī.

And the palace of Muqātil b. Ḥassān b. Thaʿlaba b. Aws b. Ibrāhīm b. Ayyūb b. Maḥrūq, one of Banū Imruʾ al-Qays b. Zayd Manāt b. Tamīm.

He said: Al-Sawādiyya in Kūfa was named after Sawād b. Zayd b. ʿAdī b. Zayd, the ʿIbādī poet. His grandfather was Ḥammād b. Zayd b. Ayyūb b. Maḥrūq.

The village of Abū Ṣalāba on the Euphrates was named after Ṣalāba b. Mālik b. Ṭāriq b. Jabr b. Hammām al-ʿAbdī.

Aqsās Mālik was named after Mālik b. Qays b. ʿAbd Hind b. Lajm, one of Banū Ḥudhāfa b. Zuhr b. Iyād b. Nizār.

The monastery of al-Aʿwar belonged to a man of Iyād, of Banū Umayya b. Ḥudhāqa, who was called al-Aʿwar. Concerning it Abū Duʾād al-Iyādī says: “And a monastery of which the scouts say: ‘What a house is the house of al-Ḥudhāqī!’”

The monastery of Qurra was named after Qurra, one of Banū Umayya b. Ḥudhāqa. The monastery of al-Sawā was also named after them. Al-sawā means equity: they would come to it and deal equitably with one another there, and swear oaths to one another concerning rights. Some transmitters say that al-Sawā was a woman of their people.

He said: The monastery of the Skulls belonged to Iyād. There was a war between them and Banū Bahrāʾ b. ʿAmr b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa and Banū al-Qayn b. Jasr b. Shayʿ Allāh b. Wabara b. Taghlib b. Ḥulwān b. ʿImrān b. al-Ḥāf. A great many of Iyād were killed in it. When the battle ended, they buried their dead beside the monastery. Afterward people would dig, and skulls came out, so it was called the monastery of the Skulls. This is the account of al-Sharqī b. al-Quṭāmī.

718Muḥammad b. al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī said: Mālik al-Rimāḥ b. Muḥriz al-Iyādī killed a group of Persians and set up their skulls beside the monastery, so it was called the monastery of the Skulls.

It is said that the monastery of Kaʿb belonged to Iyād, and it is said that it belonged to others.

The monastery of Hind belonged to the mother of ʿAmr b. Hind, who was ʿAmr b. al-Mundhir b. Māʾ al-Samāʾ. His mother was a Kindī woman.

And the house of Qumām bt. al-Ḥārith b. Hāniʾ al-Kindī, which is beside the house of al-Ashʿath b. Qays.

He said: The church of Banū ʿAdī was named after Banū ʿAdī b. al-Dhamīl of Lakhm.

719They said: Ṭayzanābādh used to be called Ḍayzanābādh, but they changed its name. It was named after al-Ḍayzan b. Muʿāwiya b. al-ʿUbayd al-Salīḥī. Salīḥ’s name was ʿUmar b. Ṭarīf b. ʿImrān b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa. The mistress of al-Khaḍrāʾ was al-Naḍīra bt. al-Ḍayzan. Al-Ḍayzan’s mother was Jayhala bt. Tazīd b. Ḥaydān b. ʿAmr b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa.

He said: The man after whom the mosque of Simāk in Kūfa was named was Simāk b. Makhrama b. Ḥumayn al-Asadī, of Banū al-Hālik b. ʿAmr b. Asad. He is the one to whom al-Akhṭal says: “Simāk has built glory for his family Until death, and hastens to do good. I used to think him a smith, knowing him well; Today he has sent sparks flying from his clothes.”

Al-Hālik was the first to work iron, and his descendants were taunted for that. Simāk said to al-Akhṭal: “Woe to you, how inarticulate you are! You meant to praise me, but you have satirized me.” He had fled from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib out of Kūfa and settled in al-Raqqa.

720Ibn al-Kalbī said: In Kūfa is the quarter of Banū Shayṭān. He was Shayṭān b. Zuhayr b. Shihāb b. Rabīʿa b. Abī Sūd b. Mālik b. Ḥanẓala b. Mālik b. Zayd Manāt of Tamīm.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: The site of the house of ʿĪsā b. Mūsā, by which it is known today, belonged to al-ʿAlāʾ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥriz b. Ḥāritha b. Rabīʿa b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. ʿAbd Shams b. ʿAbd Manāf. Al-ʿAlāʾ was in charge of a quarter of Kūfa in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr.

The lane of Ibn Muḥriz is named after him.

In Kūfa there is a lane named after ʿUmayra b. Shihāb b. Muḥriz b. Abī Shamir al-Kindī, whose sister was married to ʿUmar b. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ and bore him Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar.

The open ground of Shabath was named after Shabath b. Ribʿī al-Riyāḥī, of Banū Tamīm.

721They said: The house of Ḥujayr in Kūfa was named after Ḥujayr b. al-Jaʿd al-Jumaḥī.

He said: The well of al-Mubārak in the cemetery of Juʿfī was named after al-Mubārak b. ʿIkrima b. Ḥimyarī al-Juʿfī. Yūsuf b. ʿUmar had appointed him over part of the Sawād.

The mill of ʿUmāra was named after ʿUmāra b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ b. Abī ʿAmr b. Umayya.

He said: The cemetery of Sām was named after Sālim b. ʿAmmār b. ʿAbd al-Ḥārith, one of Banū Dārim b. Nahār b. Murra b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa b. Muʿāwiya b. Bakr b. Hawāzin. Banū Murra b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa are named after their mother, Salūl bt. Dhuhl b. Shaybān.

722They said: The open ground of al-Bardakht was named after al-Bardakht, the Ḍabbī poet, whose name was ʿAlī b. Khālid.

723They said: The mosque of Banū ʿAnz was named after Banū ʿAnz b. Wāʾil b. Qāsiṭ.

The mosque of Banū Jadhīma was named after Banū Jadhīma b. Mālik b. Naṣr b. Quʿayn b. al-Ḥārith b. Thaʿlaba b. Dūdān b. Asad. It is also said to have been named after Banū Jadhīma b. Rawāḥa al-ʿAbsī. In it are the money changers’ shops.

He said: In Kūfa there is a mosque named after Banū al-Muqāṣif b. Dhakwān b. Zubayna

b. al-Ḥārith b. Qaṭīʿa b. ʿAbs b. Baghīḍ b. Rayth b. Ghaṭafān b. Saʿd b. Qays b. ʿAylān. None of them remained.

He said: The mosque of Banū Bahdala was named after Banū Bahdala b. al-Mathal b. Muʿāwiya, of Kinda.

He said: The well of al-Jaʿd in Kūfa was named after al-Jaʿd, the client of Hamdān.

He said: The house of Abū Arṭāt was named after Arṭāt b. Mālik al-Bajalī.

He said: The house of al-Muqaṭṭaʿ was named after al-Muqaṭṭaʿ b. Sunayn al-Kalbī b. Khālid b. Mālik.

Of him Ibn al-Riqāʿ says: “On one bearing a marker, whose form the eye recognizes, As guests recognize the house of al-Muqaṭṭaʿ.”

He said: The palace of the ʿAdasiyyūn, on the edge of al-Ḥīra, belonged to Banū ʿAmmār b. ʿAbd al-Masīḥ b. Qays b. Ḥarmala b. ʿAlqama b. ʿAdas al-Kalbī.

They were named after their grandmother, ʿAdasa bt. Mālik b. ʿAwf al-Kalbī, who was the mother of al-Rammāḥ and al-Mishaẓẓ, the two sons of ʿĀmir al-Mudhamma‌m.

724A shaykh from the people of al-Ḥīra told me, who said: It was found in documents concerning the demolition of the palaces of al-Ḥīra that had belonged to the house of al-Mundhir that the congregational mosque in Kūfa was built with some of the materials salvaged from those palaces, and their value was credited to the people of al-Ḥīra against their jizya.

725Abū Masʿūd and another told me, who said: Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Asad b. Kurz al-Qasrī was of Bajīla. He built his mother a church, which is today the postal-service lane in Kūfa.

His mother was a Christian.

He said: Khālid built shops that he established, making their roofs vaults arched with baked brick and gypsum.

Khālid dug the canal known as al-Jāmiʿ.

He established in the village a palace known as the Palace of Khālid.

His brother Asad b. ʿAbd Allāh established the village known as Sūq Asad.

He made it a market and moved people to it, so it was called Sūq Asad.

The other crossing was the estate of ʿAttāb b. Warqāʾ al-Riyāḥī. When he departed for Khurāsān as its governor, his encampment was beside this market of his.

726Abū Masʿūd said: During his governorship of Iraq, ʿUmar b. Hubayra b. Muʿayya al-Fazārī constructed the arched bridge of Kūfa. Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī subsequently repaired and strengthened it.

It was repaired several times thereafter.

He said: Some of our shaykhs said: The first to build it was a man of the ʿIbād from Juʿfī, in the pre-Islamic period. Then it collapsed, and a bridge was made in its place. Subsequently, in Islam, it was built by Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān, then Ibn Hubayra, then Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh, then Yazīd b. ʿUmar b. Hubayra. It was subsequently repaired several times after the Umayyads.

727Abū Masʿūd and others told me, who said: Yazīd b. ʿUmar b. Hubayra built a town in Kūfa on the Euphrates and settled there, while a small part of it remained unfinished.

A letter from Marwān then reached him, ordering him to avoid living near the people of Kūfa, so he abandoned it.

He built the palace known as the Palace of Ibn Hubayra near the bridge of Sūrā.

When the Commander of the Faithful Abū al-ʿAbbās came to power, he settled in that town, completed some enclosed residences in it, added buildings there, and named it al-Hāshimiyya.

People continued, out of habit, to associate it with Ibn Hubayra. He said: “I do not think the mention of Ibn Hubayra will ever fall away from it.”

He therefore abandoned it and built opposite it the town of al-Hāshimiyya.

He then chose to settle in al-Anbār and built his well-known town there. When he died, he was buried there.

Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr succeeded to the caliphate and settled in the town of al-Hāshimiyya in Kūfa. He completed something that had remained unfinished, added buildings to it, and arranged it as he wished. He then moved from it to Baghdad.

He built his town, laid out Baghdad as a city, and named it Madīnat al-Salām. He repaired its old wall, which begins at the Tigris and ends at al-Ṣirāṭ.

At al-Hāshimiyya, al-Manṣūr imprisoned ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥasan b. Ḥasan b. ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib on account of his two sons, Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm. His grave is there.

Al-Manṣūr built al-Ruṣāfa in Kūfa and ordered his client Abū al-Khaṣīb Marzūq to build for him, on an old foundation, the palace known as Abū al-Khaṣīb.

It is also said that Abū al-Khaṣīb built it for himself, and that al-Manṣūr used to visit him there.

As for al-Khawarnaq, it was an ancient Persian building, built by al-Nuʿmān b. Imruʾ al-Qays—who was the son of al-Shaqīqa bt. Abī Rabīʿa b. Dhuhl b. Shaybān—for Bahrām Jūr b. Yazdajird b. Bahrām b. Sābūr Dhū al-Aktāf.

Bahrām Jūr was in his care.

This al-Nuʿmān was the one who abandoned his kingship and wandered abroad, and whom ʿAdī b. Zayd al-ʿIbādī mentioned in his poetry.

When the blessed dynasty came to power, al-Khawarnaq was granted to Ibrāhīm b. Salama, one of the propagandists in Khurāsān . He was the grandfather of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Isḥāq the judge, who was in Madīnat al-Salām during the caliphates of al-Maʾmūn and al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh ﵏. He was a client of al-Ribāb (?).

Ibrāhīm added the dome of al-Khawarnaq during the caliphate of Abū al-ʿAbbās; it had not existed before that.

728Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me: Yaḥyā b. Salama b. Kuhayl al-Ḥaḍramī told us, from shaykhs of the people of Kūfa, that when the Muslims conquered al-Madāʾin, they captured an elephant there. They had previously killed whatever elephants they encountered.

They wrote to ʿUmar about it.

He wrote to them: “Sell it if you can find a buyer for it.”

A man from the people of al-Ḥīra bought it. He kept it, showing it to people, covering it with a cloth, and taking it around the villages. It remained with him for a time.

Then Umm Ayyūb bt. ʿUmāra b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, the wife of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba—whom Ziyād married after him—wished to look at it. She was residing in her father’s house.

It was brought and stationed at the gate of the mosque that is today called the Elephant Gate.

She began looking at it, gave its owner something, and sent him away. It had taken only a few steps when it fell down dead.

The gate was therefore named the Elephant Gate.

It has also been said that the woman who looked at it was the wife of al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ.

It has been said that a sorcerer made people see him bringing an elephant out through this gate upon a donkey. That is false.

It has been said that the basin in the mosque was carried on an elephant and brought in through this gate, which was therefore named the Elephant Gate.

Some said: An elephant belonging to one of the governors forced its way through this gate, so it was named after it.

The first report is the best established of these reports.

729Abū Masʿūd told me, who said: The cemetery of Maymūn in Kūfa was named after Maymūn, the client of Muḥammad b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh. He was the father of Bishr b. Maymūn, the proprietor of the arcades in Baghdad near the Syrian Gate.

The open ground of Umm Salama was named after Umm Salama bt. Yaʿqūb b. Salama b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. Makhzūm, the wife of Abū al-ʿAbbās.

Abū Masʿūd told me, who said: Al-Manṣūr compelled the people of Kūfa to dig its trench and required each of them to pay forty dirhams toward its expense.

He censured them for their inclination toward the Ṭālibids and their spreading alarming rumors about the ruling authority.

730Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Isrāʾīl, from Jābir, from ʿĀmir, who said: ʿUmar wrote to the people of Kūfa: “The head of the Arabs.”

731Al-Ḥusayn told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Sufyān, from Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit,

from Nāfiʿ b. Jubayr b. Muṭʿim, who said: ʿUmar said: “In Kūfa are the foremost people.”

732Al-Ḥusayn and Ibrāhīm b. Muslim al-Khwārazmī told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Yūnus b. Abī Isḥāq, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: ʿUmar wrote to the people of Kūfa: “To the head of Islam.”

733Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Qays b. al-Rabīʿ, from Shamir b. ʿAṭiyya, who said: ʿUmar said, mentioning Kūfa: “They are God’s spear, the treasure of faith, and the skull of the Arabs. They guard their frontier posts and reinforce the people of the garrison towns.”

734Abū Naṣr al-Tammār told us: Sharīk b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sharīk al-ʿĀmirī told us, from Jundab, from Salmān, who said: “Kūfa is the dome of Islam. A time will come upon people when no believer will remain except one who is there or whose heart yearns toward it.”

Chapter 61

Wāsiṭ

The Affairs of Wāsiṭ in Iraq

735ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Wāsiʿ al-Khuttalī, the reckoner, told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told me, from al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ, who said: The first congregational mosque built in the Sawād was the mosque of al-Madāʾin. Saʿd and his companions built it. It was subsequently enlarged and its construction strengthened; this was carried out by Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān.

Ḥudhayfa died at al-Madāʾin in the year thirty-six.

Then the mosque of Kūfa was built, then the mosque of al-Anbār.

He said: Al-Ḥajjāj founded the town of Wāsiṭ in the year eighty-three or the year eighty-four.

He built its mosque, its palace, and the Green Dome there.

Wāsiṭ had been land covered in reeds, so it was called Wāsiṭ al-Qaṣab.

The distance between it and al-Ahwāz, Baṣra, and Kūfa

is the same.

Ibn al-Qirriyya said: “He built it in a land other than his own, and his offspring will leave it to someone else.”

736A shaykh from the people of Wāsiṭ told me, from shaykhs among them, that when al-Ḥajjāj had finished Wāsiṭ, he wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān: “I have established a town in a belly of the land, between al-Jabal and the two garrison towns, and have named it Wāsiṭ.”

For that reason, the people of Wāsiṭ were called al-Karshiyyūn.

Before establishing Wāsiṭ, al-Ḥajjāj had intended to settle at al-Ṣīn in Kaskar. He dug the canal of al-Ṣīn, assembled laborers for it, and ordered that they be chained so that they would not stray away and become idle.

Then he changed his mind and founded Wāsiṭ.

He settled there and dug al-Nīl and al-Zābī, naming it Zābī because it drew from the old al-Zābī.

He brought into cultivation the lands along these two canals and founded the town known as al-Nīl, laying it out as a city.

He turned his attention to estates that ʿAbd Allāh b. Darrāj, the client of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, had reclaimed for him during his administration of the land tax of

Kūfa under al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba, from abandoned waste land, pools of standing water, drainage depressions, and reed beds. He constructed embankments around them, then uprooted their reeds, took possession of them for ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān, and developed them.

Al-Ḥajjāj transferred doors to his palace and the congregational mosque in Wāsiṭ from Zandaward, al-Dawqara, Dārwasāṭ, Dayr Māsarjisān, and Sharābīṭ.

The people of these towns raised an outcry and said: “We were granted security for our towns and our property.”

He paid no attention to what they said.

He said: Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī dug al-Mubārak. Al-Farazdaq said : “It is as though you were at al-Mubārak after a month, With piebald dogs wading through its depths.”

Then he said in a long poem of his: “He gave his caliph, through Khālid’s strength, A canal that pours forth for him over the canals. Al-Mubārak, true to its name, waters The crops of the Sawād and luxuriant tall palms.

And the Tigris, when its flood advances, is like An aged she-camel for which a train-rope is stretched.”

737Muḥammad b. Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṭaḥḥān told me: Our shaykhs told me that Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī wrote to Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik, asking his permission to build an arched bridge over the Tigris.

Hishām wrote to him: “Had this been possible, the Persians would have done it first.”

He wrote to him again, and he wrote back: “If you are certain that it will be completed, build it.”

He built it and spent a great deal on it. It was not long before the water broke it apart.

Hishām made him repay what he had spent on it.

738They said: The canal known as al-Bazzāq was ancient. In Nabataean it was called al-Bassāq, meaning that which cuts the water off from what lies beside it and draws it to itself.

It is a canal into which the surplus waters of the reed beds of al-Sīb collect, together with some water from the Euphrates.

People therefore said al-Bazzāq.

As for al-Maymūn, the first to dig it was an agent of Umm Jaʿfar Zubayda bt. Jaʿfar b. al-Manṣūr, called Saʿīd b. Zayd.

Its mouth was beside a village called the Village of Maymūn.

It was moved in the days of al-Wāthiq bi-llāh by ʿUmar b. Faraj al-Rukhkhajī. It was named al-Maymūn so that the mention of Yemen would not fall away from it.

739Muḥammad b. Khālid told me, who said: Al-Mahdī, the Commander of the Faithful, ordered the digging of the Canal of Grants. It was dug, and the lands along it were brought into cultivation. Its revenue was assigned to grants for the people of the two sanctuaries and to expenditure there.

He had stipulated for the cultivators whom he attracted to it the terms under which they operate today, for fifty years, on condition that after the fifty years had elapsed they would share the produce on a half-share basis.

As for the Canal of the Amīr, it was named after ʿĪsā b. ʿAlī and lies within his land grant.

740Muḥammad b. Khālid told us, who said: Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim had presented al-Ḥajjāj with an elephant from Sind. He crossed the marshes in a boat and brought ashore at the landing place called the Elephant Landing.

That landing place was therefore named the Elephant Landing and the Elephant Wharf.

Chapter 62

The marshes

The Matter of the Marshes

741A group of learned men told me that the Persians used to speak of the passing of their kingdom and relate that earthquakes and a flood would occur as a sign of it.

The Tigris used to empty into the Tigris of Baṣra, which is called al-ʿAwrāʾ, through channels branching from its main course, in which the remainder of its water flowed; it was like one of those channels.

In the time of Qubādh b. Fayrūz, a great breach opened in lower Kaskar. It was neglected until its water overwhelmed the land and submerged many cultivated tracts. Qubādh was feeble and paid little attention to his affairs.

When his son Anūshirwān assumed power, he ordered that this water be dealt with, and it was blocked by embankments until some of those lands returned to cultivation.

Then, in the year in which the Messenger of God ﷺ sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥudhāfa al-Sahmī to Kisrā Abarwīz—which was the year seven of the Hijra, though the year six is also reported—the Euphrates and the Tigris rose enormously, as had never been seen before or since.

Great breaches opened. Abarwīz strove to dam them, but the water overcame him and turned toward the site of the marshes, spreading over cultivated lands and crops and submerging several ṭassūjs that were there.

Kisrā rode out in person to close those breaches. He scattered money on leather mats and killed laborers in sufficient numbers; at some of the breaches, it is said, he crucified forty bridge builders in one day, yet he could devise no means of controlling the water.

Then the Arabs entered the land of Iraq and occupied the non-Arabs with wars. Breaches would burst open without receiving attention, and the dihqāns were unable to close the largest of them. Thus the marsh expanded and broadened.

When Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān assumed power, he appointed his client ʿAbd Allāh b. Darrāj to administer the land tax of Iraq. He reclaimed lands in the marshes for him whose revenue reached five million. He did this by cutting the reeds and overcoming the water with embankments.

Then came Ḥassān al-Nabaṭī—the client of Banū Ḍabba, the man associated with Ḥassān’s Pool in Baṣra, and the one after whom Ḥassān’s Tower in the marshes is named. He reclaimed tracts of marshland for al-Ḥajjāj during the days of al-Walīd, and for Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

742They said: Before the marshes came into being, there was a canal in Kaskar called al-Janb. The postal road to Maysān, Dast Maysān, and al-Ahwāz lay on its southern side.

When the marshes formed, the part on the side of the postal road that became overgrown with reeds was called the Reed Beds of the Postal Road. The other side was called the Reed Beds of Aghmar Banī. This means the Great Reed Beds. Today the canal appears in the dry lands that have recently been reclaimed.

743Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from his elders, who said: The marshes came into being after the Prophet’s emigration ﷺ when Abarwīz was king of the Persians. This happened because great breaches opened which Kisrā was unable to close, and the rivers overflowed until the marshes came into being.

Then, during the days when the Muslims were fighting the non-Arabs, there was a rise in the water and breaches which no one attended to closing. The marsh consequently expanded and grew larger.

The Umayyads had reclaimed some of its lands. In the time of al-Ḥajjāj, these were submerged, because breaches burst open and al-Ḥajjāj was not assisted in closing them, to the detriment of the dihqāns, whom he had accused of supporting Ibn al-Ashʿath when he rebelled against him.

Ḥassān al-Nabaṭī also reclaimed tracts of marshland for Hishām.

Abū al-Asad—after whom the Abū al-Asad Canal was named—was one of the commanders of al-Manṣūr, Commander of the Faithful, among those he had sent to Baṣra during ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAlī’s stay there. He was the one who brought ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAlī into Kūfa.

744ʿUmar b. Bukayr told me that al-Manṣūr ﵀ dispatched Abū al-Asad, the client of the Commander of the Faithful, and he encamped between him and the army of ʿĪsā b. Mūsā when he was fighting Ibrāhīm b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥasan b. al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib.

He dug the canal known as Abū Asad near the marsh.

Someone else said: He stayed at the mouth of the canal because boats could not enter it, as it was too narrow for them. He widened it, and it was named after him.

Abū Masʿūd said: During the days of the blessed dynasty, breaches opened which further enlarged the marshes. Reed beds also formed from the Euphrates, some of which were reclaimed.

745Abū Masʿūd told me, from ʿAwāna, who said: The breaches opened in the days of al-Ḥajjāj. Al-Ḥajjāj wrote to al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik informing him that he had estimated three million dirhams for closing them.

Al-Walīd considered this excessive. Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik said to him: “I will spend money on them, on condition that you grant me the low-lying lands in which water remains after the expenditure of three million dirhams, with your trusted and faithful adviser al-Ḥajjāj overseeing their expenditure.” He agreed to this.

Thus he acquired lands in contiguous ṭassūjs. He dug al-Sībayn, won over the cultivators and farmers, and brought those lands into cultivation. People placed many estates there under his protection to gain strength through him.

When the blessed dynasty came and the Umayyads’ properties were seized, all of al-Sībayn was granted to Dāwūd b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās. It was subsequently purchased from his heirs, with its rights and boundaries, and became one of the caliphate’s estates.

Chapter 63

Madīnat al-Salām

The Matter of Madīnat al-Salām

746They said: Baghdādh was ancient. The Commander of the Faithful al-Maṣnūr ﵀ made it a city and built a city there, beginning it in the year one hundred and forty-five.

When news reached him of the revolt of Muḥammad and Ibrāhīm, the two sons of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥasan b. Ḥasan, he returned to Kūfa. Then, in the year one hundred and forty-six, he transferred the treasuries, storehouses, and administrative bureaus from Kūfa to Baghdādh. He named it Madīnat al-Salām.

He completed the construction of his city’s wall, all its works, and the construction of the wall of old Baghdādh in the year one hundred and forty-seven. He died in the year one hundred and fifty-eight at Mecca and was buried beside the well of Maymūn b. al-Ḥaḍramī, the ally of Banū Umayya.

Al-Manṣūr built al-Ruṣāfa for al-Mahdī on the eastern side of Baghdādh. This side was called al-Mahdī’s Camp because he had encamped there when he set out for al-Rayy.

When he returned from al-Rayy, al-Manṣūr having changed his mind about sending him to Khurāsān to reside there, he settled in al-Ruṣāfa. This was in the year one hundred and fifty-one. Before settling him on the eastern side, al-Manṣūr had ordered the construction for al-Mahdī of his palace known as the Palace of al-Waḍḍāḥ, the Palace of al-Mahdī, and al-Sharqiyya. It lies toward Bāb al-Karkh. Al-Waḍḍāḥ was a man from al-Anbār who had supervised expenditure on it, so it was named after him.

Al-Manṣūr built the two mosques of Madīnat al-Salām. He built the New Bridge over al-Ṣarāt and purchased the land of Madīnat al-Salām from some of the owners of the villages of Bādūrayā, Quṭrabbul, Nahr Būq, and Nahr Bīn. He granted it to members of his household, his commanders, his troops, his companions, and his secretaries. He established the gathering place of the markets at al-Karkh and ordered the merchants to build shops, imposing rent upon them.

747Al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, who said: Al-Mukharrim in Baghdādh was called al-Mukharrim because Mukharrim b. Shurayḥ b. Ḥazn al-Ḥārithī settled there.

He said: The area of the Bardān Bridge belonged to al-Sarī b. al-Ḥuṭaym, the man associated with al-Ḥuṭaymiyya, which is known in Baghdādh.

748Elders from the people of Baghdādh told me that al-Ṣāliḥiyya in Baghdādh was named after Ṣāliḥ b. al-Manṣūr.

They said: Al-Ḥarbiyya was named after Ḥarb b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Balkhī, who was in charge of the police of Jaʿfar b. Abī Jaʿfar at al-Mawṣil.

Al-Zuhayriyya, known as Bāb al-Tibn, was named after Zuhayr b. Muḥammad, of the people of Abīward.

ʿĪsābādh was named after ʿĪsā b. al-Mahdī, who was in the care of Manāzil al-Turkī. He was the son of al-Khayzurān.

The Palace of ʿAbdawayh, toward Barāthā, was named after a man of al-Azd called ʿAbdawayh, who was one of the leading men of the dynasty.

749They said: Al-Manṣūr granted Sulaymān b. Mujālid the site of his house in Baghdādh—Mujālid was Sharwā, a client of ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh.

He granted Muhalhil b. Ṣafwān a tract in the city; Darb Muhalhil is named after him. Ṣafwān was a client of ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh.

Muhalhil’s name had been Yaḥyā. Muḥammad b. ʿAlī asked him to recite poetry, and he recited to him:

“O our night at Dhū Ḥushum, shine!”

It was [a poem] by Muhalhil, so he named him Muhalhil. Muḥammad emancipated him (?).

Al-Manṣūr granted ʿUmāra b. Ḥamza the district known by his name behind the square of Shabīb b. Wāj.

He granted Maymūn, the father of Bishr b. Maymūn, a tract beside Bustān al-Qass, in the direction of Bāb al-Shām. The Arcades of Bishr are named after this Bishr b. Maymūn. Maymūn was a client of ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh.

He granted his client Shubayl a tract beside the house of Yaqṭīn. There is a mosque there known by Shubayl’s name.

He granted a tract to Umm ʿUbayda, who was a nurse to them and a client of Muḥammad b. ʿAlī. The Arcades of Umm ʿUbayda near the bridge are named after her.

He granted land to Munīra, the client of Muḥammad b. ʿAlī. Darb Munīra and Khān Munīra on the eastern side are named after her.

He granted Raysāna a place known as the Mosque of Banū Raghbān, the client of Ḥabīb b. Maslama (296) al-Fihrī, which falls within the palace of ʿĪsā b. Jaʿfar or Jaʿfar b. Jaʿfar b. al-Manṣūr. Darb Mahrawayh on the eastern side was named after Mahrawayh al-Rāzī, who was among the captives of Sunfādh; al-Mahdī emancipated him.

Al-Manṣūr ﵀ remained in Madīnat al-Salām until the last years of his caliphate. He then departed from it on pilgrimage and died at Mecca.

After him, al-Mahdī, Commander of the Faithful, resided there. He then departed from it for Māsabadhān and died there. Most of his residence in Madīnat al-Salām was at ʿĪsābādh, in buildings he constructed there.

Then al-Hādī Mūsā b. al-Mahdī resided there and died there.

Al-Rashīd Hārūn b. al-Mahdī resided there, then departed from it for al-Rāfiqa and stayed there. From there he traveled to Khurāsān and died at Ṭūs.

Muḥammad b. al-Rashīd resided there and was killed there.

Al-Maʾmūn ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Rashīd came there from Khurāsān and stayed there. He then departed from it on campaign, died at al-Fadhdandūn, and was buried at Ṭarsūs.

The Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh resided there, then departed from it for al-Qāṭūl. He settled in a palace of al-Rashīd which he had built when he dug his Qāṭūl canal, which he called Abū al-Jund because the lands it irrigated provided his troops’ maintenance.

He then constructed a building at al-Qāṭūl in which he resided, and gave that palace to his client Ashnās al-Turkī. He intended to establish a city there and began building a city which he abandoned.

Then he decided to establish a city at Surra Man Raʾā. He made it a city, transferred people to it, and resided there. He built a congregational mosque at the edge of the markets and named it Surra Man Raʾā.

He settled his client Ashnās, together with the commanders he had attached to him, at Karkh Fayrūz. He settled some of his commanders at al-Dūr, known as al-ʿArabāyī.

He died ﵀ at Surra Man Raʾā in the year two hundred and twenty-seven.

Hārūn al-Wāthiq bi-llāh resided at Surra Man Raʾā in a building he constructed and named al-Hārūnī, until he died there.

Then the Commander of the Faithful Jaʿfar al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh ﵀ was made caliph in Dhū al-Ḥijja of the year two hundred and thirty-two. He resided at al-Hārūnī, constructed many buildings, and granted people tracts behind Surra Man Raʾā, in the enclosure which al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh had fenced off there, giving them more room.

He built a large congregational mosque and spent an enormous amount ? on it. He ordered its minaret to be raised so that the voices of the muezzins upon it would carry high, until it could be seen from parasangs away. The people assembled in it and abandoned the first mosque.

Then he founded a city which he named al-Mutawakkiliyya, built it up, and resided there. He granted people tracts within it and situated it between al-Karkh known as Fayrūz and al-Qāṭūl known as Kisrā. Thus al-Dūr and the village known as al-Māḥūza were incorporated into it.

He built a congregational mosque there. Months elapsed between his beginning it and his taking up residence there. He took up residence there at the beginning of the year two hundred and forty-six.

Then he died there ﵀ in Shawwāl of the year forty-seven,

and on this night al-Muntaṣir bi-llāh was made caliph. He moved from it to Surra Man Raʾā on Tuesday, ten nights having elapsed of Shawwāl, and died there.

750They said: The springs of al-Ṭaff, such as ʿAyn al-Ṣayd, al-Quṭquṭāna, al-Ruhayma, ʿAyn Jamal, and others like them, belonged to those assigned to the frontier posts beyond the Sawād. These are the springs of Sābūr’s Trench, which he dug between himself and the Arabs, those assigned to the frontier posts of the trench and others.

This was because Sābūr had granted them its land, and they cultivated it without his imposing any land tax upon them.

When the day of Dhū Qār came and God granted the Arabs victory through His Prophet ﷺ the Arabs took control of a portion of those springs. Some remained in the hands of the non-Arabs.

Then, when the Muslims arrived at al-Ḥīra, the non-Arabs fled after filling in most of those in their hands. Those in the hands of the Arabs remained, and they embraced Islam while possessing them. The lands they had cultivated became subject to the tithe.

When the affair of al-Qādisiyya and al-Madāʾin had passed, the lands of those springs whose inhabitants had departed were handed over to the Muslims and granted to them, and they too became subject to the tithe. Thus the springs of al-Ṭaff and their lands were treated like the outlying districts of Medina and the villages of Najd, and all their alms levy was entrusted to the officials of Medina.

When Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm b. Muṣʿab assumed the governorship of the Sawād for al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, he added them to what was under his control, took charge of administering their tithe, and made them Sawād land. They remain so to this day.

Springs have also been opened in Islamic times; the lands watered by their springs follow this same treatment.

751One of the elders told me that a camel died beside ʿAyn al-Jamal, and it was named after it.

Some of the people of Wāsiṭ said: The man who opened it was called Jamal.

They said: The spring was called ʿAyn al-Ṣayd because musk collects in it.

752One of the Kurayzīs informed me that ʿAyn al-Ṣayd was among the springs that had been filled in. While a Muslim man was riding about there, his horse’s legs sank into it.

He dismounted and dug, and water appeared. He gathered some people who helped him remove the earth and mud from it and clear it out, until it returned to its former condition.

It subsequently passed to ʿĪsā b. ʿAlī.

ʿĪsā had purchased it from the descendants of Ḥasan b. Ḥasan b. ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib. He was married to one of their women, Umm Kulthūm bt. Ḥasan b. Ḥasan. Muʿāwiya had granted this ʿAyn Ṣayd, together with other properties, to al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī in compensation for the caliphate.

ʿAyn al-Raḥba was among the springs filled in long ago. A pilgrim from Kirmān saw it seeping water. When he returned from his pilgrimage, he came to ʿĪsā b. Mūsā, offering him sincere counsel, and showed it to him. He obtained a grant of it and its land, and the Kirmānī excavated it for him. He cultivated the lands watered by it and planted the date palms along the road to al-ʿUdhayb.

Several farsakhs from Hīt are springs called al-ʿAraq, which follow this same arrangement; their tithes go to the official in charge of Hīt.

753Al-Athram told me, from Abū ʿUbayda, from Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ, who said: When the Arabs saw the abundance of villages, date palms, and trees, they said: “We have never seen more dark mass.”

Sawād means a person; hence al-Sawād was called al-Sawād.

754Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: Muḥammad b. ʿUbayd told us, from Muḥammad b. Abī Mūsā, who said: ʿAlī went out to the market and saw that its people had appropriated their places. He said: “They have no right to that. The Muslims’ market is like their place of prayer: whoever reaches a place first has it for that day, until he leaves it.”

755Abū ʿUbayd told me: Marwān b. Muʿāwiya told me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿUbayd, from his father, who said: We used to go early to the market in the time of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba. Whoever sat in a place had the stronger claim to it until nightfall.

When Ziyād took office, he said: “Whoever sits in a place has the stronger claim to it as long as he remains there.”

Marwān said: Al-Mughīra governed Kūfa twice, once for ʿUmar and once for Muʿāwiya.

Chapter 64

The transfer of the Persian register

756Al-Madāʾinī, ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. Abī Sayf, told me, from his elders, who said: The land-tax register of al-Sawād and the rest of Iraq had always been in Persian. When al-Ḥajjāj became governor of Iraq, he appointed Zādān Farrūkh b. Bīrī as his secretary. With him was Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, a client of Banū Tamīm, who wrote in his presence in Arabic and Persian.

Ṣāliḥ’s father was one of the captives of Sijistān. Zādān Farrūkh brought Ṣāliḥ into contact with al-Ḥajjāj, who took a liking to him.

One day Ṣāliḥ said to him: “You are my means of access to the governor. I see that he has taken a liking to me, and I fear that he may promote me above you and that you may lose your position.”

He said: “Do not think that. He needs me more than he needs you, for he can find no one other than me to handle his accounts.”

He said: “By God, if I wished to convert the accounts into Arabic, I could do so.”

He said: “Then convert a portion of them so that I may see.”

He did so.

He said to him: “Feign illness.”

He feigned illness, and al-Ḥajjāj sent his physician to him, but he found no ailment in him.

Zādān Farrūkh learned of this and ordered him to appear.

Then Zādān Farrūkh was killed during the days of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath al-Kindī, while going out from a house where he had been to his own house or someone else’s house.

Al-Ḥajjāj appointed Ṣāliḥ as his secretary in his place.

He informed him of what had passed between himself and Zādān Farrūkh concerning the transfer of the register.

Al-Ḥajjāj resolved to have the register kept in Arabic.

He entrusted this to Ṣāliḥ.

Mardānshāh b. Zādān Farrūkh said to him: “What will you do with dahwiyya and shashwiyya?” He said: “I shall write a tenth and half a tenth.”

He said: “What will you do with wīd?” He said: “I shall write that too.”

Wīd is the surplus and the increment that is added.

He said: “May God cut off your root from this world, just as you have cut off the root of Persian.”

He was offered one hundred thousand dirhams to profess himself incapable of transferring the register and to desist from

that, but he refused and transferred it.

ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd b. Yaḥyā, the secretary of Marwān b. Muḥammad, used to say: “God bless Ṣāliḥ! How great is his service to the secretaries!”

757ʿUmar b. Shabba told me: Abū ʿĀṣim al-Nabīl told me, saying: Sahl b. Abī al-Ṣalt reported, saying: Al-Ḥajjāj allowed Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān a period of time in which to convert the register.

Chapter 65

Al-Jibāl: Ḥulwān

The Conquests of al-Jibāl—Ḥulwān

758They said: When the Muslims had finished dealing with Jalūlāʾ, the site of the battle, Hāshim b. ʿUtba b. Abī Waqqāṣ attached a large cavalry force to Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī and stationed him at Jalūlāʾ, to stand between the Muslims and their enemy.

Then Saʿd sent them some three thousand Muslims and ordered him to advance with them and those already with him to Ḥulwān.

When he was close to it, Yazdajird fled toward Iṣbahān.

Jarīr conquered Ḥulwān by agreement, on condition that he refrain from attacking them and grant security to their lives and property, and that those among them who wished to flee should not be molested.

Then he left Jarīr behind in Ḥulwān with ʿAzra b. Qays b. Ghaziyya al-Bajalī and proceeded toward al-Dīnawar, but did not conquer it. He conquered Qarmāsīn on the same terms on which he had conquered Ḥulwān.

He came to Ḥulwān and remained there as its governor until ʿAmmār b. Yāsir arrived in Kūfa.

He wrote to him, informing him that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb had ordered him to send him as reinforcement to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. Jarīr left ʿAzra b. Qays in charge of Ḥulwān and traveled until he reached Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī in the year nineteen.

759Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Muḥammad b. Najjād, from ʿĀʾisha bt. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ, who said: When Muʿāwiya killed Ḥujr b. ʿAdī al-Kindī, my father said: “Had Muʿāwiya seen the great service rendered by the springs of ʿAyn Qanṭara at Ḥulwān, he would have known that he had rendered great service on behalf of Islam.”

Al-Wāqidī said: Some of the descendants of Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh settled in Ḥulwān, and they alternate residence there.

Chapter 66

The conquest of Nihāwand

759. They said: When Yazdajird fled from Ḥulwān in the year nineteen, the Persians and the people of al-Rayy, Qūmis, Iṣbahān, Hamadhān, and the two Māhs corresponded with one another and assembled around Yazdajird. This was in the year twenty. He appointed Mardānshāh Dhū al-Ḥājib to command them, and they brought out their banner, the Dirafshkābiyān. The polytheists numbered sixty thousand that day; it is also said one hundred thousand.

ʿAmmār b. Yāsir had written to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb with news of them. He contemplated campaigning against them himself, but then feared that the affairs of the Arabs in Najd and elsewhere would fall into disorder. He was advised to send the people of Syria on campaign from their Syria, and the people of Yemen from their Yemen. He feared that, if he did so, the Byzantines would return to their territories and the Abyssinians would seize the lands adjoining them.

He wrote to the people of Kūfa, ordering two-thirds of them to march and one-third to remain to guard their country and their homes.

He dispatched a contingent from the people of Baṣra.

He said: “I shall appoint a man who will be foremost in meeting the spearpoints.”

He wrote to al-Nuʿmān b. ʿAmr b. Muqarrin al-Muzanī, who was with al-Sāʾib b. al-Aqraʿ al-Thaqafī, appointing him to command the army. He said: “If you are struck down, the commander is Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān; if he is struck down, then Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī; if he is struck down, then al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba; if he is struck down, then al-Ashʿath b. Qays.”

Al-Nuʿmān was governor of Kaskar and its district. It is also said that he was in Medina, and that ʿUmar personally appointed him to command this army, whereupon he departed from there.

760Shaybān told me: Ḥammād b. Salama told us, from Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī, from ʿAlqama b. ʿAbd Allāh, from Maʿqil b. Yasār, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb consulted al-Hurmuzān and asked: “What do you think? Shall we begin

with Iṣbahān or Ādharbayjān?” Al-Hurmuzān said: “Iṣbahān is the head, and Ādharbayjān the two wings. If you cut off the head, the two wings and the head will fall.”

He said: ʿUmar entered the mosque and saw al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin. He sat down beside him, and when he had finished his prayer, he said: “I am going to appoint you.”

Al-Nuʿmān said: “As a tax collector, no; but as a warrior, yes.”

He said: “Then you are a warrior.”

He sent him off and wrote to the people of Kūfa to reinforce him.

They reinforced him, and among them was al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba.

Al-Nuʿmān sent al-Mughīra to Dhū al-Ḥājibayn, the chief of the Persians at Nihāwand. He began tearing his carpets with his spear until he stood before him. Then he sat on his throne, whereupon he ordered him dragged away.

He said: “I am an envoy.”

Then the Muslims and the polytheists met. They chained every ten men together in a chain, and every five men in a chain, so that they would not flee.

He said: They shot at us until they had wounded a number of us. This was before the fighting.

Al-Nuʿmān said: “I was present with the Prophet ﷺ. When he did not fight at the beginning of the day, he would wait for the sun to decline, the winds to blow, and victory to descend.”

Then he said: “I shall shake my banner three times. After the first shake, let each man perform his ablution and relieve himself. After the second shake, let each man inspect his sword—or he said, his sandal strap—and prepare himself and put his affairs in order. At the third, when it comes, God willing, charge, and let no one turn aside for anyone else.”

He shook his banner, and they did as he had ordered them. His coat of mail weighed heavily upon him. He fought, and the men fought, and he ﵀ was the first to be killed.

He said: The Persian fell from his mule, and his belly split open.

He said: I came to al-Nuʿmān while a spark of life remained in him and washed his face with water from a water vessel I had with me.

He said: “Who are you?” I said: “Maʿqil.”

He said: “What have the Muslims done?” I said: “Rejoice in God’s conquest and victory.”

He said: “Praise be to God. Write to ʿUmar.”

761Shaybān told me: Ḥammād b. Salama told us: ʿAlī b. Zayd b. Judʿān told me, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said: I went to ʿUmar with the good news.

He said: “What happened to al-Nuʿmān?” I said: “He was killed.”

He said: “Indeed, we belong to God, and to Him we return.”

Then he wept. I said: “By God, he was killed along with others whom I do not know.”

He said: “But God knows them.”

762Aḥmad b. Ibrāhīm told me: Abū Usāma, Abū ʿĀmir al-ʿAqadī, and Salm b. Qutayba all told us, from Shuʿba, from ʿAlī b. Zayd, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said: I saw ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, when news of al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin’s death reached him, put his hand on his head and begin to weep.

763Al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us: Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī told us, from al-Nahhās b. Qahm, from al-Qāsim b. ʿAwf, from his father, from al-Sāʾib b. al-Aqraʿ—or from ʿAmr b. al-Sāʾib, from his father; al-Anṣārī was uncertain—who said: A force advanced against the Muslims the like of which had never been seen.

He related the account of ʿUmar’s contemplation of campaigning in person, his appointment of al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin, and his sending his letter to him with al-Sāʾib. He put al-Sāʾib in charge of the spoils and said: “Do not submit a false claim or withhold a rightful due.”

Then he described the battle.

He said: Al-Nuʿmān was the first to be killed on the day of Nihāwand.

Then Ḥudhayfa took the banner, and God granted them victory.

Al-Sāʾib said: I gathered those spoils and then divided them. Then Dhū al-ʿUwaynatayn came to me and said: “The treasure of al-Nakhīr Khān is in the citadel.”

He said: I climbed up to it, and there I found two chests

containing jewels the like of which I had never seen.

He said: I then came to ʿUmar, to whom the news had been slow in coming, while he was going about Medina making inquiries. When he saw me, he said: “Woe to you! What news have you?” I told him about the battle and the killing of al-Nuʿmān, and mentioned the matter of the two caskets. He said: “Take them away and sell them, then divide their price among the Muslims.”

I brought them to Kūfa, where a young man of Quraysh called ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth came to me and bought them with the stipends of the dependants and fighting men. He then took one of them to al-Ḥīra and sold it for the amount for which he had bought both from me. The other remained as his surplus, and that was the first hoard of wealth he acquired.

764Some authorities on historical accounts said: They fought at Nihāwand on Wednesday and Thursday, then disengaged, then fought on Friday. He related an account of the battle similar to the account of Ḥammād b. Salama.

765Ibn al-Kalbī said, from Abū Mikhnaf, that al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin encamped at al-Isbīdhahān and placed al-Ashʿath b. Qays over his right wing and al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba over the left wing. They fought, and al-Nuʿmān was killed; then the Muslims prevailed. That conquest was therefore called the Conquest of Conquests.

He said: The conquest of Nihāwand took place in the year nineteen, on a Wednesday; it is also said, in the year twenty.

766Al-Rifāʿī told us: al-ʿAnqazī told us, from Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad, who both said: The battle of Nihāwand took place in the year twenty-one.

767Al-Rifāʿī told me: al-ʿAnqazī told us, from Abū Maʿshar, from Muḥammad b. Kaʿb, to the same effect.

768They said: When the army of the non-Arabs was defeated and the Muslims prevailed, Ḥudhayfa, who was then in command of the men, besieged Nihāwand. Its people would come out and fight, and the Muslims defeated them.

Then one day Simāk b. ʿUbayd al-ʿAbsī pursued one of their men, who had eight horsemen with him. Whenever one of them came out against him , he killed him, until only the man himself remained. He surrendered and threw down his weapons, and Simāk took him prisoner. He spoke in Persian, so Simāk summoned a man who understood his speech and interpreted it. What he was saying was: “Go to your commander so that I may make a settlement with him on behalf of this land and pay him the jizya. I shall give you whatever you wish for having taken me prisoner, for you have shown me kindness by not killing me.”

He asked him: “What is your name?” He replied: “Dīnār.” He took him to Ḥudhayfa, who made a settlement with him on terms of kharāj and jizya, and granted the people of his city, Nihāwand, security for their property, walled gardens, and dwellings. Nihāwand was therefore called Māh Dīnār. Dīnār thereafter used to visit Simāk, bring him gifts, and treat him generously.

769Abū Masʿūd al-Kūfī told me, from al-Mubārak b. Saʿīd, from his father, who said: Nihāwand was among the conquests of the people of Kūfa, and al-Dīnawar among the conquests of the people of Baṣra. When the Muslims in Kūfa became numerous, they needed an increase in the districts whose kharāj was apportioned among them. Al-Dīnawar was therefore assigned to them, and the people of Baṣra were compensated with Nihāwand, because it belonged to Iṣbahān. The excess of the kharāj of al-Dīnawar over that of Nihāwand thus went to the people of Kūfa. Nihāwand was consequently called Māh Baṣra, and al-Dīnawar Māh Kūfa. That was during the caliphate of Muʿāwiya.

770A group of learned men told me that Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān—he was Ḥudhayfa b. Ḥusayl b. Jābir al-ʿAbsī, an ally of the Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal of the Anṣār, and his mother was al-Rabāb bt. Kaʿb b. ʿAdī of ʿAbd al-Ashhal—and Ḥudhayfa’s father had been killed on the day of Uḥud: ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd al-Hudhalī killed him by mistake, thinking him an unbeliever. The Messenger of God, may God bless

him and grant him peace, ordered that his blood money be paid, but Ḥudhayfa gave it to the Muslims.

Al-Wāqidī used to say: Ḥusayl was called al-Yamānī because he used to trade in Yemen. Whenever he came to Medina, they would say: “Al-Yamānī has arrived.”

Al-Kalbī said: He was Ḥudhayfa b. Ḥusayl b. Jābir b. Rabīʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarwa. Jarwa was al-Yamān, to whom Ḥudhayfa was ascribed, with several forefathers between them . He had incurred bloodguilt in the time of ignorance, fled to Medina, and entered into an alliance with the Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal. His people therefore said: “He is a Yamān,” because he had allied himself with the Yemenis.

Chapter 67

Al-Dīnawar, Māsabadhān and Mihrjānqadha

Al-Dīnawar, Māsabadhān, and Mihrjānqadha f

771They said: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī returned from Nihāwand, having gone there in person at the head of the expeditionary force of the people of Baṣra to reinforce al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin. He passed by al-Dīnawar and remained before it for five days, on only one of which he was fought. Its people then acknowledged their obligation to pay jizya and kharāj and requested security for themselves, their property, and their children. He granted them that, and left his official there with a cavalry force.

He then proceeded to Māsabadhān, whose people did not fight him. The people of al-Sīrawān made a settlement with him like that of al-Dīnawar, undertaking to pay jizya and kharāj. He dispatched raiding parties among them and gained control of its territory.

Some people say that Abū Mūsā conquered Māsabadhān before the battle of Nihāwand. Abū Mūsā ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays al-Ashʿarī sent al-Sāʾib b. al-Aqraʿ al-Thaqafī—who was his son-in-law through his daughter, the mother of Muḥammad b. al-Sāʾib—to al-Ṣaymara, the city of Mihrjānqadhaf. He conquered it by a settlement providing for the sparing of lives, the taking of no captives, the relinquishment of claims to gold and silver, and the payment of jizya and land kharāj. He conquered all the districts of Mihrjānqadhaf. The better-established account is that he dispatched al-Sāʾib from al-Ahwāz, and he conquered it.

772Muḥammad b. ʿUqba b. Mukram al-Ḍabbī told me, from his father, from Sayf b. ʿUmar al-Tamīmī, from elders of the people of Kūfa, that when the Muslims invaded al-Jibāl, they passed the eastern summit called Sinn Samīra—Samīra was a woman of Ḍabba, of the Banū Muʿāwiya b. Kaʿb b. Thaʿlaba b. Saʿd b. Ḍamma, one of the women who emigrated—and it had a tooth, so that place was called Samīra’s Tooth.

Ibn Hishām al-Kalbī said: The bridges of al-Nuʿmān were named after al-Nuʿmān b. ʿAmr b. Muqarrin al-Muzanī. He encamped beside them, and they were ancient.

773Al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from ʿAwāna, who said: Kathīr b. Shihāb b. al-Ḥuṣayn b. Dhī al-Ghuṣṣa al-Ḥārithī was a partisan of ʿUthmān who disparaged ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and discouraged people from supporting al-Ḥusayn. He died shortly before the rising of al-Mukhtār b. Abī ʿUbayd, or in its earliest days. It was of him that al-Mukhtār b. Abī ʿUbayd said in his rhymed prose: “By the Lord of the clouds, severe in punishment, swift in reckoning, who sent down the Book, I shall indeed dig up the grave of Kathīr b. Shihāb, the lying fabricator!”

Muʿāwiya had appointed him over al-Rayy and Dastabā for a time, on his own behalf and on behalf of his two governors, Ziyād and al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba. Then he became angry with him, imprisoned him in Damascus, and beat him, until Shurayḥ b. Hāniʾ al-Murādī travelled to him concerning his case and secured his release.

Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya had praised his partisanship and compliance with his wishes. He therefore wrote to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād concerning his appointment over Māsabadhān, Mihrjānqadhaf, Ḥulwān, and the two Māhs, and granted him estates in al-Jabal. Then his palace, known as the Palace of Kathīr, was built, which belongs to the administrative territory of al-Dīnawar.

Zuhra b. al-Ḥārith b. Manṣūr b. Qays b. Kathīr b. Shihāb acquired estates in Māsabadhān.

774One of the descendants of Khashram b. Mālik b. Hubayra al-Asadī told me that the Khashārima first settled in Māsabadhān in the last days of the Banū Umayya. Their ancestor moved there from Kūfa.

775Al-ʿUmarī told me, and from al-Haytham b. ʿAdī, who said: Ziyād was on a journey when the safshaq of his qabāʾ came apart. Kathīr b. Shihāb took out a needle that was stuck into his cap and some thread he had with him, and repaired the safshaq. Ziyād said to him: “You are a prudent man. Someone like you should not be left without employment.” He appointed him over part of al-Jabal.

Chapter 68

The conquest of Hamadhān

776They said: Al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba, who was ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb’s governor over Kūfa after the dismissal of ʿAmmār b. Yāsir, sent Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī to Hamadhān. That was in the year twenty-three. Its people fought him, and resistance was offered in its defence. His eye was struck by an arrow, and he said: “I seek its recompense from God, who adorned my face with it and gave me light for as long as He wished, then took it from me in His path.”

He then conquered Hamadhān on terms like the settlement of Nihāwand. That was at the end of the year twenty-three. Its people fought him, and it was defended; he gained control of its territory and took it by force.

Al-Wāqidī said: Jarīr conquered Nihāwand in the year twenty-four, six months after the death of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵀.

Some have related that al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba marched to Hamadhān, with Jarīr commanding his vanguard, and conquered it, and that al-Mughīra added Hamadhān to the jurisdiction of Kathīr b. Shihāb al-Ḥārithī.

777ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from his grandfather and ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam, that when Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ governed Kūfa for ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān, he appointed al-ʿAlāʾ b. Wahb b. ʿAbd b. Wahbān, one of the Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy, over Māh and Hamadhān. The people of Hamadhān acted treacherously and broke their agreement. He fought them, and then they submitted to his judgment.
