He made a settlement with them providing that they pay the kharāj of their land and the poll jizya and give him one hundred thousand dirhams for the Muslims, after which no interference would be made with their property, protected persons, or children.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: The fortress known as Mādhirān was named after al-Sarī b. Nusayr b. Thawr al-ʿIjlī. He had encamped before it until he conquered it .

778Ziyād b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Balkhī told me, from elders of the people of Sīsar, who said: Sīsar was so named because it lies in a depression in the land between the summits of thirty hills. Thus it was called “thirty heads.” Sīsar used to be called Sīsar Ṣadkhāniya, meaning “thirty heads and one hundred springs.” It has many springs, amounting to one hundred.

779They said: Sīsar and its environs had always been pastureland for the livestock of the Kurds and others. There were meadows there for the riding animals and sheep of al-Mahdī, Commander of the Faithful. They were supervised by a client of his called Sulaymān b. Qīrāṭ, the proprietor of Ṣaḥrāʾ Qīrāṭ in Madīnat al-Salām, together with an associate called Sallām al-Ṭayfūrī. Ṭayfūr had been a client of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, who gave him to al-Mahdī.

When the brigands and malefactors became numerous and spread through al-Jabal during the caliphate of al-Mahdī, Commander of the Faithful, they made this district their refuge and protected territory. They would waylay travellers and take shelter there, and were not pursued because it was on the boundary of Hamadhān, al-Dīnawar, and Ādharbayjān.

Sulaymān b. Qīrāṭ and his associate wrote to al-Mahdī with news of them, complaining of their attacks on the riding animals and sheep in their charge. He sent a great army against them and wrote to Sulaymān and Sallām, ordering them to build a city in which they, their assistants, and their herdsmen could take shelter, and in which they could safeguard the riding animals and sheep against those whom they feared might attack them.

They built the city of Sīsar, fortified it, and settled people in it. The rural district of Mā Yanharaj from al-Dīnawar was attached to it, together with the rural district of al-Jūdhama from Ādharbayjān, from the district of Barza, and Rasṭaf and Khābanjar. It was constituted a district with these rural districts, and a separate governor was appointed over it, to whom its kharāj was paid.

Then the brigands became numerous during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd and wrought havoc in Sīsar. He ordered its repair and fortification and stationed there one thousand men from the followers of Khāqān, the Sogdian eunuch. There are people there descended from them.

Then, toward the end of al-Rashīd’s days, Murra b. Abī Murra al-Rudaynī al-ʿIjlī was dispatched to Sīsar.

ʿUthmān al-Awdī attempted to wrest it from him but could not do so; he did, however, wrest from him what he held of Ādharbayjān, or most of it.

Murra b. al-Rudaynī continued to pay the kharāj for Sīsar during the days of Muḥammad al-Rashīd, under a fixed assessment agreed with him, until the civil strife broke out.

Then it was taken from ʿĀṣim b. Murra and removed from his control during al-Maʾmūn’s caliphate. It thus reverted to the caliphate’s estates.

780Elders from the people of al-Mafāza, which borders Sīsar, told me that when al-Jurashī was appointed governor of al-Jabal, the people of al-Mafāza departed from it and abandoned it.

Al-Jurashī had a commander called Hammām b. Hāniʾ al-ʿAbdī. Most of the people of al-Mafāza placed their estates under his protection, and he gained control of what was there. He paid the treasury’s due on it until he died. His children were unable to manage it.

When al-Maʾmūn, Commander of the Faithful, came from Khurāsān after the killing of Muḥammad b. Zubayda, bound for Madīnat al-Salām, one of Hammām’s descendants and a local man called Muḥammad b. al-ʿAbbās intercepted him. They told him its story and that all its inhabitants were willing to give him ownership of its land and become his cultivators there, on condition that they be given strength and protected from the ṣaʿālīk and others.

He accepted it and ordered that they be provided with resources and assistance for its cultivation and improvement. It thus became one of the caliphate’s estates.

781Al-Madāʾinī told me that Laylā al-Akhyaliyya came to al-Ḥajjāj, who gave her a gift. She asked him to write on her behalf to his governor at al-Rayy. When she reached Sāwa, she died and was buried there.

Chapter 69

Qum, Qāshān and Iṣbahān

782They said: When Abū Mūsā ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays al-Ashʿarī departed from Nahāwand, he proceeded to al-Ahwāz and went through its districts.

Then he came to Qum, remained before it for some days, and conquered it. He dispatched al-Aḥnaf b. Qays, whose name was al-Ḍaḥḥāk b. Qays al-Tamīmī, to Qāshān, and he conquered it by force. Then he joined him.

ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb dispatched ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl b. Warqāʾ al-Khuzāʿī to Iṣbahān in the year twenty-three. It is also said that ʿUmar instead wrote to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, ordering him to dispatch him with an army to Iṣbahān, and he dispatched him. ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl conquered Jayy by agreement after fighting, on condition that its inhabitants pay the kharāj and the jizya and receive security for their persons and possessions, except for the weapons in their hands.

ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl dispatched al-Aḥnaf b. Qays, who was in his army, to al-Yahūdiyya. Its inhabitants concluded an agreement with him on the same terms. Ibn Badīl gained control of the territory of Iṣbahān and its ṭasāsīj. He remained its governor until a year of ʿUthmān’s caliphate had passed; then ʿUthmān appointed al-Sāʾib b. al-Aqraʿ over it.

783Muḥammad b. Saʿd, client of Banū Hāshim, told me: Mūsā b. Ismāʿīl told us, from Sulaymān b. Muslim, from his maternal uncle Bashīr b. Abī Umayya, that al-Ashʿarī encamped at Iṣbahān and offered them Islam, but they refused. He then offered them the jizya, and they concluded an agreement with him on that basis. They spent the night under an agreement, but by morning had acted treacherously. He fought them, and God gave him victory over them.

Muḥammad b. Saʿd said: I think he was speaking of the people of Qum.

784Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: Al-Haytham b. Jamīl told me, from Ḥammād b. Salama, from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, who said: ʿUmar b. Badīl al-Khuzāʿī was dispatched to Iṣbahān.

Its marzbān was an elderly man called al-Fādūsfān. He besieged him and corresponded with the inhabitants of the city, discouraging them from supporting him. When the old man saw the people turning against him, he selected thirty archers whose courage and obedience he trusted. Then he fled the city, intending to go to Kirmān to follow Yazdajird and join him.

News of him reached ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl, who pursued him with a large cavalry force. The Persian, having climbed a height, turned toward him and said: “Spare yourself, for no arrow of those you see misses its mark. If you charge, we shall shoot you; if you wish to engage us in single combat, we shall engage you.”

He engaged the Persian in single combat, and he struck him a blow that landed on the pommel of his saddle, breaking it and severing the breast strap. Then he said to him: “Man! I do not wish to kill you, for I see that you are sensible and brave. Would you agree that I return with you and conclude an agreement with you to pay the jizya on behalf of the people of my land, so that whoever remains shall be under protection and whoever flees shall not be molested, and that I hand the city over to you?”

Ibn Badīl returned with him, conquered Jayy, and fulfilled what he had granted him. He said: “People of Iṣbahān! I saw that you were base and deserted one another, so I was entitled to do what I did to you.”

785They said: Ibn Badīl proceeded through the districts of Iṣbahān, its plains and mountains, and gained control of them. He made arrangements with them concerning the kharāj similar to those made with the people of al-Ahwāz.

786They said: The conquest of Iṣbahān and its territory took place during part of the years twenty-three and twenty-four.

787It has been related that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb dispatched ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl with an army, and he reached Abū Mūsā after he had conquered Qum and Qāshān. They campaigned together against Iṣbahān, with al-Aḥnaf b. Qays commanding the vanguard of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. The two conquered al-Yahūdiyya together on the terms we have described. Then Ibn Badīl conquered Jayy, and the two proceeded together through the territory of Iṣbahān and gained control of it.

The soundest accounts are that Abū Mūsā conquered Qum and Qāshān, and that ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl conquered Jayy and al-Yahūdiyya.

788Abū Ḥassān al-Ziyādī told me, from a man of Thaqīf, who said: ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī had a memorial site at Iṣbahān.

789Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā al-Tamīmī told us, from his elders, who said: The nobles among the people of Iṣbahān had strongholds at Jafrabādh, in the rustāq of al-Thaymara al-Kubrā, at Hajāwarsān, and at a fortress known as Mārbīn. When Jayy was conquered, they submitted on condition that they pay the kharāj. They disdained the jizya and embraced Islam.

790Al-Kalbī and Abū al-Yaqẓān said: Al-Hudhayl b. Qays al-ʿAnbarī governed Iṣbahān in the days of Marwān. From that time, the ʿAnbarīs came to it.

791They said: The grandfather of Abū Dulaf and Abū Dulaf himself—al-Qāsim b. ʿĪsā b. Idrīs b. Maʿqil al-ʿIjlī—used to work with perfumes and milk sheep. He came to al-Jabal with a number of his family, and they settled in a village of Hamadhān called Mass. Then they became wealthy and acquired estates.

Idrīs b. Maʿqil attacked a merchant against whom he had a monetary claim and strangled him. It is also said that he instead strangled him and took his money. He was taken to Kūfa and imprisoned there during Yūsuf b. ʿUmar al-Thaqafī’s governorship of Iraq, in the time of Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

Then ʿĪsā b. Idrīs settled at al-Karaj, gained control of it, and built its fortress, which had been dilapidated.

The position of Abū Dulaf al-Qāsim b. ʿĪsā grew stronger, and his standing with the ruler increased. He enlarged that fortress and developed al-Karaj into a town, so it was called Karaj Abī Dulaf. Al-Karaj today is one of the towns.

Al-Maʾmūn had dispatched ʿAlī b. Hishām al-Marwazī to Qum, whose inhabitants had rebelled, defied authority, and withheld the kharāj. He ordered him to fight them and reinforced him with armies. He did so, killed their leader, Yaḥyā b. ʿImrān, demolished their city wall and razed it to the ground, and collected from it seven million dirhams and a further amount. Previously, its inhabitants had complained of being wronged by an assessment of two million dirhams.

They broke their agreement during the caliphate of Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Muʿtazz bi-llāh b. al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh. He dispatched against them Mūsā b. Bughā, his governor of al-Jabal, to fight the Ṭālibids who had risen in Ṭabaristān. It was conquered by force, and a great many of its inhabitants were killed. Al-Muʿtazz bi-llāh wrote ordering that a group of its leading men be brought to him.

.

Chapter 70

The killing of Yazdajird

The Killing of Yazdajird b. Shahriyār b. Kisrā Abarwīz b. Hurmuz b. Anūsharwān

790. They said: Yazdajird fled from al-Madāʾin to Ḥulwān, then to Iṣbahān. When the Muslims had finished with the affair of Nahāwand, he fled from Iṣbahān to Iṣṭakhr. After conquering Iṣbahān, ʿAbd Allāh b. Badīl b. Warqāʾ set out in pursuit of him but could not catch him.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī reached Iṣṭakhr and attempted to conquer it, but could not do so. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī struggled against it but could not take it.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz came to Baṣra in the year twenty-nine, when all of Fārs had been conquered except Iṣṭakhr and Jūr. Yazdajird considered going to Ṭabaristān, for its marzbān had offered, while he was at Iṣbahān, that he come there, and had told him of its defensibility. Then he changed his mind and fled to Kirmān. Ibn ʿĀmir sent Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd al-Sulamī and Haram b. Ḥayyān al-ʿAbdī in pursuit of him. Mujāshiʿ proceeded and encamped at Baymandh in Kirmān. The people were struck by the damaq, and his army perished; only a few escaped. The fortress was therefore called the Fortress of Mujāshiʿ. Mujāshiʿ returned to Ibn ʿĀmir.

One day Yazdajird was sitting in Kirmān when its marzbān entered his presence. He did not speak to him, out of arrogance, so he ordered that he be dragged by the leg and said: “You are not fit to govern a village, let alone a kingdom. Had God known any good in you, He would not have reduced you to this condition.”

He proceeded to Sijistān, whose king honored him and treated him with great respect. When some days had passed, he asked him about the kharāj, and he became hostile toward him.

When Yazdajird saw this, he traveled to Khurāsān. When he reached the boundary of Marw, Māhawayh, its marzbān, met him with honor and reverence. Nīzak Ṭarkhān came to him, and he provided him with a mount, bestowed a robe of honor upon him, and honored him. Nīzak stayed with him for a month, then departed and wrote to him asking for his daughter’s hand. This enraged

Yazdajird, who said: “Write to him: You are merely one of my slaves. What has emboldened you to ask me for a marriage alliance?” He ordered an accounting from Māhawayh, the marzbān of Marw, and questioned him about the funds.

Māhawayh wrote to Nīzak, inciting him against him and saying: “This is the man who arrived defeated and driven out, to whom you showed favor so that his kingdom might be restored to him; yet he wrote you what he wrote.”

Then the two joined forces to kill him. Nīzak advanced with the Turks until he encamped at al-Junābidh. They fought him, and the Turks held their own; then the tide turned against him. His companions were killed and his camp plundered.

He came to the city of Marw, but its gates were not opened for him. He dismounted and walked until he entered a miller’s house on the Murghāb. It is said that Māhawayh sent his messengers to him when news of him reached him, and they killed him in the miller’s house.

It is also said that he secretly sent word to the miller, ordering him to kill him, and he killed him. Then he said: “The killer of a king ought not to live.” He ordered that the miller be killed, and he was killed.

It is also said that the miller served him food, and he ate. He brought him a drink, which he drank, and he became intoxicated. When evening came, he took out his crown and placed it on his head. The miller saw it and coveted it. He took a millstone and cast it upon him. When he had killed him, he took his crown and clothes and threw him into the water. Then Māhawayh learned his story, killed the miller and his household, and took the crown and clothes.

It is also said that Yazdajird became aware of Māhawayh’s messengers, fled, and entered the water. He was sought from the miller, who said: “He has left my house.” They found him in the water. He said: “Leave me alone, and I shall give you my belt, my ring, and my crown.” They withdrew out of his sight.

He asked them for something with which to eat bread, and one of them gave him four dirhams. He laughed and said: “I was indeed told that you would come to need four dirhams.”

Then some men whom Māhawayh had dispatched to seek him came upon him. He said: “Do not kill me. Take me to the king of the Arabs, so that I may make an agreement with him on my behalf and yours.” They refused and strangled him with a bowstring. Then they took his clothes, which were put in a leather bag, and threw his body into the water.

Fīrūz b. Yazdajird, so they claim, reached the Turks. They married him to one of their women, and he remained among them.

.

Chapter 71

The conquest of al-Rayy and Qūmis

791. Al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to ʿAmmār b. Yāsir, his governor of Kūfa, two months after the battle of Nahāwand, ordering him to dispatch ʿUrwa b. Zayd al-Khayl al-Ṭāʾī to al-Rayy and Dastabā with eight thousand men. He did so.

ʿUrwa proceeded there. The Daylam assembled against him, and the people of al-Rayy reinforced them. They fought him, and God gave him victory over them; he killed them and swept them away.

Then he left his brother Ḥanẓala b. Zayd in charge and came to ʿAmmār, asking him to send him to ʿUmar. This was because he had been the one who had brought him the news of the Bridge, and he wished to bring him something that would gladden him.

When ʿUmar saw him, he said: “Indeed, we belong to God, and indeed, to Him we return.” [Source note 1: Sūrat al-Baqara, 2, part of verse 156.] ʿUrwa said: “Rather, praise God, for He has granted us victory and made us prevail.” He told him his story, and he said: “Why did you not remain and send word?” He said: “I left my brother in charge, and I wished to come to you myself.” So he called him al-Bashīr, the bearer of glad tidings.

ʿUrwa said: “I went forth against the people of al-Qādisiyya bearing a distinguishing mark; / not everyone who enters the fray bears such a mark. And on a day before it, in the environs of al-Nukhayla, / I was present and never ceased bleeding and being wounded. On the day of the Daylamīs I knew with certainty / that whenever I turned my face toward the people, they would be routed, Out of zeal to defend, for I am a man of protective ardor; / when I find no place to fall back, I advance.”

Al-Mundhir b. Ḥassān b. Ḍirār, one of Banū Mālik b. Zayd, shared in the bloodshed against Mihrān on the day of al-Nukhayla.

(*)

792They said: When ʿUrwa withdrew, Ḥudhayfa sent Salama b. ʿAmr b. Ḍirār al-Ḍabbī at the head of his army; it is also said that it was al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib. ʿUrwa’s battle had broken the Daylam and the people of Rayy. He encamped before the fortress of al-Farrukhān b. al-Zaynabadī , whom the Arabs call al-Zaynabī, and who was called ʿĀrīn.

After fighting, Ibn al-Zaynabī concluded a settlement with him on condition that they should become protected subjects, paying the poll tax and land tax. He gave him five hundred thousand on behalf of the people of Rayy and Qūmis, on condition that he should kill none of them, take none captive, and demolish none of their fire temples, and that they should be treated like the people of Nihāwand regarding their land tax.

He also concluded a settlement with him on behalf of the people of the Rayy division of Dastabī. Dastabī had two divisions, one belonging to Rayy and one to Hamadhān.

Sulaymān b. ʿUmar al-Ḍabbī—or, it is said, al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib—sent cavalry to Qūmis. They offered no resistance and opened the gates of al-Dāmghān.

Then, when ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb dismissed ʿAmmār and appointed al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba governor of Kūfa, al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba appointed Kathīr b. Shihāb al-Ḥārithī governor of Rayy and Dastabī.

Kathīr had distinguished himself at the battle of al-Qādisiyya.

When they reached Rayy, he found that its people had broken their agreement. He fought them until they returned to obedience and submitted to the land tax and poll tax.

He raided the Daylam and inflicted a defeat upon them, and he raided the Babr and the Ṭaylasān.

793Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī told me, from al-Haytham b. ʿAdī, from Ibn ʿAyyāsh al-Hamadhānī and others, that Kathīr b. Shihāb governed Rayy, Dastabī, and Qazwīn. He was handsome, resolute, and unable to walk. He used to say: “There is no man unable to walk who is not a burden upon his family, except me.”

When he rode, his two little shins stuck out like two plows.

When he went on a raid, he required every man accompanying him to have a shield, a coat of mail, a helmet, a large needle, five needles, linen threads, an awl, shears, and a large sack.

He was miserly. He had a large bowl placed before him, and whenever someone came to him he would say: “May you have no father! Did you have a spy watching us?” And he said

one day: “Boy! Give us something to eat.”

He replied: “There is nothing on hand except bread and greens.”

He said: “Did Persia and Rome fight one another over anything but bread and greens?”

He also governed Rayy and Dastabī for a time during Muʿāwiya’s days.

He said: When Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ was appointed governor of Kūfa for the second time, he came to Rayy.

It was in disrepair, and he set it right.

He raided the Daylam, at the beginning of the year twenty-five, and then withdrew.

794Bakr b. al-Haytham told me, from Yaḥyā b. Ḍurays, the judge of Rayy, who said: After its conquest in Ḥudhayfa’s days, Rayy continued to rebel and be reconquered until the last person to conquer it was Qaraẓa b. Kaʿb al-Anṣārī, during Abū Mūsā’s governorship of Kūfa for ʿUthmān. Thereafter it remained obedient.

Its governors used to reside in the fortress of al-Zanabadī and hold Friday prayers in a mosque established beside it.

That has now been incorporated into the outer enclosure of the newly built city.

They used to raid the Daylam from Dastabī.

He said: Qaraẓa subsequently governed Kūfa for ʿAlī and died there. ʿAlī ﵁ led the funeral prayer over him.

795ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: ʿAlī appointed Yazīd b. Ḥujba b. ʿĀmir b. Taym Allāh b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUkāba governor of Rayy and Dastabī.

He left a shortfall in the land tax, so he imprisoned him. He got out and joined Muʿāwiya.

Abū Mūsā had personally raided Rayy after its people broke their agreement, and conquered it on its original terms.

796Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad al-Rāzī told me, saying: The Commander of the Faithful al-Mahdī arrived during al-Manṣūr’s caliphate and built the city of Rayy in which the people live today, and dug a trench around it,

and built a congregational mosque within it. This was carried out under the supervision of ʿAmmār b. Abī al-Khaṣīb, and his name was inscribed on its wall.

Its construction was dated to the year one hundred and fifty-eight.

He provided it with an outer enclosure surrounded by two brick fāriqs, and named it al-Muḥammadiyya. The people of Rayy call Rayy the inner city, and call the outer enclosure the outer city.

The fortress of al-Zanabadī lies within al-Muḥammadiyya.

Al-Mahdī had ordered its repair and resided in it.

It overlooks the congregational mosque and the governor’s residence, and was subsequently made into a prison.

He said: In Rayy there is a household called Banū al-Ḥarīsh, who settled there after the city was built.

He said: The city of Rayy was called Arāzī in pre-Islamic times. It is said that the earth swallowed it up.

It lies six parasangs from al-Muḥammadiyya, and Rayy was named after it.

He said: When al-Mahdī first arrived at Rayy, he stayed in a village called al-Sīrwān.

He said: Concerning the citadel of al-Farrukhān, the poet al-Ghaṭmash b. al-Aʿwar b. ʿAmr al-Ḍabbī says:

At the accursed pavilion in Rayy, unceasingly, upon its summit the herald of death flashes.

797Bakr b. al-Haytham said: Yaḥyā b. Ḍurays the judge told me, saying: Al-Shaʿbī entered Rayy with Qutayba b. Muslim.

He asked him: “What drink do you like best?” He replied:

“That which is easiest to find and hardest to do without.”

He said: Saʿīd b. Jubayr also entered Rayy. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk met him and wrote down Qurʾānic interpretation from him.

He said: ʿAmr b. Maʿdī Karib al-Zubaydī raided Rayy when it was first raided. On his return he died, and was buried above Rūdha and Būsana, at a place called Kirmānshāhān.

Al-Kisāʾī the grammarian, whose name was ʿAlī b. Ḥamza, was buried in Rayy.

He had traveled there with al-Rashīd ﵀ who was heading for Khurāsān.

Al-Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāh died there.

He had traveled there with al-Mahdī, and his kunya was Abū Arṭāh.

Al-Kalbī said: Qaṣr Jābir in Dastī was attributed to Jābir, one of the Banū Zaybān b. Taym Allāh b. Thaʿlaba.

798They said: Rayy’s assessment remained twelve million dirhams until al-Maʾmūn passed through it on his return from Khurāsān, heading for Madīnat al-Salām. He remitted two million dirhams of its assessment and issued a written deed to its people to that effect .

Chapter 72

The conquest of Qazwīn and Zanjān

799Several people from Qazwīn told me, as did Bakr b. al-Haytham, from an elder of the people of Rayy. They said: The fortress of Qazwīn was called Kashwīn in Persian, meaning “the frontier watched over,” that is, guarded.

Between it and the Daylam lies a mountain. Persian fighting men from the asāwira had continually been stationed there, maintaining a frontier garrison. They repelled the Daylam when there was no truce between them, and protected their country from their marauders and others when peace had been concluded between them.

Dastabī was divided between Rayy and Hamadhān, one division being called the Rayy division and another the Hamadhān division.

When al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba became governor of Kūfa, he appointed Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh governor of Hamadhān and al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib governor of Qazwīn. He ordered him to march there and, if God granted him its conquest, to raid the Daylam from it. Previously their raids had been launched only from Dastabī.

Al-Barāʾ marched with Ḥanẓala b. Zayd al-Khayl until he reached Abhar.

He took up position before its fortress. It was a fortress built by one of the non-Arabs over springs that he had blocked with ox hides and wool. He constructed a platform over them, then erected the fortress upon it.

They fought him, then requested safe-conduct. He granted them safe-conduct on the same terms on which Ḥudhayfa had granted it to the people of Nihāwand, and concluded a settlement with them on that basis. He gained control of the lands of Abhar.

Then he raided the people of the fortress of Qazwīn.

When they learned that the Muslims were advancing against them, they sent to the Daylamites asking for their support, and they promised to provide it.

Al-Barāʾ and the Muslims encamped in their environs. They came out to fight them, while the Daylamites stood on the mountain, raising no hand against the Muslims.

When they saw this, they requested a settlement.

He offered them what he had granted the people of Abhar, but they disdained the poll tax and professed Islam.

It is said that they accepted Islam on the same terms as the asāwira of Baṣra had accepted it, on condition that they could associate with whomever they wished.

They settled in Kūfa and entered into an alliance with Zuhra b. Ḥawiyya, and were called the Ḥamrāʾ of the Daylam.

It is also said that they embraced Islam and remained where they were, and their lands became subject to the tithe.

Al-Barāʾ stationed five hundred Muslim men with them, including Ṭulayḥa b. Khuwaylid al-Asadī, and granted them lands over which no one had any claim.

Bakr said: A man from Qazwīn recited to me verses by his father’s grandfather, who had been with al-Barāʾ:

The Daylam have learned, as they wage war, when the son of ʿĀzib came with his army, that the polytheists’ expectation is false. How many have we crossed in the darkness of deep gloom, rugged mountains and open plains!

He raided the Daylam until they paid him tribute.

He raided Jīlān, the Babr, and the Ṭaylasān.

He conquered Zanjān by force.

When al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ b. Abī ʿAmr b. Umayya became governor of Kūfa for ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān, he raided the Daylam from the direction of Qazwīn. He raided Ādharbayjān, and raided Jīlān, Mūqān, the Babr, and the Ṭaylasān, then withdrew.

Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Umayya was appointed after al-Walīd. He raided the Daylam and established Qazwīn as a garrison town.

It became the frontier post of the people of Kūfa, and their buildings were in it.

800Aḥmad b. Ibrāhīm al-Dawraqī told me, saying: Khalaf b. Tamīm told us, saying: Zāʾida b. Qudāma told us, from Ismāʿīl b. Murra al-Hamadhānī, who said: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵁ said: “Whoever among you is unwilling to fight Muʿāwiya alongside us should take his stipend and go out against the Daylam and fight them.”

He said: I was among the selected men. We took our stipends and went out against the Daylam, numbering four thousand or five thousand.

801ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-ʿIjlī told us, from Ibn Yamān, from Sufyān, who said: ʿAlī ﵁ sent al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym al-Thawrī to raid the Daylam and gave him command over four thousand Muslims.

802One of the people of Qazwīn told me, saying: In Qazwīn, the mosque of al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym is well known. In it there was a tree against which the common people used to rub themselves.

It is said that he planted his tooth-stick in the ground and it put forth leaves, until the tree grew from it. An official of Ṭāhir b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṭāhir cut it down during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh, fearing that the people would be led astray by it.

803They said: When Mūsā al-Hādī came to Rayy, he visited Qazwīn and ordered a city to be built opposite it.

It is known as the City of Mūsā.

He purchased land called Rustamābādh and endowed it for the city’s needs.

His client ʿUmar al-Rūmī administered it, and after him Muḥammad b. ʿAmr administered it.

Al-Mubārak al-Turkī had built a fortress called the City of al-Mubārak, and some of his clients are there.

804Muḥammad b. Hārūn al-Iṣbahānī told me, saying: Al-Rashīd passed through Hamadhān on his way to Khurāsān. The people of Qazwīn approached him and informed him of their position in relation to enemy territory and their effectiveness in fighting the enemy. They asked him to attend to their interests and reduce what they owed as a tithe on their yields in the qaḍba.

He imposed on them a fixed annual payment of ten thousand dirhams.

Al-Qāsim, son of the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd, had become governor of Jurjān, Ṭabaristān, and Qazwīn. The people of Zanjān placed under his protection

their estates, seeking strength through him and protection from the depredations of brigands and the oppression of officials. They drew up deeds of sale for him covering them and became his tenant cultivators.

Today they are among the estates.

Al-Qāqazān was subject to the tithe, because its people had embraced Islam while possessing it and had brought it under cultivation after Islam. They also placed it under al-Qāsim’s protection, on condition that they assign him a second tithe in addition to the tithe of the public treasury.

It too became part of the estates.

Dastabī continued in its two divisions, part belonging to Rayy and part to Hamadhān, until a man in Qazwīn from Banū Tamīm, called Ḥanẓala b. Khālid and bearing the kunya Abū Mālik, pursued its affairs until all of it was attached to Qazwīn.

A man from his town heard him say: “I have made it into a ball, and I am Abū Mālik.”

He replied: “Rather, you have ruined it, and you are Abū Hālik.”

805Al-Madāʾinī and others told me that the Kurds wrought havoc and destruction during the days of the revolt of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath.

Al-Ḥajjāj sent ʿAmr b. Hāniʾ al-ʿAbsī against them with the people of Damascus. He inflicted a defeat upon them and killed a great many of them .

Then he ordered him to raid the Daylam. He raided them with twelve thousand men, among whom were eighty from Banū ʿIjl and their clients from the people of Kūfa, including Muḥammad b. Sinān al-ʿIjlī.

806ʿAwf b. Aḥmad al-ʿAbdī told me, saying: Abū Ḥanash al-ʿIjlī told me, from his father, who said: I met a man from among the Tamīmī ʿIjlīs whom al-Ḥajjāj had dispatched to maintain a frontier garrison against the Daylam. He told me, saying: I saw a man from among the clients of Banū ʿIjl who claimed to be a member by blood (?). I said: “Your father did not wish to exchange his lineage among the non-Arabs for an affiliation among the Arabs. On what grounds, then, do you claim to be a member by blood (?)?”

He replied: “My mother told me that.”

I said: “She is to be believed; she knows your father better.”

807They said: Muḥammad b. Sinān al-ʿIjlī had settled in a village belonging to the villages of Dastabā. Then he went to Qazwīn and built a house in its suburb.

The people of the frontier town reproached him, saying: “You have exposed yourself to destruction and us to weakness, should the enemy inflict harm upon you.”

He paid no attention to what they said. He instructed his children and household to build alongside him outside the city. Subsequently, people moved there and built until the city’s suburb was complete.

808They said: Abū Dulaf al-Qāsim b. ʿĪsā had campaigned against the Daylam during the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn, and he was a governor during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh, when al-Afshīn governed al-Jibāl.

He conquered fortresses, including Iqlīsim, whose inhabitants he made peace with for a tribute payment. Among them was Būmaj, which he conquered by force; then he made peace with its inhabitants for a tribute payment. Among them were al-Ablām and Andāq, as well as other fortresses.

Al-Afshīn also sent someone other than Abū Dulaf on campaign, and he too conquered fortresses belonging to the Daylam.

In the year 253, the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtazz bi-llāh sent his client Mūsā b. Bughā al-Kabīr against the Ṭālibids who had risen in al-Daylam and the region of Ṭabaristān. The Daylamites had rallied around a man from among them known as al-Kawkabī. He campaigned against al-Daylam and penetrated deeply into their country. They fought him, but he inflicted a defeat upon them. His pressure upon them grew heavy, and the harm he inflicted became severe.

809A man from Qazwīn informed me that the graves of these drinking companions are at Rāwand, in the district of Iṣbahān, and that what the poet actually said was:

“Did you two not know that I am alone at Rāwand?”

810ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-ʿIjlī told me, who said: It has reached me that three men from Kūfa were in the army of al-Ḥajjāj that he sent against al-Daylam. The three used to drink together and associate with no one else. While they were living thus, one of them died, and his two companions buried him.

The two would drink beside his grave, and when the cup came to his turn, they poured it out over his grave and wept.

Then the second died, and the survivor buried him beside him.

He would sit beside their two graves and drink, then pour some over the grave nearest him, and then over the other, and weep. One day he began to recite:

“My two friends, wake up! Long have you slept; I think you two will never finish your sleep. Did you two not know that I am alone at Qazwīn, And that I have no friend here besides you two? Remaining beside your two graves, I shall not depart Through the long nights, until your echoes answer. I shall weep for you both throughout my life; yet what Does weeping for you restore to one consumed by grief?”

Then it was not long before he died, and he was buried beside his two companions. Their graves are known as the Graves of the Drinking Companions.

Chapter 73

The conquest of Ādharbayjān

811Al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAmr al-Ardabīlī told us, from Wāqid al-Ardabīlī, from elders whom he had met, that al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba came to Kūfa as governor on behalf of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, carrying a letter to Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān appointing him governor of Ādharbayjān. He sent him to him while he was at Nihāwand or nearby.

He marched until he reached Ardabīl, the principal city of Ādharbayjān, where its marzbān resided and to whom the collection of its land tax belonged. The marzbān had assembled fighting men from Bājarwān, Maymadh , al-Narīr, Sarāt, al-Shīz, al-Mayānij, and elsewhere.

They fought the Muslims fiercely for several days. Then the marzbān made peace with Ḥudhayfa on behalf of all the inhabitants of Ādharbayjān for eight hundred thousand dirhams of eight-weight standard, on condition that he kill none of them or take any captive, demolish no fire temple, leave unmolested the Kurds of al-Balāsajān, Sabalān, and Sātarūdān, and not prevent the people of al-Shīz in particular from dancing at their festivals and publicly displaying what they had previously displayed.

Then he campaigned against Mūqān and Jīlān, inflicted a defeat upon them, and made peace with them for a tribute payment.

812They said: Then ʿUmar dismissed Ḥudhayfa and appointed ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī governor of Ādharbayjān. He came there from al-Mawṣil; it is also said that he came there from Shahrazūr, by way of the salq known today as Muʿāwiya al-Awdī.

When he entered Ardabīl, he found its inhabitants abiding by the agreement. Some districts rebelled against him, so he campaigned against them, prevailed, and took booty. ʿUmar b. ʿUtba the ascetic was with him.

Al-Wāqidī related through his chain of transmission that al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba campaigned against Ādharbayjān from Kūfa in the year 22, reached it, conquered it by force, and imposed the land tax upon it.

Ibn al-Kallī related, from Abū Mikhnaf, that al-Mughīra campaigned against Ādharbayjān in the year 20 and conquered it. Then they repudiated their allegiance

so al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī campaigned against it, conquered the fortress of Bājarwān, and made peace with them on the terms of al-Mughīra’s agreement. Al-Ashʿath’s agreement has remained in force to this day.

Abū Mikhnaf Lūṭ b. Yaḥyā used to say: ʿUmar appointed Saʿd, then ʿAmmār, then al-Mughīra; then he reinstated Saʿd and wrote to him and to the governors of the garrison towns to come to Medina in the year in which he died. For that reason Saʿd attended the council of consultation, and he instructed whoever assumed the caliphate to restore him to his post.

Someone else said: ʿUmar died while al-Mughīra was his governor of Kūfa. He instructed that Saʿd be appointed governor of Kūfa and that Abū Mūsā be appointed governor of Baṣra. ʿUthmān appointed them both, then dismissed them.

813Al-Madhāʾinī told me, from ʿAlī b. Mujāhid, from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, from al-Zuhrī, who said: When God defeated the polytheists at Nihāwand, the people returned to their garrison towns, while the people of Kūfa remained with Ḥudhayfa. He campaigned against Ādharbayjān, and they made peace with him for one hundred thousand.

814Al-Madāʾinī told me, from ʿAlī b. Mujāhid, from ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said: ʿUmar dismissed Ḥudhayfa from Ādharbayjān and appointed ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī over it. He sent him portions of khabīṣ wrapped in coarse cotton cloth.

When they reached him, he said: “Is it silver?” They said: “No.” He said: “What is it, then?” He said: “A gift he has sent.” When he looked at it, he said: “Send it back to him.”

He wrote to him: “O son of Umm ʿUtba! You are indeed eating khabīṣ without your father’s toil.”

ʿUtba said: I came from Ādharbayjān on a visit to ʿUmar, and there before him was a camel’s sinew.

815Al-Madāʾinī told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Qāsim, from Farwa b. Laqaṭ, who said: When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵁ assumed office, he appointed

al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, who dismissed ʿUtba from Ādharbayjān, whereupon they broke the agreement.

Al-Walīd campaigned against them in the year twenty-five, with ʿAbd Allāh b. Shibl al-Aḥmasī commanding his vanguard. He raided the people of Mūqān, al-Babr, and al-Ṭaylasān, taking booty and captives. The inhabitants of the districts of Ādharbayjān requested peace, and he made peace with them on the terms of Ḥudhayfa’s agreement.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵁ appointed Saʿīd b. Sāriya al-Khuzāʿī over Ādharbayjān, and then al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī.

816ʿAbd Allāh b. Muʿādh al-ʿAnqazī told me, from his father, from Saʿd b. al-Ḥakam b. ʿUtayba, from Zayd b. Wahb, who said: When God defeated the polytheists at Nihāwand, the people of the Ḥijāz returned to their Ḥijāz and the people of Baṣra to their Baṣra, while Ḥudhayfa remained at Nihāwand with the people of Kūfa. He campaigned against Ādharbayjān, and they made peace with him for eight hundred thousand dirhams .

ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to them: “You are in a land whose inhabitants’ food and clothing are mingled with carrion. Eat only what has been duly slaughtered, and wear only pure garments.” He meant furs.

817Al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd al-Narsī told me, who said: ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. Ziyād told us, who said: ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal told us, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said: I was with ʿUtba b. Farqad when he conquered Ādharbayjān. He prepared two baskets of khabīṣ, covered them with hides and felt, and then sent them to ʿUmar with Suḥaym, ʿUtba’s client.

When he came to him, he said: “What have you brought? Gold or silver?” He ordered it to be uncovered, tasted the khabīṣ, and said: “This is indeed delicious—athar! Have the Emigrants all eaten any of it?” He said: “No. It is something he has set aside especially for you.”

He wrote to him: “From God’s servant ʿUmar, Commander of the Faithful, to ʿUtba b. Farqad. To proceed: it is not from your toil

nor your mother’s toil, nor your father’s toil. We eat only that of which the Muslims can eat their fill in their dwellings.”

818Al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAmr and Aḥmad b. Muṣliḥ al-Azdī told me, from elders of the people of Ādharbayjān, who said: Al-Walīd b. ʿUqba came to Ādharbayjān with al-Ashʿath b. Qays. When al-Walīd departed, he appointed him governor of Ādharbayjān, but it rebelled. He wrote to him requesting reinforcements, and he reinforced him with a great army of the people of Kūfa.

Al-Ashʿath b. Qays pursued them enclosure by enclosure—al-ḥān means an enclosure in the language of the people of Ādharbayjān—and conquered them on terms like those of Ḥudhayfa and ʿUtba b. Farqad. He settled in them Arabs who received stipends and were enrolled in the register, and instructed them to call the people to Islam.

Then Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī assumed the governorship and campaigned against the people of Ādharbayjān, inflicting a defeat upon the people of Mūqān and Jīlān. A multitude of Armenians and people of Ādharbayjān assembled against him in the region of Aram and Balwānkarḥ (?). He sent Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī against them, and he defeated them, captured their leader, and crucified him upon the fortress of Bājarwān.

It is said that al-Shammākh b. Ḍirār al-Thaʿlab was with Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī on this campaign. Bukayr b. Shaddād b. ʿĀmir, the rider of Aṭlāl, was with them on this campaign. It is of him that al-Shammākh says:

“You rendered unnecessary horsemen at Mūqān who abandoned Bukayr of the Banū al-Shaddākh, the rider of Aṭlāl.”

He was of the Banū Kināna, and he was the one who, during ʿUmar’s caliphate, heard a Jew reciting:

“Many a disheveled man whom Islam made unwary of me— I was alone with his wife on the night of the full moon,”

and killed him.

Then ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib appointed al-Ashʿath governor of Ādharbayjān. When he arrived there, he found that most of its inhabitants had embraced Islam and recited the Qurʾān. He settled at Adrabīl a group of Arabs who received stipends and were enrolled in the register, made it a garrison town, and built its mosque, although it was enlarged afterward.

Al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAmr said: Wāqid informed me that when the Arabs settled in Ādharbayjān, their clans gravitated toward them from the two garrison towns and Syria. Each group took possession of whatever it could. Some bought lands from the non-Arabs, and villages were compelled to resort to them for protection, so that their inhabitants became cultivators for them.

Al-Ḥusayn said: Warthān was a bridge like the two bridges of Waḥsh and Arshaq, which were constructed recently, in the days of Bābak. Marwān b. Muḥammad b. Marwān b. al-Ḥakam built it up, brought its land into cultivation, and fortified it, and it became an estate of his.

Then it was confiscated along with the other estates of the Banū Umayya that were confiscated, and passed to Umm Jaʿfar Zubayda bt. Jaʿfar b. al-Manṣūr, Commander of the Faithful. Her agents demolished its wall. It was then repaired and renewed recently. Al-Warthānī was one of her clients.

He said: Barzand was a village. Al-Afshīn Ḥaydar b. Kāwūs, the governor of Ādharbayjān, Armīniya, and al-Jabal for the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh, encamped there during his war against the unbeliever Bābak al-Khurramī and fortified it.

819They said: Al-Marāgha used to be called Iqrāhrūdh. Marwān b. Muḥammad, while governor of Armīniya and Ādharbayjān, encamped near it on his return from the campaign against Mūqān and Jīlān. There was much dung there, and his beasts and those of his companions used to roll in it. They began saying: “Come to the village of the rolling-place.” Then people dropped “village” and said “al-Marāgha.”

Its inhabitants had placed it under Marwān’s protection, and he built it up. His agents attracted people, who became numerous there in order to gain strength, and developed it.

Then it was confiscated along with the other estates of the Banū Umayya that were confiscated. It passed to one of the daughters of al-Rashīd, Commander of the Faithful.

When al-Wajnāʾ al-Azdī and Ṣadaqa b. ʿAlī, the client of al-Azd, ran rampant and wrought devastation, and Khuzayma b. Khāzim b. Khuzayma was appointed governor of Armīniya and Ādharbayjān during al-Rashīd’s caliphate, he built its wall, fortified it, made it a garrison town, and stationed a large force there.

Then, when Bābak al-Khurramī rose at al-Badhdh, people sought refuge there, settled in it, and fortified themselves within it. During al-Maʾmūn’s days, several of his governors repaired its wall, among them Aḥmad b. al-Junayd b. Farzandī and ʿAlī b. Hishām. Then people settled in its suburb and fortified themselves.

As for Marand, it was a small village. Ḥalbas, the father of al-Baʿīth, settled there. Then al-Baʿīth fortified it, and afterward his son Muḥammad b. al-Baʿīth. Muḥammad built palaces there.

He had rebelled during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Mutawakkil ʿalā Allāh. Bughā al-Ṣaghīr, the client of the Commander of the Faithful, fought him until he captured him and conveyed him to Surra Man Raʾā, and demolished the wall of Marand and that palace.

Al-Baʿīth was a descendant of ʿAtīb b. ʿAmr b. Wahb b. Aqṣā b. Duʿmī b. Jadīla b. Asad b. Rabīʿa. It is also said that he was ʿAtīb b. ʿAwf b. Sinān. The ʿAtabīs say this, and God knows best .

As for Urmiya, it is an ancient city. The Magians claim that Zardusht, their master, came from it. Ṣadaqa b. ʿAlī b. Ṣadaqa b. Dīnār, the client of al-Azd, fought its inhabitants until he entered it and gained control of it. He and his brothers built palaces there.

As for Tabrīz, al-Rawwād al-Azdī settled there, then al-Wajnāʾ b. al-Rawwād. He and his brothers erected buildings there, and he fortified it with a wall. People settled there with him.

As for al-Mayānij and Khalbāthā, they are the settlements of the Hamdānīs. ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaʿfar al-Hamdānī developed his quarter in al-Mayānij into a town, and the sultan established a pulpit there.

As for the district of Barza, it belongs to al-Awd. Its chief town belongs to a man of theirs who gathered people there and built a fortress in it. In the year 239, a pulpit was established there against the wishes of the Awdī.

As for Narīr, it was a village with an old, dilapidated palace. Murr b. ʿAmr al-Mawṣilī al-Ṭāʾī settled there, built in it, and settled his children there.

Then they built palaces there and developed it into a town. They built the market of Jābarwān and enlarged it. The ruling authority assigned it separately to them, and they came to administer it independently of Ādharbayjān.

As for Sarāt, there is a group of Kinda there. One of them told me that he was descended from someone who had been with al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī.

Chapter 74

The conquest of Mosul

820They said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī governor of Mosul in the year twenty.

The people of Nineveh fought him, and he took its fortress, which is the eastern one, by force. He crossed the Tigris, and the people of the other fortress made terms with him for payment of the jizya and permission for anyone who wished to depart to do so.

He found monasteries at Mosul, and their inhabitants made terms with him for payment of the jizya.

Then he conquered al-Marj and its villages, the territory of Bāhadhrā, Bāʿadhrā, Ḥabtūn, al-Ḥannāna, al-Muʿalla, Dāmīr, and all the Kurdish strongholds.

He came to Bānʿāthā in Ḥazza and conquered it.

He came to Tall al-Shahārija and al-Salq, which is known as Banū al-Ḥurrayn. Ṣāliḥ b. ʿUbāda al-Hamdānī, commander of the garrison of Mosul, conquered all of that, and the Muslims gained control of it.

821Muʿāfā b. Ṭāwus informed me, from elders among the people of Mosul, who said: Urmiya was among the conquests of Mosul; ʿUtba b. Farqad conquered it.

For a time its kharāj went to Mosul.

The same was true of al-Ḥawr, Khuyy, and Salmās.

Muʿāfā said: I also heard that ʿUtba conquered it when he was appointed governor of Ādharbayjān.

God knows best.

822Al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The first to lay out Mosul, settle the Arabs there, and establish it as a garrison town was Harthama b. ʿArfaja al-Bāriqī.

823Abū Mūsā al-Harawī told me, from Abū al-Faḍl al-Anṣārī, from Abū al-Muḥārib al-Ḍabbī, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb dismissed ʿUtba from Mosul and appointed Harthama b. ʿArfaja al-Bāriqī its governor.

There were a fortress, Christian churches, a few dwellings belonging to them near those churches, and the Jewish quarter there.

Harthama established it as a garrison town, settled the Arabs in their dwellings, and laid out plots for them. Then he built the congregational mosque.

824Al-Muʿāfā b. Ṭāwūs told me, saying: The one who paved Mosul with stones was Ibn Talīd, chief of police under Muḥammad b. Marwān b. al-Ḥakam.

Muḥammad was governor of Mosul, al-Jazīra, Armenia, and Ādharbayjān.

825Al-Wāqidī said: ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān appointed his son Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān, the proprietor of Nahr Saʿīd, governor of Mosul.

He appointed his brother Muḥammad governor of al-Jazīra and Armenia.

Saʿīd built the wall of Mosul, which al-Rashīd demolished when he passed through it.

They had previously rebelled. Saʿīd paved it with stones.

826I was told, on the authority of one of the people of Bābaghīsh, that the Muslims had sought an opportunity to catch unawares the inhabitants of an area belonging to it, toward Dāmīr, called Zarān.

They came upon them on one of their festival days, when they had no weapons, blocked them from reaching their citadel and captured it.

827They said: When Harthama laid out Mosul and settled the Arabs there, he came to al-Ḥadītha. It was an old village containing two churches and Christian houses. He established it as a garrison town and settled there a group of

Arabs. It was called al-Ḥadītha because it came after Mosul.

He built a fortress near it.

It is said that Harthama first settled at al-Ḥadītha and established it as a garrison town and laid it out before Mosul, and that it was called al-Ḥadītha only when some of the people of al-Anbār moved there, after Ibn al-Rufayl was appointed over them in the days of al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf and oppressed it.

Among them were people from Ḥadīthat al-Anbār. They built a mosque there and named the town al-Ḥadītha.

828They said: ʿUtba b. Farqad conquered al-Ṭayrahān and Tikrīt. He granted the people of the fortress of Tikrīt security for their lives and property. He proceeded through the district of Bājarmā, then went to Shahrazūr.

829An elder from the people of Tikrīt told me that they had possessed a document of safe-conduct

and stipulations in their favor.

Al-Jurashī tore it up when he laid waste the villages of Mosul: Narsābādh, Hāʿila, and those associated with them.

Al-Haytham b. ʿAdī maintained that when ʿAbbāḍ b. Ghanm conquered Balad, he came to Mosul and conquered one of the two fortresses.

God Most High knows best.

Chapter 75

Shahrazūr, al-Ṣāmaghān and Darābādh

830Isḥāq b. Sulaymān al-Shahrazūrī told me, saying: My father told us, from Muḥammad b. Marwān, from al-Kalbī, from one of the family of ʿAzra al-Bajalī, that ʿAzra b. Qays attempted to conquer Shahrazūr while he was governor of Ḥulwān during the caliphate of ʿUmar, but was unable to take it.

ʿUtba b. Farqad then campaigned against it and conquered it after fighting, on terms like those of the settlement of Ḥulwān.

Scorpions would sting a man among the Muslims, and he would die.

831Isḥāq told me, from his father, from their elders, who said: The people of al-Ṣāmaghān and Darābādh made terms with ʿUtba for payment of the jizya and kharāj, on condition that they would not be killed or taken captive, and would not be barred from any road they traveled.

832Abū Rajāʾ al-Ḥulwānī told me, from his father, from the elders of Shahrazūr, who said: Shahrazūr, al-Ṣāmaghān, and Darābādh were among the conquests of ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī.

He conquered them and fought the Kurds, killing a great many of them. He wrote to ʿUmar: “Through my conquests I have reached Ādharbayjān.”

He appointed him its governor.

He appointed Harthama b. ʿArfaja governor of Mosul.

833They said: Shahrazūr and its dependencies remained attached to Mosul until they were separated at the end of al-Rashīd’s caliphate.

A separate man was appointed governor of Shahrazūr, al-Ṣāmaghān, and Darābādh.

The stipend of the administrator of each district of Mosul was two hundred dirhams, so six hundred dirhams were deducted for these districts.

Chapter 76

Jurjān, Ṭabaristān and their regions

Jurjān, Ṭabaristān, and Their Surrounding Regions

834They said: ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵀ appointed Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī b. Umayya governor of Kūfa in the year twenty-nine.

The marzbān of Ṭūs wrote to him and to ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz b. Rabīʿa b. Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams, who was governor of Baṣra, inviting them both to Khurāsān, on condition that whichever of them prevailed and was victorious would make him ruler over it.

Ibn ʿĀmir set out for it, and Saʿīd set out.

Ibn ʿĀmir reached it before him, so Saʿīd campaigned against Ṭabaristān. With him on his campaign, it is said, were al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, the sons of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵈.

It has also been said that Saʿīd campaigned against Ṭabaristān without any letter having reached him from anyone, and that he headed there from Kūfa. God knows best.

Saʿīd conquered Ṭamīsa and Nāmana, which is a village.

He made terms with the king of Jurjān for two hundred thousand dirhams; it is said, for three hundred thousand full-weight Baghlī dirhams. He would pay these to the Muslim campaigning forces.

Saʿīd conquered the plain of Ṭabaristān, al-Rūyān, and Dunbāwand. The people of the mountains gave him money.

The Muslims would campaign against Ṭabaristān and its surrounding regions. Sometimes they paid the tribute voluntarily, and sometimes they paid it after fighting.

Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān appointed Maṣqala b. Hubayra b. Shibl—one of the Banū Thaʿlaba b. Shaybān b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUkāba—governor of Ṭabaristān, all of whose inhabitants were at war.

He assigned him ten thousand men, or, it is said, twenty thousand. The enemy plotted against him and made a show of being in awe of him, until he penetrated deep into the country with those accompanying him.

When they had passed beyond the narrow passes, the enemy seized these against them and rolled rocks down from the mountains onto their heads.

That entire army perished, and Maṣqala perished. People made him proverbial,

saying: “Until Maṣqala returns from Ṭabaristān.”

Then ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān appointed Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath b. Qays al-Kindī governor of Ṭabaristān.

He made peace with them and concluded an agreement with them. Then they gave him time until he had entered, whereupon they seized the narrow passes against him, killed his son Abū Bakr, and battered him. Then he escaped.

The Muslims would campaign on that frontier while taking care not to penetrate deep into enemy territory.

835ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf and others, who said: When Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān assumed power, he appointed Yazīd b. al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra governor of Iraq.

He set out for Khurāsān because of Qutayba b. Muslim’s insubordination and opposition to Sulaymān, and Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd al-Tamīmī’s killing of him.

Ṣūl the Turk intercepted him on his way as he was heading for Khurāsān.

He wrote to Sulaymān requesting permission to campaign against him, and he granted him permission.

He campaigned against Jīlān and Sāriya, then came to Dihistān, where Ṣūl was, and besieged it with a large army of men from the two garrison towns, Syria, and Khurāsān.

The people of Dihistān would come out and fight them. Yazīd pressed them hard and cut off their supplies.

Then Ṣūl sent to Yazīd asking for peace, on condition that he grant him security for his life, property, and household, and that he hand over to him the city, its inhabitants, and everything in it.

Yazīd accepted this, made peace with him on those terms, and fulfilled his undertaking to him.

Yazīd killed fourteen thousand of the Turks and appointed a deputy over it.

Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said that Ṣūl was killed, but the first account is better established.

836Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: Yazīd came to Jurjān.

Its inhabitants met him with the tribute on which Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣī had made terms with them, and he accepted it.

Then the people of Jurjān broke the agreement and acted treacherously.

He sent Jahm b. Zaḥr al-Juʿfī against them, and he conquered it.

He said: It is said that he went to Marw and spent his winter there, then campaigned against Jurjān

with one hundred thousand and twenty thousand men from Syria, al-Jazīra, the two garrison towns, and Khurāsān.

837ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī told me, saying: Yazīd b. al-Muhallab spent a winter in Khurāsān, then campaigned against Jurjān. Around it was a wall of baked brick with which they had fortified themselves against the Turks, one end of it reaching the sea. Then the Turks gained control of it, and their king was called Ṣūl.

Yazīd said: “May God make Qutayba abominable! He left these people in the heart of the Arabs’ domain and intended to campaign against China”—or he said: “and campaigned against China.”

Yazīd left Mukhlad b. Yazīd in charge of Khurāsān.

He said: When he reached Jurjān, he found that Ṣūl had taken up a position in al-Buḥayra.

He besieged him for six months and fought him repeatedly.

He requested peace, on condition that he grant him security for his life, property, and three hundred members of his household, and that he hand over to him al-Buḥayra and everything in it.

He made peace with him, then proceeded to Ṭabaristān.

He appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Maʿmar al-Yashkurī over Dihistān and al-Bayāsān, while he was with four thousand men. He sent his son Khālid b. Yazīd and his brother Abū ʿUyayna b. al-Muhallab against the iṣbahbadh, and he defeated it until he drove the two of them back to Yazīd’s army.

The iṣbahbadh wrote to the marzbān—also called the marūzbān: “We have killed Yazīd’s men, so kill the Arabs who are with you.”

He killed ʿAbd Allāh b. Maʿmar al-Yashkurī and those with him while they were unsuspecting in their quarters.

The news reached Yazīd, and he sent Ḥayyān, the mawlā of Maṣqala, who was one of the captives from al-Daylam. He said to the iṣbahbadh: “I am a man of your people and belong with you, even though religion divides us. I cannot be sure that there will not come against you, from the Commander of the Faithful and the armies of Khurāsān, forces that you have no power to withstand and against which you cannot hold out.

“I have sounded Yazīd out for you and found him quick to make peace, so make peace with him.”

He continued to deceive him until he made peace with Yazīd for seven hundred thousand dirhams and four hundred loads of saffron.

The iṣbahbadh said to him: “The ten are to weigh six.”

He said: “No, rather the weight of seven.”

He refused.

Ḥayyān said: “I undertake to bear

The surplus between the two weights.

He undertook it.

Ḥayyān was among the noblest and most eminent of the clients,

and was kunya-named Abū Maʿmar.

838Al-Madāʾinī said: Yazīd learned that the people of Jurjān had broken their agreement and treacherously acted, so he marched toward it a second time.

When the marzbān learned of his advance, he went to Wajeh and fortified himself there; around it were thickets and dense brush.

He laid siege to it for seven months, unable to gain access.

They fought him repeatedly, and he set up a mangonel against it.

Then a man showed him a path to their fortress and said, “There is no way but to use a ladder of hides.”

Yazīd appointed Jahm b. Zaḥr al-Juʿfī and said to him, “If you cannot prevail in staying alive, do not fail to prevail in dying.”

Yazīd ordered that fire be set to the firewood.

This alarmed them. Some of them came out, then went back in.

Jahm reached the fortress. Some of the men stationed at its gate fought him, but he drove them away.

The enemy did not realize until late afternoon that the takbīr was being proclaimed behind them.

The fortress was opened, and they surrendered on Yazīd’s terms.

Jahm led them to the Wādī of Jarmujān and kept killing them until blood flowed and ran through the valley.

He built the city of Jurjān.

Yazīd set out for Khurāsān, and gifts reached him.

Then he appointed his son Mukhlad over Khurāsān and returned to Sulaymān.

Sulaymān wrote to him that he had with him twenty-five million dirhams.

The letter fell into the hands of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who seized Yazīd on its account and imprisoned him.

839ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf or ʿAwānah b. al-Ḥakam, who said: Yazīd marched to Ṭabaristān.

The Iṣbahbadh sought the Daylam’s aid, and they came to his support.

Yazīd fought him, then made peace with him in return for a cash payment of four million dirhams, seven hundred thousand dirhams in mithqāls each year, four hundred loads of saffron, and the provision of four hundred men, each carrying a shield and a ṭaylasān, with a silver bowl and a silk cushion.

Some transmitters say: a burnous.

Yazīd conquered al-Rūyān and Dunbāwand in return for money, garments, and vessels.

Then he proceeded to Jurjān. Its people had treacherously acted and killed his deputy, and he sent Jahm b. Zaḥr b. Qays al-Juʿfī ahead of him.

He entered the city while its people were unsuspecting and heedless. Ibn al-Muhallab came to him and killed many of its people and took their children captive. He crucified those he had killed on the right and left sides of the road.

He appointed Jahm over it, and imposed the jizya and land tax on its people; his rule weighed heavily upon them.

840They said: The people of Ṭabaristān continued sometimes to pay the terms of the treaty and at other times to refuse payment, alternating between fighting and making peace.

When it was the time of Marwān b. Muḥammad b. Marwān b. al-Ḥakam, they acted treacherously and broke their agreement. Then, when Abū al-ʿAbbās, Commander of the Faithful, became caliph, he sent his governor against them, and they made peace with him.

Then they broke their agreement, acted treacherously, and killed Muslims during the caliphate of al-Manṣūr, Commander of the Faithful.

He sent Khāzim b. Khuzayma al-Tamīmī and Rūḥ b. Ḥātim al-Muhallabī against them, along with Marzūq Abū al-Khaṣīb, his client, after whom Qaṣr Abī al-Khaṣīb in Kūfa was named.

When the matter had grown prolonged and difficult for them, Marzūq asked them to strike him and shave his head and beard. They did so.

He made his way to the Iṣbahbadh and said to him, “These two men suspected me of treachery and did to me what you see. I have fled to you. If you accept my defection and grant me the standing I deserve from you, I will show you the Arabs’ vulnerable points and will be a hand with you against them.”

He clothed him, gave him gifts, and displayed confidence in him and consulted him.

He made it appear that he was his sincere adviser and concerned for him.

When he had learned his affairs and vulnerabilities , he wrote to Khāzim and Rūḥ what they needed to know about them, and contrived to open the gate.

The Muslims entered the city and conquered it, then marched through the lands and subdued them.

ʿUmar b. al-ʿAlāʾ was a butcher from al-Rayy. He assembled a force and fought Sanfādh when he emerged there.

He made a successful recovery and inflicted losses. Juhūr b. Marrār al-ʿIjlī sent him as an envoy to al-Manṣūr, who appointed him commander,

showed him favor, and granted him a rank.

Then he was appointed over Ṭabaristān, where he was martyred during the caliphate of al-Mahdī, Commander of the Faithful.

Muḥammad b. Mūsā b. Ḥafṣ b. ʿUmar b. al-ʿAlāʾ and Māzdyār b. Qārin conquered the Shīrwīn Mountains of Ṭabaristān. They are the most impregnable and difficult of its mountains, and the most densely wooded and overgrown, during the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn ﵀.

Then al-Maʾmūn appointed Māzdyār over the districts of Ṭabaristān, al-Rūyān, and Dunbāwand, gave him the name Muḥammad, and granted him the rank of Iṣbahbadh.

He continued as governor until al-Maʾmūn died.

Then Abū Isḥāq al-Muʿtaṣim bi-Allāh, Commander of the Faithful, became caliph and confirmed him in his office.

Then, six years and some months into his caliphate, he renounced the faith and acted treacherously.

He wrote to ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṭāhir b. al-Ḥusayn b. Muṣʿab, his governor over Khurāsān, al-Rayy, Qūmis, and Jurjān, ordering him to fight Māzdyār.

ʿAbd Allāh sent his uncle al-Ḥasan b. al-Ḥusayn against him with men from Khurāsān.

Al-Muʿtaṣim bi-Allāh sent Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm b. Muṣʿab with troops he had assigned to him from the caliphal army.

When the armies had gathered in Māzdyār’s lands, a brother of his named Fūhyār b. Qārin wrote to al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad, informing them that he was on their side against him.

He had harbored resentment over various acts of disrespect he had suffered.

The people of his governorship had grown weary of his conduct because of his arrogance and oppression.

Al-Ḥasan wrote, advising him to lie in ambush at a place he named. He said to Māzdyār, “Al-Ḥasan has arrived, and is at such-and-such a place”—and he named a different place—“and he is inviting you to a safe-conduct and wants to speak with you face to face, so I have heard.”

Māzdyār set out to meet al-Ḥasan.

When he came near the place where al-Ḥasan was lying in ambush , Fūhyār notified al-Ḥasan of his arrival.

He came out against him with his companions, who were dispersed in the thickets, and they began converging upon him.

Māzdyār tried to flee, but Fūhyār seized him by his belt.

They surrounded him

Al-Ḥasan’s companions took him captive without any pact or agreement.

He was brought to Surr man raʾā in the year

two hundred and twenty-five. He was flogged severely with whips before al-Muʿtaṣim bi-Allāh, and when the whips were lifted from him, he died.

He was crucified at Surr man raʾā alongside Bābak al-Khurramī, on the rise by the police headquarters.

Some of Fūhyār’s brother’s close associates rose against Fūhyār, and he was killed in Ṭabaristān.

Ṭabaristān, its plain and its mountains, was conquered, and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṭāhir and, after him, Ṭāhir b. ʿAbd Allāh governed it.

Part Five

Southern Iraq and the armies of Baṣra

Chapter 77

The districts of the Tigris

The Conquests of the Districts of the Tigris

841They said: Suwayd b. Quṭba al-Dhuhlī—and some say Quṭba b. Qatāda—used to raid the Persians in the vicinity of al-Khurayba in Baṣra, just as al-Muthannā b. Ḥāritha al-Shaybānī used to raid in the vicinity of al-Ḥīra.

When Khālid b. al-Walīd arrived in Baṣra intending to go to Kūfa in the year 12, Suwayd helped him fight the people of al-Ubulla, and Khālid left Suwayd behind.

It is said that Khālid did not leave Baṣra until he had conquered al-Khurayba, which was a Persian garrison post; he killed and took captives there.

He left there a man from Banū Saʿd b. Bakr b. Hawāzin, called Shurayḥ b. ʿĀmir.

It is said that he came to Nahr al-Marʾa and conquered the palace by treaty. Nawshajān b. Jassansamā made the treaty on its behalf, and the woman who owned the palace was Kāmin Dār, daughter of Narsī; she was Nawshajān’s cousin.

The place was called “the woman’s” because Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī had stayed there. She provisioned him with khabīṣ, and he kept saying, “Give us some of the woman’s flour.”

Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Wāqidī used to deny that Khālid b. al-Walīd had come to Baṣra after he had finished dealing with the people of al-Yamāma and al-Baḥrayn.

He said: He arrived in Medina, then set out from there for Iraq by way of Fayd and al-Thaʿlabiyya. God knows best.

842They said: When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb heard what Suwayd b. Quṭba was doing in Baṣra,

he decided to appoint a man of his own over it, so he appointed ʿUtba b. Ghazwān b. Jābir b. Wahb b. Nasīb—one of Banū Māzin b. Manṣūr b. ʿIkrima b. Khaṣafa.

He was an ally of Banū Nawfal b. ʿAbd Manāf and among the earliest Emigrants—and he said to him: “Indeed …”

Al-Ḥīra had been conquered, a great Persian leader—that is, Mihrān—had been killed, and the Muslims’ horses had trodden the land of Babylon.

So turn toward the Baṣra region and occupy the people there, from al-Ahwāz, Fārs, and Maysān, keeping them from sending aid to their brothers against your brothers.”

ʿUtba went there, and Suwayd b. Quṭba and those with him from Bakr b. Wāʾil and Banū Tamīm joined him.

There were seven settlements at Baṣra: two at al-Khurayba, two at al-Zābūqa, and three at the site of today’s Dār al-Azd.

ʿUtba distributed his companions among them; he settled at al-Khurayba, which was a Persian garrison post. Khālid b. al-Walīd had conquered it, and it had been emptied of them.

ʿUtba wrote to ʿUmar, informing him where he and his companions had settled.

ʿUmar wrote back, ordering him to settle them in a place near water and pasture.

He proceeded to the site of Baṣra.

Abū Mikhnaf said: It had gravel and black stones, so it was said that it was called Baṣra.

It is also said that they named it Baṣra because its ground was soft.

843They said: They pitched tents, domed tents, and pavilions there.

They had no buildings.

ʿUmar reinforced ʿUtba with Harthama b. ʿArfaja al-Bāriqī, who had been in al-Baḥrayn and later went to al-Mawṣil.

844They said: ʿUtba b. Ghazwān raided al-Ubulla and conquered it by force.

He wrote to ʿUmar, informing him of this and telling him that al-Ubulla was the port of al-Baḥrayn, ʿUmān, India, and China.

He sent the letter with Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith al-Thaqafī.

845al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me: Marḥūm al-ʿAṭṭār told us, from his father,

from Shuways al-ʿAdawī, who said: We went out with the commander of al-Ubulla and gained victory there.

Then we crossed the Euphrates. The people of the Euphrates came out against us with their spades, but we defeated them and conquered al-Furāt.

846ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. Ghiyāth told me: Ḥammād b. Salama told us, from his father, from Ḥumayrī b. Kurātha al-Rabʿī, who said: When they entered al-Ubulla, they found white-flour bread.

They said, “This is what they used to say makes one grow fat.”

When they ate it, they began looking at their forearms and saying, “By God, we see no fat.”

He said: I found a shirt with an opening at the chest, green in color, and I used to attend Friday prayer wearing it.

847Al-Madāʾinī told me, from Jahm b. Ḥassān, who said: ʿUtba conquered al-Ubulla, sent Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd to the Euphrates, appointed al-Mughīra to lead the prayer, and set off to see ʿUmar.

848Al-Madāʾinī told me, from his authorities, that the territory from al-Fahraj to the Euphrates was conquered by treaty, while the rest of al-Ubulla was conquered by force.

849ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-Muqriʾ told me: ʿAbda b. Sulaymān told me, from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq b. Yasār, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb sent ʿUtba b. Ghazwān, an ally of Banū Nawfal, with eight hundred men to Baṣra, and reinforced him with troops.

He settled the people in tents.

When they had grown numerous, a group of them built seven mud-brick settlements: two at al-Khurayba, one at al-Zābūqa, two in the Azd quarter, and two in Tamīm.

Then he went out to al-Ubulla, fought its people, and conquered it by force.

He came to the Euphrates, with Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd al-Sulamī at the head of his vanguard, and conquered it by force.

He came to al-Madhār, whose marzbān came out against him and fought him. God routed him, and most of his men drowned.

He was taken captive and ʿUtba struck off his head.

ʿUtba marched to Dasht Maysān, whose people had assembled

They were gathering against the Muslims and intended to march against them. He decided to attack them swiftly, so that this would weaken their resolve and give their hearts greater confidence. He met them; God routed them, and he killed their landowners.

ʿUtba immediately turned back to Abr Qubādh, and God granted him its conquest.

850They said: Then ʿUtba asked ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb for permission to visit him and perform the pilgrimage.

ʿUmar gave him permission.

He appointed Ibn Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd al-Sulamī as his deputy, although he was away from Baṣra, and ordered al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba to act in his place until his arrival.

He said, “Shall I put a man of the people of the desert over a man of the people of settled lands?” ʿUtba asked to be relieved of the governorship of Baṣra, but ʿUmar did not relieve him. He set out, and died on the road.

ʿUmar appointed al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba governor of Baṣra.

People had asked ʿUtba about Baṣra, and he told them of its fertility, so many people set out for it.

851ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from ʿAwāna, who said: Uzdah bt. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada was with ʿUtba b. Ghazwān.

When ʿUmar appointed ʿUtba b. Ghazwān, Nāfiʿ, Abū Bakra, and Ziyād came with him.

Then ʿUtba fought the people of the city of the Euphrates. His wife Uzdah urged the people to fight, saying, “If they defeat you, they will penetrate us with their circumcised [members].” God granted the Muslims victory over that city, and they acquired much booty.

No one among them could write and calculate except Ziyād.

He was put in charge of distributing that booty, and he was given two dirhams each day, though he was a youth with a lock of hair on his head.

Then ʿUtba set out to see ʿUmar.

He wrote to Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd informing him that he had appointed him in his place, though he was away, and ordered al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba to lead the people in prayer until Mujāshiʿ arrived.

Then the dihqān of Maysān renounced Islam and apostatized. al-Mughīra met him at al-Munʿaraj and killed him.

al-Mughīra wrote to ʿUmar informing him of the conquest.

ʿUmar summoned ʿUtba and said, “Did you not tell me that you had appointed Mujāshiʿ as your deputy?” He replied, “Yes.”

“But al-Mughīra has written to me saying such-and-such.”

He said, “Mujāshiʿ was away, so I ordered al-Mughīra to act as his deputy and lead the people in prayer until his return.”

ʿUmar said, “By my life, the settled people were more entitled to be appointed than the nomads.”

Then he wrote to al-Mughīra confirming his appointment over Baṣra and sent the letter to him.

al-Mughīra remained in office as long as God willed.

Then he became enamored of the woman.

852ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told me, from ʿAbda, from Muḥammad b. Isḥāq, who said: al-Mughīra campaigned against Maysān and conquered it by force after fierce fighting, gaining control of its land.

Then the people of Abruqbādh treacherously broke their pact, and al-Mughīra conquered it by force.

853Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin told me: Wahb b. Jarīr b. Ḥāzim told us, from his father, who said: ʿUtba b. Ghazwān conquered al-Ubulla, the Furat, Abruqbādh, and Dast Maysān, and al-Mughīra conquered Maysān.

The people of Abruqbādh broke their pact treacherously, and al-Mughīra conquered it.

854ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī said: People used to call Maysān, Dast Maysān, the Furat, and Abruqbādh “Maysān.”

855They said: Among the captives of Maysān were Abū al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and his brother Saʿīd b. Yasār.

Yasār’s name had been Fīrūz.

Abū al-Ḥasan came to belong to a woman of the Anṣār called al-Rabīʿ bt. al-Naḍr, the paternal aunt of Anas b. Mālik.

It is said that he belonged to a woman of Banū Salama called Jamīla, the wife of Anas b. Mālik.

856al-Ḥasan related: “My father and mother belonged to a man of Banū al-Najjār.

“He married a woman of Banū Salama and gave them to her as part of her bridal gift.

“That woman emancipated them, so our clientage belongs to her.”

al-Ḥasan was born in Medina in the last two years of ʿUmar’s caliphate. He left it a year after Ṣiffīn and died in Baṣra in the year 110, aged eighty-nine.

857They said: al-Mughīra began making frequent visits to a woman of Banū Hilāl called Umm Jamīl bt. Miḥjan b. al-Afḳam b. Shuʿaytha b. al-Hazm.

She had a husband from Thaqīf called al-Ḥajjāj b. ʿUtayk.

This came to the attention of Abū Bakra b. Masrūḥ, the client of the Prophet ﷺ one of the Thaqīf born in Islam; Shibl b. Maʿbad b. ʿUbayd al-Bajalī; Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada al-Thaqafī; and Ziyād b. ʿUbayd. They kept watch on him.

When he entered her place, they rushed in upon him and found them naked, with him lying between her legs.

They went out and came to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, testifying before him to what they had seen.

ʿUmar said to Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, “I intend to send you to a town where Satan has nested.”

He replied, “Then provide me with a contingent of Anṣār.”

He sent al-Barāʾ b. Mālik, ʿImrān b. al-Ḥuṣayn Abū Najīd al-Khuzāʿī, and ʿAwf b. Wahb al-Khuzāʿī with him, appointed him over Baṣra, and ordered him to bring al-Mughīra in.

He brought him in three days after his own arrival.

When he reached ʿUmar, ʿUmar brought him together with the witnesses.

Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith said, “I saw him on top of the woman, moving over her, and I saw what he had with him enter and come out like a kohl-stick in its container.”

Then Shibl b. Maʿbad testified in accordance with his testimony, then Abū Bakra. Then Ziyād came as the fourth.

When ʿUmar saw him, he said, “I see before me the face of a man from whose hand I hope no Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ will be stoned, nor will he be disgraced by his testimony.”

al-Mughīra had come from Egypt, embraced Islam, and witnessed al-Ḥudaybiya with the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Ziyād said, “I saw an ugly sight and heard a loud breath. I do not know whether he entered her or not.” It is said that he testified to nothing.

ʿUmar ordered the three to be flogged.

Shibl said, “Will you flog witnesses to the truth and set aside the prescribed punishment?” When Abū Bakra was flogged, he said, “I testify that al-Mughīra is an adulterer.”

ʿUmar said, “Flog him.”

He said, “Only if you make it testimony. Then stone your companion.”

Abū Bakra swore that he would never speak to Ziyād again; they were maternal half-brothers, their mother being Sumayya.

Then ʿUmar sent them back to their province.

Some people have related that Abū Mūsā was in Baṣra, and that ʿUmar wrote to him appointing him over it and ordering him to bring al-Mughīra in.

The first account is more firmly established.

It is related that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ had ordered Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ ﵁ to send ʿUtba b. Ghazwān to Baṣra, and he did so.

ʿUtba was too proud to correspond with him, and for that reason asked to be excused. ʿUmar ﵁ reinstated him as governor, but he died on the way.

Abū Mūsā’s governorship of Baṣra was in the year 16; it is also said, in the year 17. He surveyed the districts of the Tigris and found their inhabitants submitting in obedience. He ordered the land measured and the land tax imposed according to its capacity.

The established account is that Abū Mūsā was appointed over Baṣra in the year 16 .
