858Shaybān b. Farrūkh al-Ubullī told me: Abū Hilāl al-Rāsibī told us: Yaḥyā b. Abī Kathīr told us that a scribe of Abū Mūsā wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, “From Abū Mūsā.”

ʿUmar wrote back to him, “When this letter of mine reaches you, strike your scribe with a whip and dismiss him from his post.”

Chapter 78

The founding of Baṣra

859ʿAlī b. al-Mughīra al-Athram told me, from Abū ʿUbayda, who said: When ʿUtba b. Ghazwān settled at al-Khurayba, he wrote to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb informing him that he had settled there and that the Muslims needed a place where they could spend the winter when winter came and rest when they returned from their campaigns.

He wrote back to him: “Gather your companions in one place.

“Let it be near water and pasture.

“Write to me describing it.”

He wrote back: “I have found land with abundant reeds at the edge of the desert toward the cultivated land, and beyond it are pools of water with reeds.”

When ʿUmar read the letter, he said, “This is fertile land, near watering places, pasture, and firewood.”

He wrote to him ordering him to settle the people there.

He settled them there.

They built dwellings of reeds.

ʿUtba built a mosque of reeds, in the year 14.

It is said that he himself directed the mosque’s layout.

It is said that Muḥajjir b. al-Adraʿ al-Bāhilī of Sulaym laid it out.

It is said that Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada laid it out when he marked out his house.

Or, it is said, al-Aswad b. Sarīʿ al-Tamīmī laid it out; he was the first to judge cases there.

Mujāshiʿ and Mujālid, the sons of Masʿūd, said to him, “May God have mercy on you! You have made yourself conspicuous.”

He said, “I will not do it again.”

ʿUtba built the governor’s residence below the mosque, in the open space now called the open space of Banū Hāshim.

It was called al-Dahnāʾ.

The prison and the register were there.

When they went on campaign, they would ...

they removed those reeds, bundled them, and stored them until they returned from the campaign.

When they returned, they rebuilt it.

The situation continued in this way.

Then people laid out plots and built houses.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī built the mosque and the governor’s residence of mud brick and clay, and roofed them with grass; he also enlarged the mosque.

When the imam came to pray, he would pass the people toward the qibla on a raised platform.

One day ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir left the governor’s residence, heading toward the qibla, wearing a dark silk brocade robe.

The Bedouins began saying, “The governor is wearing a bear’s hide!”

860Abū Muḥammad al-Thawrī told me, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: When ʿUtba b. Ghazwān settled at al-Khurayba, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakra was born there.

He was the first child born in Baṣra.

His father slaughtered a camel, enough to feed the people of Baṣra.

Then, when Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān appointed Ziyād over Baṣra, Ziyād enlarged the mosque considerably, built it with baked brick and plaster, roofed it with teak, and said, “The imam ought not to have to pass through the people.”

He moved the governor’s residence from al-Dahnāʾ to the qibla side of the mosque.

The imam would leave the residence through the door in the qibla wall.

When Ziyād had built the mosque and governor’s residence, he would walk around them and inspect the construction. Then he would say to the leading men of Baṣra with him, “Do you see any flaw?” They would reply, “We know of no construction more soundly built.”

He said, “Indeed, there is: these pillars, each of which has four arches. If only they were thicker than the other pillars.”

It is related from Yūnus b. Ḥabīb the grammarian, who said: Not once did those pillars suffer a crack or defect.

861Ḥāritha b. Badr al-Ghudānī said—and it is also said that al-Buʿayth al-Mujāshiʿī said this:

Ziyād built for the remembrance of God a structure of stone, not made of clay. Were human hands not to take turns raising it, we would have called it the work of devils.

862al-Walīd b. Hishām b. Qaḥdham said: When Ziyād built the mosque, he made five columns for its front portico.

He built its minaret of stone.

He was the first to make a screened enclosure.

He moved the governor’s residence to the qibla side of the mosque.

It was built of mud brick and clay until Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sijistānī, the client of Banū Tamīm, built it of baked brick and plaster while he was in charge of Iraq’s land tax under Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād enlarged it and the mosque of Kūfa.

He said, “I prayed to God to grant me jihad, and He did so. I prayed to Him to grant me the building of the two congregational mosques in the two garrison cities, and He did so. I prayed to Him to make me Ziyād’s successor, and He did so.”

863Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: When Ziyād built the mosque, its columns were brought from the mountains of al-Ahwāz.

The people who undertook their transport and cutting were al-Ḥajjāj b. ʿUtayk al-Thaqafī and his son.

He made a fortune.

It was said, “How fine is the governorship, even over stones!”

It became a proverb.

He said: Some people say that Ziyād saw people dusting off their hands when they became dusty during prayer. He said, “I cannot be sure that, over the passage of time, people will not come to think that dusting off the hands during prayer is a sunna.”

He ordered gravel to be gathered and spread in the mosque.

Those assigned to this task were harsh with the people, made unreasonable demands of them, and showed them gravel they had selected.

They said, “Bring us the same in its ...”

sizes and colors, and they took bribes for doing so.

The speaker said, “How fine is the governorship, even over stones!”

Abū ʿUbayda said: The mosque’s northern side was set at an angle because there was the house of Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada there.

His sons refused to sell it.

When Muʿāwiya appointed ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād over Baṣra, ʿUbayd Allāh said to his companions, “When ʿAbd Allāh b. Nāfiʿ departs for the farthest part of his estate, inform me.”

He departed for his white palace on the marsh.

ʿUbayd Allāh was informed of this.

He sent laborers, who demolished as much of the house as was needed to square off the mosque.

Ibn Nāfiʿ returned and complained to him about it.

He placated him by giving him five cubits for every cubit taken.

He opened a small door for him in the wall, leading to the mosque.

The small door remained in his wall until the Commander of the Faithful al-Mahdī enlarged the mosque.

The entire house was incorporated into it, and the governor’s residence was incorporated into it as well, during the caliphate of al-Rashīd ﵀.

Abū ʿUbayda said: When al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf arrived in Iraq, he was told that Ziyād had built the governor’s residence in Baṣra.

He wanted to erase Ziyād’s name from it and resolved to build it in plaster and baked brick.

He was told, “You will only make his name in it more firmly established.”

He demolished it and left it.

Most of the houses around it were built from its clay, mud bricks, and doors.

There was no governor’s residence in Baṣra until Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik became caliph.

He appointed Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān over the land tax of Iraq.

Ṣāliḥ told him the story of al-Ḥajjāj and what he had done to the governor’s residence.

He ordered him to rebuild it.

He rebuilt it in baked brick and plaster on its foundations and raised its height.

When ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ﵁ became caliph and appointed ʿAdī b. Arṭāt al-Fazārī over Baṣra, ʿAdī wanted to build upper rooms on it.

ʿUmar wrote to him: “May your mother lose you, son of ʿAdī’s mother! Is a house that sufficed for Ziyād and the family of Ziyād beyond your means?” ʿAdī refrained from completing those upper rooms and left them.

When Sulaymān b. ʿAlī b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās became governor of Baṣra for Abū al-ʿAbbās, the Commander of the Faithful, he built with clay on top of what ʿAdī had raised of the walls for the upper rooms; then he abandoned it and moved to al-Mirbad, where he took up residence.

When al-Rashīd became caliph, the residence was incorporated into the qibla side of the mosque. Thus, the governors of Baṣra have no governor’s residence.

864al-Walīd b. Hishām b. Qaḥdham said: No one enlarged the mosque after Ibn Ziyād until al-Mahdī.

He bought the house of Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada al-Thaqafī, the house of ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra, the house of Rabīʿa b. Kalada al-Thaqafī, the house of ʿAmr b. Wahb al-Thaqafī, the house of Umm Jamīl al-Hilālīya, whose affair with al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba was what it was, and other houses, and added them to the mosque during the time Muḥammad b. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī governed Baṣra.

Then Hārūn, the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd, ordered ʿĪsā b. Jaʿfar b. al-Manṣūr, during his governorship of Baṣra, to incorporate the governor’s residence into the mosque, and he did so.

  1. al-Walīd b. Hishām said: My father told me, from his father, who had been appointed by Yūsuf b. ʿUmar over the register of the Arab troops: I examined the total number of fighters in Baṣra in Ziyād’s time and found them to number eighty thousand.

I found their dependents to number one hundred and twenty thousand.

I found the Arab fighters of Kūfa to number sixty thousand, and their dependents eighty thousand.

865Muḥammad b. Saʿīd told me, from al-Wāqidī, in his chain of transmission, who said: ʿUtba b. Ghazwān was with Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ ...

ʿUmar wrote to him: “Dig your military camp at Kūfa.”

He sent ʿUtba b. Ghazwān to Baṣra.

He went out with eight hundred men and set up a tent of haircloth; the people set up alongside him.

ʿUmar sent him reinforcements.

When their numbers grew, a group of them built seven mud-brick quarters: two at al-Khurayba, one at al-Zābūqa, two among Banū Tamīm, and two among al-Azd.

Then ʿUtba went to the Euphrates at Baṣra and opened it up.

Then he returned to Baṣra.

Saʿd used to correspond with ʿUtba, and this grieved him.

He asked ʿUmar’s leave to go to him.

He caught up with him

and appointed al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba as his deputy.

When he arrived in Medina, he complained to ʿUmar of Saʿd’s overbearing conduct toward him.

ʿUmar said to him: “What harm is there in your acknowledging the authority of a man of Quraysh who has companionship [with the Prophet] and distinction?” But he refused to return.

ʿUmar insisted on sending him back.

On the road he fell from his mount and died in the year 16.

Muḥajjir b. al-Adraʿ had laid out the site of the mosque of Baṣra but had not built it.

People prayed in it while it remained unbuilt.

ʿUtba built it of reeds; then Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī rebuilt it, and built after that.

866Al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī b. al-Aswad al-ʿIjlī told me: Yaḥyā b. Ādam related to us: Abū Muʿāwiya related to us, from al-Shaybānī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī, who said: In Baṣra there was a man kunya’d Abū ʿAbd Allāh and called Nāfiʿ. He was the first to clear pastureland in Baṣra. He came to ʿUmar and said: “In Baṣra there is land that is not among the tax-paying lands and does no harm to any Muslim.”

Abū Mūsā wrote to ʿUmar about this on his behalf.

ʿUmar wrote back to him, instructing him to grant it to him.

867Saʿīd b. Sulaymān related to us: ʿAbbād b. al-ʿAwwām related to us,

from ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī, who said: I read ʿUmar’s letter to Abū Mūsā: “Abū ʿAbd Allāh asked me for land on the bank of the Tigris where he can pasture his horses.

If it is outside the land subject to the poll tax, and no poll-tax land’s water is diverted to it, then grant it to him.”

ʿAbbād said: I was told that he was Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalda, the physician of the Arabs.

He asked me for land on the bank of the Tigris where he could pasture his horses.

If it is outside the land subject to the poll tax, and no poll-tax land’s water is diverted to it, then grant it to him.

ʿAbbād said: I was told that he was Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalda, the physician of the Arabs.

868Al-Walīd b. Hishām b. Qaḥdham said: I found a document in our possession that read: “In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

From ʿUmar, servant of God and Commander of the Faithful, to al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba.

Peace be upon you.

I praise God to you, there being no god but Him.

To proceed: Abū ʿAbd Allāh mentioned that he planted crops in Baṣra during the governorship of Ibn Ghazwān and pastured the offspring of horses

at a time when no one among the people of Baṣra pastured them. What he did was good.

Assist him with his crops and his horses.

I have given him permission to plant crops.

Give him the land he planted, unless it is land subject to the poll tax among the lands of the non-Arabs, or water from land subject to the poll tax is diverted to it.

Do not deal with him except kindly.

Peace be upon you, and God’s mercy.

Muʿayqīb b. Abī Fāṭima wrote this with me in Ṣafar of the year 17.”

Al-Walīd b. Hishām said: My paternal uncle told me, from Ibn Shubruma, that he said: “If I were appointed governor of Baṣra, I would collect their revenues, because ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb granted land there to no one except Abū Bakra and Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith.

ʿUthmān granted land in Baṣra only to ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn and Ibn ʿĀmir—he granted him his house—and to Ḥumrān, his freedman.”

He said: “It is also said that Ziyād granted ʿImrān a holding.”

869Hishām al-Kalbī said: The first house built in Baṣra was the house of Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith, then the house of Maʿqil b. Yasār al-Muzanī.

ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān had taken the house of ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī and wrote that land should be given to him in Baṣra.

He was given his land, known as the bank of ʿUthmān, opposite al-Ubulla.

It was marshy, so he reclaimed it and cultivated it.

The Gate of ʿUthmān in Baṣra is named after ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

870They said: Ḥumrān b. Abān belonged to al-Musayyab b. Najba al-Fazārī.

He had captured him at ʿAyn al-Tamr, and ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān bought him from him, taught him writing, and made him his scribe.

He became displeased with him because he had sent him to investigate the charges brought against al-Walīd b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ; Ḥumrān took a bribe from him and denied what had been said about him.

Later ʿUthmān became certain that this was true.

He was displeased with him and said: “He shall never live with me again.”

He gave him the choice of a town to live in other than Medina.

He chose Baṣra.

He asked him to grant him a house there,

and named a very large area.

ʿUthmān thought it excessive and said to Ibn ʿĀmir: “Give him a house like one of your houses.”

So he granted him his house in Baṣra.

871They said: The house of Khālid b. Ṭalīq al-Khuzāʿī, the judge, had belonged to Abū al-Jarrāḥ, the judge and custodian of Ibn al-Zubayr’s prison.

Salm b. Ziyād bought it for him because he had escaped from al-Zubayr’s prison.

872Ibn al-Kalbī said: The lane of Banū Samura in Baṣra belonged to ʿUtba b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samura b. Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams b. ʿAbd Manāf.

The mosque of ʿĀṣim was named after ʿĀṣim, one of Banū Rabīʿa b. Kilāb b. Rabīʿa b. ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa.

The house of Abū Nāfiʿ in Baṣra was named after Abū Nāfiʿ, the client of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakra.

873Al-Qaḥdhamī said: The house of Abū Yaʿqūb al-Khaṭṭābī belonged to Saḥāma b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Aṣamm al-Ghanawī, the muezzin of al-Ḥajjāj.

He was among those who fought alongside Yazīd b. al-Muhallab.

Muslima b. ʿAbd al-Malik killed him on the Day of al-ʿAqr.

It is beside the house of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba.

874They said: The house of Ṭāriq was named after Ṭāriq b. Abī Bakra.

Opposite it was the plot of al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī.

The house of Ziyād b. ʿUthmān was one that ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād had bought for his nephew Ziyād b. ʿUthmān.

Next to it was the plot that included the house of Bāba bt. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

The house of Sulaymān b. ʿAlī had belonged to Salm b. Ziyād. Bilāl b. Abī Burda seized it during his governorship of Baṣra under Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh; then Sulaymān b. ʿAlī came and took up residence in it.

875They said: The house of Mūsā b. Abī al-Mukhtār, the client of Thaqīf, belonged to a man from

Banū Dārim.

Fayrūz Ḥuṣayn wanted to buy it from him for ten thousand.

He said: “I would not sell my neighborhood to you for a hundred thousand.”

Fayrūz gave him ten thousand and let him keep the house.

876Abū al-Ḥasan said: The man of Banū Dārim wanted to sell his house and said: “I will sell it for ten thousand dirhams: five thousand for its price and five thousand for Fayrūz’s neighborhood.”

When Fayrūz heard this, he said: “Keep your house.”

He gave him ten thousand dirhams.

The house of Ibn Tabaʿ was named after ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Tabaʿ al-Ḥīrī.

He was in charge of Ziyād’s grants of land.

Damūn was from the people of Ṭāʾif.

Abū Mūsā married his daughter, and she bore him Abū Burda.

Damūn had a plot in Baṣra.

The people of Baṣra used to say of him: “Prosperity and sons, bread and cumin, in Damūn’s house.”

877Al-Qaḥdhamī and others said: The first bathhouse established in Baṣra was the bathhouse of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī. It stood on the site of the garden of Sufyān b. Muʿāwiya at al-Khurayba, near the palace of ʿĪsā b. Jaʿfar.

The second was the bathhouse of Fayl, the client of Ziyād.

The third was the bathhouse of Muslim b. Abī Bakra at Bilāl-Ābādh.

It later came into the possession of ʿAmr b. Muslim al-Bāhilī.

For a long time, Baṣra had no bathhouses other than these.

878Al-Madāʾinī told me: Abū Bakra said to his son Muslim: “My son, by God, you have held no office, and I do not see you as falling short of your brothers in usefulness.”

He replied: “If you keep it secret, I will tell you.”

He said: “I will.”

He said: “I make a thousand dirhams each day from this bathhouse of mine, as well as a great deal of food.”

Then Muslim fell ill. He bequeathed [his affairs] to his brother ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakra and told him about the bathhouse’s income.

He disclosed it and asked the authorities for permission to build a bathhouse.

Bathhouses could be built in Baṣra only with the governors’ permission.

He gave him permission.

He sought permission from ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra, and he gave it to him; he sought permission from al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ, and he gave it to him.

He sought permission from Sīāh al-Aswārī, and he gave it to him.

He sought permission from al-Ḥuṣayn b. Abī al-Ḥurr al-ʿAnbarī, and he gave it to him.

Rīṭa bt. Ziyād sought permission, and he gave it to her.

Lubāba bt. Awfā al-Jurashī sought permission, and he gave it to her for two bathhouses: one in Aṣḥāb al-Qabāʾ and the other among Banū Saʿd.

Al-Minjāb b. Rāshid al-Ḍabbī sought permission, and he gave it to him.

Muslim b. Abī Bakra recovered from his illness, and his bathhouse income had been ruined for him.

They began cursing ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and saying: “What is the matter with him? May God sever his ties of kinship!”

879They said: Fayl was Ziyād’s chamberlain and client. Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī and Anas b. Zanīm rode with him. Fayl was riding a sleek mule, while the two of them were on poor, slow horses.

Jealousy overcame them.

Anas said: “I will requite Abū al-Aswad.”

He said: “Go ahead.”

He said:

“By your father’s life, Kisrā’s bathhouse is not even two-thirds of Fayl’s bathhouse.” Abū al-Aswad said:

“Why should our dancing around the clients

be according to our custom in the Prophet’s time?”

Abū Mufarrigh said to Ṭalḥa al-Ṭalḥāt, namely Ṭalḥa b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khalaf:

“Ṭulayḥa promises me a thousand thousand;

you have promised me a distant hope.

You are not a noble free man, but rather

for a dark woman who bears slaves.

Even if I were admitted to Fayl’s bathhouse

and clothed in brocade and fine robes.”

Someone said when death came upon him:

“O my Lord, how often someone asks, worn out,

‘How does one get to the bathhouse of al-Minjāb?’”

He meant the bathhouse of al-Minjāb b. Rāshid al-Ḍabbī.

ʿAbbās, the client of Banū Usāma, said: “I remembered the band in ʿAmr’s bathhouse, but I did not leave until after the evening meal.”

The donkey of Balj was named after Balj b. Nashba al-Saʿdī, to whom Ziyād said: “And one on guard against his like is himself a guard.” 880. Hishām al-Kalbī said: The Palace of Aws in Baṣra was named after Aws b. Thaʿlaba b. Ruqayy, one of Banū Taym Allāh b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUkāba.

He was among the prominent men who were in Khurāsān.

He held important offices there.

He was the one who passed by Tadmur and said of its two idols:

“You two who have come to Tadmur, tell me:

Have you not grown weary of standing so long?

How many an age has passed over you, then another age,

for your people, and year after year?”

The Palace of Anas was named after Anas b. Mālik al-Anṣārī, the servant of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said: “The one who built the minaret of Banū Asīd was Ḥassān b. Saʿd, one of them.

The Red Palace belonged to ʿAmr b. ʿUtba b. Abī Sufyān; today it belongs to the family of ʿUmar b. Ḥafṣ b. Qubayṣa b. Abī Ṣafra.

The Palace of the Two Travelers belonged to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ziyād.

Al-Ḥajjāj had the dependents of those who had gone with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath al-Kindī sent to him, and he imprisoned them in it.

It is a palace within a palace, and adjoining it is the palace of ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād, with a pavilion beside it.

881Al-Qaḥdhamī said: The Palace of al-Nawāhiq is Ziyād’s palace.

The ruffians gave it that name.

The Palace of al-Nuʿmān belonged to al-Nuʿmān b. Ṣahbān al-Rāsibī, who arbitrated between Muḍar and Rabīʿa when Yazīd died.

He said: ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād added to al-Nuʿmān b. Ṣahbān’s palace here.

Al-Nuʿmān said: “What a wretched possession this is, Abū Ḥātim! If the water rises, you will drown; if it falls, you will thirst.”

And so it was,

as he had said.

The water became scarce, and everyone there died.

The Palace of Zarbā was named after Zarbā, the client of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir.

He was in charge of his horses.

The house was for his mounts.

The Palace of ʿAṭiyya was named after ʿAṭiyya al-Anṣārī.

The mosque of Banū ʿAbbād was named after Banū ʿAbbād b. Riḍāʾ b. Shaqra b. al-Ḥārith b. Tamīm b. Murra.

The house of ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī had belonged to his paternal aunt Dujāja, the mother of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir.

She granted it to him.

He was ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim b. Asmāʾ b. al-Ṣalt.

She was Dujāja bt. Asmāʾ.

882Al-Madāʾinī told me, from Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī,

and al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām, from his father, from ʿAwāna, both of whom said: Al-Aḥnaf b. Qays came to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ with the people of Baṣra.

He began asking them one by one, while al-Aḥnaf sat at the side of the room in silence, not speaking.

ʿUmar said to him: “Do you have no need?” He replied: “Yes, Commander of the Faithful.

The keys of good are in God’s hand. Our brothers among the people of the garrison towns settled in the abodes of bygone peoples, between fresh waters and lush gardens, while we settled in a marshy, saline place whose dampness never dries and whose pasture does not grow.

To its east lies the briny sea, and to its west the open plain. We have neither crops nor livestock. Our supplies and provisions come to us in a quantity as slight as an ostrich’s gullet.

A weak man goes out and fetches sweet water from two farsakhs away. A woman goes out for the same purpose and leaves her child tied up as one ties a young goat, for fear of a sudden enemy attack or a beast devouring it.

If you do not raise our lowly standing and remedy our poverty, we will become like a people who perished.”

ʿUmar enrolled the dependents of the people of Baṣra in the stipends and wrote to Abū Mūsā, instructing him to dig a canal for them.

883A group of learned men told me: They said: The blind Tigris—that is, the Tigris of Baṣra—had an inlet, a channel for water that no one had dug, through which rainwater flowed

to it, and its water recedes into it at high tide and dries up at low tide.

Its length was about one farsakh.

Its bank on the side facing Baṣra had a hollow and a broad area called al-Ajānah in the Jāhiliyya; the Arabs called it al-Jazzārah in Islam.

It lay about three farsakhs from Baṣra, measured by the measure according to which the entire Nahr al-Ubullah was four farsakhs. From there began the canal known today as Nahr al-Ajānah.

When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ ordered Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī to dig a river for the people of Baṣra, he began digging at al-Ajānah and carried it for three farsakhs until it reached Baṣra.

Thus Nahr al-Ubullah was four farsakhs long.

Then the stretch between Baṣra and the breach of al-Ḥayrī silted up; this was about one farsakh from Baṣra.

Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān was in charge of the dīwān and the treasury on behalf of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz, while ʿAbd Allāh was then in charge of Baṣra on behalf of ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān.

He advised Ibn ʿĀmir to continue digging Nahr al-Ubullah from where it had silted up until it reached Baṣra.

He delayed this and kept putting it off.

When Ibn ʿĀmir departed for Khurāsān and appointed Ziyād as his deputy, Ziyād left Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī’s excavation as it was.

He dug the river from where it had silted up until it reached Baṣra.

He put ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakrah in charge of this.

When ʿAbd al-Raḥmān released the water, he made his horse gallop, while the water was almost outpacing him.

Ibn ʿĀmir returned from Khurāsān and grew angry with Ziyād, saying: “You only wanted to take the fame and renown of this river away from me.”

The two remained estranged until they died.

Their sons, too, were estranged because of it.

Yūnus b. Ḥabīb the grammarian said: “I knew the families of Ziyād and Ibn ʿĀmir to be estranged from one another.”

884Al-Athram related to me, from Abū ʿUbaydah, who said: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī led Nahr al-Ubullah from al-Ajānah to Baṣra.

Before that, people drew water from a place called Dayr Qāwūs, whose mouth was

in the Tigris, above al-Ubullah by four farsakhs; it ran through salt marshes, with no buildings along its banks.

The winds would bury it.

He said: When Ziyād dug the Fayd of Baṣra after completing the repair of Nahr al-Ubullah, Ibn ʿĀmir returned from Khurāsān, reproached him, and said: “You wanted to take the fame and renown of this river away from me.”

For that reason, the two men and their families became estranged.

885Abū ʿUbaydah said: He dug the Fayd from the house of Fīl, Ziyād’s freedman and chamberlain, as far as the bridge site.

886Muḥammad b. Saʿd related, from al-Wāqidī and others, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ordered Abū Mūsā to dig the other river and have it run under the direction of Maʿqil b. Yasār al-Muzanī; it was therefore attributed to him.

887Al-Wāqidī said: Maʿqil died in Baṣra during the governorship of ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād over Baṣra for Muʿāwiyah.

888Al-Walīd b. Hishām al-Qaḥdhamī and ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. Abī Sayf al-Madāʾinī said: Al-Mundhir b. al-Jārūd al-ʿAbdī spoke to Muʿāwiyah b. Abī Sufyān about digging Nahr Thār.

He wrote to Ziyād, and Ziyād dug Nahr Maʿqil.

Some said: It was made to run under the direction of Maʿqil b. Yasār.

So it was attributed to him.

889Others said: Rather, Ziyād had it run under the direction of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakrah, or someone else.

When he had finished it and they wanted to open it, Ziyād sent Maʿqil b. Yasār to open it, seeking a blessing through him, because he was one of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ.

The people said: “Maʿqil’s River.”

Al-Qaḥdhamī related that Ziyād gave a man one thousand dirhams and told him: “Go to the Tigris and ask who owns this river. If a man tells you that it is Ziyād’s River, give him the thousand.” The man reached the Tigris, then returned and said: “I met no one who did not say, ‘Maʿqil’s River.’”

Ziyād said: “That is God’s bounty; He grants it to whomever He wills.” (1)

890They said: Dubays’s River was named after a tailor called Dubays, who used to tailor clothes on it.

The breach of al-Ḥayrī was named after a Nabataean from al-Ḥīrah; it is said that he was Ziyād’s freedman.

891They said: When Ziyād had extended Maʿqil’s River as far as the dome where the troops were reviewed, he turned it toward the south until he brought it out to the recipients of alms at al-Jabal.

That bend was called Dubays’s River.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir dug his river by the house of Fīl.

It is the one known as the River of the Asāwirah.

Some said that the Asāwirah dug it.

ʿAmr’s River was named after ʿAmr b. ʿUtbah b. Abī Sufyān, and Umm Ḥabīb’s River was named after Umm Ḥabīb bt. Ziyād.

There was a palace with many doors on it, so it was called al-Hazārdar.

892ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī said: Shirūyah al-Aswārī married Marjānah, the mother of ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād.

He built her a palace with many doors, so it was called Hazārdar.

(1) Sūrat al-Ḥadīd, 57:21.

(*)

Abū al-Ḥasan said: Some said it was called Hazārdar because Shirūyah made a thousand doors in his palace.

Others said that a thousand Asāwirah settled in that place in a thousand houses; Kisrā settled them there, and so it was called Hazārdar.

The River of Ḥarb was named after Ḥarb b. Salm b. Ziyād.

ʿAbd al-Aʿlā b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir claimed that the land on which it lay belonged to Ibn ʿĀmir, and disputed it with Ḥarb.

When the judgment was turning in ʿAbd al-Aʿlā’s favor, Ḥarb came to him and said: “I disputed this river with you, and I have regretted doing so.

You are the elder and chief of the clan; it is yours.”

ʿAbd al-Aʿlā b. ʿAbd Allāh said: “Rather, it is yours.”

Ḥarb left. In the evening, ʿAbd al-Aʿlā’s freedmen and advisers came and said: “By God, Ḥarb did not come to you until the judgment was turning against him in your favor.”

He said: “By God, I shall never take back what I gave him.”

The river known as Yazīdān was named after Yazīd b. ʿUmar al-Asīd, the chief of police under ʿAdī b. Arṭāh.

He was the most prominent man of Baṣra in his time.

893They said: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz granted ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmayr b. ʿAmr b. Mālik al-Laythī—his maternal half-brother, through Dajājah bt. Asmāʾ b. al-Ṣalt al-Sulamī—eight thousand jarībs.

He dug for it the river known as Ibn ʿUmayr’s River.

894They said: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir dug the river of Umm ʿAbd Allāh Dajājah, and Ghaylān b. Kharashah al-Ḍabbī took charge of it.

It is the river about which Ḥārithah b. Badr al-Ghudanī said to ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir, as he rode alongside him: “I have seen no river more blessed than this one.

The weak draw water from the doors of their houses, and it brings their needs in it right to their homes; it is a drain

for their waters.

Then, later during his governorship, he rode alongside Ziyād and said: “I have seen no river worse than it: their houses leak from it, they have to make holes for it in their homes, and their children drown in it.”

Some transmit that Ghaylān b. Kharashah was the speaker.

The former account is more firmly established.

Salm’s River was named after Salm b. Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir dug a river overseen by his freedman Nāfidh, and it became known by his name, as Nāfidh’s River.

It belongs to the family of al-Faḍl b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbbās b. Rabīʿah b. al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.

895Abū al-Yaqẓān said: ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān granted al-ʿAbbās b. Rabīʿah b. al-Ḥārith a house in Baṣra and gave him one hundred thousand dirhams.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbbās was nicknamed “Mule Trainer” because he rode mules so well.

People followed his example after Ibn al-Ashʿath fled to Sijistān, and he fled from al-Ḥajjāj.

The two Ṭalḥahs were the river of Ṭalḥah b. Abī Nāfiʿ, the freedman of Ṭalḥah b. ʿUbayd Allāh.

Ḥumaydah’s River was named after a woman of the family of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samurah b. Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams, called Ḥumaydah.

She was the wife of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir.

The two Khayrāns belonged to Khayrah bt. Ḍamrah al-Qushayrī, al-Muhallab’s wife.

She had two Muhallabs.

Al-Muhallab had given them to her.

It is said, rather, that they belonged to her and were named after al-Muhallab.

She was the mother of his son Abū ʿUyaynah.

The two Jubayrs belonged to Jubayr b. Ḥayyah.

The two Khalafāns were a grant to ʿAbd Allāh b. Khalaf al-Khuzāʿī, Abū Ṭalḥah of the Ṭalḥahs.

The two Ṭulayqāns belonged to the family of ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn al-Khuzāʿī, descendants of Khālid b. Ṭulayq b. Muḥammad b. ʿImrān.

Khālid had served as judge of Baṣra.

896Al-Qaḥdhamī said: Murrah’s River belonged to Ibn ʿĀmir. Murrah, the freedman of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, had been put in charge of digging it for him, and his name came to predominate in its attribution.

897Abū al-Yaqẓān and others said: Murrah’s River was named after Murrah b. Abī ʿUthmān, the freedman of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, who was a notable man.

He asked ʿĀʾishah, Mother of the Believers, to write to Ziyād on his behalf and to put his name first in the address of her letter. She wrote to him, recommending Murrah, and addressed it: “To Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān, from ʿĀʾishah, Mother of the Believers.”

When Ziyād saw that she had written to him and associated him with Abū Sufyān, he was pleased, and treated Murrah with honor and kindness.

He said to the people: “This is the letter of the Mother of the Believers to me,” and showed it to them so that they could read its address.

Then he granted him one hundred jarībs along Nahr al-Ubullah and ordered him to dig a river for it; it was named after him.

ʿUthmān b. Murrah was one of the notables of Baṣra. The grant passed out of his descendants’ hands and came to belong to the family of al-Ṣaffāq b. Ḥujr b. Bujayr al-ʿAqawī of al-Azd.

898They said: Darjāh Jank was one of the properties of Thaqīf; it was called that because of disputes that took place over it.

Jank means “clamor” in Persian.

Anasān was named after Anas b. Mālik, on a grant from Ziyād.

Bashshār’s River was named after Bashshār b. Muslim b. ʿAmr al-Bāhilī, the brother of Qutaybah.

He had given al-Ḥajjāj a horse on which he won a race.

Al-Ḥajjāj granted him seven hundred jarībs; it is said, four hundred jarībs.

He dug a river for it.

Fayrūz’s River was named after Fayrūz Ḥuṣayn; it is said that it was named after Bāshkār, who was called Fayrūz.

Al-Qaḥdhamī said: It was named after Fayrūz, the freedman of Rabīʿah b. Kildah al-Thaqafī.

Al-ʿAlāʾ’s River was named after al-ʿAlāʾ b. Sharīk al-Hudhalī. He presented something to ʿAbd al-Malik that pleased him, so he granted him one hundred jarībs.

Dhiraʿ’s River was named after Dhiraʿ al-Namarī of Rabīʿah.

He was the father of Hārūn b. Dhiraʿ.

Ḥabīb’s River was named after Ḥabīb b. Shihāb al-Shāmī, a merchant on a grant from Ziyād; it is said, from ʿUthmān.

Abū Bakrah’s River was named after Abū Bakrah b. Ziyād.

899Al-ʿAqawī the broker related to me, saying: The island between the two rivers was a salt marsh, and Muʿāwiyah granted it to one of his nephews.

When the young man came to inspect it, Ziyād ordered water to be sent into it.

The young man said: “The Commander of the Faithful granted me only a marsh, which I have no use for.”

Ziyād bought it from him for two hundred thousand dirhams and dug its canals.

He granted Rawādān, part of it, to Rawād b. Abī Bakrah.

A fish called al-Rāʾ was caught in the River of al-Rāʾ, and it was named after it.

Ḥumrān’s land, which Muʿāwiyah had granted him, lies along it.

Makkḥūl’s River was named after Makkḥūl b. ʿUbayd Allāh al-Aḥmasī, who was the cousin of Shaybān, the owner of the cemetery of Shaybān b. ʿAbd Allāh, who had been chief of police under Ibn Ziyād.

Makkḥūl composed poetry about horses, and his grant came from ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān.

900Al-Qaḥdhamī said: Makkḥūl’s River was named after Makkḥūl b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Saʿdī,

Al-Qaḥdhamī said: ʿUthmān’s Riverbank was purchased by ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī from ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān with property he owned in al-Ṭāʾif.

It is said that he purchased it in exchange for a house of his in Madīnah, which ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān added to the mosque.

ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ granted Ḥafṣān to his brother Ḥafṣ b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

He granted Umayyatān to Abū Umayyah b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

He granted Ḥakamān to al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

He granted Mughīratān to his brother al-Mughīrah.

He said: The River of the Waterwheels belonged to Abū ʿAmr b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī.

901Al-Madāʾinī said: Ziyād granted al-Jumūm on the riverbank; these were the two Ziyāds.

He said to ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUthmān: “I grant only what you cultivate.”

He would grant a man a tract and leave it with him for two years; if he cultivated it, otherwise he took it back from him.

Al-Jumūm belonged to Abū Bakrah, then passed to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakrah.

The two Azraqāns were named after al-Azraq b. Muslim, a freedman of Banū Ḥanīfah.

The two Muḥammads were named after Muḥammad b. ʿAlī b. ʿUthmān al-Ḥanafī.

The two Ziyāds were named after Ziyād, a freedman of Banū al-Haytham. He was the grandfather of Muʾnis b. ʿImrān b. Jamīʿ b. Yasār, and the maternal grandfather of ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar the grammarian and Ḥājib b. ʿUmar.

Abū al-Khaṣīb’s River was named after Abū al-Khaṣīb Marzūq, the freedman of al-Manṣūr, the Commander of the Faithful.

The Commander’s River in Baṣra was dug by al-Manṣūr, who then gave it to his son Jaʿfar.

It used to be called the Commander of the Faithful’s River, then it was called the Commander’s River; then al-Rashīd bought it, granted some of it, and sold some.

Ribā’s River belonged to al-Rashīd and was named after Sūrajī.

The Qurashī and the Arab: ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Aʿlā al-Kurayzī and ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. al-Ḥakam al-Thaqafī disputed it, then settled on each taking half of it.

So it was called “the Qurashī and the Arab.”

Al-Qandal is a creek among the creeks of the Tigris. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī dammed it, and al-Mundhir b. al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām held an allotment there.

There is also the canal of al-Nuʿmān b. al-Mundhir, lord of al-Ḥīrah.

In the days of Kisrā

There was a palace of al-Nuʿmān there.

The canal of Muqātil was named after Muqātil b. Jāriyah b. Qudāmah al-Saʿdī.

ʿUmayrān was named after ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmayr al-Laythī.

Sayḥān belonged to the Barmakids, who named it Sayḥān.

Al-Jawbarah: a jawbarah was hunted there, so it was named after that.

Ḥuṣaynān belonged to Ḥuṣayn b. Abī al-Ḥurr al-ʿAnbarī.

ʿUbaydalān belonged to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah.

ʿUbaydān belonged to ʿUbayd b. Kaʿb al-Numayrī.

Munqidhān belonged to Munqidh b. ʿIlāj al-Sulamī.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmānān had belonged to Abū Bakrah b. Ziyād, then Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the client of Hishām, bought it.

Nāfiʿān belonged to Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith al-Thaqafī.

Aslamān belonged to Aslam b. Zurʿah al-Kilābī.

Ḥumrānān belonged to Ḥumrān b. Abān, the client of ʿUthmān.

Qutaybatān belonged to Qutaybah b. Muslim.

Khashkhashān belonged to the family of al-Khashkhāsh al-ʿAnbarī.

902Al-Qaḥdhamī said: The Canal of the Daughters belonged to Ziyād’s daughters; he granted each daughter sixty jarībs.

He likewise used to grant allotments to the common people.

He said: Ziyād ordered ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Tabaʿ al-Ḥimyarī, who was in charge of his allotments, to allot to Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith al-Thaqafī as far as he walked.

He walked until his sandal strap broke, then sat down and said, “That is enough for you.”

He replied, “Had I known, I would have walked as far as al-Ubullah.”

He said, “Let me throw it so that it reaches ʿAlī.”

He threw it until it reached al-Ajānah .

Saʿīdān belonged to the family of Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbbād b. Usayd.

Sulaymānān was an allotment belonging to ʿUbayd b. Qusayṭ, the owner of the watercourse, in the days of al-Ḥajjāj.

A man of ascetic devotion called Sulaymān b. Jābir kept watch there, and it was named after him.

ʿUmrān belonged to ʿUmar b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Muʿammar al-Tamīmī.

Faylān belonged to Fayl, the client of Ziyād.

Khālidān was named after Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayyah.

The canal of Yazīd al-Ibāḍī: he was Yazīd b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥimyarī.

Al-Mismāriyyah was an allotment of Mismār, the client of Ziyād.

He had an estate in Kūfah.

Al-Qaḥdhamī said: Bilāl b. Abī Burdah was the one who opened the Canal of Maʿqil at the inundation of Baṣra.

Before that, it was broken and overflowed toward the dome where Ziyād used to review the troops.

Bilāl dug the Canal of Bilāl, built shops along both its banks, moved the market there, and assigned it to Yazīd b. Khālid al-Qasrī.

903They said: Bashīr b. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah dug al-Marghāb and named it

by the name Marghāb of Marw.

The allotment containing al-Marghāb belonged to Hilāl b. Aḥwaz al-Māzinī; Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik granted it to him. It was eight thousand jarībs.

Bashīr dug al-Marghāb, its irrigation canals, and its cross-channels by force, and said, “This is an allotment of mine.”

Ḥumayrī b. Hilāl disputed with him, so Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī wrote to Mālik b. al-Mundhir b. al-Jārūd, who was in charge of the security forces of Baṣra: “Let al-Ḥimyarī have access to al-Marghāb, and satisfy him.”

That was because Bashīr had been summoned before Khālid and lodged a complaint, and Khālid accepted his statement.

ʿAmr b. Yazīd al-Asīdī was concerned for Ḥumayrī and supported him.

He said to Mālik b. al-Mundhir, “May God set you right! This is not ‘let him have access’; it is ‘release al-Marghāb to Ḥumayrī.’”

He said: Ṣaʿṣaʿah b. Muʿāwiyah, al-Aḥnaf’s uncle, had an allotment opposite al-Marghāb and next to it.

Muʿāwiyah b. Ṣaʿṣaʿah b. Muʿāwiyah came to support Ḥumayrī.

Bashīr said, “This is the pasture for our camels, cows, donkeys, beasts of burden, and sheep” .

Muʿāwiyah said, “Is it because of the dung of a mangy cow and a lustful she-ass that you want to deprive us of our right?” ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd came and said, “Our land and our allotment.”

Muʿāwiyah said to him, “Have you heard of the one who stepped over the fire and got the flame into his backside? That is you.”

904They said: Suwaydān was an allotment belonging to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah, measuring four hundred jarībs.

He gave it to Suwayd b. Manjūf al-Sadūsī.

That was because Suwayd fell ill, and Ibn Abī Bakrah visited him and said, “How are you feeling?” He replied, “Well, if you wish.”

He said, “I do wish it; what is it?” He replied, “If you give me the like of what you gave Ibn Muʿammar, I’ll be all right.”

He gave him Suwaydān, and it was named after him.

905Al-Madāʾinī said: Yazīd b. al-Muhallab dug the Canal of Yazīd in an allotment

belonging to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah.

He said to Bashīr b. ʿUbayd Allāh, “Write me a document stating that this canal is my right.”

He replied, “No. If you are dismissed, I will bring a claim against you.”

Jabrān belonged to the family of Kulthūm b. Jabr.

The Canal of Ibn Abī Bardhaʿah was named after Abū Bardhaʿah b. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah.

Al-Masraqānān was an allotment belonging to the family of Abū Bakrah. Its original area was one hundred jarībs, but al-Manṣūr’s survey measured it at one thousand jarībs.

They were confirmed in possession of one hundred of them, and the rest was seized.

The allotment of Humayān belonged to Humayān b. ʿAdī al-Sadūsī.

Kathīrān belonged to Kathīr b. Sayyār.

Bilālān belonged to Bilāl b. Abī Burdah.

The allotment had belonged to ʿAbbād b. Zayd, and he bought it.

Shiblān belonged to Shibl b. ʿUmayrah b. Yathribī al-Ḍabbī.

The Canal of Salm was named after Salm b. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakrah. The River of al-Rabāḥī was named after Rabāḥ, the client of the family of Jadʿān. The Sabkhat ʿĀʾishah was named after ʿĀʾishah bt. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khalaf al-Khuzāʿī.

906They said: Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Sulamī, Abū al-ʿĀj, the agent of Yūsuf b. ʿUmar al-Thaqafī in Baṣra, dug a canal from the Canal of Ibn ʿAtabah to al-Khistal, and it was named after him .

The Canal of Abū Shaddād was named after Abū Shaddād, the client of Ziyād.

The breach of Sayyār belonged to Fayl, the client of Ziyād, but the overseer of it was Sayyār, the client of Banū ʿAqīl, and the name prevailed from him.

The land of the Iṣfahānīs was purchased from some Arabs.

These Iṣfahānīs were

people who had embraced Islam and migrated to Baṣra.

It is said that they were among the Asāwirah who settled in Baṣra.

The house of Ibn al-Iṣfahānī in Baṣra was named after ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Iṣfahānī. He had four hundred mamlūks and fought al-Mukhtār alongside Muṣʿab, serving on Muṣʿab’s right wing.

907ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from one of the family of al-Ahtam, who said: Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to ʿUmar b. Hubayrah: “The Commander of the Faithful has no cultivated land in the lands of the Arabs, so go through the allotments and take their surplus for the Commander of the Faithful.”

ʿUmar began going to each allotment, asking about it, then measuring it.

Until he came to a piece of land.

He said, “Whose is this?” Its owner said, “It is mine.”

He said, “How did it come to be yours?” He replied, “We inherited it from fathers of good repute, and we leave it as an inheritance to our sons when we die.” He said: Then the people complained loudly about this, and he stopped.

They said: Ṣaltān was named after al-Ṣalt b. Ḥurayth al-Ḥanafī. Qāsimān was an allotment of al-Qāsim b. ʿAbbās b. Rabīʿah b. al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; his brother ʿAwn inherited it from him. The Canal of Khālidān, al-Ajmah, belonged to the family of Khālid b. Asīd and the family of Abū Bakrah. The Canal of Māsūrān: there was a wicked man there who went about stirring people up and investigating them, so the canal was named after him.

In Persian, māsūr means “bold, wicked.” Jabayrān was also an allotment of Jubayr b. Abī Zayd of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār.

Maʿqalān was an allotment granted by Ziyād to Maʿqil b. Yasār. His descendants say it was from ʿUmar, but ʿUmar granted no one either of the two canals.

Jandilān belonged to ʿUbayd Allāh b. Jandal al-Hilālī. The Canal of al-Tūt was an allotment of ʿAbd Allāh b. Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith al-Thaqafī .

909Al-Qaḥdhamī said: The Canal of Sulaymān b. ʿAlī belonged to Ḥassān b. Abī Ḥassān al-Nabaṭī.

The River of al-Ghawthī had a garrison commander there called Ghawth, and it was named after him.

Some said: He made it a place of refuge for al-Marghāb, so it was called al-Ghawth.

Dhāt al-Ḥaffāfayn, on the Canal of Maʿqil and the Tigris, belonged to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakrah; ʿArabī al-Tammār, the client of Ummat Allāh bt. Abī Bakrah, bought it.

The Canal of Abū Sabrah al-Hudhalī was an allotment.

Ḥarbānān was an allotment belonging to Ḥarb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

The allotment of al-Ḥubāb? [belonged to] Ḥubāb b. Yazīd al-Majāshiʿī.

The Canal of Jaʿfar belonged to Jaʿfar, the client of Salm b. Ziyād, and was subject to land tax.

The breach of Shīrīn was named after Shīrīn, the wife of Kisrā b. Hurmuz.

910Al-Qaḥdhamī and al-Madāʾinī said: Muhallabān, which is known in the register as the allotment of ʿUmar b. Hubayrah, belonged to ʿUmar b. Hubayrah.

Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik granted it to him when he seized the property of Yazīd b. al-Muhallab, his brothers, and his son.

It had belonged to al-Mughīrah b. al-Muhallab, and there was a canal in it that Zādān Farrūkh had dug, so it became known by his name.

Today it belongs to the family of Sufyān b. Muʿāwiyah b. Yazīd b. al-Muhallab. He appealed to Abū al-ʿAbbās, the Commander of the Faithful, regarding it, and he granted it to him. The family of al-Muhallab disputed with him over it, and he said, “It belonged to al-Mughīrah.”

They said, “We accept that.”

Al-Mughīrah b. al-Muhallab had died before his father, so his daughter inherited half; “Your inheritance from your mother is yours.”

The remainder returned to his father, so it belongs among the heirs.

He said, “Did al-Mughīrah have a son?” They said, “What concern have you with al-Mughīrah’s son? You do not inherit from him; he is only your maternal uncle.”

He gave them nothing. It was one thousand five hundred jarībs.

Kawsajān was named after ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr al-Thaqafī al-Kawsaj.

Al-Madāʾinī said: Kawsajān belonged to Abū Bakrah.

His brother Nāfiʿ disputed with him, and they went out to it, each claiming it.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr al-Kawsaj went out there too.

He said to them, “I see you are disputing; let me arbitrate between you.”

They appointed him as arbiter .

He said, “I have judged it to be mine.”

They surrendered it to him.

He said: It is also said that al-Kawsaj had no water share.

He said to Abū Bakrah and Nāfiʿ, “Give me a water share equal to a leap.”

They agreed to that.

It is said that he leapt thirty cubits.

911They said: Along the Euphrates there were lands whose inhabitants had embraced Islam when the Muslims entered them, and lands that passed from their inhabitants into the hands of Muslim people through gifts and other means of ownership. They were made subject to the tithe, though they had been subject to land tax.

Al-Ḥajjāj returned them to land tax; then ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz returned them to the alms levy; then ʿUmar b. Hubayrah returned them to land tax.

When Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik assumed rule, he returned some of them to the alms levy.

Then al-Mahdī, the Commander of the Faithful, made all of them lands subject to the alms levy.

He said: Jaʿfarān belonged to Umm Jaʿfar bt. Mujzaʾah b. Thawr al-Sadūsī, the wife of Aslam, the owner of Aslamān.

912Al-Qaḥdhamī said: Arqam b. Ibrāhīm told me that he saw Ḥassān

the Nabaṭī pointing from the bridge, accompanied by ʿAbd al-Aʿlā b. ʿAbd Allāh, [measuring] with a cubit all that lay from the boundary of the Canal of al-Fayḍ to the land of the descendants of Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

When he reached the house of ʿAbd al-Aʿlā, he raised the measuring rod.

When the Blessed Dynasty came to power, it seized all of that. Abū Jaʿfar al-Jabbān was placed in charge of it, among the lands placed in charge of the people of al-Madīnah.

Al-Mahdī granted al-ʿAbbāsah, his daughter and the wife of Muḥammad b. Sulaymān al-Sharqī, ʿAbbādān. [He also granted] an allotment to Ḥumrān b. Abān, the client of ʿUthmān, [which had come] from ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān.

Some of it, they say, came from Ziyād.

Ḥumrān was among the captives of ʿAyn al-Tamr; he claimed to be from al-Nimr b. Qāsiṭ.

One day al-Ḥajjāj said, with ʿAbbād b. Ḥuṣayn al-Ḥabaṭī present, “What does Ḥumrān say? If he claims Arab descent and does not say that his father is my father and that he is a client of ʿUthmān, I will strike off his head.”

ʿAbbād hurried out from al-Ḥajjāj and informed Ḥumrān of what he had said.

He gave him the [garbled] of the canal and retained al-Sharqī.

It was named after ʿAbbād b. al-Ḥuṣayn.

913Hishām b. al-Kalbī said: The first to keep watch at ʿAbbādān was ʿAbbād b. al-Ḥuṣayn.

He said: Al-Rabīʿ b. Ṣubḥ, the jurist and client of Banū Saʿd, collected money from the people of Baṣra, fortified ʿAbbādān with it, and kept watch there. Al-Rabīʿ transmitted from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. He had gone on a naval expedition to India and died; he was buried on one of the islands in the year 160.

914Al-Qaḥdhamī said: Khālidān al-Qaṣr and Khālidān Habsāʾ belonged to Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd.

Khālidān also belonged to Yazīd b. Ṭalḥah al-Ḥanafī, whose teknonym was Abū Khālid.

He said: The ʿAdī Canal had been a branch of the Baṣra River, until ʿAdī b. Arṭāʾ al-Fazārī, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s governor, cut it through from the Shīrīn weir.

He said: Sulaymān had granted Yazīd b. al-Muhallab whatever land he reclaimed in the marshes.

He reclaimed al-Sharqī, al-Jabbān, al-Khasht, al-Rayḥiyya, two places called Mughayratān, and others, and they became his domain. Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik seized them, then Hishām granted them to his son; after him, they were taken into possession.

Al-Qaḥdhamī said: al-Ḥajjāj had granted ʿAbbāsān to Khayra bt. Ḍamra al-Qushayriyya, al-Muhallab’s wife.

Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik seized it and granted it to al-ʿAbbās b. al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik.

Then it was seized, and Abū al-ʿAbbās, the Commander of the Faithful Sulaymān b. ʿAlī, granted it.

He said: al-Qāsimiyya was among the lands from which the water had receded. Al-Qāsim b. Sulaymān, Ziyād’s client, forged a document claiming that it was a grant to him from Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya.

Al-Khālidiyya belonged to Khālid b. Ṣafwān b. al-Ahtam.

It belonged to al-Qāsim b. Sulaymān.

Al-Mālikiyya belonged to Mālik b. al-Mundhir b. al-Jārūd.

Al-Ḥātimiyya belonged to Ḥātim b. Qabīṣa b. al-Muhallab.

915A group of Baṣrans told me: ʿAdī b. Arṭāʾ wrote to ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and ordered the people of Baṣra to write about digging a canal for them.

Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd al-Tamīmī wrote to him: “If you do not dig a canal for us, Baṣra will be no home for us.”

It is said that ʿAdī sought thereby to harm Bahz b. Yazīd b. al-Muhallab, but it benefited him.

They said: ʿUmar wrote granting him permission to dig a canal.

ʿAdī’s Canal was dug, and the people came out to watch it.

ʿAdī mounted al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī on a donkey that he had, and began walking.

916They said: When ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz arrived as governor of Iraq on behalf of Yazīd b. al-Walīd, the people of Baṣra came to him and complained about the salinity of their water. They brought him two bottles: one contained water from Baṣra, the other water from the marshes.

He saw a difference between them.

They said: “If you dig a canal for us, we shall drink this fresh water.”

He wrote about this to Yazīd.

Yazīd wrote back: “If the cost of this canal amounts to the revenue of Iraq, while it is in our hands, spend it on it.”

He dug the canal known as Ibn ʿUmar’s Canal.

One day a man said in Ibn ʿUmar’s assembly: “By God, I think the cost of this canal will reach three hundred thousand, or more.”

Ibn ʿUmar said: “Even if it reached the revenue of Iraq, I would spend it on it.”

917They said: The governors and notables in Baṣra used to obtain fresh water from the Tigris.

They dug cisterns.

Al-Ḥajjāj had a well-known cistern there in which rainwater collected.

Ibn ʿĀmir, Ziyād, and Ibn Ziyād had cisterns that they made available to the people.

918They said: On his first visit to Baṣra, al-Manṣūr ﵀—built his palace by the Great Prison, in the year 142.

On his second visit, he built the prayer ground in Baṣra.

Al-Qaḥdhamī said: The Great Prison is Islamic-era.

They said: Muḥammad b. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī endowed an estate of his on the basins he had constructed in Baṣra; its yield was spent on their waterwheels, camels, and upkeep.

919Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin told me, from his uncle Abū Hishām, from his father, who said: The people of Baṣra came to Ibn ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz at Wāsiṭ.

They asked him to dig a canal for them, so he dug Ibn ʿUmar’s Canal for them.

The water that came was scant and little.

Most of the water of the marshes flowed into the Dayr Canal.

People used to get fresh water from al-Ubulla until Sulaymān b. ʿAlī came to Baṣra, established al-Mughītha, and built its embankments along the marshes.

He held back the water from the Dayr Canal and diverted it to Ibn ʿUmar’s Canal.

He spent one million dirhams on al-Mughītha.

He said: The people of Baṣra complained to Sulaymān about the salinity of the water and the great quantity of seawater that reached them.

So he dammed al-Qandal, and their water became fresh.

He said: Sulaymān b. ʿAlī bought the site of the prison, in the house of Ibn Ziyād, with his own money and made it a prison. He dug the basin in al-Dahnāʾ, which is the open space of Banū Hāshim.

920A scholar of the estates of Baṣra told me: The people of al-Shuʿaybiyya, by the Euphrates, assigned it to ʿAlī, son of the Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd, during al-Rashīd’s caliphate, on the condition that they farm it for him and that their assessed share be reduced.

He spoke on its behalf, and it was made subject to the tithe as alms. He assessed its people according to what they accepted, and Shuʿayb b. Ziyād al-Wāsiṭī managed its affairs for him. One of his sons had a house in Wāsiṭ on the Tigris, and it was named after him.

921A number of Baṣrans told me, among them Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin: When Sulaymān b. ʿAlī established al-Mughītha, al-Manṣūr wanted to reclaim an estate from the marshes and ordered the establishment of al-Sabīṭiyya.

Sulaymān b. ʿAlī and the people of Baṣra disliked this, and the people of Baṣra gathered at the door of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAlī, who at that time was with his brother Sulaymān, fleeing from

al-Manṣūr. They shouted: “Commander of the Faithful, come down to us so that we may pledge allegiance to you!”

Sulaymān restrained them and dispersed them. He sent to al-Manṣūr Sawwār b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Tamīmī, then al-ʿAnazī; Dāwūd b. Abī Hind, client of Banū Bashīr; and Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba—whose name was Bahrān. They came to him carrying a map of the marshes and told him that they feared their water would become saline.

He said: “I do not think it is as you suppose.”

He ordered them to stop.

Then he came to Baṣra and ordered the reclamation of al-Sabīṭiyya, and it was reclaimed for him.

Among it was a thicket belonging to a landholder called Sabīṭ.

The agent whom he had appointed to manage and reclaim the estate withheld some of its price from him and beat him. Sabīṭ kept waiting at al-Manṣūr’s door, demanding the remainder of the price of his thicket, and repeatedly going to his chancery about it, until he died.

The estate was named after him because of his thicket, and so it was called al-Sabīṭiyya.

922They said: The Qurrat Bridge in Baṣra was named after Qurra b. Ḥayyān al-Bāhilī. There had formerly been a canal by it, which Umm ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir then bought and gave as a charitable drain for the people of Baṣra.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir bought the market and gave it in charity.

923They said: On the day Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya’s death was announced, ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād passed by Umm ʿAbd Allāh’s Canal. It had palm trees, so he ordered them cut down; he also demolished Ḥumrān b. Abān’s bathhouse. Its site is now used for making rabāb.

924They said: The Mosque of al-Ḥāmira was named after a group who came to al-Yamāma, non-Arabs from ʿUmān.

Then they traveled from there to Baṣra on donkeys and settled opposite this mosque.

Some said: They built it, and it was later renovated.

925ʿAlī al-Athram told me, from Abū ʿUbayda, from Abū ʿAmr b. al-ʿAlāʾ, who said: Qays b. Masʿūd al-Shaybānī was in charge of al-Ṭaff on behalf of Kisrā. He established al-Manjashāniyya six miles from Baṣra.

It was carried out by a man called Manjashān, and was named after him.

He said: Above that was Rawḍat al-Khayl, where his mounts used to graze.

926Ibn al-Kalbī said: The water known as al-Ḥawʾab was named after al-Ḥawʾab bt. Kalb b. Wabra.

She was married to Mur b. ʿAdd b. Ṭābikha.

The protected pasture of Ḍariyya was named after Ḍariyya bt. Rabīʿa b. Nizār, who was the mother of Ḥulwān b. ʿImrān b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa.

They said: Ḥulwān was named after this Ḥulwān.

Chapter 79

The Asāwira and the Zutt

927A group of scholars told me: Sīyāh al-Aswārī was at the head of Yazdegerd’s vanguard .

Then he sent him to al-Ahwāz, where he settled at al-Kalbāniyya, while Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī was besieging al-Sūs.

When he saw Islam’s ascendancy and the strength of its adherents, that al-Sūs had been conquered, and that reinforcements were arriving in succession for Abū Mūsā, he sent him this message: “We wish to enter your religion, on the terms that we fight your enemies among the Persians alongside you; that, if a disagreement arises among you, we do not fight one another; that if the Arabs fight us, you protect us from them and aid us against them; that we settle in whichever towns we choose, and join whichever of you we choose; and that we be assigned a place among those who receive the stipends, with the commander who sent you formalizing this for us.”

Abū Mūsā said: “Rather, you shall have what we have and bear what we bear.”

They said: “We are not satisfied with that.”

Abū Mūsā wrote about this to ʿUmar.

ʿUmar wrote back: “Grant them everything they have asked for.”

They set out and joined the Muslims.

They took part with Abū Mūsā in the siege of Tustar, but did not show any hostility.

He said to Sīyāh: “ʿAwn, you and your companions are not as we had supposed.”

He replied: “I tell you, our insight is not like yours, nor do we have among you kin whom we fear for and fight to protect. We entered this religion at its beginning as a precaution, although God has granted us much good.”

Then he assigned them a place among those who received the stipends.

When they reached Baṣra, they asked which tribal group was closest in lineage to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

They were told: “Banū Tamīm.”

They had intended to ally with the Azd, but left them and allied with Banū Tamīm.

Then their plots of land were laid out and they settled,

and dug their canal, which is known as the Asāwira Canal.

It is said that ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir dug it.

928Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī said: Shīrūya al-Aswārī wanted to settle among Bakr b. Wāʾil with Khālid b. al-Muʿammar and Banū Sadūs, but Sīyāh refused.

They settled among Banū Tamīm.

At that time, the Azd and ʿAbd Shams were not in Baṣra.

He said: The Sayābija joined the Asāwira. Before Islam they had been on the coasts; likewise the Zutt, who had been in the riverine lowlands following the pasture.

When the Asāwira, Zutt, and Sayābija gathered , Banū Tamīm disputed over them, eager to have them.

The Asāwira joined Banū Saʿd, and the Zutt and Sayābija joined Banū Ḥanẓala.

They stayed with them, fighting the polytheists, and went with Ibn ʿĀmir to Khurāsān. They took no part with them at the Battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, or in any of their battles, until the Day of Masʿūd.

After the Day of Masʿūd, they took part in al-Rabadha and joined Ibn al-Ashʿath in his affair.

Al-Ḥajjāj oppressed them: he demolished their houses, reduced their stipends, and exiled some of them.

He said: “Your agreement stipulated that you would not assist one of us against another.”

It has also been related that when the Asāwira withdrew to al-Kalbāniyya, Abū Mūsā sent al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād al-Ḥārithī against them, and he fought them.

Then they sought a guarantee of safety on the terms that they would submit, fight the enemy, ally with whomever they wished, and settle wherever they liked.

929They said: A group of Persian fighters who had no land joined these Asāwira. They came to them after the fighting in the regions had subsided, stayed with them, and entered Islam.

930Al-Madāʾinī said: When Yazdegerd set out for Iṣfahān, he summoned Sīyāh and sent him

to Iṣṭakhr with three hundred men, among them seventy of their leading men, and ordered him to choose whoever he wished from among the people and fighters of each town.

Then Yazdegerd followed him.

When he reached Iṣṭakhr, he sent him to al-Sūs, which Abū Mūsā was besieging.

He sent al-Hurmuzān to Tustar.

Sīyāh settled at al-Kalbāniyya.

When the people of al-Sūs learned of Yazdegerd’s situation and flight, they asked Abū Mūsā for peace, and he made peace with them.

Sīyāh remained at al-Kalbāniyya until Abū Mūsā marched to Tustar. Sīyāh then moved and settled between Rāmhurmuz and Tustar, until ʿAmmār arrived.

Sīyāh gathered the leaders who had come with him from Iṣfahān and said: “You know what we used to say: that these people would gain control of this kingdom and their mounts would graze in the īwān of Iṣṭakhr.

Their situation is unfolding before you as you see. Consider your own interests and enter their religion.”

They agreed to do so.

Shīrūya sent ten men to Abū Mūsā. They obtained a guarantee on the conditions we have described , and entered Islam.

931Someone other than al-Madāʾinī told me, from ʿAwāna, who said: The Asāwira allied with the Azd.

Then they asked which of the two groups—the Azd or Banū Tamīm—was closer in lineage to the Prophet and the caliphs, and which was nearer in reinforcements.

They were told: “Banū Tamīm.”

So they allied with them.

The leader of Banū Tamīm at that time was al-Aḥnaf b. Qays.

A group of Asāwira took part in the Battle of al-Rabadha in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr. They killed a number of men equal to their own number with arrows, and not one of them missed his shot.

As for the Sayābija, Zutt, and Andaghār, they were among the Persian forces, taken captive by them and assigned stipends; they were from the people of Sind.

Some were captives of the first expeditions.

When they heard what had happened with the Asāwira, they embraced Islam and came to Abū Mūsā, who settled them in Baṣra as he had settled the Asāwira.

932Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin told me: Yaʿqūb b. al-Ḥaḍramī told me, from Sallām, who said: al-Ḥajjāj was brought a large number of Zutt from Sind and various kinds of peoples from there, along with their families, children, and buffaloes. He settled them in the lower reaches of Kaskar.

Rūḥ said: They came to dominate the marshes and multiplied there.

Then some runaway slaves, clients of Bāhila, the retainers of Muḥammad b. Sulaymān b. ʿAlī, and others joined them and emboldened them to waylay travelers and openly defy the authorities through disobedience.

Before that, their whole aim had been to ask for a trifling thing and seize an opportunity against the people of a boat, taking from it whatever they could steal.

During some days of al-Maʾmūn’s reign, people had avoided passing through their territory, and all the goods carried by ship from Baṣra to Baghdad had stopped arriving there.

When al-Muʿtaṣim bi-Allāh became caliph, he set himself to deal with them and put a man from Khurāsān named ʿAjīf b. ʿAnbasa in charge of fighting them. He assigned him a large number of commanders and troops and withheld none of the funds he requested.

He stationed lean, fleet horses, their tails cropped, between the marshes and the City of Peace.

News of the Zutt reached him in the City of Peace within a few hours during the day or at the beginning of the night.

ʿAjīf was ordered to dam the water against them with great engineering works, until they were captured; not one of them escaped.

They were brought to the City of Peace in small boats. Some were settled at Khāniqīn, and the rest were dispersed to ʿAyn Zarba and the frontier districts.

933They said: A group of Sīyābija were then assigned to guard the treasury of Baṣra. It is said they numbered forty, and it is also said four hundred.

When Ṭalḥa b. ʿUbayd Allāh and al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām arrived in Baṣra, where ʿUthmān b. Ḥunayf al-Anṣārī had been appointed by ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, they refused to hand over the treasury until ʿAlī ﵁ arrived.

They came upon them at dawn and killed them.

ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr was in charge of their affairs, among a group who rushed at them with him.

At that time, Abū Sālima al-Zuṭṭī was in charge of the Sīyābija; he was a righteous man.

Muʿāwiya had earlier transferred some of the old Zutt and Sīyābija to the coasts of Syria and Antioch.

Al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik had also transferred some Zutt to Antioch and its environs.

934They said: ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād had taken a great many people from Bukhara captive.

It is said instead that they submitted to his terms; it is also said that he invited them to accept security and the poll tax, and they submitted to that and welcomed it.

He settled them in Baṣra.

When al-Ḥajjāj built the city of Wāsiṭ, he transferred many of them there.

Among their descendants there today are people, including Khālid al-Shāṭir, known as Ibn Mārqalā.

He said: The Andaghār are from the region of Kirmān, toward Sijistān.

Chapter 80

The districts of al-Ahwāz

935They said: During his governorship, al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba raided the market town of al-Ahwāz, when ʿUtba b. Ghazwān had departed from Baṣra at the end of the year 15 or the beginning of the year 16.

Al-Bīrūz, its dihqān, fought him, then made peace with him for a payment.

Then he broke the agreement, and Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī raided it when ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb appointed him over Baṣra after al-Mughīra.

He conquered the market town of al-Ahwāz by force and took the Tīrī canal by force. He led this campaign himself in the year 17.

936Abū Mikhnaf and al-Wāqidī said in their account: Abū Mūsā arrived in Baṣra and appointed Ziyād as his secretary. ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb then sent ʿImrān b. al-Ḥuṣayn al-Khuzāʿī to him and put him in charge of teaching the people jurisprudence and the Qurʾān, and of acting as Abū Mūsā’s deputy whenever he left Baṣra.

Abū Mūsā set out for al-Ahwāz and continued conquering district after district and canal after canal, while the Persians fled before him. He gained control of all its land except al-Sūs, Tustar, Manādhir, and Rāmhurmuz.

937al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me: Marḥūm al-ʿAṭṭār told me, from his father, from Shuways al-ʿAdawī, who said: We came to al-Ahwāz, where there were people from among the Zutt and the Asāwira. We fought them fiercely, overcame them, and defeated them. We took many captives and divided them among ourselves.

ʿUmar wrote to us: “You are not capable of cultivating the land, so release the captives in your possession and impose the land tax on them.”

We returned the captives and did not make them our property.

938They said: Abū Mūsā marched to Manādhir and besieged its people; the fighting grew fierce.

In the army was al-Muhājir b. Ziyād al-Ḥārithī, the brother of al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād b. al-Dayyān.

He intended to sell his life in battle, and he was fasting. Al-Rabīʿ said to Abū Mūsā: “Al-Muhājir has resolved to sell his life in battle while fasting.”

Abū Mūsā said: “I have resolved that every fasting man must either break his fast or not go out to fight.”

Al-Muhājir drank a mouthful of water and said: “I have fulfilled my commander’s resolve! By God, I did not drink it because I was thirsty.”

Then he went out with the warriors and fought until he was martyred.

The people of Manādhir took his head and set it up on their citadel between two battlements.

A poet said of him:

“At Manādhir, when their host surged forth, al-Muhājir went out with fine camels. The house is the house of the sons of al-Dayyān, as we know, among Āl Madhḥij, like a precious jewel.”

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī appointed al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād over Manādhir and marched to al-Sūs. Al-Rabīʿ conquered Manādhir by force, killed the fighting men, and took the children captive. Greater and Lesser Manādhir came into the hands of the Muslims, and Abū Mūsā appointed ʿĀṣim b. Qays b. al-Ṣalt al-Sulamī over them.

He appointed Samura b. Jundab al-Fazārī, the ally of the Anṣār, over the market town of al-Ahwāz.

Some said that ʿUmar wrote to Abū Mūsā while he was besieging Manādhir, ordering him to leave a deputy over it and march to al-Sūs; he left al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād.

939Saʿdawayh told me: Sharīk told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra, who said: We besieged Manādhir and took captives. ʿUmar wrote: “Manādhir is like one of the villages of al-Sawād, so return to them what you took.”

940They said: Abū Mūsā marched to al-Sūs and fought its people, then besieged them

until their provisions ran out, and they pleaded for safe conduct.

Their marzbān asked that eighty of them be granted security on condition that he open the city gate and surrender it.

He named the eighty and excluded himself from among them.

Abū Mūsā ordered that his neck be struck. He did not harm the eighty, but killed the remaining combatants, seized the property, and took the children captive.

Abū Mūsā saw a chamber in their citadel with a curtain over it. He asked about it and was told: “Inside is the body of Daniel the Prophet ﷺ and upon God’s prophets and messengers. They had suffered a drought and asked the people of Babylon to send him to them,

so that they could pray for rain by means of him, and they did so.

Nebuchadnezzar had taken Daniel captive and brought him to Babylon, where he died.

Abū Mūsā wrote about this to ʿUmar.

ʿUmar wrote back: “Shroud him and bury him.”

Abū Mūsā dammed a river until its water had receded, buried him, and then let the water flow over him.

941Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: Marwān b. Muʿāwiya told us, from Ḥumayd al-Ṭawīl, from Ḥabīb, from Khālid b. Zayd al-Muzanī, whose eye had been injured at al-Sūs, who said: We besieged its city, with Abū Mūsā as our commander, and we faced great hardship.

Then its dihqān made terms with him: he would open the city to him and grant security to one hundred of his people. He did so and received Abū Mūsā’s pledge.

He said to him: “Set them apart.”

He began setting them apart, while Abū Mūsā said to his companions: “I hope God will make him overcome himself.”

He set apart the hundred and the enemy of God remained.

Abū Mūsā ordered that he be killed.

He cried out: “Wait! I will give you a great deal of money!” But Abū Mūsā refused and had him beheaded. 942. They said: Abū Mūsā made a truce with the people of Rāmhurmuz. When their truce expired, he sent Abū Maryam al-Ḥanafī to them, who made peace with them for eight hundred thousand dirhams.

942Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin told me: Yaʿqūb told me, from Abū ʿĀṣim al-Rāmhurmuzī, who had reached a hundred years of age or nearly so, who said: Abū Mūsā made peace with the people of Rāmhurmuz for eight hundred thousand or nine hundred thousand.

Then they treacherously broke the agreement, and it was later conquered by force; Abū Mūsā conquered it in the last days of his life.

943They said: Abū Mūsā also conquered Saraq on terms like those of the peace agreement with Rāmhurmuz.

Then they treacherously broke the agreement, and he sent Ḥāritha b. Badr al-Ghudanī against it with a large army, but he did not conquer it.

When ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir arrived, he conquered it by force.

Ḥāritha later governed Saraq.

Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī said of him:

“O Ḥār b. Badr, you have been appointed to office, so be a rat there, cheating and stealing. For all people are either liars, saying whatever you like, or truthful. They make statements based on suspicion and conjecture; if asked to produce proof, they cannot prove them. Do not be incapable, for incapacity is the worst habit; your share of the wealth of the two Iraqs is theft.”

When the poem reached Ḥāritha, he said:

“May the God of mankind reward you with the best reward, for you spoke well and gave sound counsel. You advised me to act with resolve; had you advised otherwise, you would have found me disobeying your command.”

944They said: Abū Mūsā marched to Tustar, where the enemy’s strength was concentrated and their leaders were gathered.

He wrote to ʿUmar asking for reinforcements.

ʿUmar wrote to ʿAmmār b. Yāsir, ordering him to march to him with the people of Kūfa.

ʿAmmār sent Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī ahead, then marched until he reached Tustar. On his right wing—that is, Abū Mūsā’s right wing—was al-Barāʾ b. Mālik, the brother of Anas b. Mālik,

On his left wing was Mujazʾa b. Thawr al-Sadūsī; over the cavalry was Anas b. Mālik; on ʿAmmār’s right wing was al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib al-Anṣārī; on his left wing was Ḥudhayfa b. al-Yamān al-ʿAbsī; over his cavalry was Qarẓa b. Kaʿb al-Anṣārī; and over his infantry was al-Nuʿmān b. Muqarrin al-Muzanī. The people of Tustar fought them fiercely.

The people of Kūfa charged until they reached the gate of Tustar.

Al-Barāʾ b. Mālik fought them at the gate until he was martyred ﵀. Al-Hurmuzān and his companions entered the city in a sorry state. Nine hundred of them had been killed in the battle, and their heads were later struck off.

Al-Hurmuzān was from Mihr Jānaqadh, and had been present at the battle of Jalūlāʾ with the Persians.

Then a man from among the non-Arabs sought safe conduct from the Muslims on condition that he guide them to the vulnerable point of the polytheists.

He became Muslim and stipulated that a stipend be assigned to his son and to him.

Abū Mūsā made an agreement with him on

that basis, and sent with him a man from Shaybān named Ashras b. ʿAwf. He crossed the Dujayl with him over a ridge of stones, then brought him up to the city and showed him al-Hurmuzān, then returned him to the army.

Abū Mūsā called for forty men to go with Mujazʾa b. Thawr and sent two hundred men after them. This was at night, and the man who had sought safe conduct led them.

He brought them into the city, where they killed the guards and raised the takbīr on the city wall.

When al-Hurmuzān heard them, he fled to his citadel, where his treasury and property were kept.

In the morning Abū Mūsā crossed over and entered the city, taking control of it.

Al-Hurmuzān said: “Only one of those among us who saw their fortunes rise and ours decline could have shown the Arabs our vulnerable point.”

The Persian began killing his own family and children and throwing them into the Dujayl, fearing the Arabs might capture them.

Al-Hurmuzān asked for safe conduct, but Abū Mūsā refused to grant it except on ʿUmar’s judgment.

He submitted to that condition.

Abū Mūsā killed those in the citadel who had no guarantee of safety, and took al-Hurmuzān to ʿUmar, who spared his life and assigned him a stipend.

Then he was accused of aiding Abū Luʾluʾa, the slave of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba, in the killing of ʿUmar ﵁

ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar said: “Come with me; let us go look at a horse of mine.”

He went, with ʿUbayd Allāh behind him. ʿUbayd Allāh struck him with a sword while he was unaware and killed him.

945Abū ʿUbayda told us: Marwān b. Muʿāwiya told us, from Ḥumayd, from Anas, who said: We besieged Tustar. Al-Hurmuzān came down, and I was the one who brought him to ʿUmar; Abū Mūsā had sent me.

ʿUmar said to him: “Speak.”

He said: “Am I to speak as a living man or as a dead one?” He said: “Speak; there is no harm.”

Al-Hurmuzān said: “We non-Arabs, so long as God left us and you apart, would keep you at a distance and kill you.

But when God was with you, we had no two hands against you.”

ʿUmar said: “What do you say, Anas?” I said: “I left behind me a formidable force and a savage enemy.

If you kill him, the people will despair of staying alive, and their force will become stronger. If you spare him, the people will hope to live.”

ʿUmar said: “Anas! Glory be to God—[what of] the slayers of al-Barāʾ b. Mālik and Mujazʾa b. Thawr al-Sadūsī?”

I said: “You have no right to kill him.”

He said: “Why not? Did you take a payment from him?” I said: “No, but you told him, ‘There is no harm.’”

He said: “When did I say that? You must bring someone with you who witnessed it, or I shall begin by punishing you.”

He said: “I left him, and al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām had remembered what I remembered.

He testified for me.

So he released al-Hurmuzān.

He became Muslim, and ʿUmar assigned him a stipend.”

946Isḥāq b. Abī Isrāʾīl told me: Ibn al-Mubārak told us, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, who said: “I spared you the trouble: Tastur had made a peace agreement, but then broke it.

The Emigrants marched against it , killed the fighting men, and took the children captive. They remained in the hands of their masters until ʿUmar wrote: ‘Release those in your possession.’

He said: Abū Mūsā marched against Jundaysābūr. Its people were disarmed, and they asked for a guarantee of safety. He made peace with them on condition that he kill none of them, take none captive, and not interfere with their property, except for their weapons.

Then a group of its people set out for al-Kalbāniyya. Abū Mūsā sent al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād against them; he killed them and conquered al-Kalbāniyya.

The asāwira asked for a guarantee of safety, and Abū Mūsā granted them one, whereupon they embraced Islam.

It is said that they had asked for a guarantee of safety before that, joined Abū Mūsā, and were present at Tustar.

God knows best.

947ʿUmar b. Ḥafṣ al-ʿUmarī told me, from Abū Ḥudhayfa, from Abū al-Ashhab, from Abū Rajāʾ, who said: “Al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād conquered al-Thaybān by force on Abū Mūsā’s behalf.
