Then they broke their agreement, and Munjūf b. Thawr al-Sadūsī conquered it.

He said: Among the places ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir conquered were Sanbīl and al-Zuṭṭ. Their people had apostatized, and Kurds from among these Kurds gathered there.

Aydhaj was conquered after fierce fighting.

Abū Mūsā conquered al-Sūs, Tastur, and Dūrq by force.”

Al-Madāʾinī said: Thābit b. Dhī al-Ḥurra al-Ḥimyarī conquered the fortress of Dhī al-Rināq.

948Al-Madāʾinī told me, from his authorities, and ʿUmar b. Shabba, from Mujālid b. Yaḥyā, that Muṣʿab b. al-Zubayr appointed Muṭarrif b. Saydān al-Bāhilī, one of the Banū Jiʾāwa, as chief of his police during one of the periods when he governed Iraq on behalf of his brother ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.

Muṭarrif brought before him al-Nābī b. Ziyād b. Ẓabyān, one of the Banū ʿĀʾish b. Mālik b. Taym Allāh b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUkāba, and a man from Banū Numayr, who had committed highway robbery. He killed al-Nābī, flogged the Numayrī, and let him go.

When Muṭarrif was dismissed from the police and appointed governor of al-Ahwāz , ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād b. Ẓabyān raised a force against him and set out to attack him.

They met and faced one another, with a river between them. Muṭarrif b. Saydān crossed it, and Ibn Ẓabyān swiftly attacked him, stabbed him, and killed him.

Muṣʿab sent Makram b. Muṭarrif to pursue him.

He marched until he reached the place now known as ʿAskar Makram, but did not encounter Ibn Ẓabyān.

Ibn Ẓabyān joined ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān and fought Muṣʿab alongside him; he killed Muṣʿab and cut off his head.

ʿAskar Makram was named after this Makram b. Muṭarrif.

Al-Buʿayth al-Sukkarī said:

“We gave Ibn Saydān a draught in a brimming cup, Which sufficed us; the best affair is one that suffices.”

It is also said that ʿAskar Makram was named after Makram b. al-Fizr, one of the Banū Jaʿūna b. al-Ḥārith b. Numayr.

Al-Ḥajjāj had sent him to fight Kharzād b. Bās when the latter rebelled, went to Aydhaj, and fortified himself in a fortress known by his name.

When the siege grew long, Kharzād came down secretly in disguise to join ʿAbd al-Malik.

Makram captured him, with two pearls in his qalansuwa, took him, and sent him to al-Ḥajjāj, who struck off his head.

949They related that near ʿAskar Makram there was an ancient village, to which he joined the building

afterward; then it continued to be enlarged until it grew extensive.

All of that was called ʿAskar Makram, and today it is a congregational city.

950Abū Masʿūd told me, from ʿAwāna, who said: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr appointed Ḥamza b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr governor of Baṣra.

He went out to al-Ahwāz, and when he saw its mountain, he said: “It is like Quʿayqiʿān.”

951Al-Thawrī said: In Persian, al-Ahwāz was named Hūz Masīr.

It was called al-Akhwāz, but people changed it and said al-Ahwāz.

He cited these verses by a Bedouin:

“Do not return me to al-Akhwāz a second time, And to Quʿayqiʿān, which lies beside the market, And the Nahr Baṭṭ, which keeps me awake at night, With mosquitoes biting without mercy. What did his soul promise him, out of desire, From al-Ḥuṣaynī or ʿAmr, truthfully?”

He said: Nahr al-Baṭṭ was a river beside which there were pastures for ducks. The common people said “Nahr Baṭṭ,” just as they said “Dār Baṭṭīkh.”

I heard someone say that the river belonged to a woman called al-Baṭṭiʾa, so it was named after her, and then part of the name was dropped.

952Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh, from al-Zuhrī, who said: “ʿUmar conquered al-Sawād and al-Ahwāz by force.

ʿUmar was asked about dividing

that. He said: ‘What, then, is the share of those Muslims who come after us?’ He left them in the status of protected people.

953Al-Madāʾinī told me, from ʿAlī b. Ḥammād and Suḥaym b. Ḥafṣ and others, who said: Abū al-Mukhtār Yazīd b. Qays b. Yazīd b. al-Ṣaʿq said some verses in which he appealed to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ against the officials of al-Ahwāz and others:

“Convey a message to the Commander of the Faithful, For you are God’s trustee in what is forbidden and what is commanded. You are God’s trustee over us; whoever is Trustworthy to the Lord of the Throne will have his breast made safe. Do not let the people of the districts and villages Enjoy God’s wealth amid abundant hides. Send for al-Ḥajjāj and examine his accounts, And send for Juzʾ, and send for Bishr. Do not forget either of the two Nāfiʿs, Nor Ibn Ghulāb, one of the chiefs of Banū Naṣr. ʿĀṣim is no empty purse among them, And that man in the market is a client of Banū Badr. Send for al-Nuʿmān and examine his accounts, And the in-law of Banū Ghazwān—for I am well informed. And Shibl: ask him about the wealth; and Ibn Muḥarrish, For he was well known among the people of the districts. Divide their wealth, may my family be your ransom; they Will be content if you divide half from them. Do not summon me to testify, for I Am absent, but I see the age’s marvels. We return when they return, and raid when they raid; How could they have wealth when we are not people of wealth? When the merchant from Dār brings a marten pelt Of musk, it wafts among their forelocks.”

ʿUmar divided the wealth of the men whom Abū al-Mukhtār had named, taking half from each, until he took one sandal and left the other.

Abū Bakra was among them and said: “I have done nothing for you.”

He replied: “Your brother is in charge of the treasury and the tithes of al-Ubulla, and he gives you money to trade with.”

He took ten thousand from him.

It is said that he divided half of his wealth with him.

He said: The al-Ḥajjāj mentioned was al-Ḥajjāj b. ʿAtīk al-Thaqafī, who was in charge of the Euphrates.

Juzʾ b. Muʿāwiya, al-Aḥnaf’s uncle, was in charge of Suraq.

Bishr b. al-Muḥtafiz was in charge of Jundaysābūr.

The two Nāfiʿs were Nufayʿ, Abū Bakra, and his brother Nāfiʿ b. al-Ḥārith b. Kalada.

Ibn Ghulāb was Khālid b. al-Ḥārith of Banū Dahmān; he was in charge of the treasury at Iṣfahān.

ʿĀṣim b. Qays b. al-Ṣalt al-Sulamī was in charge of Manādhir.

The man in the market was Samura b. Jundab, in charge of the market of al-Ahwāz.

Al-Nuʿmān b. ʿAdī b. Naḍla b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. Ḥarthān, one of the Banū ʿAdī b. Kaʿb b. Luʾayy, was in charge of the districts of the Tigris.

He is the one who said:

“Who will tell the beautiful woman that her lover At Maysān drinks from glass and a clay jar? Whenever you wish, the landowners of a village sing to me, And a songstress dances to every stride. Perhaps the Commander of the Faithful would be displeased That we carouse in the dilapidated palace.”

When ʿUmar heard his poem, he said: “By God, that does displease me.”

He dismissed him.

The in-law of Banū Ghazwān was Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd al-Sulamī.

He was married to the daughter of ʿUtba b. Ghazwān.

He was in charge of the land of Baṣra and its alms.

Shibl b. Maʿbad al-Bajalī, later al-Aḥmasī, was in charge of collecting the spoils.

Ibn Muḥarrish, Abū Maryam al-Ḥanafī, was in charge of Rām Hurmuz.

ʿAwsaja b. Ziyād the secretary said : “The Commander of the Faithful al-Rashīd granted ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Mahdī a sharecropping lease on land in al-Ahwāz.

Some doubt arose about it, so a group brought the matter to al-Maʾmūn. He ordered it examined and investigated: whatever was free of doubt he approved, and whatever he doubted he designated as the doubtful matter.

This is well known in al-Ahwāz.”

Chapter 81

The districts of Fārs and Kirmān

954They said: Al-ʿAlāʾ b. al-Ḥaḍramī, ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb’s governor in al-Baḥrayn, sent Harthama b. ʿUrfaja al-Bāriqī, of the Azd, who conquered an island in the sea toward Fārs.

Then ʿUmar wrote to al-ʿAlāʾ, ordering him to reinforce ʿUtba b. Farqad al-Sulamī with him, and he did so.

Then ʿUmar appointed ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī over al-Baḥrayn and ʿUmān. He subdued them, and their people’s obedience was secured. He sent his brother al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ across the sea to Fārs with a large army of ʿAbd al-Qays, the Azd, Tamīm, Banū Nājiya, and others. He conquered the island of Abrakāwān.

Then he went to Tūj, which is in the land of Ardashīr Khurra. The meaning of Ardashīr Khurra is “the glory of Ardashīr.” According to the account of Abū Mikhnaf, ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ himself crossed the sea to Fārs, landed at Tūj, conquered it, built mosques there, made it a residence for the Muslims, and settled there ʿAbd al-Qays and others.

From there he would raid Arrajān, which adjoins it.

Then he departed from Fārs for ʿUmān and al-Baḥrayn, because of ʿUmar’s letter to him about that, and left his brother al-Ḥakam as his deputy.

Someone other than Abū Mikhnaf said that al-Ḥakam conquered Tūj and settled Muslims there from ʿAbd al-Qays and others in the year nineteen.

955They said: Shahrak, the marzbān of Fārs and its governor, was more alarmed than ever by the Arabs’ arrival in Fārs, and it weighed heavily on him, and news reached him of the damage they inflicted, their might, and their victories over

all of the enemy they encountered.

He assembled a great force and marched in person until he reached Rāshahr in the land of Sābūr, near Tūj. Al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ came out against him, with Sawwār b. Hammām al-ʿAbdī at the head of his advance guard.

They fought fiercely.

There was a wadi there, which Shahrak had assigned to a man from among his captains with a group of men, ordering him to kill any of his companions who fled across it.

A brave man from among the asāwira came fleeing from the battle.

The man intended to kill him.

The asāwira said to him: “Do not kill me; we are only fighting a people who are granted victory, with God on their side.”

He placed a stone down and shot it, splitting it. Then he said: “Do you see this arrow that split the stone? By God, if it were shot at one of them, it would not even scratch him.”

He said: “I must kill you.”

While this was happening, news arrived that Shahrak had been killed.

The one who killed him was Sawwār b. Hammām al-ʿAbdī. He charged him and struck him with a spear, striking him so that he fell from his horse, then struck him with his sword until he breathed his last.

Shahrak’s son charged Sawwār and killed him. God routed the polytheists, and Rāshahr was conquered by force. In its difficulty and the great blessing it brought the Muslims, that day was like the day of al-Qādisiyya.

ʿAmr b. al-Ahtam al-Tamīmī carried the news of the victory to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, saying:

“I came swiftly to the Imam to tell him The true account of the ʿAbdī, Sawwār: A most valiant man, auspicious in his fortune, Put to use in God’s cause, a bold warrior.”

Some people of Tūj said that Tūj was made a garrison town after Shahrak was killed.

God knows best.

956They said: Then ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ wrote to ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ ordering him to go to Fārs.

He left his brother al-Mughīra in charge of his post. It is said that it was Ḥafṣ b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ.

He was resolute.

He arrived at Tūj and settled there.

He would raid from there and then return to it.

ʿUmar wrote to Abū Mūsā, who was in Baṣra, ordering him to support ʿUthmān b. Abī al-

al-ʿĀṣī and assist him. He would raid Fārs from Baṣra and then return to it. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī sent Hurm b. Ḥayyān al-ʿAbdī to a fortress called Shabīr, which he took by force after a siege and fighting. Some say: Hurm took the fortress of al-Satūj by force, while ʿUthmān took Khurra from Sābūr and conquered it and its surrounding land, after its inhabitants fought him, under a treaty requiring them to pay the jizya and land tax and to be sincere toward the Muslims. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī took Kāzarūn from Sābūr and gained control of its land. ʿUthmān also took al-Nūbandajān from Sābūr and gained control of it. Abū Mūsā and ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī joined forces at the end of ʿUmar’s caliphate ﵁ and took Arrajān by treaty, in return for the jizya and land tax. They took Shīrāz, which is in the land of Ardashīr Khurra, on condition that its people be protected subjects who paid the land tax, except for whoever among them wished to leave; they were not to be killed or enslaved. They took Sīnaz in the land of Ardashīr Khurra, leaving its people to cultivate the land. ʿUthmān took the fortress of Junāba under a guarantee of safety. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī came to Dārābjird, where their sacred pavilion was their place of worship and religion, and it was under the charge of the herbad. The herbad made a treaty with him in return for money he gave him, and on the condition that all the people of Dārābjird would have the same status as the people of Persia whose lands had been conquered. A force gathered for him in the region of Jahram, and he dispersed them and conquered the land of Jهرم. ʿUthmān came to Fasā, and its chief made a treaty with him on terms like those of the treaty of Dārābjird. It is said that the herbad also made a treaty on its behalf. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī came to the city of Sābūr in the year 23, though it is said, in the year 24, before ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān appointed Abū Mūsā governor of Baṣra.

[The people of Sābūr] found its inhabitants in fear of the Muslims. Shahrak’s brother saw in a dream that a man from among the Arabs entered upon him and stripped him of his shirt. This unsettled his heart; he held out for a little while, then sought a guarantee of safety and a treaty. ʿUthmān made a treaty with him on the condition that no one be killed or taken captive, that he be granted protected status, and that he pay money promptly. Then the people of Sābūr broke their treaty and betrayed it . It was taken by force in the year 26; Abū Mūsā took it, with ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī at the head of his vanguard. 957. Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā and others said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ordered al-Jārūd al-ʿAbdī in the year 22 to be sent to the fortresses of Persia. When he was between Khurra and Shīrāz, he fell behind his companions at a mountain pass there before dawn to relieve himself. He had a waterskin with him. A group of Kurds surrounded him and killed him. That pass was called the Pass of al-Jārūd. 958. They said: When ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz was appointed governor of Baṣra by ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, after Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, he marched to Iṣṭakhr in the year 28, and Māhak made a treaty with him on behalf of its people. Then he set out for Jūr. When he had left it, they broke the treaty and killed his governor there. After he took Jūr, he turned back against them and took it. 959. They said: Hurm b. Ḥayyān was stationed at Jūr, a city in Ardashīr Khurra. The Muslims would attack it and then withdraw; they would attack Iṣṭakhr and raid districts that kept rebelling against them. When Ibn ʿĀmir came down there, they fought him and then fortified themselves, but he took it by the sword, by force, in the year 29. Ibn ʿĀmir also took Kāriyān and Fashajātan, which is al-Fīshajān of Dārābjird. These two had not been included in the treaty of the herbad, and they had rebelled.

960A group of scholars told me that Jūr was raided for several years, but could not be taken until Ibn ʿĀmir conquered it. The reason for its conquest was that one of the Muslims stood praying one night, with a bag containing bread and meat beside him. A dog came, dragged it away, and ran with it until it entered the city through a hidden entrance. The Muslims then kept watch on that entrance until they entered through it and took the city. 961. They said: When ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir had finished taking Jūr, he turned against the people of Iṣṭakhr and took it by force after fierce fighting and bombardment with mangonels. He killed forty thousand Persians there and exterminated most of the prominent families and leading asāwira, who had taken refuge there . Some transmitters say that Ibn ʿĀmir returned to Iṣṭakhr when he heard that they had broken their treaty and took it. Then he proceeded to Jūr, with Hurm b. Ḥayyān at the head of his vanguard, and took it. 962. Al-Ḥasan b. ʿUthmān al-Ziyādī related that the people of Iṣṭakhr betrayed their treaty during ʿAlī’s governorship of Iraq by ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbbās ﵄ and that he took it. 963. al-ʿAbbās b. Hishām told me, from his father, from Abū Mikhnaf, who said: Ibn ʿĀmir set out for Iṣṭakhr and sent ʿUbayd Allāh b. Maʿmar al-Taymī at the head of his vanguard. The people of Iṣṭakhr Barāma-jird met him and fought him; they killed him, and he was buried in the garden of Barāma-jird. The news reached Ibn ʿĀmir, who came swiftly until he engaged them. Abū Barza Naḍla b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Aslamī was on his right wing, Maʿqil b. Yasār al-Muzanī on his left wing, ʿImrān b. Ḥuṣayn al-Khuzāʿī with the cavalry, and Khālid b. al-Muʿammar al-Dhuhlī with the infantry. He fought them and routed them, driving them into Iṣṭakhr. God granted him its conquest by force, and he killed there about one hundred thousand. He came to Dārābjird and took it; it had rebelled. Then he sent toward Kirmān. 964. ʿUmar al-Nāqid told me: Marwān b. Muʿāwiya al-Fazārī related to us, from ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal, from Fuḍayl b. Zayd al-Raqāshī, who said: We besieged Shahrīyāj for a whole month. We thought we would take it that very day. One day we fought its people and returned to our camp, while a slave whom they thought had deserted, stayed behind. He wrote them a guarantee of safety and shot it to them on an arrow. He said: We went out to fight, but they had come out of their fortress and said, “Here is your guarantee of safety!” We wrote about this to ʿUmar, and he wrote to us: “The Muslim slave is one of the Muslims; his guarantee of safety is like theirs, so let him carry out his guarantee.” We carried it out. 965. al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: Abū al-Naḍr related to us, from Shuʿba, from ʿĀṣim, from al-Fuḍayl, who said: We were arrayed against the enemy at Sīrāf. Then he mentioned something similar. 966. Saʿdawayh related to us: ʿAbbād b. al-ʿAwwām related to us, from ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal, from al-Fuḍayl b. Zayd al-Raqāshī, who said: The Muslims besieged a fortress. A slave wrote a guarantee of safety and shot it to them in an arrowhead. The Muslims said, “His guarantee of safety is of no account.” The people said, “We do not distinguish a free man from a slave.” This was written to ʿUmar, and he wrote: “The Muslims’ slave is one of them; his guarantee of safety is like theirs.” 967. A man from among the people of Persia informed me that the fortress of Sīrāf is called Sūriyānj. The Arabs named it Shahrīyāj. In Fasā there is a fortress known as Khirsha b. Masʿūd of Banū Tamīm, then of Banū Sharqa. He was with Ibn al-Ashʿath and fortified himself in this fortress, then obtained a guarantee of safety and died at Wāsiṭ. He has descendants in Fasā.

Chapter 82

Kirmān

968As for Kirmān, ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī encountered its marzbān on the island of Abrakāwān while he was in a light detachment, and killed him. The position of the people of Kirmān was weakened and their hearts were shaken. When Ibn ʿĀmir arrived in Fārs, he sent Mujāshiʿ b. Masʿūd al-Sulamī to Kirmān in pursuit of Yazdegerd. He came to Bīmend, where his army perished. Then, when Ibn ʿĀmir set out for Khurāsān, he appointed Mujāshiʿ over Kirmān. He took Bīmend by force and spared its people, granting them a guarantee of safety. There is a palace there known as Mujāshiʿ’s Palace. Mujāshiʿ took Barūkhrawa, then came to Shīrjān, the city of Kirmān, and stayed there a few days. Its people were fortified, and cavalry had come out against them. He fought them, took it by force, and left a man there. Then many of its people left. Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī had sent al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād, who took the area around Shīrjān and made treaties with the people of Bam and al-Andaghār. Its people feared and broke their treaty, so Majāmiʿ b. Masʿūd took it. He took Jīruft by force and subdued Kirmān as he marched through it. He came to al-Qafṣ, and a large number of people who had left Persia gathered against him at Hurmuz . He fought them, defeated them, and prevailed over them. Many of the people of Kirmān fled by sea; some reached Makrān and some went to Sijistān. The Arabs were assigned their dwellings and lands; they cultivated them, paid the tithe on them, and dug subterranean channels in some places. Al-Ḥajjāj appointed Qaṭan b. Qubayṣa b. Mukhāriq al-Hilālī over Fārs and Kirmān, and he was who reached a river, but his companions could not cross it. He said, “Whoever crosses will receive a thousand dirhams.” They crossed, and he fulfilled his promise to them. That was the first day on which the prize was so called. The poet, al-Jaḥḥāf b. Ḥakīm, said: “May my family and property be ransom for the noblest, the Banū Hilāl, despite their shortcomings! They established the prizes among Maʿadd, and through the passage of nights it became another custom. Their lances increase beyond eight and ten when the spear-shafts clash.” Qubayṣa b. Mukhāriq was one of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. The poet said of Qaṭan: “How many an emir have I struck down, his favor having been my share, and another whose emirate brought me only grief. Is Qaṭan anything but like those who came before him? So patience with what Qaṭan brings one day.” 969. They said: Ibn Ziyād appointed Shurayk b. al-Aʿwar al-Ḥārithī, who was Shurayk b. al-Ḥārith, over Kirmān. Yazīd b. Ziyād b. Rabīʿa b. Mufarrigh al-Ḥimyarī wrote to him, and he granted him land in Kirmān, which he sold after Ibn Ziyād fled from Baṣra. Al-Ḥajjāj appointed al-Ḥakam b. Nuhayk al-Hujaymī over Kirmān, after having appointed him over Fārs. He built the mosque of Arrajān and its governor’s residence.

Chapter 83

Sijistān and Kābul

970ʿAlī b. Muḥammad and others told me that ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz b. Rabīʿa b. Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams set out for Khurāsān in the year 30. He encamped his army on the side of Shīrjān in Kirmān . He sent al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād b. Anas b. al-Dayyān al-Ḥārithī to Sijistān. He marched until he camped at al-Fahraj. Then he crossed the desert, which was seventy-five farsakhs, and reached the rural district of Zāliq. Zāliq was five farsakhs from Sijistān, and Zāliq was a fortress. He raided its people on the day of Mihragān and seized their dihqān. The latter ransomed himself by planting a lance and covering it with gold and silver, and the dihqān made a treaty with him to spare his life. 971. Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: He made a treaty with him on the condition that his town would have the same status as some of the lands conquered in Fārs and Kirmān. Then he came to a village called Karkūya, five miles from Zāliq; its people made a treaty with him and did not fight. Then he camped in a rural district called Haysūn. Its people provided him with lodging and made a treaty with him without fighting. Then he came to Zāliq and took guides from there to Zarang. He marched until he camped at Hindmand and crossed a valley from which a stream called Nūq issues. He came to Zūsht, two-thirds of a mile from Zarang. Its people came out against him and fought fiercely, and men among the Muslims were struck down. Then the Muslims charged again and routed them, driving them into the city after killing many of them.

Then al-Rabīʿ came to Nāsharūdh, a village. He fought its people and defeated them. There ʿAbd al-Raḥmān captured Abū Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the man who had written for al-Ḥajjāj in place of Zād Nafrukhh b. Nayrī, and who administered the Iraqi land tax for Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik and his mother. A woman of Ibn Tamīm, from Banū Murra b. ʿUbayd b. Muqāʿis b. ʿAmr b. Kaʿb b. Saʿd b. Zayd b. Tamīm, named ʿAbla, bought him. Then he proceeded from Nāsharūdh to Sharwādh, a village. He gained control of it and captured there the ancestor of Ibrāhīm b. Bassām, who became the property of Ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī. Then he besieged the city of Zarang, after its people had fought him. Its marzbān, Parwīz, sent to ask him for a guarantee of safety so that he could make a treaty with him . He ordered one of the corpses to be brought and placed for him. He sat on it and leaned against another, and seated his companions on the corpses. Al-Rabīʿ was dark-skinned, wide-mouthed, and tall. When the marzbān saw him, he was awed, and made a treaty with him for a thousand young servants, each with a gold cup. Al-Rabīʿ entered the city. Then he came to Sanārūdh, a valley, crossed it, and came to the two villages. There was Rustam’s horse-station. They fought him, but he prevailed. Then he arrived in Zarang and stayed there for two years. Then Ibn ʿĀmir came and left there as his deputy a man from Banū al-Ḥārith b. Kaʿb; they expelled him and shut its gates. Al-Rabīʿ’s governorship lasted two and a half years. During this governorship he took forty thousand captives. His secretary was al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. Then Ibn ʿĀmir appointed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samura b. Ḥabīb b. ʿAbd Shams over Sijistān. He came to Zarang and besieged its marzbān in his palace on one of their feast days. He made a treaty with him for two million dirhams and two thousand young servants. Ibn Samura gained control of the lands between Zarang and Kash, on the Indian side. From the direction of the route to al-Rukhkhaj, he gained control of the territory between him and the land of al-Dāwar. When he reached the land of al-Dāwar, he besieged them on Mount al-Zūr, then made a treaty with them. The number of Muslims with him was eight thousand. Each man received four thousand. He entered upon al-Zūr, an idol of gold with two ruby eyes.

dirhams and two thousand serving boys. Ibn Samura gained control of the territory between Zaranj and Kash on the Indian side. From the direction of the road to al-Rukhkhaj, he gained control of the territory between it and the lands of al-Dāwar. When he reached the lands of al-Dāwar, he besieged them on Mount al-Zūr, then made peace with them. The number of Muslims with him was eight thousand. Each man received four thousand [dirhams]. He entered upon al-Zūr, an idol of gold whose eyes were two rubies. He cut off its hand and took the two rubies. Then he said to the marzbān, “Keep the gold and jewels; I only wanted to show you that it can neither harm nor benefit.” He conquered Bist and Zābul under a treaty.

972al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me; Wakīʿ told us, from Ḥammād b. Zayd, from Yaḥyā b. ʿAtīq, from Muḥammad b. Sīrīn, that he disapproved of taking captives from Zābul and said, “ʿUthmān made a treaty with them.” Wakīʿ said, “He concluded a pact with them, which is below a treaty.”

973They said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān came to Zaranj and stayed there until ʿUthmān’s affairs became unsettled. Then he appointed Amīr b. Aḥmar al-Yashkurī as his deputy and departed from Sijistān. Ziyād al-Aʿjam says of Amīr:

“Had it not been for Amīr, Yashkur would have perished— And Yashkur is doomed in any case.”

Then the people of Zaranj expelled Amīr and shut its gates. When ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib had finished with the Battle of the Camel, Ḥasaka set out ...

b. ʿAttāb al-Ḥabṭī and ʿImrān b. al-Fuḍayl al-Barjamī, among the Arab vagabonds, until they reached Zāliq, whose people had broken their agreement. They seized property there and took captive the grandfather of al-Bukhturī al-Aṣamm, Ibn Mujāhid, the client of Shaybān. Then they came to Zaranj, whose marzbān feared them and made peace with them, and they entered it. The rajaz poet said:

“Give Sijistān glad tidings of hunger and war, With Ibn al-Fuḍayl and the Arab vagabonds; Neither silver nor gold will avail them.”

ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib sent ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Juzʾ al-Ṭāʾī to Sijistān, but Ḥasaka killed him. ʿAlī said, “I shall kill four thousand of the Ḥabṭīs.” He was told, “The Ḥabṭīs do not number five hundred.”

974Abū Mikhnaf said: ʿAlī ﵁ sent ʿAwn b. Jaʿda b. Hubayra al-Makhzūmī to Sijistān. Bahdhalī, the Ṭāʾī bandit, killed him on the road to Iraq. ʿAlī wrote to ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās, ordering him to appoint a man over Sijistān with four thousand men. He dispatched Rubʿī b. al-Kaʾs al-ʿAnbarī with four thousand. Al-Ḥuṣayn b. Abī al-Ḥurr went with him—and Abū al-Ḥurr’s name was Mālik b. al-Khashkhāsh al-ʿAnbarī—as did Thāt b. Dhī al-Ḥurra al-Ḥimyarī. Thāt was at the head of the vanguard. When they arrived in Sijistān, Ḥasaka fought them, and they killed him. Rubʿī took control of the country. Their rajaz poet said:

“We are those who stormed Sijistān, Against Ibn ʿAttāb and the army of Satan; The noble ʿAbd al-Raḥmān leads us. In the illuminating Furqān we found That we must not ally ourselves with the party of Ibn ʿAffān.”

Thāt was called ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Fīrūz Ḥuṣayn was affiliated with Ḥuṣayn b. Abī al-Ḥurr. This is the one from among those taken captive in Sijistān. Then, when Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān came to power, he appointed Ibn ʿĀmir over Baṣra. He appointed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samura over Sijistān. He came there with ʿAbbād b. al-Ḥuṣayn al-Ḥabṭī as his chief of police. Among the notables with him were ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Maʿmar al-Taymī, ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī, Qaṭarī b. al-Fujāʾa, and al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra. He would raid a land whose people had become unbelievers, conquering it by force or making peace with its people, until he reached Kabul. When he arrived there, he encamped and besieged its people for months. He fought them and attacked them with a mangonel until a great breach was made. ʿAbbād b. al-Ḥuṣayn spent a night at the breach, thrusting with his spear against the polytheists until morning, and they could not manage to close it. Ibn Khāzim fought alongside him there. When morning came, the unbelievers came out to fight the Muslims. Ibn Khāzim struck an elephant they had with them, and it fell across the gate through which they had come out, so they could not close it. The Muslims entered by force. Abū Mikhnaf said: It was al-Muhallab who hamstrung the elephant. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī used to say, “I never thought one man could stand in the place of a thousand until I saw ʿAbbād b. al-Ḥuṣayn.”

975They said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samura sent ʿUmar b. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Maʿmar and al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra with news of the conquest. Then ʿAbd al-Raḥmān set out and crossed the Wādī Nasl. Then he came to Khuwāsh and Qūzān in Bist and conquered them by force. He marched to Razān; its people fled, and he took control of it. Then he marched to Khushk, whose people made peace with him.

Then he came to al-Rukhkhaj. They fought him, but he defeated them and conquered it. Then he marched to Dhābilistān. They fought him, having broken their agreement, but he conquered it and took captives. He came to Kabul, whose people had broken their agreement, and conquered it. Then Muʿāwiya appointed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samura over Sijistān on his behalf and sent him his commission. He remained over it until Ziyād arrived in Baṣra. Ziyād confirmed him in office for some months, then appointed al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād. Ibn Samura died in Baṣra in the year fifty, and Ziyād performed the funeral prayer over him. He was the one to whom the Prophet ﷺ said: “Do not ask for authority. If it is given to you without your asking, you will be helped in it; but if it is given to you upon your asking, you will be left to it. If you swear an oath and then see that something else is better, do what is better and make expiation for your oath.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had brought boys from among the captives of Kabul, and they built him a mosque in his palace in Baṣra in the style of Kabul.

976They said: Then the Kabul Shah assembled the Muslims and expelled from Kabul those of them who were there. Rutbīl came and took control of Dhābilistān and al-Rukhkhaj, reaching as far as Bist. Al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād went out with the people, fought Rutbīl at Bist and routed him. He pursued him until he came to al-Rukhkhaj, fought him there, then went on and conquered the lands of al-Dāwar. Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān then dismissed al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād al-Ḥārithī and appointed ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra over Sijistān. He raided; when he was at Razān, Rutbīl sent to him asking for peace concerning his lands and the lands of Kabul, in return for one million two hundred thousand. ʿUbayd Allāh agreed to this. Rutbīl asked him to gift him two hundred thousand, and he did so. The peace was thus concluded for one million dirhams. ʿUbayd Allāh visited Ziyād and informed him of this, and Ziyād approved the treaty.

Then ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra returned to Sijistān and stayed there until Ziyād died. After Ziyād’s death, ʿAbbād b. Ziyād governed Sijistān on behalf of Muʿāwiya. Then, when Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya came to power, he appointed Salm b. Ziyād over Khurāsān and Sijistān. Salm appointed his brother Yazīd b. Ziyād over Sijistān. At the time of Yazīd’s death, or shortly before it, the people of Kabul betrayed their agreement and broke it, and captured Abū ʿUbayda b. Ziyād. Yazīd b. Ziyād marched against them and fought them while they were at Janza. Yazīd b. Ziyād was killed, along with many of those with him, and the rest of the people were routed. Among those who were martyred were Zayd b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Mulayka b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Judʿān al-Qurashī, and Ṣila b. Ashyam Abū al-Ṣahbāʾ al-ʿAdawī, the husband of Muʿādhā al-ʿAdawiyya. Salm sent Ṭalḥa b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khalaf al-Khuzāʿī, known as Ṭalḥa al-Ṭaḥḥāt, who ransomed Abū ʿUbayda for five hundred thousand dirhams. Ṭalḥa went from Kabul to Sijistān as governor on behalf of Salm b. Ziyād. He collected the revenues, gave gifts to his visitors, and died in Sijistān. He appointed a man from Banū Yashkur as his deputy, but the Muḍarīs expelled him. Partisanship broke out, and each group took control of its own city. Rutbīl coveted them. Then ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir arrived as governor of Sijistān on behalf of al-Qubāʿ—who was al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī—in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr. They admitted him into the city of Zaranj and fought Rutbīl. Abū ʿAfrāʾ ʿUmayr al-Māzinī killed him, and the polytheists were routed. ʿAbd Allāh b. Nāshira al-Tamīmī sent word to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: “Take everything in the treasury and withdraw.” He did so. Ibn Nāshira arrived and entered Zaranj, while Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd al-Tamīmī went on, brought back ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and admitted him into the city when it was opened for the woodcutters; Ibn Nāshira was expelled and gathered a force. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. ʿAbd Allāh and Wakīʿ with him fought him. Ibn Nāshira’s horse stumbled, and he was killed.

Abū Ḥuzāba—or, it is said, Ḥanẓala b. ʿArāda—said:

“Ah, there is no young man after the young Ibn Nāshira, And everything has passed away and turned its back. Was he a harvest reaped from deaths? Why did they disdain him? Why did they not leave the plant while it was still green? A young man of Ḥanẓala, whose right hand continually Gives generously in what is good and rejects what is evil. By my life, Quraysh have brought down our tents With a noble, generous man, blooming in the evenings.”

ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān appointed Umayya b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ over Khurāsān. He sent his son ʿAbd Allāh b. Umayya to Sijistān and appointed him over it while he was in Kirmān. When ʿAbd Allāh arrived there, he raided King Rutbīl, who came after the first Rutbīl, who had been killed. He had feared the Muslims. When ʿAbd Allāh encamped at Bist, Rutbīl made peace with him for one million. He agreed and sent him gifts and slaves, but ʿAbd Allāh refused to accept them and said, “The furnishings of this portico must be gold, or else there is no peace between us.” He was a raider, so Rutbīl left the country open to him; when he had penetrated far into it, Rutbīl blocked the mountain passes and narrow defiles against him. ʿAbd Allāh asked them to let him go without taking anything from them. Rutbīl refused and said, “Rather, you will take three hundred thousand dirhams as tribute, write us a document for it, and not raid our country as long as you are governor; you shall neither burn nor destroy.” ʿAbd Allāh agreed. When ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān heard of this, he dismissed him. Then, when al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf governed Iraq, he sent ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra to Sijistān. He grew apprehensive and weak. He came to al-Rukhkhaj; the land was suffering a drought, and he marched until he encamped near Kabul. He reached a mountain pass, where the enemy seized it against him, and Rutbīl caught up with them. ʿUbayd Allāh made peace with them on the condition that they give him five hundred thousand dirhams and send him three of his sons—Nahār, al-Ḥajjāj, and Abū Bakra—as hostages, and write them a document that he would not raid them as long as he was ...

governor. Shurayḥ b. Hāniʾ al-Ḥārithī said to him, “Fear God and fight these people. If you do what you intend to do, you will weaken Islam on this frontier, and you will have fled from the death to which you are destined.” They fought, and Shurayḥ charged and was killed. The people fought and escaped, exhausted; they took the desert route of Bist, and many people perished from thirst and hunger. ʿUbayd Allāh b. Abī Bakra died of grief over what had befallen the people. It is said that he complained of pain in his ear and died. He appointed his son Abū Bardʿa as his deputy over the people. Then ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muḥammad b. al-Ashʿath rebelled and went to Sijistān in opposition to ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān and al-Ḥajjāj. He made a truce with Rutbīl and went over to him. Then Rutbīl handed him over, fearing al-Ḥajjāj. This was because al-Ḥajjāj wrote to Rutbīl threatening him. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān threw himself down from above a ?-b-l—and it is said, from a roof—and the man who was guarding him fell with him; he had chained himself to him, and he died. His head was brought to al-Ḥajjāj. Al-Ḥajjāj made peace with Rutbīl on the condition that he would not raid him for seven years; it is said, nine years, in return for an annual payment thereafter of one thousand dirhams in kind. When the years had passed, al-Ḥajjāj appointed al-Ashhab b. Bishr al-Kalbī over Sijistān. He dealt harshly with Rutbīl regarding the goods in kind he paid. Rutbīl wrote to al-Ḥajjāj complaining of him, and al-Ḥajjāj dismissed him.

977They said: Then, when Qutayba b. Muslim al-Bāhilī governed Khurāsān and Sijistān in the days of al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik, he appointed his brother ʿAmr b. Muslim over Sijistān. ʿAmr demanded from Rutbīl a peace payment in coined dirhams. Rutbīl said that he could pay only the goods in kind that he had agreed upon with al-Ḥajjāj. ʿAmr wrote this to Qutayba, and Qutayba marched to Sijistān. When Rutbīl learned of his arrival, he sent him word: “We have not withdrawn a hand from obedience; you only made terms with us ...”

for goods in kind, so do not wrong us.” Qutayba said to the troops, “Accept the goods in kind from him, for this is an ill-omened frontier.” They agreed. Then Qutayba returned to Khurāsān after sowing a crop in the land of Zaranj, so that the enemy would despair of his departure and submit to him. When the crop was harvested, snakes prevented them from taking it, and he ordered it burned. Qutayba appointed over Sijistān Ibn ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmayr al-Laythī, the maternal half-brother of ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir. Then Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik came to power and appointed Yazīd b. al-Muhallab over Iraq. Yazīd appointed his brother Mudrik b. al-Muhallab over Sijistān. Rutbīl gave him nothing. Then Muʿāwiya b. Yazīd came to power, and Rutbīl paid him a little. Then Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik came to power, and Rutbīl gave none of his officials anything. He said, “What has happened to the people who used to come to us with empty bellies and black faces from prayer, their sandals woven from palm fibers?” They said, “They have passed away.” He said, “Those people were more faithful to their agreements and stronger in battle, even if your faces are better-looking than theirs.” He was asked, “Why did you pay al-Ḥajjāj the tribute but not us?” He said, “Al-Ḥajjāj was a man who, when he attained what he sought, did not consider what he had spent, even if not a single dirham came back to him. You, however, do not spend a dirham unless you hope to get ten back in its place.” Then he gave none of the officials of the Umayyads, nor those of Abū Muslim over Sijistān, any of that tribute.

978They said: When the Commander of the Faithful al-Manṣūr was acknowledged as caliph, he appointed Maʿn b. Zāʾida al-Shaybānī over Sijistān. Maʿn arrived there and appointed his officials over it. He wrote to Rutbīl, ordering him to deliver ...

the tribute which al-Ḥajjāj had agreed upon in a treaty.

He sent camels, Turkish pavilions, and slaves, and doubled the value of each item.

Maʿn became angry and set out for al-Rukhkh, with Yazīd b. Mazyad at the head of his vanguard.

He found that Rutbīl had left it and gone to Dhābilistān to spend the summer there.

He conquered it and took many captives.

Among them were Faraj al-Rukhkhī, a boy, and his father Ziyād.

Faraj used to relate that Maʿn saw a cloud of dust raised by the hooves of wild asses and thought that an army had come against him to fight him and free the captives and prisoners from his hands.

So he turned the sword on them and killed many of them.

Then he learned what had caused the dust, saw the asses, and stopped.

Faraj said: “I saw my father when Maʿn ordered the sword turned on us. He bent over me and said, ‘Kill me, but do not kill my son.’”

979They said: The number of those taken captive and imprisoned was nearly thirty thousand.

Māwand, Rutbīl’s deputy, sought a safe-conduct on the condition that he be taken to the Commander of the Faithful.

He granted him safe-conduct and sent him to Baghdad with five thousand of their fighters. al-Manṣūr treated him generously and assigned him a stipend.

980They said: Maʿn feared the onset of winter and withdrew to Bist.

A group of Khārijites disapproved of his conduct and infiltrated themselves among workers who were building at his residence. When they reached the roofing, they contrived to conceal their swords in bundles of reeds. Then they entered his domed chamber while he was being cupped and attacked him. One of them cut open his belly with a dagger he had with him.

They concealed their swords in bundles of reeds. Then they entered his domed chamber while he was being cupped and attacked him. One of them cut open his belly with a dagger he had with him.

One of them said: “Abū al-Ghulām al-Ṭāqī struck him on the head.”

Al-Ṭāq is a district near Zaranj. Yazīd b. Mazyad killed them, and none of them escaped.

Then Yazīd took charge of Sijistān, and his rule weighed heavily upon its Arabs and non-Arabs.

Some Arabs devised a scheme and wrote a letter in his name to al-Manṣūr, informing him that the letters

addressed to al-Mahdī had bewildered and astonished him, and asking him to excuse him from dealing with it.

This angered al-Manṣūr, who reviled him. He read the letter to al-Mahdī, who dismissed him, ordered him imprisoned, and ordered everything he owned sold.

Zaranj. Then—someone interceded for him, and he was brought to the City of Peace.

He remained there in disgrace until the Khārijites encountered him on the bridge, and he fought them.

His fortunes then improved somewhat.

Then he went to Yūsuf al-Barm in Khurāsān, and his fortunes continued to rise.

The governors of al-Mahdī and al-Rashīd, may God have mercy on them, continued to collect the tribute from Rutbīl of Sijistān according to their strength and weakness, and to appoint their own governors over the districts that Islam had conquered.

When al-Maʾmūn was in Khurāsān, the tribute was paid to him in a doubled amount.

He conquered Kābul, and its king professed Islam and obedience. He installed his governor there, and the postal service was connected to it. From there, the king sent him fresh myrobalan. After that, matters remained settled for a time.

981ʿUmarī told me, from al-Haytham b. ʿAdī, who said: Among the ancient treaties of Sijistān was the condition that their weasels not be killed, because of the many snakes there.

He said: The first to call the people of Sijistān to the doctrine of the Khārijites was a man of Banū Tamīm called ʿĀṣim or Ibn ʿĀṣim.

Title page of volume 3 of the Cairo edition

Chapter 84

Khurāsān

982They said: Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī dispatched ʿAbd Allāh b. Budayl b. Warqāʾ al-Khuzāʿī on a raid. He came to Kirmān and proceeded until he reached al-Ṭabasayn, two fortresses, one called Ṭabas and the other Kurīn.

They were sanctuaries with palm trees, and the two gateways to Khurāsān.

He obtained booty.

Some people of al-Ṭabasayn came to ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb and made peace with him for sixty thousand; it is said, seventy-five thousand. He wrote them a document.

It is also said that ʿAbd Allāh b. Budayl had set out from Iṣfahān on his own initiative.

When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān became caliph, in the year 28 he appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz governor of Baṣra; it is also said, in the year 29. He was twenty-five years old. He conquered what he conquered of the land of Fārs, then raided Khurāsān in the year 30. He appointed Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān as his deputy in Baṣra and sent al-Aḥnaf b. Qays at the head of his vanguard. It is also said that it was ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim b. Asmāʾ b. al-Ṣalt b. Ḥabīb al-Sulamī. He confirmed the treaty of al-Ṭabasayn.

Ibn ʿĀmir sent al-Aḥnaf b. Qays to Qūhistān.

He had asked which city was closest to al-Ṭabasayn, and was directed to it.

The Hayāṭila met him—they are Turks; it is also said that they were a people of Fārs who practiced sodomy, whom Fīrūz exiled to Herat, where they joined the Turks and became allies of the people of Qūhistān. He defeated them and conquered Qūhistān by force.

It is also said that he drove them into their fortress.

Then Ibn ʿĀmir came to him, and they asked for peace. He made peace with them for six hundred thousand dirhams.

983Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: The commander who went to Qūhistān was Amīr b. Aḥmar al-Yashkurī.

That is the land of Bakr b. Wāʾil to this day.

Ibn ʿĀmir sent Yazīd al-Jurashī, Abū Sālim b. Yazīd, to the district of Zām in Nīshāpūr, and he conquered it by force.

He also conquered Bākharz, a district of Nīshāpūr, and conquered Juwayn as well, taking captives.

Ibn ʿĀmir sent al-Aswad b. Kulthūm al-ʿAdawī, of ʿAdī al-Ribāb, who was an ascetic, to Bayhaq, a district of Nīshāpūr.

He entered one of its inhabitants’ walled enclosures through a breach in it, and a group of Muslims entered with him. The enemy then blocked that breach against them.

Al-Aswad fought until he and those with him were killed.

Adham b. Kulthūm took command of the people after him.

He prevailed and conquered Bayhaq.

Al-Aswad used to pray to his Lord that He gather him up from the bellies of beasts and birds. His brother did not shroud him, but buried those of his companions who had been martyred.

Ibn ʿĀmir conquered Bisht of Nīshāpūr, Ashband, Rukh, Zāwa, Khwāf, Isfarāyīn, and Arghiyān of Nīshāpūr.

Then he came to Abrashahr, which is the city of Nīshāpūr, and besieged its people for months.

A man was assigned to each of its quarters.

The governor of one of those quarters sought a guarantee of safety on the condition that he admit the Muslims into the city.

It was granted to him.

He let them in by night.

They opened the gate, while its marzbān fortified himself in the inner citadel with a group of men. He sought a guarantee of safety on the condition that he make peace on behalf of all Nīshāpūr for a fixed levy to be paid.

He made peace with him for one million dirhams; it is said, seven hundred thousand dirhams.

When Nīshāpūr was conquered, he appointed Qays b. al-Haytham al-Sulamī over it.

Ibn ʿĀmir sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī to Ḥamrāndiz of Nasā, which is a district, and he conquered it.

The ruler of Nasā came to him and made peace for three hundred thousand dirhams; it is said, on the condition that the land’s assessed tax be borne, and that no one be killed or taken captive.

Bahmana, the ruler of Abīward, came before Ibn ʿĀmir and made peace for four hundred thousand. It is also said that Ibn ʿĀmir sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim there, and he made peace with its people for four hundred thousand dirhams.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim to Sarakhs.

He fought them, then Zādhūya, its marzbān, sought peace on the condition that a hundred men be granted safe-conduct and that the women be handed over to him.

His daughter fell to Ibn Khāzim as a share, and he took her and named her Maythāʾ.

Ibn Khāzim gained control over the land of Sarakhs.

It is said that he made peace with him on condition that a hundred persons be granted safe-conduct.

He named the hundred but did not name himself, so Ibn Khāzim killed him and entered Sarakhs by force.

From Sarakhs, Ibn Khāzim sent Yazīd b. Sālim, the client of Sharīk b. al-Aʿwar, to Kayf and Bīna, and he conquered them.

The marzbān of Ṭūs, [name unclear in the Arabic text], came to Ibn ʿĀmir and made peace with him on behalf of Ṭūs for six hundred thousand dirhams.

Ibn ʿĀmir sent an army to Herat, commanded by Aws b. Thaʿlaba b. Ruqayy; it is also said, Khulayḍ b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥanafī. When the ruler of Herat learned of this, he went to Ibn ʿĀmir and made peace with him on behalf of Herat, Bādhghīs, and Būshanj—except Ṭāghūn and Bāghūn, which were conquered by force.

Ibn ʿĀmir wrote for him:

“In the name of God, Most Gracious, Most Merciful.

This is what ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir ordered for the ruler of Herat, Būshanj, and Bādhghīs.

He ordered him to fear God, to be sincere toward the Muslims, and to put in good order the lands under his authority.

He made peace with him on behalf of Herat, its plain and its mountain, on the condition that he pay the jizya agreed upon, and that it be apportioned fairly among the lands.

Whoever withholds what is due from him shall have neither treaty nor protection.”

Rabīʿ b. Nahshal wrote it, and Ibn ʿĀmir sealed it.

It is also said that Ibn ʿĀmir himself marched with the troops to Herat.

He fought its people, then its marzbān made peace with him on behalf of Herat, Būshanj, and Bādhghīs for one million dirhams.

The marzbān of Marw al-Shāhijān sent asking for peace, so Ibn ʿĀmir sent Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān al-Bāhilī to Marw, and he made peace with him for two million two hundred thousand dirhams.

Some said: one million dirhams and two hundred thousand jarībs of wheat and barley.

Some said: one million and one hundred thousand ūqiyyas.

Their treaty stipulated that they make room for the Muslims in their homes, and that they were responsible for apportioning the money; the Muslims had only to collect it .

All of Marw made peace, except for a village there called al-Sanj, which was taken by force.

984Abū ʿUbayda said: He made peace with him for female and male attendants, mounts, and goods.

At that time, the people had no cash.

The entire tax was in that form until Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya became caliph and turned it into money.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir sent al-Aḥnaf b. Qays toward Ṭukhāristān.

He came to the place called Qaṣr al-Aḥnaf, a fortress belonging to Marw al-Rūdh, which had a large district known as the district of al-Aḥnaf and called Bishq al-Juradh.

He besieged its people, and they made peace with him for three hundred thousand.

Al-Aḥnaf said: “I will make peace with you on condition that one of our men enter the fortress, make the call to prayer there, and remain among you until I depart.” They agreed.

The treaty covered the whole district.

Al-Aḥnaf went on to Marw al-Rūdh and besieged its people. They fought him fiercely, but the Muslims defeated them and forced them back into their fortress.

The marzbān was a descendant of Bādhām, the ruler of Yemen, or a relative of his.

He wrote to al-Aḥnaf: “The Islam of Bādhām has called me to make peace.”

He made peace with him for sixty thousand.

985Al-Madāʾinī said: Some people said six hundred thousand.

Al-Aḥnaf had sent out cavalry that captured a district called Bagh and drove off livestock from it. The treaty was made after that.

986Abū ʿUbayda said: al-Aḥnaf fought the people of Marw al-Rūdh on several occasions.

Then he passed by a man cooking a pot or kneading dough for his companions. He heard him say, “The commander ought to fight them from one direction, from inside the ravine.” He said to himself, “The man’s advice is right.” He fought them with the Murghāb on his right and the mountain on his left. The Murghāb is a river that flows through Marw al-Rūdh, then disappears into sand and emerges at Marw al-Shāhijān. He routed them and the Turks with them. Then they asked for safe-conduct, and he made peace with them.

987Someone other than Abū ʿUbayda said: The people of Ṭukhāristān rallied against the Muslims. The people of al-Jūzjān, al-Ṭālaqān, al-Fāriyāb , and those around them gathered, reaching thirty thousand. The people of al-Ṣaghāniyān also came to them; they were on the eastern side of the river. Al-Aḥnaf returned to his fortress, and its people honored their agreement with him.

He went out at night and heard people in a tent talking. A man said, “The commander should march against them and engage them wherever he meets them.” A man tending a fire beneath his cooking pot, or kneading dough, said, “That is not sound advice! The sound advice is to camp between the Murghāb and the mountain, with the Murghāb on his right and the mountain on his left, so that, however numerous his enemies may be, he will face no more of them than the number of his own companions.” He thought this was sound and acted on it.

He had five thousand Muslims with him: four thousand Arabs and one thousand non-Arab Muslims. They met, and he raised his banner and charged, and they charged. The king of al-Ṣaghāniyān made for al-Aḥnaf and thrust at him with his spear. Al-Aḥnaf wrenched the spear from his hand and fought fiercely, killing three of those among them who had drums. He would make straight for the man with the drum and kill him.

Then God turned the unbelievers back. The Muslims slew them in a great slaughter and laid down their arms among them wherever they wished. Al-Aḥnaf returned to Marw al-Rūdh. Some of the enemy reached al-Jūzjān, so al-Aḥnaf sent al-Aqraʿ b. Ḥābis

al-Tamīmī with cavalry. He said, “O Banū Tamīm! Love one another and give generously to one another, and your affairs will be set right.

“Begin by waging jihād against your bellies and your private parts, and your religion will be set right for you.

“Do not embezzle, and your jihād will be sound.”

Al-Aqraʿ marched and encountered the enemy at al-Jūzjān. The Muslims suffered a setback, then rallied, routed the unbelievers, and took al-Jūzjān by force.

Ibn al-Gharīza al-Nahshalī said:

May the rain clouds pour, when they break forth, on the slain young men at al-Jūzjān, up to the two palaces of the rural district of Ḥawf; there al-Aqraʿān brought them to ruin.

Al-Aḥnaf took al-Ṭālaqān by treaty and took al-Fāriyāb. It is also said that Amīr b. Aḥmar took it .

Then al-Aḥnaf marched to Balkh, a city of Ṭukhārā. Its people made peace with him for four hundred thousand; it is also said seven hundred thousand, and that is the more reliable account. He appointed Asīd b. al-Mutashammis over Balkh.

Then he marched to Khwārazm, which lies within the lands watered by the river, with its city on the eastern side. He could not take it, so he returned to Balkh, where Asīd had collected its tribute under the treaty.

988Abū ʿUbayda said: Ibn ʿĀmir conquered the lands up to the river. When the people beyond the river learned of his campaign, they asked him to make peace with them, and he did so. It is said that he crossed the river and went to each place in turn. It is also said that they came to him and made peace, and he sent someone to collect it. Pack animals, male and female attendants, silk, and clothing came to him; then he entered the state of consecration in gratitude to God. No one other than him mentioned his crossing the river and making peace with the people on the eastern side.

989They said: He entered the state of consecration for an ʿumra and came to ʿUthmān. He appointed Qays b. al-Haytham as his deputy.

Qays marched after departing the land of Ṭukhāristān. He came to no town there without making peace with its people, who submitted to him, until he reached Samanjān. They resisted him, so he besieged them until he took it by force.

It has also been said that Ibn ʿĀmir divided Khurāsān among three men: al-Aḥnaf b. Qays, Ḥātim b. al-Nuʿmān al-Bāhilī, and Qays b. al-Haytham. The first account is more reliable.

Then Ibn Khāzim fabricated a commission in Ibn ʿĀmir’s name and took over Khurāsān. The Turks gathered there in great numbers, and he dispersed them. Then he came to Baṣra before ʿUthmān was killed.

990Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told me: Wakīʿ b. al-Jarrāḥ told us, from Ibn ʿAwn, from Muḥammad b. Sīrīn, that ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān made an appointment for the people beyond the river.

991They said: Māhūyah, the marzbān of Marw, came to ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib during his caliphate, while he was in Kūfa. He wrote to the dihqāns, the asāwira, and the dahshlarīs, ordering them to pay him the jizya. Khurāsān rebelled against them, so he sent Jaʿda b. Hubayra al-Makhzūmī —his mother was Umm Hāniʾ bt. Abī Ṭālib—but he did not conquer it. Khurāsān remained unsettled until ʿAlī ﵇ was killed.

992Abū ʿUbayda said: The first of ʿAlī’s governors over Khurāsān was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abzā, a client of Khuzāʿa; then Jaʿda b. Hubayra b. Wahb b. ʿAmr b. ʿĀʾidh b. ʿImrān b. Makhzūm. He did not concern himself with the people who had broken their agreement, but collected the tribute from those who had made peace. He was in charge of it for a year, or nearly a year.

  1. They said: Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān appointed Qays b. al-Haytham b. Qays b. al-Ṣalt al-Sulamī over Khurāsān, then dismissed him and appointed Khālid b. al-Muʿammar, who died at Qaṣr Muqātil or at ʿAyn al-Tamr. It is said that Muʿāwiya regretted appointing him and sent him a poisoned garment. It is also said that a shard of glass entered his leg, and he bled until he died.

Then Muʿāwiya added Khurāsān to ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir’s charge along with Baṣra. Ibn ʿĀmir appointed Qays b. al-Haytham al-Sulamī over Khurāsān.

The people of Bādghīs, Herat, Būshanj, and Balkh had broken their agreements. He marched to Balkh and destroyed its Nawbahār. The man who carried this out was ʿAṭāʾ al-Sāʾib, client of the Banū al-Layth, who was al-Khashal. ʿAṭāʾ was called al-Khashal for this reason. He built bridges over three rivers a parasang from Balkh, and they were called the Bridges of ʿAṭāʾ.

Then the people of Balkh asked for peace and a return to obedience. Qays made peace with them, then came to Ibn ʿĀmir, who flogged him a hundred times and imprisoned him. He appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim. The people of Herat, Būshanj, and Bādghīs sent to him seeking safe-conduct and peace. He made peace with them and sent money to Ibn ʿĀmir.

In the year 45, Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān became governor of Baṣra and appointed Amīr b. Aḥmar over Marw, Khulayḍ b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥanafī over Abrashahr, Qays b. al-Haytham over al-Ṭālaqān and al-Fāriyāb, and Nāfiʿ b. Khālid al-Ṭāʾī, of al-Azd, over Herat, Bādghīs, Būshanj, and Qādis, in Anwārān.

Amīr was the first to settle Arabs in Marw . Then Ziyād appointed al-Ḥakam b. ʿAmr al-Ghifārī, who was upright and had been a Companion. He said to his doorkeeper Fayl, “Bring me al-Ḥakam,” meaning al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī. The daughter of ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī was married to him. The doorkeeper brought him al-Ḥakam b. ʿAmr, and when Ziyād saw him he regarded it as a blessing and said, “A righteous man among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

He appointed him over Khurāsān, where he died in the year 50. Al-Ḥakam was the first to pray beyond the river.

994Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Juʿfī told me: I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Mubārak say to a man from al-Ṣaghāniyān, who used to study ḥadīth with us, “Do you know who conquered your land?” He said, “No.” He replied, “Al-Ḥakam b. ʿAmr al-Ghifārī conquered it.”

Then, in the year 51, Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān appointed al-Rabīʿ b. Ziyād al-Ḥārithī over Khurāsān and transferred with him from the two garrison cities about fifty thousand people with their families. Among them was Burayda b. al-Ḥuṣayb al-Aslamī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh, who died in Marw during the days of Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya. Also among them was Abū Barza al-Aslamī, ʿAbd Allāh b. Naḍla, and [others] at Bahāmāt. He settled them south of the river.

Al-Rabīʿ was the first to order the troops to share provisions by contribution. When news reached him of the killing of Ḥujr b. ʿAdī al-Kindī, he was grieved by it and prayed for death. He collapsed that very day and died in the year 53.

He appointed his son ʿAbd Allāh as his deputy. The son fought the people of Āmul—which is Āmūya—and Zam. Then he made peace with them and returned to Marw. He stayed there two months, then died.

Ziyād died, and Muʿāwiya appointed ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād over Khurāsān, when he was twenty-five years old. He crossed the river with twenty-four thousand and came to Baykand. Khātūn was in the city of Bukhārā. She sent to the Turks asking them for aid, and a multitude of them came to her. The Muslims met them, defeated them, and seized their camp. The Muslims advanced, demolishing and burning. Khātūn sent to them asking for peace and safe-conduct. He made peace with her for one million and entered the city. He took Rāmidīn and Baykand, two parasangs apart. Rāmidīn is attributed to Baykand. It is said that he conquered al-Ṣaghāniyān.

He came to Baṣra with a multitude of people from Bukhārā and assigned them stipends. Then Muʿāwiya appointed Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān over Khurāsān. He crossed the river. He was the first to cross it with his troops.

Rafīʿ Abū al-ʿĀliya al-Riyāḥī accompanied him; he was a client of a woman of Banū Riyāḥ. He said: “Rafīʿ Abū al-ʿĀliya means elevation and eminence.”

When Khātūn learned that he had crossed the river, she brought him terms of peace. The people of al-Sughd, the Turks, and the people of Kash and Nasaf—which is Nakhshab—came to Saʿīd in a force of one hundred and twenty thousand. They met at Bukhārā. Khātūn had regretted paying the tribute and had broken the agreement. A slave belonging to some of those assembled was present, then went away with his people, and the rest were routed. When Khātūn saw this, she gave him the hostages and renewed the peace. Saʿīd entered the city of Bukhārā.

Then Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān raided Samarqand, and Khātūn aided him with the people of Bukhārā. He camped at the gate of Samarqand and swore that he would not depart until he conquered it and hurled a projectile at its citadel. He fought its people for three days; their fighting was fiercest on the third day. His eye and the eye of al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra were put out. It is said that al-Muhallab’s eye was put out at al-Ṭālaqān.

Then the enemy held to the city, and wounds had spread among them. A man came to him and showed him a fortress containing the sons of their kings and notables. He marched against them and besieged them. When the people of the city feared that the fortress would be taken by force and those inside killed, they asked for peace. He made peace with them for seven hundred thousand dirhams, on condition that they give him hostages from among the sons of their notables, that he enter the city, and that whoever wished could leave by the other gate. They gave him fifteen sons of their kings; it is also said forty, and it is also said eighty. He hurled a projectile at the citadel, and the stone lodged in its embrasure. Then he departed.

When he reached Tirmidh, Khātūn brought him terms of peace. He remained at Tirmidh until he took it by treaty. Later, when ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī was killed, Mūsā, his son, came to the king of Tirmidh, who granted him protection and refuge, along with some men who were with him. He expelled him from it and took control of it , acting in defiance. When he was killed, it came into the hands of the governors. Then its people rebelled, and Qutayba b. Muslim conquered it.

Mālik b. al-Rayb says of Saʿīd:

A cold north wind blew and shook down leaves, and the wormwood on the plain turned yellow after its greenness.

Depart, may you be guided, and do not make our booty snow lashed by the wind at Tirmidh.

Winter is an enemy with which we are fighting; return, may you be guided, while the padded coat lies cast aside.

It is said that these verses were by Nahār b. Tawsīʿa, about Qutayba, and that their opening is:

Khurāsān was a land when Yazīd was there; every gate to good fortune stood open.

She exchanged [him] for a curly-toed colt, its face as though splashed with vinegar.

Qutham b. al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was with Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān and died at Samarqand. It is also said that he was martyred there. When news of his death reached ʿAbd Allāh b. al-ʿAbbās, he said, “How far apart his birth and his grave are!” Then he began to pray. They asked him, “What is this?” He replied, “Have you not heard God say: ‘Seek help through patience and prayer; it is indeed hard except for the humble’?” (1)

995ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told me: Sharīk told us, from Jābir, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: Qutham came to Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān in Khurāsān. Saʿīd said to him, “I will give you a thousand shares from the booty.” He replied, “No, but give me one share for myself and one share for my horse.”

Saʿīd proceeded with the hostages he had taken from al-Sughd until he reached the city. He gave their clothes and belts to his clients, dressed them in woolen cloaks, and set them to drawing water, tending the waterwheels, and working. They entered his audience chamber and attacked him, then killed themselves.

Mālik b. al-Rayb says of Saʿīd:

On the day of al-Sughd you stood trembling, a coward, until I feared you would become a Christian.

Khālid b. ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ said :

Indeed, the best of people in soul and father is Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān, slain by the non-Arabs.

If the vicissitudes of the days have willed Saʿīd’s fate, who in this world is safe from time?

Saʿīd had contrived against his partner in the tax revenues of Khurāsān and took money from him. Muʿāwiya sent someone who met him at Ḥulwān and took the money from him. His partner was Aslam b. Zurʿa; it is also said Isḥāq b. Ṭalḥa b. ʿUbayd Allāh.

Muʿāwiya had feared that Saʿīd might depose him, and for that reason he hastened to dismiss him.

(1) Sūrat al-Baqara, verse 45. (*)

Then Muʿāwiya appointed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ziyād over Khurāsān. He was a nobleman. Muʿāwiya died while he was governor there. Then Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya appointed Salm b. Ziyād. The people of Khwārazm made peace with him for four hundred thousand and delivered it to him. He crossed the river with his wife, Umm Muḥammad bt. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣī al-Thaqafī. She was the first Arab woman by whom the river was crossed.

He came to Samarqand, and its people gave him a thousand blood-wit payments. He had a son whom he named al-Sughdī. His wife borrowed jewelry from the wife of the lord of al-Sughd, broke it while she had it, and went away with it.

While Salm b. Ziyād was in al-Sughd, he sent an army to Khujanda. Al-Aʿshā of Hamdān was among them, and they were routed. Al-Aʿshā said:

Would that my cavalry had not been routed on the day of Khujanda, and that I had not been left stripped at al-Makr!

The birds circle my place of death, and I return to God, stained with blood.

Then Salm returned to Marw. From there he raided, crossed the river, and killed Bandūn al-Sughdī. Al-Sughd had gathered against him, and he fought them.

When Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya died, the people turned against Salm and said, “How evil was Ibn Sumayya’s assumption—that he would rule over us in a time of unity and in a time of discord!” The same was said to his brother ʿUbayd Allāh in Baṣra.

He departed Khurāsān and went to ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, who charged him four million dirhams and imprisoned him. Salm used to say, “If only I had gone to Syria and not disdained serving my brother ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād——then I would have washed his foot, and I would not have gone to Ibn al-Zubayr.”

He remained in Mecca until Ibn al-Zubayr besieged al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf. He broke through the prison wall and went to al-Ḥajjāj, then to ʿAbd al-Malik. ʿAbd al-Malik said to him, “By God, if you had stayed in Mecca, it would have had no governor other than you, and there would have been no commander over you there.” He appointed him over Khurāsān. When he arrived in Baṣra, he died there.

996They said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī had met Salm b. Ziyād at Nīshāpūr when he was returning from Khurāsān.

Salm gave him a commission over Khurāsān and assisted him with one hundred thousand dirhams.

A great many men of Bakr b. Wāʾil and others gathered and said, “Why should these people consume Khurāsān to our exclusion?” They raided Ibn Khāzim’s baggage train and fought its men off, then desisted.

Sulaymān b. Marthad, one of the Banū Saʿd b. Mālik b. Ḍubayʿa b. Qays b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿUkāba, of the Marāthid branch of Rabīʿa, sent word to Ibn Khāzim: “The man who gave you the commission would have stayed in Khurāsān if he could; he would not have left it and sent you in his place.”

Sulaymān came and camped at Mashraʿat Sulaymān, while Ibn Khāzim was at Marw. They agreed to write to Ibn al-Zubayr, and that whichever of them he appointed would be the commander.

They did so, and Ibn al-Zubayr appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim over Khurāsān.

ʿUrwa b. Quṭba brought him the commission six months later.

Sulaymān refused to accept it, saying, “Ibn al-Zubayr is no caliph; he is only a man seeking refuge at the Sacred House.”

Ibn Khāzim fought him with six thousand men, while Sulaymān had fifteen thousand.

Sulaymān was killed; Qays b. ʿĀṣim al-Sulamī killed him and cut off his head.

Some of Ibn Khāzim’s men were also struck down.

Ibn Khāzim’s battle cry was, “Red ones, they shall not be helped!”

Sulaymān’s battle cry was, “O God’s victory, draw near!”

Sulaymān’s defeated troops gathered around ʿUmar b. Marthad at Ṭāliqān.

Ibn Khāzim marched against him, fought him, and killed him.

Rabīʿa gathered around Aws b. Thaʿlaba at Herat. Ibn Khāzim appointed his son Mūsā as his deputy and marched against him. There were engagements between their men, and the Turks took advantage of this, raiding until they reached the vicinity of Nīshāpūr.

Ibn Khāzim had poison administered to Aws ,

and Aws fell ill.

They gathered for battle, and Ibn Khāzim urged his men on, saying, “Make this your day, and thrust at the horses’ nostrils, for no horse has ever been thrust in its nostrils without turning back.” They fought fiercely. Aws was wounded while already ill, and died of it a few days later.

Ibn Khāzim appointed his son Muḥammad over Herat, made Bukayr b. Wishāḥ chief of his police, and Khurāsān became settled under his authority.

Then the Banū Tamīm rebelled in Herat and killed Muḥammad.

His father, ʿUthmān b. Bishr b. al-Muḥtafiz, prevailed…

He killed him in cold blood, and killed a man of the Banū Tamīm.

The Banū Tamīm gathered, deliberated, and said, “We do not think this man will leave us alone. Let a group of us go to Ṭūs; when he goes out against them, those of us in Marw will depose him.”

So Bujayr b. Wafāʾ al-Ṣuraymī, of the Banū Tamīm, went with a group to Ṭūs. They entered the fortress, then moved to Abrashahr and deposed Ibn Khāzim.

Ibn Khāzim sent his baggage train with his son Mūsā to Tirmidh, for he did not trust the Banū Tamīm in Marw with it.

A letter from ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān arrived for Ibn Khāzim appointing him governor of Khurāsān.

He fed the letter to its messenger and said, “I would be ashamed to meet God having broken my pledge to the son of the Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ and pledged allegiance to the son of the one driven away.”

ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to Bukayr b. Wishāḥ appointing him over Khurāsān.

Ibn Khāzim feared that Bukayr would come against him with the people of Marw. Bukayr had already revolted against Ibn Khāzim, seized the weapons and the treasury, and called on the people of Marw to pledge allegiance to ʿAbd al-Malik; they did so.

Ibn Khāzim set out to join his son Mūsā, who was at Tirmidh with his dependents and baggage train. Bujayr pursued him and fought him near Marw. Wakiʿ b. al-Dawraqiyya al-Qurayʿī—his father’s name was ʿUmayya, and his mother was among the captives from Dūrq, after which he was named—put on his coat of mail and armor and went out. He put it on and went out, then charged Ibn Khāzim with Bujayr b. Waqāʾ; the two stabbed him.

Wakiʿ sat on his chest and said, “O vengeance for Duwayla!” Duwayla was Wakiʿ’s maternal brother.

He had been a client of the Banū Qurayʿ; Ibn Khāzim had killed him.

Ibn Khāzim spat in Wakiʿ’s face and said, “May God curse you! You kill the ram of Muḍar for your brother’s sake, you foreigner, not worth a handful of date stones.”

Wakiʿ said: “Taste, son of ʿAjlā, what you made me taste; * Do not think I was heedless of that.” ʿAjlā was Ibn Khāzim’s mother. He was called Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Wakiʿ b. al-Dawraqiyya’s teknonym was Abū Rabīʿa.

ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim’s two sons, ʿAnbasa and Yaḥyā, were killed with him.

Ṭahmān, Ibn Khāzim’s client, was wounded; he was the grandfather of Yaʿqūb b. Dāwūd, secretary to the Commander of the Faithful al-Mahdī after Abū ʿUbayd Allāh.

Bukayr b. Wishāḥ brought Ibn Ḥāzim’s head and sent it to ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān, who had it displayed in Damascus.

They cut off his right hand and sent it to the descendants of ʿUthmān b. Bishr b. al-Muḥtafiz al-Muzanī.

Wakiʿ was rough-mannered and large of build.

One day he prayed with a plant in front of him and began eating from it.

He was asked, “Do you eat while you are praying?” He replied, “God would not have forbidden a plant that He made grow with rainwater upon the soil of the earth.”

He used to drink wine. When he was reproached for it, he said, “You reproach me over wine? It makes my urine clear until it is like silver!”

997They said: Some people were angered on Ibn Khāzim’s account, discord broke out, and one faction joined Bukayr b. Wishāḥ while another joined Bujayr.

The leading and most distinguished men of Khurāsān wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik, informing him that after the civil war Khurāsān could be governed properly only by a man of Quraysh.

He appointed Umayya b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya over Khurāsān.

He appointed Bukayr b. Wishāḥ over Ṭukhāristān,

then appointed him to campaign beyond the river.

Umayya then resolved to campaign against Bukhara and afterward go to Mūsā b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim at Tirmidh.

Bukayr returned to Marw, seized Umayya’s son and imprisoned him, and called on the people to depose Umayya; they responded.

When this reached Umayya, he made peace with the people of Bukhara for a small ransom , prepared ships—which Bukayr had burned—and returned, leaving Mūsā b. ʿAbd Allāh behind.

Bukayr fought him, then made peace with him on condition that he appoint him over whichever district he wished.

Then Umayya learned that Bukayr was afterward working to depose him,

He ordered that the man be seized when he entered his house. The man entered, and was seized. He ordered that he be imprisoned, but Bujayr b. Wafāʾ leapt upon him and killed him.

Umayya campaigned against al-Khatl. Its people had revolted after Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān had made peace with them, and Umayya conquered it.

Then al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf appointed al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra—whose name was Ẓālim b. Surāq b. Ṣubḥ b. al-ʿAtīk of al-Azd, and whose teknonym was Abū Saʿīd—over Khurāsān together with the two Iraqs, in the year 99.

He went on many campaigns and conquered al-Khatl, which had revolted.

He conquered Khujanda, and Sughd paid him tribute.

He campaigned against Kash and Nasaf, then returned and died at Zāghūl, in Marw al-Rūdh, from a carbuncle.

The beginning of his illness was grief over his son al-Mughīra b. al-Muhallab.

Al-Muhallab appointed his son Yazīd b. al-Muhallab as his deputy.

Yazīd went on many campaigns, and Makhlad b. Yazīd b. al-Muhallab conquered al-Batt.

Al-Ḥajjāj appointed Yazīd b. al-Muhallab.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-ʿAbbās b. Rabīʿa b. al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went to Herat with the defeated remnants of Ibn al-Ashʿath’s forces and others; he had gone out with Ibn al-Ashʿath.

Al-Raqqād al-ʿAtakī collected the land tax.

Yazīd marched against him. They fought, and Yazīd routed them and ordered that they not be pursued. The Hāshimī reached Sind.

Yazīd campaigned against Khwārazm and took captives.

The troops put on the captives’ clothes and died of the cold.

Then al-Ḥajjāj appointed al-Mufaḍḍal b. al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra.

He conquered Bādhghīs, which had

revolted, as well as Shūmān and other places; he took booty and distributed it among the people.

998They said: Mūsā b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khāzim al-Sulamī was at Tirmidh.

He went to Samarqand, whose king Ṭarkhūn treated him generously.

One of his companions attacked and killed a man from Sughd, so Ṭarkhūn expelled him and his men. Mūsā went to the ruler of Kash.

Then he came to Tirmidh, which was a fortress , and lodged with Tirmidh’s dihqān, who prepared food for him.

After eating, he lay down…

The dihqān said to him, “Get out.”

He replied, “I know no lodging like this one.”

He fought the people of Tirmidh until he overcame them and took it.

Its dihqān and its people went out to the Turks seeking their help, but the Turks did not help them. They said, “May God curse you! What good do you expect?

A man came to you with a hundred men, drove you out of your city, and took it from you.”

Mūsā’s companions, including those who had been with his father and others, had all come together with him.

The ruler of Tirmidh and its people remained with the Turks until the Turks aided them and surrounded Mūsā and his men on every side. Mūsā attacked them by night and captured their camp.

Sixteen Muslims were killed.

Thābit and Ḥurayth, the two sons of Quṭba al-Khuzāʿī, were with Mūsā.

They sought reinforcements from Ṭarkhūn and his men against Mūsā. Ṭarkhūn came to their aid and sent a large force with them against Mūsā.

Their influence over him grew great, and they were the ones giving orders and prohibitions in his camp.

He was told, “You have only the title; these two are the commanders of the army and the ones in charge.”

A host of people of Tirmidh, Hephthalites and Turks, came out against him. They fought fiercely, and the Muslims and those with them defeated them.

When al-Ḥajjāj heard of it, he said, “Praise be to God, who gave the hypocrites victory over the polytheists.”

Mūsā made two great towers from the heads of those who had fought him.

Ḥurayth b. Quṭba was killed by an arrow that struck him.

Mūsā’s companions said to him, “God has rid us of Ḥurayth; rid us of Thābit too, for life with him is unbearable.”

Thābit heard what they were saying. When he confirmed it, he went to Ḥashūrā and sought help from Ṭarkhūn, who came to his aid.

Mūsā marched against him and took control of the city’s outer district.

Then Sughd reinforcements grew numerous, and Mūsā returned to Tirmidh and fortified himself there. The people of Kash, Nasaf, and Bukhara aided him.

Thābit besieged Mūsā with a force of eighty thousand.

Mūsā sent Yazīd b. Huzayl as though to console Ziyād al-Qaṣīr al-Khuzāʿī, who had suffered a calamity , while he himself sought an opening against Thābit and struck him on the head with a sword blow…

He lived seven days after it, then died.

Yazīd threw himself into the river of Ṣaghāniyān and survived.

Ṭarkhūn took charge of his companions.

Mūsā attacked them by night, and the non-Arabs returned to their lands.

The people of Khurāsān used to say, “We have seen no one like Mūsā: he fought alongside his father for two years and was never routed.”

Then he came to Tirmidh, took it while he had only a small force, and drove its king out of it.
