Then he fought the Turks and non-Arabs, routed them, and inflicted losses on them.

When Yazīd b. al-Muhallab was dismissed and al-Mufaḍḍal b. al-Muhallab took over Khurāsān, he sent ʿUthmān b. Masʿūd.

ʿUthmān marched until he camped on an island at Tirmidh, now called the Island of ʿUthmān. He had fifteen thousand men.

He pressed Mūsā hard and wrote to Ṭarkhūn, who came to him.

When Mūsā saw the force that had come against him, he left the city and said to the companions he had left inside it, “If I am killed, hand the city over to Mudrik b. al-Muhallab; do not hand it over to Ibn Masʿūd.”

The Turks and Sughd stood between Mūsā and the fortress. His horse stumbled and he fell; he mounted behind one of his clients and kept saying, “Death is bitter.”

ʿUthmān looked at him and said, “Mūsā’s leap, by the Lord of the Kaʿba!” He rode straight at him until Mūsā and his client fell. They closed in around him and killed him, and his companions were killed. None escaped except Ruqayya b. al-Ḥarr, who handed himself over to Khālid b. Abī Barza al-Aslamī.

The man who finished off Mūsā b. ʿAbd Allāh was Wāṣil b. Ṭaysala al-ʿAnbarī.

The city was handed over to Mudrik b. al-Muhallab.

Mūsā was killed at the end of the year 85.

A man struck Mūsā’s shin while he was dead; when Qutayba took power, he killed that man.

999They said: Then al-Ḥajjāj appointed Qutayba b. Muslim al-Bāhilī over Khurāsān.

He set out intending to go to Akhrūn.

When he reached Ṭāliqān, the dihqāns of Balkh met him and crossed the river with him. When he had crossed, the king of Ṣaghāniyān came to him with gifts and a gold key, submitted to him, and invited him to…

…to settle in his land.

The king of Akhrūn and Shūmān had put pressure on Ṣaghāniyān and raided it; that is why he gave Qutayba what he gave him and invited him to what he invited him to.

The king of Kafiyān came to Qutayba with an offer like that made by the king of Ṣaghāniyān, and they both handed their lands over to him.

Qutayba returned to Marw and left his brother Ṣāliḥ in charge of what lay beyond the river.

Ṣāliḥ conquered Kāsān and Urusht, which are in Farghāna.

Naṣr b. Sayyār was with him in his army.

He conquered Bayʿankhar (?) and Khushkat in Farghāna, its old city.

The last to conquer Kāsān and Urusht, after their people had revolted, was Nūḥ b. Asad, during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Muntaṣir bi-llāh ﵀.

1000They said: The king of Jūzjān sent to Qutayba and made peace with him on the condition that Qutayba come to him.

Qutayba went to him, then returned and died at Ṭāliqān.

Then Qutayba campaigned against Baykand in the year 87, accompanied by Nīzak. He crossed the river from Zamm to Baykand, which is the Bukhara city nearest the river.

Its people acted treacherously and sought aid from Sughd. Qutayba fought them, raided them, and besieged them.

They asked for peace, but he conquered it by force.

Qutayba campaigned against Tūmishkat and Karmīniya in the year 88.

He appointed his brother Bishr b. Muslim as his deputy in Marw. Bishr made peace with them and conquered small fortresses.

Qutayba campaigned against Bukhara and conquered it by treaty.

Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: Qutayba came to Bukhara, and its people took precautions against him.

He said, “Let me enter it and pray two rakʿas there.”

They allowed him to do so.

He concealed some men against them, and when he entered, they overpowered the gate’s defenders and went in.

He seized immense wealth there and betrayed its people.

He said: Qutayba attacked Sughd, killed Nīzak in Ṭukhāristān and crucified him, and conquered Kash and Nasaf—which is Nakhshab—by treaty.

1001They said: The king of Khwarazm was weak, and his brother Khurzād had opposed him and grown powerful against him. The king of Khwarazm sent to Qutayba: “I will give you such-and-such, and hand over the keys to you, on condition that you install me as ruler over my lands, excluding my brother.” Khwarazm consists of three cities, surrounded by Fāriqīn (?) and Madīnat al-Fīl, the most strongly fortified of them. ʿAlī b. Mujāhid said: “Madīnat al-Fīl is in fact Samarqand.” The king settled in the most strongly fortified city and sent Qutayba the money agreed upon in their treaty, along with the keys. Qutayba sent his brother ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muslim against Khurzād; he fought him, killed him, and took four thousand prisoners, whom he fought. He installed the first king of Khwarazm as ruler according to the terms he had stipulated. The people of his kingdom said to him, “He is weak,” and rose up against him and killed him. Qutayba appointed his brother ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muslim over Khwarazm. Qutayba raided Samarqand. The kings of Soghd used to reside there in ancient times, then moved to Ishtīkhan. Qutayba besieged the people of Samarqand, and they clashed repeatedly and fought. The king of Soghd wrote to the king of al-Shāsh, who was staying at Ṭārband, and he came to him with a force of his fighters. The Muslims met them and fought fiercely. Then Qutayba attacked them and routed them. Ghawzak made peace with him for two million two hundred thousand dirhams each year, and on condition that prayer be performed in the city. Qutayba entered it, and Ghawzak had prepared food for him. He ate, prayed, and established a mosque, leaving behind a group of Muslims there, among them al-Ḍaḥḥāk b. Muzāḥim, the Qur’an commentator. It is also said that Qutayba made peace with him for seven hundred thousand dirhams and hospitality for the Muslims for three days. The treaty included the temples of idols and fire. The idols were taken out, stripped of their ornaments, and burned. The non-Arabs used to say that there were idols there such that whoever treated them lightly would perish. When Qutayba burned them with his own hand, a group of them embraced Islam. Al-Mukhtār b. Kaʿb al-Juʿfī said of Qutayba:

He subdued Soghd with the tribes until * he left Soghd sitting in the open. Abū ʿUbayda and others said: When ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became caliph, a group of people from Samarqand came to him and reported that Qutayba had entered their city and settled Muslims in it by treachery. ʿUmar wrote to his governor, ordering him to appoint a judge to examine what they had reported. If he ruled that the Muslims be expelled, they would be expelled. He appointed Jamīʿ b. Ḥāḍir al-Nājī for them. He ruled that the Muslims be expelled, on condition that they face one another on equal terms. The people of Samarqand disliked war and allowed the Muslims to remain, so they stayed among them. Al-Haytham b. ʿAdī said: Ibn ʿAyyāsh al-Hamadhānī told me: Qutayba conquered most of al-Shāsh and reached Isfījāb. It is said that the fortress of Isfījāb had been conquered long ago, then the Turks took control of it, together with some people of al-Shāsh. Then Nūḥ b. Asad conquered it during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh and built a wall around it that enclosed the vineyards and fields of its people. Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: Qutayba conquered Khwarazm and took Samarqand by force. Saʿīd b. ʿUthmān had previously made peace with its people, and Qutayba conquered it after him. They had not broken their treaty, but he considered their peace treaty insufficient. He said: He also conquered Baykand, Kash, Nasaf, and al-Shāsh, and raided Farghāna, conquering some of it; he raided Soghd and Ashrūsana. 1002. They said: Qutayba felt alienated from Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik. This was because he had worked to secure the oath of allegiance to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Walīd, seeking to divert it from Sulaymān. When al-Walīd died and Sulaymān took power, he addressed the people, saying: “The one appointed over you is Habanqa al-ʿĀʾishī.” Sulaymān used to give gifts and cultivate the favor of the people of wealth and means, while neglecting others. Habanqa was …

Yazīd b. Tharwān, who favored the fattening of his camels with fodder and pasture, saying, “I do not set right what God has ruined.” He called on the people to depose him, but no one responded. He insulted Banū Tamīm and accused them of treachery, saying, “You are not Banū Tamīm, but Banū Dhamīm.” He disparaged Banū Bakr b. Wāʾil, saying, “O brothers of Musaylima!” He disparaged the Azd , saying: “You exchanged the spears for the marādī, and the reins of the fortress for ships.” He said: “O people of the lowland—I do not say the highland!—I shall put you where God has placed you.” He said: Sulaymān wrote to Qutayba confirming his governorship and ordering him to release everyone in his prison, give the people their stipends, and permit anyone who wished to return home to do so. They had been looking forward to this. He ordered his messenger to inform the people of what he had written. Qutayba said, “This is a stratagem of his against me.” He stood and said: “People! Sulaymān has made you the marrow of the mosquito’s limbs, and you will be summoned to swear allegiance to a more luminous child whose slaughtered animal is unlawful.” They were angry with him because he had insulted them. He apologized for that, saying, “I was angry and did not know what I was saying. I wanted nothing but good for you.” They spoke and said, “If he permits us to return home, that will be best for him; if he does not, let him blame no one but himself.” This reached him, and he addressed the people, recounting his beneficence toward them, censuring their scant loyalty to him and their opposition to him, and threatening them with the non-Arabs whom he had used to reinforce himself against them. They resolved to fight him and did not answer him at all. They asked al-Ḥuḍayn b. al-Mundhir to take charge of them, but he refused and advised them to choose Wakīʿ b. Ḥassān b. Qays b. Abī Sūd b. Kalb b. ʿAwf b. Mālik b. Ghadāna b. Yarbuʿ b. Ḥanẓala al-Tamīmī. He said: “No one but he can handle this affair, for he is a rough, uncultivated Bedouin, his clan obeys him, and he is of Banū Tamīm. Qutayba has killed Banū al-Ahtam, and they seek vengeance for their blood.” They went to Wakīʿ, who gave them his hand, and they pledged allegiance to him. Before that, the intermediary between him and them had been Ḥayyān, the client of Maṣqala. At that time in Khurāsān there were forty thousand fighters from the people of Baṣra, seven thousand from the people of Kūfa, and seven thousand clients.

Wakīʿ feigned illness and stayed at home. Qutayba would send for him, and he would smear his legs and shins with red ochre, saying, “I am ill; I cannot move.” Whenever Qutayba sent men to bring him, they would slip away and go to Wakīʿ and inform him. Wakīʿ called for his weapon and a spear, and took the headscarf of his concubine and tied it around himself. A man called Idrīs met him and said, “Abū Muṭrif, you are seeking something and fearing what the man has already made you safe from. Fear God, fear God!” Wakīʿ said, “This Idrīs is the messenger of Iblīs! Would Qutayba make me safe? By God, I will not go to him until I bring his head.” He advanced toward Qutayba’s tent, and the people followed after him. Qutayba was with his household, his kin, and his clients. His brother Ṣāliḥ said to his servant, “Bring me my bow.” One of them said to him mockingly, “This is no day for a bow.” A man from Banū Ḍabba shot him and struck his lung, so he fell. He was carried into the tent and died, with Qutayba at his head. Qutayba would say to Ḥayyān, who was in command of the non-Arabs, “Charge!” He would reply, “The time for that has not yet come.” The non-Arabs charged the Arabs. Ḥayyān said, “O company of non-Arabs, why are you killing yourselves for Qutayba? Is this the excellence of his conduct toward you?” Then he withdrew with them to Banū Tamīm. The people became agitated, while Qutayba’s brothers, his household, and a group of sons of the kings of Soghd, who disdained to abandon him, stood firm with him. The guy-ropes of the tent and the awning were cut and fell on Qutayba—or the awning pole fell on his head and killed him. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAlwān cut off his head. Some of them, including Hishām b. al-Kalbī, said: Rather, they entered his tent; Jahm b. Zaḥr al-Juʿfī killed him, Saʿd b. Majd struck him, and Ibn ʿAlwān cut off his head. 1003. They said: A group of his brothers and household were killed with him, as was his concubine al-Ṣammāʾ. Ḍirār b. Muslim escaped; Banū Tamīm gave him safe-conduct.

The Azd took Qutayba’s head and his ring. Wakīʿ was brought Qutayba’s head and sent it to Sulaymān with Sulayṭ b. ʿAṭiyya al-Ḥanafī. The people began to plunder Bāhila, but he prevented them. Wakīʿ wrote to Abū Mijlaz Lāḥiq b. Ḥumayd, appointing him over Marw; he accepted, and the people approved of him. Qutayba was fifty-five years old on the day he was killed. When Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd accepted the authority in Khurāsān by force (?) and brought it under control, Sulaymān wanted to appoint him over it. He was told, “Wakīʿ is raised up by rebellion and brought low by unity; he is rough and Bedouin.” Wakīʿ used to call for a basin and urinate while people watched him. He remained for nine months, until Yazīd b. al-Muhallab, who was in Iraq, came to him. Sulaymān wrote to him to come to Khurāsān and sent him his appointment. Yazīd arrived, leaving his son Mukhlad behind. He called Wakīʿ to account and imprisoned him, saying, “Pay over God’s property.” He replied, “Was I God’s treasurer?” Mukhlad raided al-Battam and conquered it. Then its people broke their treaty after him, so he left them and turned away; they grew confident that he had withdrawn, then he turned back on them until he entered it. Jahm b. Zaḥr entered it and seized property and idols made of gold; the people of al-Battam are attributed to his clientage. Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: They used to believe that ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ahtam, Abū Khāqān, had written to al-Ḥajjāj denouncing Qutayba and reporting the wealth that had come into his possession. At that time he was Qutayba’s deputy over Marw. Whenever Qutayba raided, he appointed him over Marw. When the raid on Bukhara and its environs took place and Qutayba appointed him [over Marw], Bashīr, one of Banū al-Ahtam, came to him and said, “You have given ʿAbd Allāh too much latitude, and he is envious and full of hidden designs. We cannot be sure he will not depose you and corrupt matters against us.”

He said, “I said this only out of envy of your cousin.” He replied, “Then let that be my excuse in your eyes; if that was the case, you will excuse me.” He raided, and [ʿAbd Allāh] wrote what he had written to al-Ḥajjāj. Al-Ḥajjāj folded his letter into his own letter to Qutayba. The messenger came and stopped at al-Sikka in Marw, passed beyond it, and did not go to ʿAbd Allāh. He sensed danger and fled, reaching Syria, where for a time he sold wine and cotton goods from a bundle around his neck, walking about with it. Then he placed a rag and cotton over one of his eyes, bound it, and took the kunya Abū Ṭīna. He used to sell oil. He remained in this state until al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik died and Sulaymān took power; then he cast off that filth and rag. He delivered an address of congratulation to Sulaymān and attacked al-Ḥajjāj and Qutayba. They had pledged allegiance to ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Walīd and deposed Sulaymān. The people dispersed, saying, “Abū Ṭīna the oil seller is the most eloquent of people.” When the letter of Ibn al-Ahtam to al-Ḥajjāj reached Qutayba, after the opportunity had passed, he turned on his cousins and their sons. One of them was Shayba, Abū Shabīb; he killed nine people, one of them Bashīr. Bashīr said to him, “Remember my excuse with you.” He replied, “You advanced one man and held another back, enemy of God!” Then he killed all nine. Wakīʿ b. Abī Sūd had previously been in charge of Banū Tamīm in Khurāsān. Qutayba removed him from them and appointed a man from Banū Ḍirār al-Ḍabbī. When he killed them, he said, “May God kill me; I shall kill him.” They checked on him and found that he had not prayed noon or afternoon prayer. They said to him, “You have not prayed.” He replied, “How can I pray to a Lord who killed their children, the majority of them, and did not become angry on their behalf?” Abū ʿUbayda said: Qutayba raided Madīnat al-Fīl and conquered it. Umayya b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Khālid b. Asīd had previously conquered it. Then they broke their treaty, and Yazīd b. al-Muhallab tried to subdue them but could not. Kaʿb al-Ashqarī said: “Fīl gave herself into your hands, and rightly so; * before you, al-Fajfāja the arrogant tried for her.”

He means Yazīd b. al-Muhallab. 1004. They said: When ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became caliph, he wrote to the kings of Transoxiana, inviting them to Islam. Some of them embraced Islam. ʿUmar’s governor over Khurāsān was al-Jarrāḥ b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥakamī. He seized Mukhlad b. Yazīd and Yazīd’s officials and imprisoned them. Al-Jarrāḥ sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Muʿammar al-Yashkurī to Transoxiana. He penetrated far into the lands of al-ʿŪd, intending to enter China, but the Turks surrounded him until he ransomed himself from them, escaped, and reached al-Shāsh. ʿUmar lifted the land tax from those who embraced Islam in Khurāsān, assigned stipends to those who embraced Islam, and built caravanserais. Then reports reached ʿUmar about al-Jarrāḥ’s partisanship, and he wrote to him, “The people of Khurāsān can be set right only by the sword.” He rejected this and dismissed him. He had a debt , and [ʿUmar] paid it. He appointed ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Nuʿaym al-Ghāmidī to command the war in Khurāsān, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qushayrī over its land tax. He said: Al-Jarrāḥ b. ʿAbd Allāh used to take small pieces of silver and gold and place them under a carpet in his reception room, in various weights. When someone entered—whether one of his brothers or one who claimed his favor—he would toss each man an amount suited to his standing. Then Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik became caliph and appointed Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik over Iraq and Khurāsān. Maslama appointed Saʿīd b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Ḥārith b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya over Khurāsān. This Saʿīd was nicknamed Ḥudhayfa. This was because one of the landowners of Transoxiana entered to see him wearing safflower-dyed clothing, with his hair groomed. He said, “This is Khudhayna”—meaning, “a female landowner.” Saʿīd was Maslama’s son-in-law, married to his daughter. Saʿīd sent Sūra b. al-Ḥurr al-Ḥanẓalī …

Then his son turned toward Transoxiana and settled at Ishtīkhan, where the Turks had come to be. He fought them and defeated them, and for a time prevented the people from pursuing them. Then he met the Turks a second time, and they defeated them and killed many of his companions. Saʿīd appointed Naṣr b. Sayyār. The poet says of Saʿīd: “You set out against the enemies, sporting with a game; * your penis is exposed, and your sword is sheathed.” A group of leading men from Khurāsān went to Maslama to complain about Saʿīd, and he dismissed him. He appointed Saʿīd b. ʿAmr al-Jarashī over Khurāsān. When he arrived there, he ordered his secretary to read out his appointment, but the secretary spoke with grammatical errors. Saʿīd said, “People! The governor is not responsible for the grammatical errors you hear from this man.” He sent to Soghd, calling on them to join the community and return to obedience, and refrained from provoking them until his messengers brought word that they persisted in opposing him. He advanced against them; nearly ten thousand men broke away from their leader and left them, inclining toward obedience. Al-Jarashī conquered most of the fortresses of Soghd and inflicted a decisive defeat on the enemy. Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik had designated Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik as his successor, and al-Walīd b. Yazīd after him . When Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik died, Hishām took power. He appointed ʿUmar b. Hubayra al-Fazārī over Iraq, and ʿUmar dismissed al-Jarashī and appointed Muslim b. Saʿīd over Khurāsān. He raided Afshīn, made peace with its ruler on the terms of six thousand persons, and received his fortress; then he returned to Marw. He appointed Naṣr b. Sayyār over Ṭukhāristān. A group of Arabs rebelled against him, and he attacked them; then envoys mediated between them and they made peace. Hishām appointed Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī over Iraq. He appointed his brother Asad b. ʿAbd Allāh over Khurāsān. Muslim b. Saʿīd heard of this and marched until he reached Farghāna. He encamped at its city, cut down the trees, destroyed the cultivated area, and Khāqān of the Turks came down upon him with his army,

He departed from Farghāna. He traveled three stages in a single day, until his mounts died, and the Turks began to harry his army. One of the poets said:

You led us on a raid, fearing dismissal, in disobedience— Yet you did not escape the deceptions of this world, O Maʿn.

Asad arrived in Samarqand and appointed al-Ḥasan b. Abī al-ʿAmruṭa over it. The Turks used to raid Samarqand and attack it. Whenever they raided, al-Ḥasan would set out after them but could not catch them. One day he preached and, in his sermon, prayed against the Turks, saying, “O God, cut off their traces, hasten their appointed times, and send down steadfastness upon them.” The people of Samarqand reviled him and said, “No! May God send steadfastness down upon us and make their feet tremble.” Asad raided the mountains of Namrūd. Namrūd made peace with him and embraced Islam. Asad raided al-Khuttal. When he arrived in Balkh, he ordered its city to be built and the administrative registers to be transferred there. He went on to al-Khuttal but could achieve nothing there. The people suffered hardship and famine. Reports reached him of words spoken by Naṣr b. Sayyār, so he beat him and sent him to Khālid with three men suspected of causing unrest. Asad then left Khurāsān, leaving al-Ḥakam b. ʿAwāna al-Kalbī in charge there. Hishām appointed Ashras b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Sulamī over Khurāsān. He had with him a Nabataean secretary named ʿUmayra, kunya Abū Umayya, who made evil seem attractive to him. Ashras increased the levies in Khurāsān and treated the dihqāns contemptuously. He called on the people of Transoxiana to embrace Islam and ordered the jizya to be removed from anyone who embraced Islam. They hastened to embrace Islam, and the land tax declined. When Ashras saw this, he took the people who had made peace under his protection. They objected to this and protested against him. Thābit Quṭna al-Azdī grew angry on their behalf. He was called Quṭna because one of his eyes had been put out, and he used to place a piece of cotton over it. Ashras sent men against them to disperse their gathering. They seized Thābit and imprisoned him, then released him on a guarantee and sent him on a mission. The Turks rose against him and killed him.

In the year 112, Hishām appointed al-Junayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Murrī over Khurāsān. He encountered the Turks and fought them. He sent out advance parties, and they captured Ibn Khāqān while he was drunk and hunting. They seized him and brought him to al-Junayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who sent him to Hishām. Al-Junayd continued fighting the Turks until he drove them back. He wrote to Hishām asking for reinforcements, and Hishām reinforced him with ʿAmr b. Muslim and ten thousand men from among the people of Baṣra, and with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Nuʿaym and ten thousand men from among the people of Kūfa. He sent him thirty thousand lances and thirty thousand shields, and gave him free rein in assigning stipends, and he assigned stipends to fifteen thousand men. Al-Junayd conducted raids, and the propagandists of the Banū Hāshim spread throughout his governorship and their cause grew strong. Al-Junayd died in Marw. Hishām appointed ʿĀṣim b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Yazīd al-Hilālī over Khurāsān.

Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā said: “Some districts of Ṭukhāristān that al-Junayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had conquered broke away; he restored them to their peace agreement and their stipulated tribute.” He said: “Naṣr b. Sayyār had raided Ashrūsana in the days of Marwān b. Muḥammad, but achieved nothing there. When the Commander of the Faithful al-ʿAbbās ﵀ became caliph, and after him the caliphs who followed, they used to appoint their governors, who would diminish the boundaries of enemy territory and its outlying regions; they would fight those among the people of the qibla who broke their oath of allegiance and violated their pact, and renew the peace agreements of those who refused to honor their agreement by waging war on them.”

1005They said: When al-Maʾmūn, the Commander of the Faithful, became caliph, he sent the army on campaigns against Sughḍ, Ashrūsana, and those among the people of Farghāna who had rebelled against him, and pressed them hard with fighting and raids during his stay in Khurāsān and afterward. Alongside sending cavalry raiding parties against them, he corresponded with them, calling them to Islam and obedience and encouraging them in both. He sent an army to Kābul Shāh, and the latter paid the tribute and submitted in obedience. The post reached there, so that he sent him fresh, moist manna and myrobalan.

Kāwūs, king of Ashrūsana, had written to al-Faḍl b. Sahl, known as Dhū al-Riʾāsatayn, the vizier and secretary of al-Maʾmūn, asking him to make peace on the basis of a payment he would render, on condition that the Muslims would not raid his country. His request was granted. When al-Maʾmūn ﵀ arrived in Madīnat al-Salām, Kāwūs refused to honor the peace agreement. He had a steward who was highly favored by him and had married his daughter to al-Faḍl b. Kāwūs. The steward would praise al-Faḍl to Kāwūs, bring him close to his heart, and disparage and vilify Ḥaydar b. Kāwūs, known as al-Afshīn. Ḥaydar attacked the steward and killed him at the gate of Kanb, their city, then fled to Hāshim b. Maḥwar al-Khuttalī. Hāshim was enthroned in his own land. He asked him to write to his father to secure his approval of him. Kāwūs had married Umm Junayd when he killed his steward Ṭarādīs, and had fled with some of his dihqāns. When Ḥaydar heard of this, he openly professed Islam and set out for Madīnat al-Salām. He described to al-Maʾmūn how easy it would be to take Ashr and Sanna, played down the alarming reports people gave him about it, and described a short route there. Al-Maʾmūn sent the secretary Aḥmad b. Abī Khālid al-Aḥwal to raid it with a large army. When Kāwūs heard that he was approaching, he sent al-Faḍl b. Kāwūs to seek help from the Turks, and al-Dahmī among them came to his aid. Aḥmad b. Abī Khālid arrived in the land of Ashrūsana and encamped before its city before al-Faḍl arrived with the Turks. Kāwūs had assumed that he would take the distant roads and would not know this short route; he was at a loss and his heart failed him, so he surrendered and came out in obedience. When al-Faḍl heard of his situation, he withdrew with the Turks to a nearby desert. Then he left them and rode hard until he reached his father and entered under his protection. The Turks died of thirst. Kāwūs arrived in Madīnat al-Salām, openly professed Islam, and al-Maʾmūn installed him as ruler over his lands. After him, his son Ḥaydar, who was al-Afshīn, became ruler. Al-Maʾmūn ﵀ used to write to his governors in Khurāsān about raiding those among the people of Transoxiana who did not adhere to obedience and Islam, and would send his messengers, who assigned stipends to those who wished

to receive a stipend from the people of those districts and the sons of their kings, seeking to win them over by offering inducements. When they came to his door, he honored them and increased their gifts and stipends. Then al-Muʿtaṣim biʾllāh became caliph and followed the same course, until most of the troops in his army were soldiers from among the people of Transoxiana: from Sughḍ, Farghāna, Ashrūsana, the people of al-Shāsh, and others. Their kings came to his door, Islam prevailed among those there, and the people of those lands began to raid the Turks beyond them. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṭāhir sent his son Ṭāhir b. ʿAbd Allāh on a campaign to the lands of the Ghūziyya, and he conquered places no one before him had reached.

1006Al-ʿUmarī related to me, from al-Haytham b. ʿAdī, from Ibn ʿAyyāsh, that Qutayba settled the Arabs in Transoxiana, until he settled them in the land of Farghāna and al-Shāsh.

Chapter 85

Conquests of Sind

1007ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Sayf informed us, saying: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ appointed ʿUthmān b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Thaqafī over Baḥrayn and ʿUmān in the year fifteen. He sent his brother al-Ḥakam to Baḥrayn and went on to ʿUmān. He assigned a force to go to Tana. When the force returned, he wrote to ʿUmar informing him of this. ʿUmar wrote to him: “O brother of Thaqīf! You have loaded worms onto a stick. I swear by God, if they are attacked, I will take the same number from your people.” He also sent al-Ḥakam to Burūṣ. He sent his brother al-Mughīra b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ to the Creek of Daybul, where he encountered the enemy and prevailed. When ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵁ became caliph and appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir b. Kurayz over Iraq, he wrote to him, ordering him to send someone to the frontier of India to learn about it and return with information. He sent Ḥakīm b. Jabal al-ʿAbdī. When he returned, ʿUthmān sent for him and asked him about the condition of the lands. He said, “Commander of the Faithful, I have come to know them and explored them.” He said, “Describe them to me.” He replied, “Its water is scant, its fruit is poor, and its thief is a hero. If the army there is small, they perish; if it is large, they go hungry.” ʿUthmān said to him, “Are you a reporter or a rhymester?” He replied, “Rather, a wise chooser.” So he did not send anyone to raid it.

In the last part of the year thirty-eight and the beginning of the year thirty-nine, during the caliphate of ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib ﵁ al-Ḥārith b. Murra al-ʿAbdī went to that frontier as a volunteer, with ʿAlī’s permission. He prevailed and took booty and captives, and distributed a thousand persons in a single day. Then he and those with him were killed in the land of al-Qīqān, except for a few. He was killed in the year forty-two. Al-Qīqān is in the lands of Sind, adjacent to Khurāsān. Then al-Muhallab b. Abī Ṣufra raided that frontier in the days of Muʿāwiya, in the year forty-four. He came to Banna and Alāhū, which lie between Multān and Kābul. The enemy met him, and he and his men fought them. In the land of al-Qīqān, al-Muhallab encountered eighteen Turkish horsemen on cropped horses. They fought him and were all killed. Al-Muhallab said, “Why should these non-Arabs have the advantage over us in cropping horses?” So he cropped horses, and was the first among the Muslims to do so. Regarding Banna, al-Azdī says :

Did you not see that the Azd, on the night they were raided at Banna, Were the best of al-Muhallab’s army?

Then, in the time of Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿĀmir appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Sawwār al-ʿAbdī. It is said that Muʿāwiya had appointed him over the Indian frontier before that. He raided al-Qīqān and took booty. Then he visited Muʿāwiya and presented him with Qīqānī horses. He stayed with him, then returned to al-Qīqān, and its people sought aid from the Turks. They killed him. Regarding him, the poet says:

Ibn Sawwār, despite all his troubles, Kindled the fire and fought hunger.

He was generous; no one in his army kindled a fire other than his. One night he saw a fire and said, “What is this?” They said, “A woman has recently given birth, and khabīṣ is being made for her.” He ordered the people to be fed khabīṣ for three days. In the days of Muʿāwiya, Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān appointed Sinān b. Salama b. al-Muḥabbiq al-Hudhalī

He was virtuous and devout. He was the first to make the troops swear oaths by divorce. He came to the frontier, conquered Makrān by force, founded a garrison town there, stayed there, and secured the region. The poet says of him:

I saw Hudhayl introduce into its oath The divorce of wives for whom it had paid no bride-price.

The oath of Ibn al-Muḥabbiq was of little account When their necks were raised with yellow rings.

Ibn al-Kalbī said: “The one who conquered Makrān was Ḥakīm b. Jabal al-ʿAbdī.” Then Ziyād appointed Rāshid b. ʿAmr al-Judaydī of the Azd over the frontier. He came to Makrān, then raided al-Qīqān and prevailed, then raided al-Mīd and was killed. Sinān b. Salama took charge of the people’s affairs. Ziyād appointed him over the frontier, and he stayed there for two years. Aʿshā Hamdān said of Makrān:

You are traveling to Makrān, Though the destination and the point of departure are far away.

Makrān was not among my needs, Nor its raids, nor its trade.

I have heard of it but never visited it, And its mention has always distressed me:

That many there go hungry, And the few are afflicted.

ʿAbbād b. Ziyād raided the Indian frontier from Sijistān. He came to Sānārūdh. Then he took the route via Ḥawā Kahz to al-Rūdhbār, from the land of Sijistān to the Hindmand. He encamped at Kash and crossed the desert until he reached Qandahār. He fought its people, defeated and routed them, and conquered it after some Muslims had been killed. He saw that its people wore tall caps and made caps of that kind. They were called the ʿAbbādiyya. Ibn Mufarrigh said:

How many a man has fallen in al-Jurūm and the land of India, And how many a shroud-clad slain there lies unburied!

At Qandahār, whoever has death inscribed for him, The news is stoned before it reaches him.

Then Ziyād appointed al-Mundhir b. al-Jārūd al-ʿAbdī, kunya Abū al-Ashʿath, over the Indian frontier. He raided al-Būqān and al-Qīqān. The Muslims prevailed and took booty. He sent out raiding parties in their lands and conquered Qaṣdār and its dependencies. Sinān had conquered it earlier, but its people broke their allegiance. He died there. Al-Shāmir says:

He alighted at Qaṣdār and there came to dwell, In the grave, not returning with those who travel.

By God, Qaṣdār and its vineyards— What a young man the world and religion have brought forth!

Then ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād b. Ḥarrī al-Bāhilī was appointed. God granted the conquest of those lands through him. He fought there fiercely, prevailed, and took booty. Some people say that ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād appointed Sinān b. Salama, while Ḥarrī was in command of his raiding parties. The poet says of Ḥarrī b. Ḥarrī:

Were it not for my thrusting at al-Būqān, The raiding parties of Ibn Ḥarrī would not have returned with spoils.

The people of al-Būqān are Muslims today. ʿImrān b. Mūsā b. Yaḥyā b. Khālid al-Barmakī built a city there and named it al-Bayḍāʾ, during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim biʾllāh. When al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī ʿAqīl al-Thaqafī became governor of Iraq, he appointed Saʿīd b. Aslam b. Zurʿa al-Kilābī over Makrān and that frontier. Muʿāwiya and Muḥammad, the two sons of al-Ḥārith al-ʿAlāfī, rebelled against him and killed him. The two al-ʿAlāfīs gained control of the frontier. The name of ʿAlāf was Rabbān b. Ḥalwān b. ʿImrān b. al-Ḥāf b. Quḍāʿa. He was the father of Jarm. Al-Ḥajjāj appointed Mujāʿa b. Saʿr al-Tamīmī over that frontier. Mujāʿa raided and took booty, and conquered districts of Qundābīl. Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim completed its conquest. Mujāʿa died in Makrān a year later. The poet said:

What of your exploits that I have witnessed but its mention, O Mujāʿa, adorns you?

Then al-Ḥajjāj appointed Muḥammad b. Hārūn b. Dhurāʿ al-Namrī after Mujāʿa. During his governorship, the king of the Island of Yāqūt sent al-Ḥajjāj women born in his land, who were Muslims and whose fathers had died; their fathers had been merchants. He sought to draw near to him by means of them, but some people from Mīd al-Daybul in warships attacked the vessel in which they were. They seized the ship and everything in it. One of the women, who was from Banū Yarbuʿ, cried out, “O Ḥajjāj!” When al-Ḥajjāj heard of this, he said, “Here I am!” He sent to Dāhir asking him to release the women. He replied, “They were taken by brigands, whom I cannot control.” Al-Ḥajjāj dispatched ʿUbayd Allāh b. Nabḥān to Daybul, where he was killed. He wrote to Budayl b. Ṭahfa al-Bajalī, who was in ʿUmān, ordering him to march to Daybul. When he encountered them, his horse shied, and the enemy surrounded and killed him. Some say: “The Zutt of al-Badhaha killed him.” He said: “This island was named the Island of Yāqūt because of the beauty of its women’s faces.”

Then, in the days of al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik, al-Ḥajjāj appointed Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥakam b. Abī ʿAqīl. He campaigned in Sind. Muḥammad was in Fāris, and al-Ḥajjāj had ordered him to march to al-Rayy, with Abū al-Aswad Jahm b. Zaḥr al-Juʿfī at the head of his vanguard. He recalled him, appointed him over the frontier of Sind, and attached to him six thousand troops from the army of the people of Syria, along with a number of others. He equipped him with everything he needed, even thread and needles, and ordered him to remain in Shīrāz until his companions had all joined him and the provisions prepared for him had arrived.

Al-Ḥajjāj took ginned cotton, soaked it in sharp wine vinegar, then dried it in the shade. He said, “When you reach Sind, vinegar is in short supply there. Soak this cotton in water, then cook with it and use it as a condiment.” It is said that when Muḥammad reached the frontier, he wrote complaining that they were short of vinegar. Al-Ḥajjāj sent him cotton soaked in vinegar. Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim traveled to Makrān and stayed there several days. Then he came to Qunzabūr and conquered it,

Then he came to Armāʾīl and conquered it. Muḥammad b. Hārūn b. Dhurāʿ had met him, joined him, and marched with him; he died near there and was buried at Qanbal.

Then Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim marched from Armāʾīl with Jahm b. Zaḥr al-Juʿfī and arrived at Daybul on a Friday. Ships arrived carrying the men, weapons, and equipment he had loaded aboard them. When he encamped at Daybul, he dug a trench, planted spears along it, unfurled the banners, and positioned the men under their standards. He set up a mangonel known as al-ʿArūs, which was drawn by five hundred men. At Daybul there was a great bud with a tall mast, and on the mast was a red banner which, when the wind blew, circled around the city. It would turn.

The bud, as they report, is a great tower built with a chamber in which one or more of their idols are displayed. The idol may also be inside the tower. Anything they greatly venerate as an act of worship is called a bud by them. An idol is also a bud.

Al-Ḥajjāj’s letters were arriving to Muḥammad, and Muḥammad’s letters were being sent back to him describing what had happened and seeking his opinion on what to do, every three days. A letter from al-Ḥajjāj arrived for Muḥammad: “Set up al-ʿArūs and lower one of its supports. Let it face east. Then summon the person in charge of it and tell him to aim his shot at the mast I described to you.” He shot at the mast and broke it, and the unbelievers were greatly alarmed by this. Then Muḥammad advanced against them while they had come out to meet him, and routed them until he drove them back. He ordered ladders to be set in place, and the men climbed them. The first to climb was a man of Murād from among the people of Kūfa. It was taken by force. Muḥammad spent three days killing those inside it. Dāhir’s governor fled from it, and he killed the keeper of their temple. Muḥammad laid out a settlement there for the Muslims, built a mosque, and settled four thousand there.

1008Aḥmad b. Yaḥyā said: Manṣūr b. Ḥātim al-Naḥwī, client of the family of Khālid b. Asīd, told me that he had seen the mast that had stood on the bud’s minaret broken. He also said that ʿAnbasa b. Isḥāq al-Ḍabbī, the governor of Sind during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh ﵀—had demolished the upper part of that minaret, made it into a prison, and begun repairing the city with stones taken from that minaret. He was dismissed before completing this.

After him Hārūn b. Abī Khālid al-Marwarūdī was appointed, and he was killed there.

1009They said: Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim came to al-Bayrūn. Its people had sent some Sumanīs from among them to al-Ḥajjāj and made peace with him. They provided Muḥammad with fodder , admitted him to their city, and honored the peace agreement. Muḥammad continued to pass through city after city, conquering each, until he crossed a river below Mihrān. Sumanīs from Srībadis came to him and made peace on behalf of those they had left behind. He imposed the land tax on them and marched to Sahbān, which he conquered.

Then he marched to Mihrān and encamped in its midst. This reached Dāhir, who prepared to fight him. Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim sent Muḥammad b. Muṣʿab b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Thaqafī to Sadūsān with cavalry and donkeys. Its people asked for safe-conduct and peace. The Sumanīs mediated between him and them, and he granted them safety, imposed a land tax on them, took hostages from them, and returned to Muḥammad with four thousand Zutt, who joined Muḥammad. He appointed a man over Sadūsān.

Then Muḥammad contrived to cross Mihrān, crossing it on the side nearest the land of Rāsal, king of Qaṣṣa in India, by means of a bridge he had constructed. Dāhir was unsuspecting and heedless of him. Muḥammad and the Muslims encountered him while he was mounted on an elephant, with elephants around him and the Takākira with him. They fought an exceedingly fierce battle, the like of which had not been heard. Dāhir dismounted and fought on foot; he was killed at evening, and the polytheists fled. The Muslims killed them as they pleased. According to al-Madāʾinī’s account, the one who killed him was a man of Banū Kilāb, and he said:

The cavalry bears witness on the day of Dāhir, and the spears, and Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad, for I routed the host without turning away, until I struck down their chief with a sword, leaving him sprawled beneath the dust, his cheeks covered, unprotected.

1010Manṣūr b. Ḥātim told me: “Dāhir and the man who killed him are depicted at Burūṣ. Budayl b. Ṭahfa is depicted at Qand, and his grave is at Daybul.”

1011ʿAlī b. Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī told me, from Abū Muḥammad al-Hindī, from Abū al-Faraj, who said: “When Dāhir was killed, Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim gained control over the lands of Sind.”

Ibn al-Kalbī said: The one who killed Dāhir was al-Qāsim b. Thaʿlaba b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥiṣn al-Ṭāʾī.

1012They said: Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim took Rāwar by force. Dāhir had a woman there, who feared she would be seized, so she burned herself, her slave girls, and all her property. Then Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim came to old Brahmanābād, two farsakhs from al-Manṣūra. Al-Manṣūra did not yet exist then; its site was only a thicket. Dāhir’s defeated forces were at this Brahmanābād, and they fought him. Muḥammad took it by force, killed eight thousand there, accepted twenty-six thousand, and left his governor there; today it is in ruins.

Muḥammad marched toward al-Rūr and Baghrūr. The people of Sāwandarī met him and asked him for safe-conduct. He granted it, stipulating that they host the Muslims and guide them. The people of Sāwandarī today are Muslims. Then he proceeded to Basmand, and its people made peace on the same terms as the people of Sāwandarī.

Muḥammad reached al-Rūr, one of the cities of Sind, which lies on a mountain. He besieged them for several months and took it by treaty, on condition that he would not kill them or interfere with their bud. He said: “The bud is nothing but like the churches of the Christians and Jews and the fire temples of the Magians.” He imposed the land tax on them at al-Rūr and built a mosque.

Muḥammad marched to al-Sikka, a city below Biyās, and conquered it. Al-Sikka is now in ruins. Then he crossed the Biyās River to al-Multān. The people of al-Multān fought him. Zāʾida b. ʿUmayr al-Ṭāʾī distinguished himself, and the polytheists were routed and entered the city. Muḥammad besieged them, and the Muslims’ provisions ran out, so they ate donkeys.

Then a man who had sought safe-conduct came to them and showed them the entrance to the water from which they drank. It was water that flowed from the river at Basmand and collected in a place inside the city like a pool; they called it al-Balāḥ. He drained it. When they became thirsty, they submitted to the judgment. Muḥammad killed the combatants and took the children captive. He also took captive the keepers of the bud, who numbered six thousand. They obtained much gold.

That money was gathered in a building ten cubits by eight cubits, and whatever was deposited in it was put through an opening in its roof. Thus al-Multān was called “the opening of the House of Gold.” Al-faraj means “the frontier.” The bud of al-Multān was a bud to which money was dedicated and vows were made. The people of Sind made pilgrimage to it, circling it and shaving their heads and beards there. They claimed that an idol inside it was the prophet Ayyūb ﷺ.

1013They said: Al-Ḥajjāj considered the matter and found that he had spent sixty million on Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim, while what had been brought to him amounted to one hundred and twenty million. He said: “We have assuaged our anger, exacted our vengeance, and gained an additional sixty million dirhams and the head of Dāhir.”

Al-Ḥajjāj tortured him along with men of the family of Abū ʿAqīl until he killed him. Al-Ḥajjāj had killed Ṣāliḥ’s brother Ādam, who held the Kharijite position.

Ḥamza b. Bayḍ al-Ḥanafī said:

“Manliness, generosity, and bounty belong to Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad. He led the armies for seventeen years— how near that is to noble eminence from birth!”

Another said:

“He led the men for seventeen years, while his contemporaries were occupied elsewhere.”

Yazīd b. Abī Kabsha died eighteen days after arriving in the land of Sind. Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed Ḥabīb b. al-Muhallab to command the campaign in Sind. He arrived there after the kings of India had returned to their kingdoms. Ḥalīsha (sic) b. Dāhir returned to Brahmanābād. Ḥabīb encamped on the bank of Mihrān, and the people of al-Rūr submitted to him. He fought a group and defeated them. Then Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik died, and ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz became caliph after him. He wrote to the kings, calling them to Islam and obedience, on the condition that he would leave them in power, with the same rights and duties as the Muslims. They had already heard of his conduct and beliefs, so Ḥalīsha and the kings embraced Islam and adopted Arab names.

ʿAmr b. Muslim al-Bāhilī was ʿUmar’s governor over that frontier. He campaigned in some parts of India and was victorious. The Banū al-Muhallab fled to Sind during the days of Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik. He sent Hilāl b. Aḥwaz al-Tamīmī against them, and he encountered them and killed Mudrik b. al-Muhallab at Qandābīl. He killed al-Mufaḍḍal, ʿAbd al-Malik, Ziyād, Marwān, and Muʿāwiya, sons of al-Muhallab, and killed Muʿāwiya b. Yazīd among others.

Junayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Murrī was appointed over the frontier of Sind by ʿUmar b. Hubayra al-Fazārī, then Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed him to it.

When Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī arrived in Iraq, Hishām wrote to Junayd ordering him to correspond with him. Junayd came to Daybul, then encamped on the bank of Mihrān. Ḥalīsha prevented him from crossing and sent him word: “I have embraced Islam, and the righteous man has appointed me over my lands; I do not trust you.” Junayd gave him a hostage and took a hostage from him as security for the land tax due from his lands. Then they exchanged hostages, and Ḥalīsha renounced Islam and fought.

It is said that he did not fight, but that Junayd brought a false charge against him. He went to India, gathered forces, seized ships, and prepared for war. Junayd sailed against him in ships. They met in the eastern marsh, and Ḥalīsha was captured when his ship ran aground. Junayd killed him. Ṣaṣa b. Dāhir fled, intending to go to Iraq and complain of Junayd’s treachery. Junayd kept him company until he placed his hand in Junayd’s hand, whereupon Junayd killed him.

Junayd campaigned against al-Kīraj, whose people had broken their agreement. He fashioned battering rams and struck the city wall with them until he breached it. He entered by force, killing, taking captives, and taking booty. He sent governors to Marmad, al-Mandal, Dahanj, and Burūṣ. Junayd used to say: “Killing in panic is greater than killing with steadfastness.”

Junayd sent an army to Azīn. He sent Ḥabīb b. Murra with an army to the land of al-Māliya. They raided Azīn and campaigned at Bahrāmad, burning its outer settlement. Junayd conquered al-Baylamān and the islands. In his residence, he accumulated—apart from what he gave his visitors—forty million, and he sent an equal amount.

Jarīr said:

“Junayd’s visitors and companions have risen, they greet one with a radiant face, whose gifts are abundant.”

He appointed al-Junayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Murrī, on behalf of ʿUmar b. Hubayra al-Fazārī, over the frontier of Sind. Then Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik appointed him over it.

When Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī arrived in Iraq, Hishām wrote to al-Junayd, ordering him to correspond with him.

Al-Junayd went to al-Daybul, then encamped on the bank of the Mihrān. Ḥalīsha prevented him from crossing and sent him word: “I have become Muslim, and the righteous man has appointed me over my lands; I do not trust you.”

He gave him a hostage and took a hostage from him in exchange for the land tax due from his territory.

Then they exchanged the hostages, and Ḥalīsha apostatized and fought.

It is said that he did not fight, but that al-Junayd falsely accused him.

He went to India, gathered forces, seized ships, and prepared for war.

Al-Junayd advanced against him by ship. They met in the marsh of al-Sharqī, and Ḥalīsha was taken prisoner after his ship ran aground.

Al-Junayd killed him.

Ṣaṣa b. Dāhir fled, intending to go to Iraq and complain of al-Junayd’s treachery. Al-Junayd kept reassuring him until Ṣaṣa placed his hand in his, whereupon he killed him.

Al-Junayd raided al-Kīraj, whose people had broken their agreement.

He made battering rams and struck the city wall with them until he breached it. He entered the city by force, killing, taking captives, and seizing booty.

He sent governors to Marmad, al-Mandal, Dahnaj, and Barūṣ.

Al-Junayd used to say: “Killing in panic is greater than killing in steadfastness.”

Al-Junayd sent an army to Azīn.

He sent Ḥabīb b. Murra with an army to the land of al-Māliyya.

They raided Azīn and raided Bahrāmād, burning its outlying settlement.

Al-Junayd conquered al-Baylamān and al-Juzur. In his residence, , apart from what he gave his visitors, he amassed forty million, and he sent an equal amount.

Jarīr said:

Al-Junayd’s visitors and companions arose, Welcoming him, bright-faced, whose gifts abound.

Abū al-Juwayriya said:

If a people, through their generosity, were to sit above the sun, They would sit there, envied for the generosity they showed. May God not remove from them their wealth, which is envied.

After al-Junayd, Tamīm b. Zayd al-ʿUtbī was appointed. He proved weak and feeble, and died near al-Daybul at a watering place called the Water of the Buffaloes. It was called the Water of the Buffaloes because buffaloes were driven there to escape blue flies found on the bank of the Mihrān. Tamīm was one of the most generous of the Arabs.

Eighteen million ṭāṭirī dirhams were found in the treasury in Sind, and he spent them lavishly. A young man of Banū Yarbuʿ, called Khunays, whose mother was of Ṭayyiʾ, had accompanied him with the troops to India. His mother came to al-Farazdaq and asked him to write to Tamīm requesting that her son be sent home; she sought refuge at the grave of his father Ghālib. Al-Farazdaq wrote to Tamīm:

A woman came to me seeking refuge, Tamīm, with Ghālib, And with the grave upon which its dust has settled. So grant me Khunays, and thereby confer a favor on me, For the distress of a mother whose drink will not go down. Tamīm b. Zayd, let not my request be Neglected, nor let your answer be withheld from me. Do not make me repeat it often, for I am Weary of requests whose pursuit is slow.

He did not know whether the young man's name was Ḥubaysh or Khunays, so he ordered that everyone whose name consisted of letters like these be sent home.

During Tamīm's days, the Muslims withdrew from the lands of India and abandoned their garrisons, and they did not return to them thereafter.

Then al-Ḥakam b. ʿAwwāna al-Kalbī was appointed. The people of India had become unbelievers, except the people of Qiṣṣa. He saw no refuge to which the Muslims could flee, so beyond the lake, toward India, he built a city which he called al-Maḥfūẓa, made it a refuge and sanctuary for them, and established it as a garrison town. He said to the elders of Kalb from among the people of

Syria: “What do you think we should name it?” One of them said, “Damascus.” Another said, “Ḥimṣ.” A man among them said, “Name it Tadmur.” He replied, “May God destroy you, you fool! Rather, I shall call it al-Maḥfūẓa.” And he settled there.

ʿAmr b. Muḥammad b. al-Qāsim was with al-Ḥakam, who entrusted matters to him and charged him with his important affairs and undertakings. He sent him on a raid from al-Maḥfūẓa. When he returned to him victorious, he ordered him to build a city beyond the lake and name it al-Manṣūra; it is the city where the governors reside today.

Al-Ḥakam recovered what had been in the enemy's hands of the things they had seized, and the people were pleased with his governorship. Khālid used to say, “How strange! I appointed the young man of the Arabs, and he refused”—meaning Tamīm—“and I appointed the stingiest of men, and he accepted.” Then al-Ḥakam was killed there.

After that, the governors would fight the enemy, taking whatever they could seize and conquering districts whose people had broken their agreements.

At the beginning of the Blessed Dynasty, Abū Muslim b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Muslim appointed Mughlis al-ʿAbdī to the frontier of Sind. He took the route through Ṭukhāristān and traveled until he reached Manṣūr b. Jumhūr al-Kalbī, who was in Sind. Manṣūr met him, killed him, and routed his troops. When this reached Abū Muslim, he appointed Mūsā b. Kaʿb al-Tamīmī and then dispatched him to Sind. On his arrival there, he and Manṣūr b. Jumhūr met at Mihrān. They then clashed, and he routed Manṣūr and his army. Manẓūr killed his brother, and Manṣūr left defeated and fleeing until he reached the sandy wastes, where he died of thirst.

Mūsā governed Sind, repaired al-Manṣūra, enlarged its mosque, raided, and conquered. The Commander of the Faithful al-Manṣūr ﵀ appointed Hishām b. ʿAmr al-Taghlibī to Sind, and he conquered what had been closed off. He sent ʿAmr b. Jaml in warships to Nārand. He also sent him toward India, where he conquered Qashmīr and took many captives and slaves. He conquered al-Multān. At Qandābīl there was a usurper from among the Arabs who

The Arabs expelled them from there. He came to Qandahār by ship and conquered it. He demolished the idol temple and built a mosque in its place. The land prospered during his governorship, and the people considered him a source of blessing. He subdued the frontier and put its affairs in good order.

Then ʿUmar b. Ḥafṣ b. ʿUthmān Hazar-Mard was appointed to the frontier of Sind, then Dāwūd b. Yazīd b. Ḥātim. Abū al-Ṣamma was with him—the usurper there today—and he was a client of Kinda.

The affairs of that frontier remained in good order until Bishr b. Dāwūd was appointed to it during the caliphate of al-Maʾmūn. He rebelled and defied authority. Ghassān b. ʿAbbād, a man from the Sawād of Kūfa, was sent against him. Bishr came out to him under a guarantee of safe-conduct and arrived with it in the City of Peace. Ghassān left Mūsā b. Yaḥyā b. Khālid b. Barmak in charge of the frontier.

He killed Bāla, king of the eastern region, although Bāla had offered him five hundred thousand dirhams in return for sparing him. This Bāla had acted evasively toward Ghassān and wrote to him about the presence of his army and the kings who were with him; Ghassān refused. Mūsā made a fine record. He died in the year twenty-one and appointed his son ʿImrān b. Mūsā as his successor. The Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh then appointed him to the frontier.

He went out to the Qīqān, who are Zūṭ. He fought them and overcame them, built a city he called al-Bayḍāʾ, and settled the troops there. Then he came to al-Manṣūra and went from there to Qandābīl, a city on a mountain, where there was a usurper called Muḥammad b. al-Khalīl. He fought him, conquered it, and took its leaders to Qaṣdār. Then he raided the Mīd and killed three thousand of them, and he made an intoxicating drink known as the drink of the Mīd.

ʿImrān camped on the river al-Rūr, then summoned the Zūṭ who were nearby, and they came to him. He branded their hands, took the poll tax from them , and ordered that each man, if challenged, must have a dog with him; a dog was valued at fifty dirhams. Then he raided the Mīd with the leading Zūṭ accompanying him. He dug a canal from the sea and led it through their marsh until its water became salty, and he launched raids against them.

Then factional strife broke out between the Nizārīs and the Yemenīs, and ʿImrān sided with the Yemenīs. ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Habbārī marched against him and killed him while he was in hiding. This ʿUmar's grandfather was among those who came to Sind with al-Ḥakam b. ʿAwwāna al-Kalbī.

1014Manṣūr b. Ḥātim told me: al-Faḍl b. Māhān, a client of Banū Sāma, conquered Sindān and gained control of it. He sent a gift of an elephant to al-Maʾmūn ﵀ along with a letter. He prayed for him in a congregational mosque he had established there.

When he died, Muḥammad b. al-Faḍl b. Māhān took his place. He sailed in seventy warships to the Mīd of India, killed many of them, and conquered Fālī. He returned to Sindān, which had been seized by a brother of his called Māhān b. al-Faḍl. Māhān wrote to the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh and sent him as a gift a piece of teak such as had never been seen for its size and length. India was under his brother's authority, so they turned against him, killed him, and crucified him. Thereafter the people of India gained control of Sindān, but left its mosque for the Muslims to hold congregational prayer in and to pray for the caliph.

1015Abū Bakr, client of the Kurayziyyīn, told me that a town called al-ʿAsīfān, between Qashmīr, al-Multān, and Kābul, had a wise king. The people of that town worshipped an idol for which they had built a house and which they venerated. The king's son fell ill, so he summoned the attendants of that house and said to them, “Ask the idol to heal my son.” They were away from him for an hour, then came to him and said, “We have asked it, and it has answered our request.” The boy died soon afterward. The king sprang upon the house and demolished it, upon the idol and smashed it, and upon the attendants and killed them. Then he summoned a group of Muslim merchants, who presented him with the doctrine of God's oneness. He affirmed God's oneness and became a Muslim. This was during the caliphate of the Commander of the Faithful al-Muʿtaṣim bi-llāh ﵀ .

Part Six

Concluding essays

Chapter 86

The regulations governing kharāj lands

On the Regulations Governing Kharāj Lands

1016Bishr b. Ghiyāth said: Abū Yūsuf said: Any land taken by force, such as al-Sawād, Syria, and other lands, if the imam divides it among those who conquered it, is tithe land, and its inhabitants are slaves. If the imam does not divide it and instead returns it to the Muslims as a whole—as ʿUmar did with al-Sawād—then the poll tax is imposed on its inhabitants, and the land tax on the land; they are not slaves.

This is the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfa. Al-Wāqidī related something similar from Sufyān al-Thawrī. Al-Wāqidī said: Mālik b. Anas and Ibn Abī Dhiʾb said: If an unbeliever among the people of land conquered by force becomes Muslim, his land remains in his possession; he cultivates it and pays kharāj on it. There is no disagreement on this.

Mālik, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and Ibn Abī Laylā said concerning a man who becomes Muslim among the people of land conquered by force: kharāj is due on the land, and zakāt is due on the crop after kharāj. This is the opinion of al-Awzāʿī. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions said that kharāj and zakāt are not both imposed on one man.

Mālik, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, Sufyān, and Abū Ḥanīfa said: If a man cultivates his kharāj land several times in a year, only one kharāj is collected from him. Ibn Abī Laylā said: kharāj is collected from him whenever he harvests a crop. This is the opinion of Ibn Abī Sabra and Abū Shammar.

Abū al-Zinād, Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, Sufyān, Yaʿqūb, Ibn Abī Laylā, Ibn Abī Sabra, Zufar, Muḥammad b. al-Ḥasan, and Bishr b. Ghiyāth said: If a man leaves his land uncultivated, he is told, “Cultivate it and pay its kharāj, or hand it over to someone else to cultivate.” As for tithe land, he is not told anything about it: if he cultivates it, alms are taken from him; if he refuses, that is his own affair.

They said: If a man leaves his land uncultivated for two years, then cultivates it, he pays one kharāj. Abū Shammar said: kharāj is paid for both years.

Abū Ḥanīfa, Sufyān, Mālik, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, and Abū ʿAmr al-Awzāʿī said: If the crops are struck by a disaster or inundated, kharāj is waived for their owner.

If a kharāj land belongs to a slave, a mukātab, or a woman, Abū Ḥanīfa said that only kharāj is due on it. Sufyān, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, and Mālik said that kharāj is due on it, and the tithe on what remains of the crop.

Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī said that if a Muslim or a protected non-Muslim builds on kharāj land, whether shops or something else, nothing is due from him. If he makes it into an orchard, he is charged kharāj. Mālik and Ibn Abī Dhiʾb said: We consider him liable for kharāj, because his benefit from the building is like his benefit from cultivation. As for tithe land, he knows best what he does with it.

Abū Yūsuf said: If a Muslim revives dead land in territory conquered by force, it belongs to him, and it is kharāj land if it is irrigated from kharāj water. If he brings forth a spring for it or irrigates it with rainwater, it is tithe land. Bishr said: It is tithe land, whether irrigated from kharāj water or other water.

Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, their companions, Mālik, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, and al-Layth b. Saʿd said, concerning kharāj land not attributed to anyone, where Muslims sit, trade, and make a market: no kharāj is due on them there.

Abū Yūsuf said: If there is in a land an old foreign custom which Islam has neither changed nor abolished, and people complain about it to the imam because of the harm it causes them, he may not change it. Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī said: He should change it, even if it is longstanding, because he must abolish every oppressive custom established by a Muslim, let alone one established by the people of unbelief.

Chapter 87

The stipend in the caliphate of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb

The Stipend under the Caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁

1017ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Muslim al-ʿAjlī related to us: Ismāʿīl ibn al-Mujālid related to us, from his father Mujālid ibn Saʿīd, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: When ʿUmar conquered Iraq and Syria and collected the land tax, he assembled the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, “I have decided to assign stipends to those entitled to them.”

They said, “You have reached the right decision, Commander of the Faithful.”

He said, “With whom should I begin?” They said, “With yourself.”

He said, “No. I shall place myself where God has placed me, and begin with the family of the Messenger of God ﷺ.”

He did so, and entered ʿĀʾisha, Mother of the Believers, may God have mercy on her, for twelve thousand. He entered the rest of the Prophet’s wives ﷺ for ten thousand. He assigned ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib five thousand, and assigned the same amount to those among Banū Hāshim who had been present at Badr.

1018ʿAbd al-Aʿlā ibn Ḥammād al-Narsī related to me: Ḥammād ibn Salama related to us, from al-Ḥajjāj ibn Arṭāʾ, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit, that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to come one after another to receive their stipends.

1019Muḥammad b. Saʿd, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿĀʾidh b. Yaḥyā, from Abū al-Ḥuwayrith, from Jubayr b. al-Ḥuwayrith b. Nuqaydh: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ consulted the Muslims about establishing the dīwān.

ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib said to him: “Distribute every year whatever wealth has come to you, and keep none of it back.”

ʿUthmān said: “I think there is a great deal of wealth sufficient for the people, and if they are not counted so that it is known who has received and who has not, I fear the matter will become confused.”

Al-Walīd b. Hishām b. al-Mughīra said to him: “I came to Syria and saw that its kings had established a dīwān and organized an army.” So he established a dīwān and organized an army, and he followed his advice.

He summoned ʿAqīl b. Abī Ṭālib, Makhrama b. Nawfal, and Jubayr b. Muṭʿim, who were among the Quraysh’s scribes, and said: “Register the people according to their ranks.” They began with Banū Hāshim, then followed them with Abū Bakr and his people, then ʿUmar and his people, in order of succession. When ʿUmar saw it, he said: “By God, I wish it were so, but begin with the kin of the Prophet ﷺ the nearest and then the next nearest, until you place ʿUmar where God, Exalted is He, placed him.”

1020Muḥammad, from al-Wāqidī, from Usāma b. Zayd b. Aslam, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Banū ʿAdī came to ʿUmar and said: “You are the successor of the Messenger of God ﷺ and the successor of Abū Bakr; Abū Bakr was the successor of the Messenger of God ﷺ. If only you would place yourself where these people who made the register placed you.”

He said: “Well, well, Banū ʿAdī! You want to eat at my expense and have me give my good deeds to you. By God, no! The call must come to you, and the register must include you—even if you are written among the last people. I have two companions who followed a path; if I differ from them, I will be led astray.

By God, we attained merit in this world and hope for reward for our deeds only through Muḥammad ﷺ.”

So he is our honor, and his people are the noblest of the Arabs; then the nearest, and then the next nearest. By God, if the non-Arabs come with deeds and we come without deeds, they will have a greater claim to Muḥammad than we do on the Day of Resurrection, for whoever is held back by his deeds will not be advanced by his lineage.

1021Muḥammad b. Saʿd, from al-Wāqidī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh, from al-Zuhrī, from Saʿīd, from other men whom al-Wāqidī named—some of whose reports were incorporated into one another’s—said: When ʿUmar resolved to establish the register, in Muḥarram of the year 20, he began by summoning Banū Hāshim, then those nearest in kinship to the Messenger of God ﷺ and then the next nearest.

When people were equal in kinship, he gave precedence to those with earlier merit.

Then he came to the Anṣār. They asked, “With whom shall we begin?” He said, “Begin with the clan of Saʿd b. Muʿādh al-Ashhalī of al-Aws, then with those nearest to Saʿd.”

ʿUmar assigned stipends to the people of the register, giving precedence in the allotments to those with prior service and distinguished participation.

Abū Bakr had treated the people equally in the distribution.

ʿUmar was asked about that.

He said, “I will not make one who fought against the Messenger of God ﷺ equal to one who fought alongside him.”

He began with those among the Emigrants and Anṣār who had fought at Badr, assigning each man five thousand dirhams annually; their allies and clients were equal with them.

He assigned four thousand dirhams to each man who had embraced Islam as those at Badr had, and to those who had emigrated to Abyssinia and fought at Uḥud.

He assigned two thousand each to the sons of those who fought at Badr, except al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, whom he placed on their father’s allotment because of their kinship to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He assigned each of them five thousand.

He assigned al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib five thousand because of his kinship to the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Some said: He assigned him seven thousand dirhams.

The others said: He gave no one precedence over the people of Badr except the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: he assigned each of them twelve thousand.

He included Juwayriya bt. al-Ḥārith and Ṣafiyya bt. Ḥuyayy b. Akhṭab among them.

He assigned three thousand dirhams to each man who had emigrated before the conquest.

He assigned two thousand to each man among those who embraced Islam at the conquest.

He assigned the same as those who embraced Islam at the conquest to adolescent boys among the sons of the Emigrants.

He assigned ʿUmar b. Abī Salama four thousand.

Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh said, “Why have you given ʿUmar precedence over us? Our fathers emigrated and fought at Badr.”

ʿUmar said, “I give him precedence because of his relation to the Prophet ﷺ. Let the one who seeks aid come with a mother like Umm Salama, and I will aid him.”

He assigned Usāma b. Zayd four thousand.

ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar said, “You assigned me three thousand and Usāma four thousand.

I witnessed what Usāma did not.”

ʿUmar said, “I gave him more because he was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than you were, and his father was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than your father was.”

Then he assigned people according to their rank, their recitation of the Qurʾan, and their participation in jihad.

Then he made the rest of the people one category.

He included each Muslim who came to him in Medina at twenty-five dinars.

He assigned stipends to others along with them.

He assigned the people of Yemen and Qays in Syria and Iraq amounts for each man ranging from two thousand, to one thousand, to nine hundred, to five hundred, to three hundred; he did not reduce anyone below three hundred.

He said, “If the wealth increases, I will assign each man four thousand dirhams: one thousand for his journey, one thousand for his weapons, one thousand to leave for his family, and one thousand for his horse and its equipment.”

He assigned stipends to Emigrant women: six thousand dirhams to Ṣafiyya bt. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, one thousand to Asmāʾ bt. ʿUmays, one thousand to Umm Kulthūm bt. ʿUqba, and one thousand to Umm ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd.

Al-Wāqidī said: It has also been related that he assigned three thousand dirhams to each of the Emigrant women.

Al-Wāqidī said in his chain of transmission: ʿUmar ordered the officials of the outlying districts to write to him.

He used to provide them with provisions.

Then ʿUthmān came, and he increased their provisions and clothing.

ʿUmar used to assign one hundred dirhams to a newborn; when the child grew up, he raised it to two hundred dirhams, and when the child reached maturity, he increased it further.

When an abandoned infant was brought to him, he assigned the child one hundred and provided a monthly allowance for the guardian to take, sufficient for the child’s needs; then he moved the child up from one year to the next.

He used to urge that they be treated well and have their nursing and expenses paid from the public treasury.

1022Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to us, from al-Wāqidī, who said: Ḥizām b. Hishām al-Kaʿbī related to me, from his father, who said: I saw ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb carrying the register of Khuzāʿa until he reached Qudayd. The women would come to him at Qudayd, and no woman, virgin or previously married, was absent from him; he would give it into their hands. Then

he would go on and stop at ʿUsfān, and do the same there, until he died.

1023Muḥammad b. Saʿd, from al-Wāqidī, from Abū Bakr b. Abī Sabra, from Muḥammad b. Zayd, who said: In ʿUmar’s time, the register of Ḥimyar was separate.

1024Muḥammad b. Saʿd said: Al-Wāqidī related to us: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī related to me, from Jahm b. Abī Jahm, who said: Khālid b. ʿUrfuṭa al-ʿUdhrī came to ʿUmar, who asked him,

“About what you left behind.” He said, “I left them praying to God that He prolong your life at the expense of their own.

“Everyone who set foot at al-Qādisiyya has an allowance of two thousand or fifteen hundred.

“Every newborn, male or female, is entered on the register for one hundred and two jars of land each month.”

ʿUmar said, “It is only their due, and I am most pleased to deliver it to them. If it were the wealth of al-Khaṭṭāb, I would not have given it to them. But I know that there is a surplus in it. If, when one of these men’s allowances is paid, he were to buy some sheep and establish them in his black-soil district, and when his allowance was paid a second time, he were to buy one or two more head and add them to the flock, then if any of his children remained, they would have something they had acquired.

“I do not know what will happen after me. I will give my counsel to all those whom God has entrusted with authority, for the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘Whoever dies having acted treacherously toward his subjects will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.’”

1025Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to me, from al-Wāqidī, from Muḥammad b. ʿAmr, from al-Ḥasan, who said: ʿUmar wrote to Ḥudhayfa, “Give the people their allowances and stipends.” He wrote back, “We have done so, and much remains.”

He wrote back to him: “It is their spoils, which God has granted them; it does not belong to ʿUmar or to the family of ʿUmar, so distribute it among them.”

1026He said: Wahb b. Baqiyya and Muḥammad b. Saʿd related to us; they said: Yazīd b. Hārūn related to us; he said: Muḥammad b. ʿAmr informed us, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra, that he came to ʿUmar from Bahrain.

He said: I met him during the late evening prayer.

I greeted him, and he asked me about the people. Then he said to me, “What have you brought?”

I said, “I have brought five hundred thousand.”

He said, “Do you know what you are saying?”

I said, “I have brought five hundred thousand.”

He said, “What are you saying?” I said, “One hundred thousand, one hundred thousand, one hundred thousand,” and counted five.

He said, “You are drowsy. Go back to your family and sleep; when morning comes, come to me.”

Abū Hurayra said: I went to him in the morning.

He said, “What have you brought?” I said, “Five hundred thousand.”

He said, “Is it sound?” I said, “Yes, I know nothing to the contrary.”

He said to the people, “A great deal of wealth has come to us.

“If you wish, we can count it out for you; or, if you wish, we can measure it out for you.”

A man said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, I have seen these non-Arabs keep a register by which they give people their allotments.”

He said: He established the register and assigned five thousand to the earliest Emigrants, four thousand to the Anṣār, and twelve thousand to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

1027Yazīd said: Muḥammad said: Ibn Khuṣayfa related to me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Rāfiʿ, from Barza bt. Rāfiʿ, who said: When the allotment was issued, ʿUmar sent Zaynab bt. Jaḥsh what was due to her.

When it was brought in to her, she said, “May God forgive ʿUmar. One of my sisters other than me would have been more capable of distributing this.”

They said, “It is all yours.”

She said, “Glory be to God!” She screened herself from it with a cloth.

Then she said, “Pour it out and cover it with a cloth.”

Then she said to me, “Put your hands in and take a handful

of it; go with it to so-and-so among her relatives and to orphans of hers.”

She distributed it until some remained beneath the cloth.

Barza bt. Rāfiʿ said: I said, “May God forgive you, Mother of the Believers! By God, we had a share in this wealth.”

She said, “Then you may have what is beneath the cloth.”

We found five hundred and eighty dirhams beneath it.

Then she raised her hands to heaven and said, “O God, may no allotment from ʿUmar reach me after this year of mine.”

He said: She died.

1028Abū ʿUbayd related to us: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ related to us, from al-Layth, from Muḥammad b. ʿAjlān, who said: When ʿUmar established the registers, he said, “With whom shall we begin?” They said, “With yourself.”

He said, “No. The Messenger of God ﷺ is our leader, so we will begin with his clan, then with those nearest, and then the next nearest.”

1029ʿAmr al-Nāqid related to us; he said: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Thaqafī related to us, from Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad, from his father, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb included al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn with their father and assigned them five thousand dirhams.

1030Al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī b. al-Aswad related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad, from his father, who said: When ʿUmar established the register, he consulted the people about whom to begin with. They said, “Begin with yourself.”

He said, “No. I will begin with the nearest to the Messenger of God ﷺ” and he began with them.

1031Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us, from Sufyān, from Abū Isḥāq, from Muṣʿab b. Saʿd, that ʿUmar assigned six thousand each to the people of Badr,

and ten thousand each to the Mothers of the Believers. He gave ʿĀʾisha an additional two thousand because the Messenger of God ﷺ loved her, and assigned six thousand each to Ṣafiyya and Juwayriya. He assigned one thousand each to Emigrant women, among them Umm ʿAbd, who was the mother of ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd.

1032Al-Ḥusayn related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us, from Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid, from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, who said: ʿUmar assigned five thousand each to the people of Badr, Arabs and clients alike.

He said, “I will give them precedence over everyone else.”

1033Al-Ḥusayn related to us; Wakīʿ related to us, from Isrāʾīl, from Jābir, from ʿĀmir, who said: There were five non-Arabs among them, including Tamīm al-Dārī and Bilāl.

Wakīʿ said: Al-Dār was from Lakhm, but al-Shaʿbī said this.

1034Al-Ḥusayn related to us; he said: Wakīʿ related to us, from Sufyān, from al-Aswad b. Qays, from a shaykh of theirs, who said: I heard ʿUmar say, “If I live until next year, I will include the lowest-ranking Emigrants at two thousand each.”

1035Abū ʿUbayd related to us; he said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-Miṣrī related to us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Khālid al-Fahmī, from Ibn Shihāb, that when ʿUmar established the registers, he assigned twelve thousand dirhams each to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ whom he had married in marriage.

He assigned six thousand dirhams to Juwayriya and Ṣafiyya bt. Ḥuyayy b. Akhṭab because they were among those whom God had granted to His Messenger as spoils.

He assigned five thousand each to the Emigrants who had witnessed Badr.

He assigned four thousand each to the Anṣār who had fought at Badr.

He applied his allotment to every freeborn Arab, ally, and client who had fought at Badr, giving no one precedence over another.

1036ʿAmr al-Nāqid and Abū ʿUbayd related to us; they said: Aḥmad b. Yūnus related to us, from Abū Khaythama, who said: Abū Isḥāq related to us, from Muṣʿab b. Saʿd, that ʿUmar assigned six thousand each to the people of Badr among the Emigrants and the Anṣār.

He assigned ten thousand each to the wives of the Prophet, and gave ʿĀʾisha precedence over them, assigning her twelve thousand dirhams.

He assigned six thousand each to Juwayriya and Ṣafiyya.

He assigned one thousand each to the earliest women emigrants: Asmāʾ bt. ʿUmays, Asmāʾ bt. Abī Bakr, and Umm ʿAbd Allāh bt. Masʿūd.
