1037al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Muḥammad b. Qays al-Asadī, who said: My mother, Umm al-Ḥakam, told me that ʿAlī included her among those receiving one hundred in the stipend.

1038al-Ḥusayn told us: Wakīʿ told us, from Sufyān, from al-Shaybānī, from Yasīr b. ʿAmr, who said: Saʿd assigned two thousand each to those who had recited the Qurʾān.

He said: ʿUmar wrote to him: Do not give anyone anything on account of the Qurʾān.

1039Abū ʿUbayd told us: Saʿīd b. Abī Maryam told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿUmar assigned ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ two hundred because he was a commander, ʿUmayr b. Wahb al-Jumaḥī two hundred for his steadfastness in hardship, and Busr b. Abī Arṭāʾ two hundred because he was a conqueror.

He said: How many a conquest God has granted through his hand!

Abū ʿUbayd said: He means this number in dinars.

1040Abū ʿUbayd said: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Yazīd b. Abī Ḥabīb, that ʿUmar wrote to ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ: “Assign those who pledged allegiance beneath the tree two hundred in the stipend”—he said, meaning two hundred dinars—“and make that amount reach you yourself by virtue of your command. Assign Khārija b. Ḥudhāfa a high stipend because of his bravery.”

1041Abū ʿUbayd told us: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from al-Layth b. Saʿd, from Muḥammad b. ʿAjlān, that ʿUmar gave Usāma b. Zayd precedence over ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar.

The people kept pressing ʿAbd Allāh until he spoke to ʿUmar. He said: “Do you give precedence to someone who is no better than I? You assigned him two thousand, and me one thousand five hundred dirhams.”

ʿUmar said: “I did that because Zayd b. Ḥāritha was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than ʿUmar, and Usāma was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar.”

1042Yaḥyā b. Maʿīn told me: Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd told us, from Khārija b. Muṣʿab, from ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ or someone else, from Ibn ʿUmar, that he spoke to his father about giving Usāma precedence over him in the stipend and said: “By God, he never outdid me in anything.”

ʿUmar said: “His father was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than your father, and he was dearer to the Messenger of God ﷺ than you.”

1043Muḥammad b. al-Ṣabbāḥ al-Bazzāz told us: Hushaym told us, from Manṣūr, from al-Ḥasan, who said: Some people came to a governor of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb. He gave the Arabs among them stipends and left out the non-Arabs.

ʿUmar wrote to him: “To proceed: it is enough evil for a man that he hold his Muslim brother in contempt. Peace.”

1044Abū ʿUbayd told us: Khālid b. ʿAmr told us, from Isrāʾīl, from ʿAmmār al-Duhnī, from Sālim b. Abī al-Jaʿd, that ʿUmar set ʿAmmār b. Yāsir’s stipend at six thousand dirhams.

1045Abū ʿUbayd told us: Khālid told us, from Isrāʾīl, from Ismāʿīl b. Sumayʿ, from Muslim al-Baṭīn, that ʿUmar set Salmān’s stipend at four thousand dirhams.

1046Rūḥ b. ʿAbd al-Muʾmin told us: Yaʿqūb told me, from Ḥammād, from Ḥumayd, from Anas, who said: ʿUmar assigned al-Hurmuzān two thousand in the stipend.

1047Al-ʿUmarī told me: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṭāʾī told me, from al-Mujālid, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: When ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, in the year twenty, considered establishing the registers, he summoned Makhrama b. Nawfal and Jubayr b. Muṭʿim and ordered them to list people according to their ranks.

They wrote Banū Hāshim first, then followed them with Abū Bakr and his people, and ʿUmar and his people.

When ʿUmar looked at the register, he said: “I wish I had such a degree of kinship with the Messenger of God ﷺ. Begin with the nearest, then the next nearest. Then place ʿUmar where God has placed him.”

Al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib thanked him for that ﵀ and said: “You have upheld kinship ties.”

He said: When ʿUmar established the register, Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb said: “A register like the register of the Banū al-Aṣfar? If you assign stipends to people, they will rely on the register and abandon trade.”

ʿUmar said: “This is unavoidable, for the Muslim fayʾ has grown abundant.”

He said: ʿUmar assigned one thousand to the dihqān of the Nahr al-Malik, to Ibn al-Nakhīrkhān, to Khālid and Jamīl, the sons of Baṣbahra, dihqāns of al-Falālīj, to Basṭām b. Narsī, dihqān of Bābil and Khaṭarniyya, to al-Rafīl, dihqān of al-ʿĀl, to al-Hurmuzān, and to Jufayna al-ʿIbādī.

It is said that he gave al-Hurmuzān precedence and assigned him two thousand.

1048Abū ʿUbayd told us, from Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh, from Arṭāʾ b. al-Mundhir, from Ḥakīm b. ʿUmayr, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb wrote to the commanders of the armies: “Those of the red people whom you have freed and who have become Muslims, attach them to their patrons. They shall have what their patrons have and bear what their patrons bear. If they wish to be a tribe on their own, make them equal to their patrons in the stipend.”

1049Hishām b. ʿAmmār told us, from Baqiyya, from Abū Bakr b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Maryam, from his father, from Abū ʿUbayda, that men from the desert asked him to assign them stipends.

He said: “By God, I will not assign you stipends until I have assigned stipends to the people of the settled areas.”

1050Abū ʿUbayd told us: Abū al-Yamān told us: Ṣafwān b. ʿAmr told us: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz wrote to Yazīd b. Ḥuṣayn: “Order the army to receive the fixed allotment, and attend to the people of the settled areas.”

1051Abū ʿUbayd told us: Saʿīd b. Abī Maryam told us, from ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar al-ʿUmarī, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that ʿUmar did not assign stipends to the people of Mecca or call them up for military expeditions, saying: “They are such and such.”

1052Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim b. Sallām told us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Mahdī told us, from Shuʿba, from ʿAdī b. Thābit, from Abū Ḥāzim, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Whoever leaves dependants, they are our responsibility; whoever leaves property, it belongs to his heirs.”

1053Hishām b. ʿAmmār al-Dimashqī told me: al-Walīd b. Muslim told us, from Sulaymān b. Abī al-ʿAtīka and Kulthūm b. Ziyād, who said: Sulaymān b. Ḥabīb told me that ʿUmar assigned the allotments of ten (each) to the families of the fighters and their descendants.

He said: ʿUthmān and the governors after him upheld that practice and made the stipends inheritable, so that the heirs of a deceased person who was not on the stipend register inherited them, until the time of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

Sulaymān said: He asked me about that, and I informed him of this.

He objected to inheritance and said: “Stop it, and make the fixed allotment universal.”

I said: “I fear that those after you will follow your example in stopping inheritance but will not follow your example in making the fixed allotment universal.”

He said: “You are right,” and left them as they were.

1054Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Abū Qubayl, who said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ﵁ assigned ten to a newborn when it was born; when it reached the age at which a stipend was assigned to it, he attached it to the stipend register.

When Muʿāwiya came to power, he assigned that to a weaned child.

When ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān came to power, he stopped all of that except for whomever he chose.

1055ʿAffān told us: Yazīd told us, who said: Yaḥyā b. al-Mutawakkil reported to me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that ʿUmar did not assign a stipend to a newborn until it was weaned.

Then his herald called out: “Do not rush your children into weaning, for we assign a stipend to every child born in Islam.”

ʿAmr al-Nāqid told us: Aḥmad b. Yūnus told us, from Zuhayr b. Muʿāwiya, from Abū Isḥāq, that his grandfather passed by ʿUthmān, who said to him: “How many dependants do you have, old man?” He replied: “I have such-and-such.”

He said: “We have assigned you a stipend and assigned your dependants one hundred each.”

1056Abū ʿUbayd told us: Marwān b. Shujāʿ al-Jazarī told us: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz enrolled me for ten dinars when I was a weaned child.

1057Ibrāhīm b. Muḥammad al-Shāmī told us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Mahdī told us, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Abū al-Juḥḥāf, from a man of Khathʿam, who said: “A child was born to me, so I brought him to ʿAlī, and he enrolled him for one hundred.”

1058ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Mahdī told us, from Sufyān, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Sharīk, from Bishr b. Ghālib, who said: al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī—or, he said, al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī; ʿUmar is uncertain—was asked: “When does a newborn become entitled to a share?” He said: “When it cries aloud at birth.”

1059ʿAmr al-Nāqid told me: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna told us, from ʿAmr b. Dīnār, from al-Ḥasan b. Muḥammad, that three enslaved men belonging to the Banū ʿAffān were present at Badr.

ʿUmar used to give each of them three thousand dirhams every year.

1060Abū ʿUbayd told us: Ibn Abī ʿAdī told us, from Sufyān, from Zuhayr b. Thābit—or Ibn Abī Dhiʾb—from Dhuʾl b. Aws, that a foundling was brought to ʿAlī, and he enrolled him for one hundred.

1061ʿAmr and al-Qāsim b. Sallām told me: Aḥmad b. Yūnus told us, from Zuhayr; and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ al-Muqriʾ told me, from Zuhayr b. Muʿāwiya, who said: Abū Isḥāq told us,

From Ḥāritha b. al-Muḍarrib, that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ordered a jārīb of food to be kneaded, then baked, then crumbled into a broth with oil. Then he summoned thirty men, who ate their midday meal from it until they had eaten their fill.

Then he did the same at the evening meal.

He said: “Two jārībs suffice a man each month.”

So he used to provide people—a man, a woman, and an enslaved person—with two jārībs each month.

ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣāliḥ said: A man used to curse his companion, saying:

“May God raise your two jārībs!”

That is, may He cut them off from you through death.

This expression has remained on people’s tongues to this day.

1062Abū ʿUbayd told us: Abū al-Yamān told me, from Ṣafwān b. ʿAmr, from Abū al-Zāhiriyya, that Abū al-Dardāʾ said:

“How many a rightly guided and guiding practice has ʿUmar established for the community of Muḥammad ﷺ, among them: the two mudd measures and the two qist measures.”

1063Abū ʿUbayd told us: Saʿīd b. Abī Maryam told us, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Qays b. Rāfiʿ, who heard Sufyān b. Wahb say: ʿUmar said, taking the mudd measure in one hand and the qist measure in the other: “I have assigned every Muslim soul two mudd measures of wheat and two qist measures of vinegar each month.”

A man said: “And an enslaved person?” He replied: “Yes, an enslaved person too.”

1064Hishām b. ʿAmmār told me: Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza told us: Tamīm b. ʿAṭiyya told me: ʿAbd Allāh b. Qays told me that ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb ascended the pulpit, praised and extolled God, then said: “We have set your stipends and provisions for each month, and in his hands were the mudd and qist measures.”

and in his hands were the mudd and qist measures.

He said: He shook them and said: “May God do such-and-such to whoever diminishes them!”

And he invoked a curse against him.

1065Abū ʿUbayd told us: Ibn Abī Zāʾida told us, from Maʿqil b. ʿUbayd Allāh, from ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, that whenever a man had become entitled to his stipend and then died, he would give it to his heirs.

1066ʿAffān, Khalaf al-Bazzār, and Wahb b. Baqiyya told us: Yazīd b. Hārūn reported to us: Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid reported to us, from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, who said: After the death of ʿAbd Allāh b. Masʿūd, al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām said to ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān ﵄: “Give me ʿAbd Allāh’s stipend; his dependants have a greater right to it than the public treasury.”

He gave him fifteen thousand.

Yazīd said: Ismāʿīl said: Al-Zubayr was the executor of Ibn Masʿūd.

1067Ibn Abī Shayba told me: ʿUbayd Allāh b. Mūsā told us, from ʿAlī b. Ṣāliḥ b. Ḥayy, from Simāk b. Ḥarb, that a man died in the neighborhood after eight months of the year had passed, and ʿUmar gave him two-thirds of his stipend.

Chapter 88

The signet ring

1068ʿAffān b. Muslim told us, saying: Shuʿba told us, saying: Qatāda informed us; he said: I heard Anas b. Mālik say: When the Messenger of God ﷺ wanted to write to the king of the Romans, he was told, “They do not read a letter unless it is sealed.”

He said: So he took a silver signet ring.

It is as though I can see its whiteness on his hand.

He engraved on it: “Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.”

1069Abū al-Rabīʿ Sulaymān b. Dāwūd al-Zahrānī told us, saying: Ḥammād b. Zayd told us, saying: Ayyūb informed us, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Messenger of God ﷺ took a silver signet ring, and placed its bezel on the inside of his palm.

1070Muḥammad b. Ḥayyān al-Ḥayyānī told me, saying: Zuhayr told us, from Ḥumayd, from Anas b. Mālik, who said: The Messenger of God’s signet ring was entirely silver, and its bezel was of the same material.

1071ʿAmr al-Nāqid told us, saying: Yazīd b. Hārūn told us, from Ḥumayd, from al-Ḥasan, who said: The Messenger of God’s signet ring was made of silver, and its bezel was Abyssinian.

1072Hudba b. Khālid told us, saying: Hammām b. Yaḥyā told us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Ṣuhayb, from Anas b. Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “I have had a signet ring made, so let no one engrave an inscription like its engraving.”

1073Bakr b. al-Haytham told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq told us, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī and Qatāda, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ took a silver signet ring and engraved on it, “Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.”

Abū Bakr used to seal with it, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān. It was in his hand when it fell from his hand into the well. The well was drained, but it could not be recovered. That was in the middle of his caliphate.

He then took a signet ring and engraved on it, “Muḥammad is the Messenger of God,” in three lines.

Qatāda said: “And its inscription …” (thus in the source).

1074Hennād told us, saying: al-Aswad b. Shaybān told us, saying: Khālid b. Sumayr informed us: A man called Maʿn b. Zāʾida had himself engraved on the caliphal signet ring.

He thereby obtained money from the land tax of Kūfa during ʿUmar’s time. This reached ʿUmar, who wrote to al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba: “I have been informed that a man called Maʿn b. Zāʾida had himself engraved on the caliphal signet ring and obtained money from the land tax of Kūfa through it.

“When this letter of mine reaches you, carry out my order in this matter and obey my messenger.”

When al-Mughīra had prayed the afternoon prayer and the people had taken their seats, he went out with ʿUmar’s messenger.

The people craned their necks to watch him until he stopped before Maʿn.

Then he said to the messenger: “The Commander of the Faithful has ordered me to obey your command concerning him. So order me as you wish.”

The messenger said: “Bring me a neck collar.”

He hung it around his neck.

A neck collar was brought, and he placed it around his neck and pulled it very hard.

Then he said to al-Mughīra: “Imprison him until an order concerning him comes to you from the Commander of the Faithful.”

He did so.

The prison at that time was made of reeds. Maʿn contrived to get out and sent word to his family: “Send me my she-camel, my slave-girl, and my Qaṭawānī cloak.”

They did so.

He went out at night with his slave-girl riding behind him. He traveled until he feared the morning would expose him; then he made his camel kneel, tethered it, and hid until the pursuit had passed.

When evening came, he put the cloak back on his camel, secured it, had his slave-girl ride behind him, and traveled until he arrived before ʿUmar, who was rousing those engaged in night prayer for the dawn prayer, carrying his whip.

He left his camel and slave-girl to one side, then approached ʿUmar and said: “Peace be upon you, Commander of the Faithful, and God’s mercy and blessings.”

He replied: “And upon you.”

“Who are you?” he asked. He said: “I am Maʿn b. Zāʾida. I have come to you repentant.”

He said: “Go away; may God not welcome you.”

When he had prayed the dawn prayer, he said to the people: “Stay where you are.”

When the sun had risen, he said: “This is Maʿn b. Zāʾida. He had himself engraved on the caliphal signet ring and thereby obtained money from the land tax of Kūfa. What do you say about him?” Someone said: “Cut off his hand.”

Another said: “Crucify him.”

ʿAlī remained silent.

ʿUmar said to him: “What do you say, Abū al-Ḥasan?”

He said: “Commander of the Faithful, a man who told a lie should be punished on his body.”

ʿUmar beat him severely—or, it was said, brutally—and imprisoned him.

He remained in prison as long as God willed.

Then he sent word to a Qurashī friend of his: “Speak to the Commander of the Faithful about releasing me.”

The Qurashī spoke to him, saying: “Commander of the Faithful, you have already meted out to Maʿn b. Zāʾida the punishment he deserved. If you think fit, release him.”

ʿUmar said: “You have reminded me of the beating; I had forgotten.”

“Bring Maʿn here.”

He beat him, then ordered him back to prison.

Maʿn sent word to each of his friends: “Do not mention me to the Commander of the Faithful.”

He remained imprisoned as long as God willed.

Then ʿUmar noticed him and said: “Maʿn!”

He was brought to him, and ʿUmar made him swear an oath and released him.

1075Al-Mufaḍḍal al-Yashkurī and Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī told me, from Ibn Jābān, from Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who said: When the Persian king issued an order, the official who entered the order recorded it in his presence. The king had a servant who entered a record of it in a register compiled for each month. The king sealed it with his signet, and it was stored. Then the order was sent to the ṣāḥib al-zimām, and the seal was entrusted to him. He sent it to the official in charge, who wrote a letter from the king on its basis and made a copy in the original register. Then it was sent to the ṣāḥib al-zimām, who presented it to the king and compared it with what was in the register. Then it was sealed in the king’s presence, or in the presence of the most trusted person near him.

1076Al-Madāʾinī told me, from Maslama b. Muḥārib, who said: Ziyād b. Abī Sufyān was the first among the Arabs to adopt a dīwān for the ṣāḥib al-zimām and a signet ring, following the Persian practice.

1077Mufaḍḍal al-Yashkurī told me: Ibn Jābān told me, from Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who said: One of the Persian kings had a signet for confidential matters, a signet for dispatches, a signet for perpetuity, used to seal registers, land grants, and similar documents of honor, and a signet for the land tax.

The ṣāḥib al-zimām was in charge of these.

Sometimes a man from the king’s inner circle was assigned exclusively to the signet for confidential matters and correspondence.

1078Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī told me, from Ibn Jābān,

from Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, who said: Letters accompanying the delivery of money were read to the king, and they were written on white sheets.

Each year the land-tax official brought the king joined sheets recording the amount collected in land tax, what had been spent on the various expenditures, and what had accrued to the treasury. The king would seal them and send them on.

When Kisrā b. Hurmuz Aparwēz came to power, he was bothered by the odors of those sheets and ordered that the official in charge of his land-tax bureau submit nothing to him except on sheets colored yellow with saffron and rosewater, and that the sheets presented to him concerning the delivery of money and other matters be written only on yellowed sheets. This was done.

When Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān took charge of the land tax of Iraq, Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ undertook from him the districts of the Tigris—or, it is said, al-Bahqubādh—and remitted money. He wrote his letter on a piece of leather and colored it yellow. Ṣāliḥ laughed and said: “I had thought no one else would bring it.” That is, because of Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ’s knowledge of Persian affairs.

1079When the Commander of the Faithful al-Manṣūr came to power, he ordered his vizier Abū Ayyūb al-Mūriyānī to write letters accompanying the delivery of money on sheets and to color the sheets yellow.

The practice continued in that way.

Chapter 89

Coinage

On Coinage

1080Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Aswad told us, saying: Yaḥyā b. Ādam told us, saying: al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ told me, saying: The dirhams minted by non-Arabs varied, large and small.

They minted some weighing one mithqāl, which weighed twenty qīrāṭs; some weighing twelve qīrāṭs; and some weighing ten qīrāṭs, which were half-mithqāls.

When God brought Islam and a middle standard was needed for paying the alms tax, they took twenty qīrāṭs, twelve qīrāṭs, and ten qīrāṭs.

They found that these totaled forty-two qīrāṭs.

They minted a coin at one-third of that weight, namely fourteen qīrāṭs. The weight of the Arab dirham was thus fourteen qīrāṭs of the qīrāṭs of the esteemed dīnār, making every ten dirhams weigh seven mithqāls.

That is, 140 qīrāṭs, the weight of seven.

1081Someone other than al-Ḥasan b. Ṣāliḥ said: The non-Arab dirhams included ten weighing ten mithqāls, ten weighing six mithqāls, and ten weighing five mithqāls.

These were added together and found to total twenty-one mithqāls.

They took one-third of that, which was seven mithqāls, and minted dirhams such that ten of them weighed seven mithqāls.

The two accounts amount to one and the same thing.

1082Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, saying: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Aslamī told us, saying: ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Mawhab, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Thaʿlaba b. Ṣuʿayr, who said: In the pre-Islamic period, the dīnārs of Heraclius circulated among the people of Mecca, and Persian baghlī dirhams circulated among them.

They would trade only …

for uncoined bullion.

Among them the mithqāl had a known weight: twenty-two qīrāṭs less a fraction, and ten dirhams weighed seven mithqāls.

The raṭl weighed twelve ūqiyyas, and each ūqiyya weighed forty dirhams.

The Messenger of God ﷺ affirmed this, as did Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, and ʿAlī.

When Muʿāwiya came to power, he left it as it was.

Then Muṣʿab b. al-Zubayr minted a small number of dirhams during the days of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr; they were later withdrawn.

When ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān came to power, he inquired and investigated the matter of dirhams and dīnārs.

He wrote to al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf to mint dirhams at fifteen qīrāṭs of the qīrāṭs of the dīnārs.

He himself minted Damascus dīnārs.

ʿUthmān said: My father said: I came to Medina, where there were a number of the Companions of the Messenger of God and others among the Successors, and they did not object to that.

Muḥammad b. Saʿd said: The weight of the dirham in our current dirhams is fourteen qīrāṭs of the qīrāṭs of our mithqāl, which was set at twenty qīrāṭs.

It is the weight of fifteen qīrāṭs out of twenty-one and three-sevenths qīrāṭs.

1083Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, saying: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar told us, saying: Isḥāq b. Ḥāzim told me, from al-Muṭṭalib b. al-Sāʾib, from Abū Wadāʿa al-Sahmī, who showed him the weight of the mithqāl.

He said: I weighed it and found it to be the weight of the mithqāl of ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān.

He said: “This was in the possession of my father, Abū Wadāʿa b. Ḍubayra al-Sahmī, in the pre-Islamic period.”

1084Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, saying: al-Wāqidī told us, from Saʿīd b. Muslim b. Bābak, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Sābiṭ al-Jumaḥī, who said: Quraysh had weights in the pre-Islamic period.

When Islam came, they retained them as they had been.

Quraysh weighed silver with a weight they called a dirham, and weighed gold with a weight they called a dīnār.

Every ten of the dirham weights equaled seven of the dīnār weights.

They had the barley-grain weight, one-sixtieth of the dirham weight.

Their ūqiyya weighed forty dirhams.

The nashsh weighed twenty dirhams.

They had the nawā, which weighed five dirhams.

They traded in uncoined bullion according to these weights.

When the Prophet ﷺ came to Mecca, he affirmed these for them.

1085Muḥammad b. Saʿd, from al-Wāqidī, who said: Rabīʿa b. ʿUthmān told me, from Wahb b. Kaysān, who said: I saw the dīnārs and dirhams before ʿAbd al-Malik engraved them; they were unmarked.

They were of the same weight as the dīnārs minted by ʿAbd al-Malik.

1086Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī, from ʿUthmān b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Mawhab, from his father, who said: I asked Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab: “Who was the first to mint engraved dīnārs?” He said: “ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān. The dīnārs that circulated were Roman, while the dirhams were Sasanian and a few Ḥimyarī ones.

“Saʿīd said: I sent bullion to Damascus, and they minted it for me at the weight of the mithqāl used in the pre-Islamic period.

  1. Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, saying: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna told us, from his father, that the first to mint at the weight of seven was al-Ḥārith b. ʿAbd Allāh …”

the inscribed ones? He said: ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān. The dinars used to arrive from the Byzantines, and the dirhams were Sasanian, with a few Ḥimyarite ones.

Saʿīd said: I sent bullion to Damascus, and they struck coins for me at the weight of the mithqāl in pre-Islamic times.

1087Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna told us, from his father, that the first to strike coins at the weight of seven was al-Ḥārith, son of ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Rabīʿa al-Makhzūmī, in the days of Ibn al-Zubayr.

1088Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar told me: Ibn Abī al-Zinād told us, from his father, that ʿAbd al-Malik was the first to strike gold in the Year of Unity, in the year 74. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī said: al-Ḥajjāj struck dirhams at the end of the year 75, then ordered them struck in all the regions in the year 76.

1089Dāwūd the Critic told me: I heard our shaykhs say that the ʿubbād, who were from the people of al-Ḥīra, used to trade at a hundred weighing six—that is, sixty mithqāls’ worth of dirhams—and at a hundred weighing eight—that is, eighty mithqāls’ worth of dirhams—and at a hundred weighing five—that is, fifty mithqāls’ worth of dirhams—and at a hundred mithqāls.

Dāwūd the Critic said: I saw a dirham bearing the striking of these dirhams in Kūfa in the year 73, and the money-changers agreed that it was fabricated.

He said: I also saw an unusual dirham, unlike any others, bearing the name ʿUbayd Allāh b. Ziyād; they rejected it too.

1090Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Yaḥyā b. al-Nuʿmān al-Ghifārī, from his father, who said: Muṣʿab struck dirhams by order of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr in the year 70, following the Sasanian manner of striking. On them were the words “Blessing” and “God.”

When al-Ḥajjāj came to power, he changed them.

It is related from Hishām al-Kalbī that he said: Muṣʿab also struck dinars along with the dirhams.

1091Dāwūd the Critic told me: Abū al-Zubayr the Critic told me: ʿAbd al-Malik struck some dinars in the year 74, then struck them in the year 75; and al-Ḥajjāj struck Baghlī dirhams on which he wrote: “In the name of God.

Al-Ḥajjāj.”

Then, a year later, he wrote on them:

“God is One, God the Eternal Refuge.”

The jurists disliked this, so they were called “disliked.”

He said: It is also said that the non-Arabs disliked their reduced weight, so they were called “disliked.”

He said: The Samīriyya were named after the first person to strike them, whose name was Samīr.

1092ʿAbbās b. Hishām al-Kalbī told me, from his father, who said: ʿAwāna b. al-Ḥakam told me that al-Ḥajjāj asked about what the Persians used to do when striking dirhams.

He established a mint and gathered the die-cutters there.

He would strike money for the government from the bullion, the refined debased metal, the alloy, and the inferior mixed metal that had been collected for him.

Then he permitted merchants and others to have sheets struck for them, and he profited from the surplus of what was collected as excess wages for the artisans and die-cutters.

He sealed the hands of the die-cutters.

When ʿUmar b. Hubayra took charge of Iraq for Yazīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik, he refined the silver more thoroughly than those before him and improved the dirhams.

He was strict about the standard.

Then Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī, then al-Qasrī, took charge of Iraq for Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik. He was stricter about coinage than Ibn Hubayra, until he regulated it more thoroughly than Ibn Hubayra had.

Then Yūsuf b. ʿUmar took charge after him and was excessively severe toward the die-cutters and the people who altered coins; he cut off hands and beat bodies.

The Hubayrī, Khālidī, and Yūsufī coins were the finest Umayyad coinage.

Al-Manṣūr would accept no Umayyad coins in the land tax except these.

The earlier dirhams were therefore called “disliked.”

1093Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Ibn Abī al-Zinād, from his father, that ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān was the first to strike gold and silver after the Year of Unity.

He said: I asked my father: What do people mean when they say that Ibn Masʿūd used to order debased coins to be broken? He said: Those were debased coins struck by the non-Arabs, who adulterated them.

1094ʿAbd al-Aʿlā b. Ḥammād al-Narasī told me: Ḥammād b. Salama told us: Dāwūd b. Abī Hind told us, from al-Shaʿbī, from ʿAlqama b. Qays, that Ibn Masʿūd had a remnant in the treasury, which he sold at a loss.

ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb forbade him from doing that, and afterward he would lend it.

1095Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Qudāma b. Mūsā, that when ʿAmr and ʿUthmān found debased coins in the treasury, they would make them into silver.

1096al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Ibn Abī al-Zinād, from his father, that a man who was striking coins outside the ruler’s mint was brought to ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. He punished and imprisoned him, took his iron tools, and threw them into the fire.

1097Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Kathīr b. Zayd, from al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Ḥanṭab, that ʿAbd al-Malik b. Marwān seized a man who was striking coins outside the Muslims’ mint and intended to cut off his hand, but then refrained and punished him.

Al-Muṭṭalib said: I saw the shaykhs among our people in Medina approve of his action and praise him for it.

Al-Wāqidī said: Our associates hold that whoever engraves the caliphate’s seal should be given severe and public discipline, but should not have a hand cut off. This was the view of Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Thawrī.

Mālik, Ibn Abī Dhiʾb, and their associates said: We dislike cutting a dirham if its value is intact, and we prohibit it because it is corruption.

Al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa, and their associates said: There is no harm in cutting it if that does not harm Islam and its people.

1098ʿAmr the Critic told me: Ismāʿīl b. Ibrāhīm told us, from Ibn ʿAwn, from Ibn Sīrīn, that Marwān b. al-Ḥakam seized a man for cutting dirhams.

He cut off the man’s hand. When Zayd b. Thābit heard of it, he said: “He has certainly punished him.”

Ismāʿīl said: He meant Persian dirhams.

1099Muḥammad b. Saʿd said, and al-Wāqidī said: Abān b. ʿUthmān punished a man in Medina for cutting dirhams.

He beat him thirty times and paraded him.

In our view, this concerns someone who cut them

and inserted into them cast and debased coins.

1100Muḥammad told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Ṣāliḥ b. Jaʿfar, from Ibn Kaʿb, concerning His words, “Or that we do with our wealth whatever we wish” (1), who said: “Cutting dirhams.”

1101Muḥammad b. Khālid b. ʿAbd Allāh told us: Yazīd b. Hārūn told us: Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd informed us: A man who cut dirhams was mentioned to Ibn al-Musayyab, and Saʿīd said: “This is corruption in the land.”

1102ʿAmr the Critic told us: Ismāʿīl b. Ibrāhīm told us: Yūnus b. ʿUbayd told us, from al-Ḥasan, who said: “The people, though they were unbelievers, knew the place this dirham held among people, so they made it good and pure. When it came to you, you adulterated it and corrupted it.

“ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb once said: ‘I was minded to make dirhams from camel hides.’

“He was told: ‘Then there would be no camels.’

“So he refrained.”

(1) Sūrat Hūd, 11:87.

(*)

Chapter 90

Writing

On Writing

1103ʿAbbās b. Hishām b. Muḥammad b. al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī told me, from his father, from his grandfather, and from al-Sharqī b. al-Qaṭāmī, who said: Three men from Ṭayyiʾ gathered at Baqqa: Marāmir b. Murra, Aslam b. Sidra, and ʿĀmir b. Jadara. They devised the script and modeled the spelling of Arabic on the spelling of Syriac.

A group of people from al-Anbār learned it from them; then the people of al-Ḥīra learned it from the people of al-Anbār.

Bishr b. ʿAbd al-Malik, brother of Ukaydir b. ʿAbd al-Malik b. ʿAbd al-Jinn al-Kindī, then al-Sakūnī, lord of Dūmat al-Jandal, used to visit al-Ḥīra and stay there for a time. He was a Christian.

Bishr learned the Arabic script from the people of al-Ḥīra.

Then he came to Mecca on some business and saw Sufyān b. Umayya b. ʿAbd Shams and Abū Qays b. ʿAbd Manāf b. Zuhra b. Kilāb writing. They asked him to teach them the script, so he taught them the spelling; then he showed them the script, and they wrote.

Later Bishr, Sufyān, and Abū Qays went to al-Ṭāʾif on a trading journey. Ghaylān b. Salama al-Thaqafī accompanied them and learned the script from them.

Bishr parted from them and went to the lands of Muḍar, where he learned the script from ʿAmr b. Zurāra b. ʿAdas, who was called ʿAmr the Scribe.

Then Bishr went to Syria, and people there learned the script from him.

A man from Ṭābiḫa of Kalb also learned the script from the three men of Ṭayyiʾ. He taught it to a man from the people of Wādī al-Qurā, who went to the valley, frequented it, settled there, and taught the script to a group of its people.

1104al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ and Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me: Muḥammad b. ʿUmar al-Wāqidī told us, from Khālid b. Ilyās, from Abū Bakr b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Jahm al-ʿAdawī, who said: When Islam came, there were seventeen men among Quraysh, all of whom could write: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān, Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ, Ṭalḥa, Yazīd b. Abī Sufyān, Abū Ḥudhayfa b. ʿUtba b. Rabīʿa, Ḥāṭib b. ʿAmr, brother of Suhayl b. ʿAmr al-ʿĀmirī of Quraysh, Abū Salama b. ʿAbd al-Asad al-Makhzūmī, Abān b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ b. Umayya, his brother Khālid b. Saʿīd, ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ al-ʿĀmirī, Ḥuwayṭib b. ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā al-ʿĀmirī, Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb b. Umayya, Muʿāwiya b. Abī Sufyān, and Juḥaym b. al-Ṣalt b. Makhrama b. al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf.

Among Quraysh’s confederates was al-ʿAlāʾ al-Ḥaḍramī.

1105Bakr b. al-Haytham told me: ʿAbd al-Razzāq told us, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUtba, that the Prophet ﷺ said to al-Shifāʾ bt. ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAdawiyya, from ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb’s clan: “Will you not teach Ḥafṣa the incantation for an ant bite, just as you taught her writing?” Al-Shifāʾ had been a scribe in pre-Islamic times.

1106al-Walīd b. Ṣāliḥ told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Usāma b. Zayd, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Saʿd, who said: Ḥafṣa, the Prophet’s wife, could write.

1107al-Walīd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from ʿAlqama b. Abī ʿAlqama, from Muḥammad b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Thawbān, that Umm Kulthūm bt. ʿUqba could write.

1108al-Walīd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Farwa, from ʿĀʾisha bt. Saʿd, who said: “My father taught me writing.”

1109al-Walīd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Mūsā b. Yaʿqūb, from his paternal aunt, from her mother Karīma bt. al-Miqdād, that she could write.

1110al-Walīd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from Ibn Abī Sabra, from Ibn ʿAwn, from Ibn Miyāḥ, from ʿĀʾisha, that she used to read the muṣḥaf but could not write.

1111al-Walīd told me: al-Wāqidī told me, from ʿAbd Allāh b. Yazīd al-Hudhalī, from Sālim Sabalān, from Umm Salama, that she used to read but could not write.

1112al-Walīd and Muḥammad b. Saʿd told me, from al-Wāqidī,

from his shaykhs, who said: The first person to write for the Messenger of God ﷺ upon his arrival in Medina was Ubayy b. Kaʿb al-Anṣārī.

He was the first to write at the end of a letter, “So-and-so wrote it.”

Whenever Ubayy was not present, the Messenger of God would summon Zayd

the son of Thābit al-Anṣārī, and he wrote for him.

Ubayy and Zayd used to write down the revelation in his presence, his letters to those with whom he corresponded, what was revealed as abrogating, and other things.

Al-Wāqidī said: The first Qurashī to write for him was ʿAbd Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ. Then he apostatized, returned to Mecca, and said to Quraysh:

“I can produce the like of what Muḥammad produces.”

He would dictate “the wrongdoers,” and he would write “the unbelievers.”

He would dictate “All-Hearing, All-Knowing,” and he would write “All-Forgiving, All-Merciful,”

and things like that.

Then God revealed: “Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, ‘It has been revealed to me,’ when nothing has been revealed to him, and one who says, ‘I shall send down the like of what God has sent down’?”

[Source note 1: Sūrat al-Anʿām, 6, verse 93.]

When the day of the conquest of Mecca came, the Messenger of God ordered that he be killed.

ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān interceded for him, saying, “He is my foster-brother, and he has become Muslim.”

The Messenger of God ordered that he be spared, and ʿUthmān appointed him over Egypt.

ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān and Sharḥabīl b. Ḥasana al-Ṭābikhī, of Khandaf and an ally of Quraysh, wrote for the Messenger of God.

It is said instead that he was Kindaī.

Juhaym b. al-Ṣalt, Makhrama, Khālid b. Saʿīd, Abān b. Saʿīd b. al-ʿĀṣ, and al-ʿAlāʾ al-Ḥaḍramī also wrote for him.

When the year of the conquest came, Muʿāwiya became Muslim and also wrote for him.

One day he summoned him while he was eating, and he was slow to come, so he said, “May God never fill his belly.”

He used to say, “The Messenger of God’s prayer has caught up with me.”

He would eat seven meals a day, sometimes more and sometimes fewer.

1113Al-Wāqidī and others said: Ḥanẓala b. al-Rabīʿ b. Rabāḥ al-Asīdī, of Banū Tamīm, once wrote in the presence of the Messenger of God,

and so he was called Ḥanẓala the Scribe.

Al-Wāqidī said: Writing in Arabic among the Aws and Khazraj was limited.

Some Jews had learned Arabic writing, and boys in Medina had been taught it in the early period.

Then Islam came, and there were several among the Aws and Khazraj who could write.

They were: Saʿd b. ʿUbāda b. Dulaym, al-Mundhir b. ʿAmr, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and Zayd b. Thābit.

He wrote Arabic and Hebrew; and [there were] Rāfiʿ b. Mālik, Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr, Maʿn b. ʿAdī al-Balawī, an ally of the Anṣār, Bashīr b. Saʿd, Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ, Aws b. Khawlī, and ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī the Hypocrite.

He said: Among them, those fully accomplished—the accomplished man being one who combined writing with archery and swimming—were Rāfiʿ b. Mālik, Saʿd b. ʿUbāda, Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī, and Aws b. Khawlī.

Among the people of Yathrib in the Jāhiliyya, those who combined these skills were Suwayd b. al-Ṣāmit and Ḥuḍayr al-Katāʾib.

Al-Wāqidī said: Jafīna al-ʿIbādī, a Christian from al-Ḥīra, was a wet nurse to Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ.

ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar suspected him of supporting Abū Luʾluʾa in killing his father, so he killed him and his two sons.

1115Isḥāq b. Abī Isrāʾīl told us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī al-Zinād told us, from his father, from Khārija b. Zayd b. Thābit, who said: The Messenger of God ordered me to learn the script of the Jews for him, and said to me, “I do not trust the Jews with my writing.”

Less than half a month passed before I had learned it.

I would write to the Jews for him, and when they wrote to him, I would read their letter.

Some Jews had learned Arabic writing, and boys in Medina had been taught it in the early period.

Then Islam came, and there were several among the Aws and Khazraj who could write.

They were: Saʿd b. ʿUbāda b. Dulaym, al-Mundhir b. ʿAmr, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and Zayd b. Thābit.

He wrote Arabic and Hebrew; and [there were] Rāfiʿ b. Mālik, Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr, Maʿn b. ʿAdī al-Balawī, an ally of the Anṣār, Bashīr b. Saʿd, Saʿd b. al-Rabīʿ, Aws b. Khawlī, and ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī the Hypocrite.

He said: Among them, those fully accomplished—the accomplished man being one who combined writing with archery and swimming—were Rāfiʿ b. Mālik, Saʿd b. ʿUbāda, Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī, and Aws b. Khawlī.

Among the people of Yathrib in the Jāhiliyya, those who combined these skills were Suwayd b. al-Ṣāmit and Ḥuḍayr al-Katāʾib.

Al-Wāqidī said: Jafīna al-ʿIbādī, a Christian from al-Ḥīra, was a wet nurse to Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ.

ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar suspected him of supporting Abū Luʾluʾa in killing his father, so he killed him and his two sons.

1115. Isḥāq b. Abī Isrāʾīl told us: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī al-Zinād told us, from his father, from Khārija b. Zayd b. Thābit, who said: The Messenger of God ordered me to learn the script of the Jews for him, and said to me, “I do not trust the Jews with my writing.”

Less than half a month passed before I had learned it.

I would write to the Jews for him, and when they wrote to him, I would read their letter.

The Book of the Conquests of the Lands is complete.

Praise be to God, the One, the Requiter. May His blessings be upon our master Muḥammad, the Prophet, his family, and his Companions, and His peace.
